You said:
What is pmd and pte in Linux mm

ChatGPT said:
Good question 👍 Let’s break it down step by step.

In Linux memory management (mm), when we talk about page tables, we’re really talking about a hierarchy of levels that translate a virtual address into a physical address.

On most modern 64-bit systems (ARMv8, x86_64), Linux uses a 4- or 5-level page table hierarchy.

Page Table Levels in Linux
Each level is represented by a specific type:

PGD (Page Global Directory) → top level

P4D (Page 4th Directory) → (only on 5-level paging, otherwise folded away)

PUD (Page Upper Directory)

PMD (Page Middle Directory)

PTE (Page Table Entry) → lowest level, points to actual physical pages

PMD (Page Middle Directory)
It is one level above the PTEs.

A PMD entry (type: pmd_t) points either to:

A page table page containing PTEs, or

A large page (huge page mapping, e.g. 2MB on x86_64, 2MB/1GB on ARM).

So, PMD entries allow either "step down to PTEs" or "directly map huge pages".

Think of it like an index that tells you which page table to consult for the final mapping.

PTE (Page Table Entry)
This is the final step in translation.

A PTE entry (type: pte_t) points directly to a physical page frame (PFN) in RAM.

Each PTE contains:

Physical page frame number (PFN)

Access permissions (R/W, user/supervisor, exec)

Flags (present, dirty, accessed, cache settings, etc.)

Example: 4-level page table walk (x86_64, 48-bit VA)
Virtual Address → PGD → PUD → PMD → PTE → Physical Address
If the PMD entry points to a page table → we look into PTEs.

If the PMD entry points to a huge page → translation finishes early.

In Code (Linux mm)
You’ll often see macros/functions:

pmd_offset(pud, addr) → get PMD pointer for an address

pte_offset_kernel(pmd, addr) → get PTE pointer for an address

pte_present(pte) → check if PTE maps a valid page

pte_pfn(pte) → get physical frame number

✅ In summary:

PMD = intermediate directory entry, can point to PTE page table or huge page.

PTE = lowest-level entry, maps directly to physical memory pages.

What is compound vs thp ? What is heap and tail page in that ?
What is compound vs thp ? What is head and tail page in that ? What is anonymous page ? What is page cache and slab cache ? How is it different from VFs cache ? Where is all these used ?
ChatGPT said:
Excellent set of questions 🙌 — you’re touching many of the Linux mm fundamentals. Let’s go step by step and clarify each term in context.

1. Compound Page vs THP
In Linux, the basic unit of memory management is a struct page, which represents one physical page frame (usually 4 KB).

Sometimes, the kernel wants to treat a group of contiguous physical pages as one bigger unit → this is called a compound page.

Transparent Huge Pages (THP) are just one kind of compound page, used to back huge mappings (like 2 MB or 1 GB pages) for performance.

👉 So:

Compound page = generic concept of multiple struct pages glued together to behave as one.

THP = a special case of compound pages, used to automatically back large virtual memory areas with huge pages.

2. Head Page vs Tail Page
A compound page is built from multiple struct pages.

The first page in that set is the head page.

The remaining pages are tail pages.

The head page stores metadata (refcount, mapping, flags, etc.).

Tail pages mostly reference back to the head page.

👉 Example: A 2 MB THP = 512 × 4 KB pages.

The first page struct is the head.

The other 511 page structs are tails.

This lets the kernel track one big object while still having per-4K page granularity when needed (e.g., for splitting).

3. Anonymous Page
A page not backed by a file on disk.

Comes from malloc() / brk() / mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS), i.e., heap or stack allocations.

If evicted, it must be written to swap (not to a file).

Example: process heap, stack, BSS data.

4. Page Cache
A cache of file-backed pages in RAM.

When you read() a file, the kernel keeps its pages in memory so subsequent reads are fast.

When you write(), the kernel writes to the page cache first, and syncs to disk later.

Found in /proc/meminfo as Cached.

👉 Optimizes file I/O by avoiding frequent disk access.

5. Slab Cache
A memory management technique for kernel objects (not file data).

Kernel often allocates many small objects (task_struct, inode, dentry, etc.).

Slab allocator keeps caches of frequently used kernel objects to avoid repeated allocation/free overhead.

Found in /proc/slabinfo.

👉 Improves performance of kernel internal allocations.

6. VFS (Virtual Filesystem) Cache
The VFS layer maintains metadata caches:

Dentry cache → directory entry objects

Inode cache → file inode structures

These caches live on top of the slab allocator (they are actually slab caches of dentry/inode objects).

They speed up pathname lookups (open("/usr/bin/ls") doesn’t walk the disk every time, it reuses cached dentries/inodes).

7. Where are all these used?
Compound Pages / THP → Improve TLB efficiency and reduce page fault overhead in user processes (esp. for large memory workloads like databases, ML training).

Head & Tail Pages → Kernel bookkeeping for compound/THP.

Anonymous Pages → Back process memory (heap, stack, non-file mmap).

Page Cache → Back file I/O data in memory for faster access.

Slab Cache → Back kernel data structures (efficient object reuse).

VFS Cache → Cache filesystem metadata (path lookups, inode/dentry).

✅ In summary:

Compound Page = generic multi-page unit

THP = compound page used for huge pages

Head/Tail Page = bookkeeping for compound pages

Anonymous Page = process-private, swap-backed page

Page Cache = cache of file contents

Slab Cache = cache of kernel objects

VFS Cache = metadata cache (dentry/inode), built on slab

What are different typ s of compound pages ? What are differences especially in thp ? Why all tail pages reference back to head ? Shouldn't only last one reference back to head ? So all non file backed memory is always anonymous? What are file backed memory? Where is swap space located ?
ChatGPT said:
Perfect 👌 — you’re asking the right mm questions. Let me carefully go through each one.

1. Types of Compound Pages in Linux
Compound pages are a generic abstraction in Linux to treat multiple struct pages as one logical unit. Different subsystems use them for different reasons:

Transparent Huge Pages (THP)

Backed by large page mappings (2MB, 1GB).

Created automatically by the kernel to reduce TLB misses.

HugeTLB Pages

Reserved huge pages, allocated explicitly by user-space (mmap() with MAP_HUGETLB).

Used in DBs, HPC workloads needing deterministic hugepage allocations.

High-Order Allocations (e.g., order > 0)

The buddy allocator can allocate multiple contiguous pages at once (e.g., for DMA, networking).

These higher-order allocations are internally represented as compound pages.

👉 So: THP is just one specialized type of compound page, but not the only one.

2. Why all tail pages reference back to the head?
Each compound page has one "head" page with metadata (refcount, mapping, flags).

Tail pages are not independent — they exist only as part of the compound.

That’s why all tail pages contain a pointer back to the head.

If only the last tail page pointed back, the kernel couldn’t:

Handle arbitrary page faults inside the hugepage,

Split compound pages into smaller ones,

Correctly free/reclaim pages in the middle.

👉 So every tail → head is necessary for consistency.

3. Is all non-file-backed memory anonymous?
Yes ✅

If memory is not mapped to a file, it’s anonymous memory.

Typical examples:

Heap (malloc → brk/mmap)

Stack

BSS/data sections not backed by files

Anonymous pages have no "home" on disk → if swapped, they go to swap space.

4. What is File-Backed Memory?
Memory that comes from a file mapping.

Example:

mmap("/usr/lib/libc.so") → file-backed mapping of a shared library.

Memory-mapped files (mmap with file descriptor).

If evicted, the kernel can drop the page and reload from the file (no need for swap).

👉 Difference:

Anonymous → swap-backed

File-backed → file/disk-backed

5. Where is Swap Space Located?
Swap space is a special disk area used as a backing store for anonymous pages.

Can be:

Dedicated swap partition (common on older Linux setups).

Swap file (/swapfile) inside a filesystem.

When RAM is full:

File-backed pages → can be dropped and later reloaded from the file.

Anonymous pages → must be written to swap space to free RAM.

✅ In summary:

Compound pages: multi-page units (THP, HugeTLB, high-order allocations).

THP: one type, auto hugepages (perf optimization).

All tails → head: for consistency & uniform metadata access.

Anonymous pages: non-file-backed (heap, stack, malloc).

File-backed pages: from mmap’d files, reloadable from disk.

Swap space: disk/partition backing anonymous memory when RAM is scarce.

You said:
What is difference in page mapping anon, movable and ksm ?
ChatGPT said:
Great, now we’re getting into page mapping types — these are subtle but important distinctions in Linux mm. Let’s break them down.

🔹 1. Anonymous (anon) pages
These are non-file-backed pages (heap, stack, BSS, malloc).

They don’t have a permanent disk "home".

If memory pressure occurs, they can only be written to swap space.

Tracked via an anon_vma structure so the kernel knows which VMA they belong to.

Example:

int *p = malloc(4096);   // allocated from anon pages
👉 Key point: All "normal" process-private memory that isn’t file-mapped = anon pages.

🔹 2. Movable pages
A kernel concept to allow page migration/compaction.

Needed because long-lived kernel allocations can cause physical memory fragmentation.

Linux splits zones into:

ZONE_NORMAL: contains unmovable allocations (kernel data, page tables, etc.).

ZONE_MOVABLE: contains pages that can be relocated elsewhere.

Types of pages considered movable:

User-space anonymous pages

Page cache pages

Kernel tries to place movable pages in ZONE_MOVABLE so compaction can free up big contiguous ranges (for hugepages, DMA, etc.).

👉 Key point: Movable = not a new kind of page, but a policy designation saying the page can be migrated if needed.

🔹 3. KSM (Kernel Samepage Merging) pages
A Linux feature to deduplicate identical anonymous pages across processes.

Runs a background kernel thread ksmd that scans anon pages and merges identical ones into a single physical page (marked Copy-on-Write).

Widely used in virtualization:

Multiple VMs running the same OS may have many identical libc pages.

KSM merges them to save memory.

If one process writes, the page is copied (like COW fork).

👉 Key point: KSM pages are still anonymous pages, but with extra sharing/deduplication.

✅ Differences Recap
Type	What it means	Backing store	Special property
Anon	Process-private, non-file-backed pages (heap/stack).	Swap only	Basic anonymous memory.
Movable	Any page (anon or page cache) that can be relocated for compaction.	Swap (anon) or file (page cache)	Used to reduce fragmentation.
KSM	Deduplicated anonymous pages merged across processes.	Swap (since anon)	Shared until modified (COW).
📌 Where they are used:
Anon pages → every process uses them (heap, stack).

Movable pages → memory compaction & NUMA migration need them.

KSM pages → virtualization, container workloads, memory deduplication.

⚡ So:

All KSM pages are anon, but not all anon pages are KSM.

Many anon/page-cache pages are movable, but kernel-core pages are not.

"Anon", "Movable", "KSM" are orthogonal concepts: one is type, one is policy, one is optimization.

You said:
Which exact types of pages can be migrated and where can they be migrated and what is zram, swap space ?
ChatGPT said:
Nice 👌 you’re now hitting the memory migration and swap/zram concepts — the guts of Linux mm. Let’s carefully unwrap this.

🔹 1. Which exact types of pages can be migrated?
Linux has a subsystem called the Page Migration/Compaction framework. Migration = moving a physical page’s contents to a new physical page, then updating page tables and metadata.

Not every page can be migrated. Broadly:

✅ Migratable pages:
Anonymous pages

Heap, stack, BSS, malloc allocations.

Can be moved to a new page frame.

If swapped out → can come back anywhere.

Page cache pages (file-backed)

Mapped file contents.

Easily migratable since they can be reloaded or moved.

KSM pages (deduplicated anon pages)

Migratable since they’re just anon pages with COW semantics.

Some movable kernel allocations

Allocations explicitly marked movable (e.g., via GFP_MOVABLE).

❌ Non-migratable pages:
Kernel internal pages:

Slab pages holding kernel-critical objects (task_struct, mm_struct, page tables, etc.).

Allocated with GFP_KERNEL, not movable.

Pinned pages:

Pages locked in memory by DMA, RDMA, mlock().

Migration would break device access.

Special hardware mappings:

Device memory (GPU buffers, MMIO).

ZONE_DMA or ZONE_DEVICE pages may be unmovable.

📍 Where can they be migrated?
Migratable pages can move:

Within the same NUMA node → for compaction (to defragment RAM and create contiguous blocks for hugepages/DMA).

Across NUMA nodes → for NUMA balancing (migrate closer to the CPU accessing it).

To swap/zram → when under memory pressure (but that’s eviction, not migration within RAM).

🔹 2. What is Swap Space?
Swap = disk (or SSD) area used as a backing store for anonymous pages.

When RAM is full, anonymous pages can be written ("swapped out") to disk.

Later, when accessed, they are "swapped in" back to RAM.

Two forms:

Swap partition → dedicated block device region.

Swap file → regular file marked as swap.

⚠️ Slow compared to RAM, but prevents OOM.

🔹 3. What is ZRAM?
Compressed swap in RAM.

Uses a RAM-backed block device that stores pages in compressed form.

Instead of writing anon pages to disk, kernel swaps them into zram (compressed, e.g., LZO, ZSTD).

Trade-off:

Saves memory (2–3× effective RAM).

CPU cost for compression/decompression.

Widely used in Android phones, embedded devices, VMs where disk swap is slow or unavailable.

✅ Recap
Migratable pages: anon, page cache, KSM, GFP_MOVABLE allocations.

Non-migratable pages: kernel critical objects, pinned pages, device memory.

Migration destinations: within node (compaction), across nodes (NUMA), or to swap/zram (eviction).

Swap space: disk/SSD space for evicting anon pages.

ZRAM: compressed swap in RAM (faster, avoids disk I/O).

You said:
What is anonymous or page cache pages and how is it different from struct page ?
ChatGPT said:
Great question 🙌 — this is where many people get confused because Linux uses the word page in different contexts. Let’s break it cleanly.

🔹 1. struct page
In the kernel, every physical page frame in RAM has a corresponding struct page object.

This is the metadata, not the memory itself.

Stored in a global array mem_map[].

Contains fields like:

Flags (dirty, referenced, compound, etc.)

Refcount

Mapping pointer (which file or anon_vma owns it)

List pointers (for LRU, free lists, etc.)

👉 Think of struct page as the “business card” of a physical page — describing what it’s being used for.

🔹 2. Anonymous pages
These are physical pages that are not file-backed.

Created for process heap, stack, BSS, malloc, mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS) etc.

If they are evicted → must go to swap space.

Example:

int *p = malloc(4096);   // gets one anon page
Their struct page->mapping points to an anon_vma (anonymous VMA descriptor).

🔹 3. Page cache pages
These are physical pages that cache the contents of files.

Example:

int fd = open("file.txt");
read(fd, buf, 4096);
The file’s block is read from disk into a page cache page in RAM.

If evicted → kernel can just discard it, and later reload from disk.

Their struct page->mapping points to an address_space (file’s page cache metadata).

🔹 4. Difference between Anonymous/Page Cache vs struct page
Anonymous page = a usage type of a physical page (for private process memory).

Page cache page = a usage type of a physical page (for file-backed memory).

struct page = the data structure that tracks any physical page, regardless of use.

👉 In other words:

struct page exists for every physical frame.

Whether it is used as anon, page cache, slab, THP head/tail, etc. depends on how the kernel fills in its fields.

✅ Analogy
Physical page = actual sheet of paper.

struct page = metadata card telling you what’s written on that sheet, who owns it, whether it’s clean or dirty.

Anonymous/page cache pages = categories of how that sheet is being used (private notes vs photocopy of a book).

✅ Recap
struct page → kernel metadata per physical page.

Anonymous pages → process-private memory (heap/stack), swap-backed.

Page cache pages → file-backed memory (file contents cached in RAM).

Difference = usage, not structure; both are represented by a struct page.

Difference between page, anonymous page, file backed page, page cache page and all other pages types which I've not mentioned here
ChatGPT said:
Perfect 👌 — you’re asking the core taxonomy of pages in Linux mm.
The confusion comes because "page" can mean: physical page frame, virtual page, or kernel usage type. Let’s sort them systematically.

🔹 1. Generic "Page"
A page = the basic unit of memory in Linux (usually 4 KB).

Can be virtual (in process address space) or physical (in RAM).

Every physical page has a struct page that tracks it.

🔹 2. Anonymous Pages
Pages that are not backed by a file.

Examples: heap (malloc), stack, BSS, mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS).

If evicted → written to swap space.

Metadata: struct page->mapping = anon_vma.

🔹 3. File-Backed Pages
Pages that map to a file on disk.

Examples: shared libraries, executables, memory-mapped files.

If evicted → kernel can drop them and reload later from disk (no need for swap).

Metadata: struct page->mapping = address_space (file’s cache).

🔹 4. Page Cache Pages
Subset of file-backed pages.

Specifically: pages cached in RAM when you read() or mmap() a file.

Stored in the kernel’s page cache for faster access.

Example: reading /etc/passwd → contents sit in page cache.

👉 So:

File-backed page = any page mapped from a file.

Page cache page = the actual cached physical page holding that file’s content.

🔹 5. Other Important Page Types
(a) Slab Pages
Used internally by the kernel for caching frequently used small objects (task_struct, inode, dentry, etc.).

Allocated via slab/SLUB allocator.

Not user-visible.

(b) Compound Pages
Multiple contiguous pages grouped together.

Types:

THP (Transparent Huge Pages) → automatically created 2MB/1GB pages for efficiency.

HugeTLB Pages → pre-allocated hugepages (MAP_HUGETLB), used in databases, HPC.

High-order allocations → e.g. 4 or 8 contiguous pages for networking/DMA.

Metadata stored only in the head page, tails reference back.

(c) Movable Pages
Pages that the kernel can migrate/compact to defragment memory.

Typically: anonymous pages, page cache pages.

Not kernel-core pages (page tables, pinned DMA).

(d) KSM Pages
Deduplicated anonymous pages (Kernel SamePage Merging).

Multiple processes share a physical page if contents are identical (COW on write).

Used in virtualization (e.g., two VMs running the same OS).

(e) Pinned Pages
Pages that cannot be migrated or swapped because they’re locked.

Examples: mlock(), DMA buffers, GPU buffers.

(f) Swap Cache Pages
Temporary state when anonymous pages are swapped out.

A page in RAM but also has a copy in swap space → tracked in the swap cache until eviction completes.

(g) Zero Pages
A special shared read-only page filled with zeros.

Mapped for newly allocated memory until the process writes to it (saves RAM).

✅ Recap in Table Form
Type	Backed By	Eviction Target	Notes
Page	Physical page frame	N/A	Generic unit (4 KB).
Anonymous Page	None (private memory)	Swap	Heap, stack, malloc.
File-Backed Page	File on disk	Drop → reload file	Executables, libs.
Page Cache Page	File on disk	Drop → reload file	Cached file content.
Slab Page	N/A (kernel objects)	Free on release	Kernel structures.
Compound Page	Multiple physical pages	Depends on type	Hugepages, THP.
Movable Page	Anon or page cache	Anywhere (migratable)	Helps compaction.
KSM Page	Shared anon	Swap	Deduplicated anon.
Pinned Page	Device or locked mem	Non-evictable	DMA buffers.
Swap Cache Page	Swap device	Eventually swap out	Transitional state.
Zero Page	Shared kernel zero page	N/A	Copy-on-write.
👉 So:

struct page = metadata for every physical page.

Anon vs file-backed = based on whether there’s a file mapping.

Page cache = actual cache of file contents.

Other types (slab, KSM, compound, pinned, swap cache, zero) = special usage categories.

ChatGPT said:
Perfect 🙌 — let’s integrate everything we’ve discussed so far into a single threaded explanation + master diagram so you have a one-stop reference for Linux memory management.

🧩 Linux Memory Management — Master Thread
🔹 1. User vs Kernel Memory
User space: Each process has its own virtual address space (heap, stack, code, mmap’d regions).

Kernel space: Shared, manages all physical pages (struct page for each).

🔹 2. brk, mmap, and malloc Flow
malloc() in user space doesn’t directly allocate RAM → it asks the kernel for virtual address space via:

brk() → extend/shrink heap (small allocations).

mmap() → anonymous mapping (large allocations).

Actual physical pages are only allocated on first access → via a page fault.

🔹 3. Page Faults
On first access to a VA:

Kernel checks VMA (struct vm_area_struct).

Decides: anonymous page or file-backed page.

Allocates page from buddy allocator.

Updates page table (PTE).

Types:

Minor fault → page already in RAM but not mapped.

Major fault → must load from disk/file/swap.

🔹 4. Buddy Allocator
Core physical memory manager.

Splits RAM into power-of-two blocks (order = 0…MAX_ORDER).

APIs: alloc_pages(), __free_pages().

Supplies memory to everything: kernel allocators, user mappings, page cache.

🔹 5. Slab/SLUB/SLOB
Layer on top of buddy for kernel object caching.

Pre-caches frequently used objects (task_struct, inode, dentry).

Variants:

SLAB → original, heavy metadata.

SLUB → modern default (simpler, faster).

SLOB → tiny systems (low memory).

🔹 6. Page Types
Anonymous pages → heap, stack, malloc, MAP_ANONYMOUS. Swap-backed.

File-backed pages → executables, libs, mmap’d files. Backed by file.

Page cache pages → file-backed pages cached in RAM for faster I/O.

Compound/THP/HugeTLB → grouped contiguous pages for huge mappings.

KSM pages → deduplicated anonymous pages (COW).

Movable pages → pages eligible for migration/compaction.

Pinned pages → locked for DMA/driver use, not migratable.

Slab pages → kernel internal object caches.

Swap cache pages → transient state during swap-out.

Zero page → shared read-only page filled with zeros (saves memory).

🔹 7. Swap & ZRAM
Swap space = disk/SSD partition or file used as backing for anonymous pages under memory pressure.

ZRAM = compressed block device in RAM acting as swap → saves memory but uses CPU cycles.

🧩 Master Diagram
[ User Process Space ]
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 |                                                                 |
 |  Code (.text)   → File-backed pages (ELF, shared libs)          |
 |  Data (.data)   → mmap() file-backed regions                    |
 |                                                                 |
 |  Heap (malloc → brk/mmap) → Anonymous pages (no file)           |
 |  Stack (grows down)      → Anonymous pages (no file)            |
 |                                                                 |
 |  Syscalls: brk(), mmap()  (reserve VA only, no RAM yet)          |
 |                                                                 |
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          |          ↑
                          |          |
                          v          | Page fault (on access)
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 |                [ Kernel Virtual Memory Manager ]                |
 | - Tracks VA regions via struct vm_area_struct (VMA).            |
 | - Decides: anon vs file-backed vs shared.                       |
 | - On fault: allocates page via buddy + updates PTE.             |
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          |
                          v
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 |                    [ Buddy Allocator ]                          |
 |  - Manages all physical pages in orders of 2^n.                  |
 |  - Core API: alloc_pages(), __free_pages().                      |
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
            |                               |
            |                               |
    For Kernel allocations          For User allocations
            |                               |
   ┌────────v─────────┐             ┌───────v─────────┐
   | Kernel allocators|             | User-space pages|
   | - Slab/SLUB/SLOB |             | (anon/file)     |
   | - vmalloc()      |             | via page fault  |
   | - dma_alloc_*()  |             └─────────────────┘
   └─────────────────┘
            |
   Optimized caches of objects 
   (task_struct, inode, dentry, etc.)


[ Swap & ZRAM Sidecar ]
+--------------------------------------+
 |   Swap Disk / ZRAM (compressed RAM) |
 +--------------------------------------+
      ^                          |
      |                          v
 [ Inactive anon pages evicted ] [ Reload on fault ]


📦 Page Types
- Anonymous: heap, stack, malloc.  
- File-backed: executables, mmap’d files.  
- Page cache: cached file contents.  
- Compound/THP: grouped pages for huge mappings.  
- Slab: kernel object caches.  
- Movable/KSM/Swap cache/Zero page = special cases.  
✅ Key Takeaways
Buddy allocator is the root source of all physical pages.

Slab/SLUB/SLOB sit on top of buddy for kernel allocations.

Userspace malloc → brk/mmap → page fault → buddy.

Swap/ZRAM extend RAM capacity only for anonymous pages.

File-backed pages can always be dropped/reloaded, no swap needed.

You said:
Tell me more about minor and major faults and how those are handled?
ChatGPT said:
Perfect follow-up 🚀 — page faults are the heart of Linux virtual memory. Let’s go deep into minor vs major faults and their handling path.

🔹 Page Faults Recap
A page fault occurs when a process accesses a virtual address that is not currently mapped in its page tables (PTE invalid or missing).
The CPU traps → raises a page fault exception (#PF) → kernel’s page fault handler (do_page_fault()) is invoked.

Now, not all page faults are the same 👇

🔹 Types of Page Faults
1. Minor Page Faults
Definition: Page is not mapped in the page table, but the data is already in RAM (struct page exists).

Cause:

Copy-on-Write (COW) → forked child touches a shared page.

Lazy malloc() → first access to anon memory after brk/mmap().

A page from file cache already resident in RAM but not yet mapped into this process.

Handling:

Kernel looks up the VMA (via find_vma()).

Finds that the backing page is already in memory (anon_vma or file page cache).

Just updates the PTE to point to it (sets present bit, access flags).

Returns to user.

👉 No disk I/O involved. Fast (microseconds).

2. Major Page Faults
Definition: Page is not mapped, and the data is not in RAM — must be fetched from disk (swap or file).

Cause:

First access to a file-backed page that isn’t cached yet.

Anonymous page evicted to swap, now needs to be read back.

Handling:

Kernel looks up VMA.

Determines if it’s file-backed or anonymous.

Allocates a free page from buddy allocator.

Issues disk I/O:

File-backed → read from filesystem into page cache.

Anon → read from swap area.

Once page is filled, updates PTE → resume process.

👉 Disk I/O = slow (microseconds → milliseconds).

🔹 Handling Path
CPU raises #PF → enters page_fault() trap handler.

Kernel locates the VMA (find_vma).

If invalid (address not in any VMA) → SIGSEGV to process.

Otherwise, kernel chooses:

Anonymous fault → handled via do_anonymous_page() or do_cow_fault().

File-backed fault → handled via do_fault() → filesystem’s ->fault() handler.

Depending on whether page is in RAM (minor) or must be read in (major), kernel updates PTE.

🔹 Minor vs Major — Example
// Program:
char *buf = malloc(4096);   // reserves VA only
buf[0] = 'a';               // MINOR fault (alloc fresh anon page)

int fd = open("bigfile", O_RDONLY);
char c = buf2[0];           // MAJOR fault (file page not cached yet)
char d = buf2[0];           // Next time: no fault (already mapped)
🔹 Observability
You can see minor vs major faults via /proc/[pid]/stat fields.

Also with getrusage():

struct rusage r;
getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF, &r);
printf("minor: %ld, major: %ld\n", r.ru_minflt, r.ru_majflt);
✅ Summary
Minor fault: Page not mapped, but data already in RAM → update PTE only.

Major fault: Page not mapped, data not in RAM → must fetch from disk (swap/file).

Page fault handling flow: CPU trap → VMA lookup → anon/file path → allocate page → maybe I/O → update PTE.

What pid, tgid and fd and ioctl and how those are associated with linux kernel memory management 
ChatGPT said:
Excellent question 👍 — you’re connecting process identity (PID/TGID), file descriptors (fd), and ioctl into the Linux memory management story. Let’s carefully break it down.

🔹 PID and TGID
PID = Process ID → unique identifier in kernel for every thread.

TGID = Thread Group ID → shared by all threads in a process (in userspace terms, "process ID").

📌 Example:

$ getpid() = 1234   // PID of thread
$ gettid() = 1234   // main thread has same PID & TGID
$ pthread_create()  // new thread
getpid() = 1234     // TGID = 1234 (process ID)
gettid() = 1235     // PID = 1235 (new thread’s ID)
🔗 Relation to MM:

Each thread (task_struct) points to the same mm_struct if they share address space.

mm_struct contains page tables, VMAs, etc. → so memory management is per TGID (process), not per PID (thread).

👉 So TGID is the "owner" of the address space, while PID is per-thread execution context.

🔹 File Descriptors (fd)
fd = integer handle representing an open file within a process.

Backed by kernel object struct file.

FDs are stored in the per-process file descriptor table (files_struct).

📌 Memory management relevance:

File-backed mmap():

int fd = open("data.bin", O_RDONLY);
void *p = mmap(NULL, size, PROT_READ, MAP_SHARED, fd, 0);
Here fd ties your process memory to the underlying file.

The kernel uses struct file → address_space to fetch pages into the page cache when faults occur.

So fd is the gateway to file-backed memory mappings.

Anonymous memory → no fd.

If you call mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS), kernel doesn’t need struct file.

🔹 ioctl (Input/Output Control)
ioctl(fd, cmd, arg) = user → kernel control channel.

Not about raw read/write, but about controlling kernel objects.

📌 MM relevance:

Drivers exporting memory:

GPU, DMA, or /dev/mem can use ioctl to allocate or map special memory.

E.g. DRM (GPU driver) uses ioctl to allocate buffers, then mmap() them into process VA.

Swap/ZRAM control:

You can configure ZRAM devices (compressed RAM swap) using ioctl on /dev/zramX.

Huge pages:

Some subsystems (like hugetlbfs) expose ioctls to manage hugepage pools.

So, ioctl often bridges special memory regions between kernel and user space.

🔹 How They Connect in Memory Management
 ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
 | User Process                          |
 |                                       |
 | malloc(), brk(), mmap()               |
 | fd = open("file")                     |
 | mmap(fd) → maps file into VA          |
 | ioctl(fd, DRM_ALLOC, ...)             |
 └───────────────────────────────────────┘
                  |
                  v
 ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
 | Kernel                                |
 | task_struct (PID/TGID)                |
 |   └─ mm_struct (per TGID)             |
 |       └─ vm_area_struct (VMAs)        |
 | files_struct → fd → struct file       |
 | ioctl() → driver hooks                |
 └───────────────────────────────────────┘
PID = execution context, used for signals/scheduling.

TGID = owner of address space (mm_struct).

fd = link to file-backed memory (page cache).

ioctl = custom control to manage special memory mappings beyond standard read/write.

✅ In short:

PID/TGID: decide which process/thread owns an address space.

fd: decides what file or device backs that memory.

ioctl: custom pathway to control and allocate/manage memory regions.

What is difference between static hugepage and transparent huge page
ChatGPT said:
Let’s break this down clearly:

1️⃣ Static Huge Pages (a.k.a. "Reserved Huge Pages")
Definition:
Static huge pages are manually reserved and pinned huge pages in memory. They do not get allocated or freed automatically by the kernel.

Size: Usually 2 MB (huge page) or 1 GB (gigantic page), depending on the architecture.

Controlled via:

/proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages

/sys/kernel/mm/hugepages/hugepages-*/

API: hugetlbfs and mmap(MAP_HUGETLB).

Use-cases:

Databases like Oracle, PostgreSQL, MySQL, or DPDK (for high-performance packet processing) that need deterministic performance and no risk of memory fragmentation.

Memory regions that need to be locked in RAM without kernel reclaim.

Key properties:

Aspect	Static Huge Pages
Allocation	Manual, requires admin/root configuration
Flexibility	Inflexible — cannot grow/shrink automatically
Fragmentation	Pages are reserved at boot or manually added, preventing fragmentation issues
Overhead	Low runtime overhead — pinned and fixed
Example Path	/mnt/huge mounted as hugetlbfs
2️⃣ Transparent Huge Pages (THP)
Definition:
Transparent Huge Pages are automatically managed huge pages by the kernel. They let applications benefit from huge pages without explicit support.

Default size: 2 MB huge pages (not 1 GB by default).

Kernel tries to coalesce adjacent 4 KB pages into a 2 MB THP when possible.

Can be enabled/disabled:

cat /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled
Modes: always, madvise, never.

Use-cases:

General-purpose workloads like JVM apps, Redis, or large in-memory analytics workloads.

Key properties:

Aspect	Transparent Huge Pages
Allocation	Automatic at runtime
Flexibility	Flexible — kernel decides dynamically
Fragmentation	Can fail under heavy fragmentation (falls back to 4K pages)
Overhead	Some overhead in background collapsing/khugepaged daemon
Example	malloc() → normal mapping → kernel upgrades to THP
3️⃣ Key Differences
Feature	Static Huge Page	Transparent Huge Page (THP)
Management	Manual (via sysctl, mount, or nr_hugepages)	Automatic by kernel
Flexibility	Inflexible, fixed size and count	Highly dynamic
Fragmentation Tolerance	Allocated early to avoid fragmentation	Can fail if fragmentation is high
Pinning	Always pinned in RAM	Not pinned; can be reclaimed or split
Performance	Predictable, low-latency	Good for general workloads but with slight runtime overhead
Use Case	Databases, DPDK, RT apps needing deterministic memory	General workloads, JVM, Redis, etc.
4️⃣ When to Use Which
Use Static Huge Pages

When you need real-time performance, pinned memory, and strict control.

Example: mmap() large buffers for DPDK or high-frequency trading systems.

Use Transparent Huge Pages

For ease of use with memory-hungry applications that don’t handle memory allocation explicitly.

Example: Running big data applications or caching servers.

5️⃣ Code-Level View
Static Huge Page allocation:

int fd = open("/mnt/huge/myfile", O_CREAT | O_RDWR, 0755);
void *addr = mmap(NULL, 2*1024*1024, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE,
                  MAP_SHARED, fd, 0);
Transparent Huge Pages:
Just do a normal malloc() or mmap(), and the kernel transparently upgrades regions to 2 MB pages if possible.

ChatGPT said:

Thought for 49s
Great set of follow-ups! Here’s a crisp, side-by-side view of how Transparent Huge Pages (THP) and Static (hugetlb) huge pages behave and interact with the rest of Linux mm.

1) Under memory pressure (reclaim/oom)
THP (mostly anonymous)

Can be reclaimed like normal anon/file pages.

Kernel will often split the THP into 4 KiB pages first, then reclaim/swap those base pages (there’s also THP-swap support that can swap a whole THP as a cluster when possible).

If anon: can be swapped; if file THP: can be written back or dropped.

Static huge pages (hugetlb/hugetlbfs)

Not swappable and not reclaimed by the usual LRU reclaim path.

Essentially pinned/reserved from a hugetlb pool; pressure elsewhere won’t free them.

When freed by the app, they return to the hugetlb pool, not the general LRU.

2) Can they be split?
THP: Yes. The kernel may split for reclaim, migration, mprotect/mremap, partial unmap, writeback quirks, etc.

Hugetlb: Generally no. You free the entire huge page back to the hugetlb pool; you don’t split it into base pages.

3) Fragmentation behavior
THP: Sensitive to fragmentation. Allocation tries an order-9 (2 MiB) page; if it can’t, khugepaged may collapse adjacent 4 KiB pages later. Memory compaction/migration helps create big contiguous ranges.

Hugetlb: Designed to avoid runtime fragmentation by reserving huge pages early (boot or runtime increase of nr_hugepages). Gigantic pages (1 GiB) often must be reserved at boot. Uses a dedicated MIGRATE_HUGETLB pool.

4) Where do the physical pages come from?
(“mmap/slab/slub/slob” are not sources of physical memory; they are APIs or allocators layered above.)

Both ultimately come from the buddy allocator.

THP: buddy allocates a high-order page (order 9 for 2 MiB). Anonymous THP typically placed as MOVABLE so they can be migrated/compacted.

Hugetlb: pages are carved out of the buddy into the hugetlb pool (per-node). The pool uses its own free lists (pageblocks tagged MIGRATE_HUGETLB).

mmap(): establishes virtual mappings; the actual physical frames still come from buddy on fault (THP) or from the hugetlb pool (hugetlb).

SLAB/SLUB/SLOB: kernel object allocators that themselves get base pages from buddy; they don’t supply huge pages for user memory.

5) Movable to zram/swap?
THP (anon): Yes—may be split and swapped as 4 KiB pages (or swapped as a large cluster when supported). zram is just a swap backend, so THP anon can end up in zram.

Hugetlb: No. Not swappable; won’t go to zram or disk swap.

6) File-backed?
THP:

Commonly anonymous; also file THP exists (notably tmpfs/shmem, and increasingly large-folio page cache in some FS). File THP follow page-cache/writeback rules.

Hugetlb:

Typically mapped via hugetlbfs (looks “file-backed” in API), but not the normal page cache; it uses the hugetlb pool, not generic VFS page cache machinery.

7) Which zones?
THP: From whatever node/zone can satisfy the order-9 allocation (often ZONE_NORMAL, sometimes DMA32 on x86, HIGHMEM on 32-bit). Marked MOVABLE when possible to aid compaction.

Hugetlb: Also per-node from the buddy, but placed into MIGRATE_HUGETLB pageblocks; NUMA/node policy and cpusets can constrain where the pool lives. Gigantic pages may be limited to specific zones/nodes.

8) Relationship to VFS & other cache types
THP anon: Lives on the anonymous LRU; no VFS participation.

THP file: Lives in the page cache (VFS address_space), can be written back/dropped like regular page-cache pages (subject to filesystem support for large folios).

Hugetlb: Bypasses the generic page cache; hugetlbfs has its own mechanics. Not part of normal VFS page-cache/LRU reclaim.

Other caches: slab caches (inode/dentry) ride on SLUB/SLAB and don’t use THP/hugetlb.

9) Can kmalloc()/vmalloc() use them?
kmalloc (SLUB/SLAB): No—allocates kernel objects, not huge pages for user mappings. It may occasionally use higher-order base pages for slab slabs, but not THP/hugetlb semantics.

vmalloc: Creates virtually contiguous regions backed by 4 KiB base pages (non-physically contiguous). Does not give you THP/hugetlb.

To use huge pages in kernel or user space you use hugetlb APIs/hugetlbfs (static) or rely on THP (transparent, via khugepaged/MADV).

10) Interaction with user-space malloc()
THP:

malloc() → typically brk/mmap reserves VA; on first touch you fault in 4 KiB pages; the kernel/khugepaged may later coalesce them into a THP.

madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) can encourage THP; MADV_NOHUGEPAGE discourages it.

Under pressure, THP may be split before reclaim/swap.

Hugetlb:

Normal malloc() doesn’t use it. You must explicitly allocate via mmap(MAP_HUGETLB) (often with hugetlbfs) or use libraries like libhugetlbfs or app-specific hugepage allocators.

Once allocated, those pages are not swapped and are isolated from general reclaim.

Quick matrix
Aspect	THP	Static Huge (hugetlb)
Reclaimable?	Yes (often after split)	No (kept in hugetlb pool)
Swappable?	Anon THP: Yes (may split or swap as cluster)	No
Splittable?	Yes	No (free whole huge page)
Source	Buddy (order-9)	Buddy → hugetlb pool
Fragmentation sensitivity	High (needs compaction)	Low (reserved early)
File-backed	Anon common; file THP exists (tmpfs/shmem, some FS)	Via hugetlbfs, not generic page cache
Zones	Normal/DMA32/Highmem per node	Per node; MIGRATE_HUGETLB blocks
VFS/page cache	Anon: no; File THP: yes	Not in generic page cache
kmalloc/vmalloc	No	No
malloc() usage	Transparent (optional)	Explicit (MAP_HUGETLB/hugetlbfs)
If you want, I can also sketch a compact flow diagram: fault on malloc’d memory → THP collapse → reclaim path (split → swap/zram) vs hugetlb mapping → hugetlb pool free path.

What are hugepag size range and how those are determined? One told me that if 64kb is based page size, first hugepage size will be 512mb because of pmd block? Why ?
ChatGPT said:
Let’s break this down step by step because the range of hugepage sizes — and why they differ with base page size — depends on MMU translation levels, architectural granularity, and kernel configuration.

1. Page Table Levels Refresher (ARMv8-A, x86_64 similar concept)
The MMU uses multiple levels of page tables to translate virtual → physical addresses.

For a 4-level page table (most ARM64 configs):

Level	Name	Typical Size (4 KB base)	Typical Size (64 KB base)
PGD	Page Global Directory	~512 GiB	~32 TiB
PUD	Page Upper Directory	~1 GiB	~512 GiB
PMD	Page Middle Directory	2 MiB (block mapping)	512 MiB (block mapping)
PTE	Page Table Entry	4 KB	64 KB
2. How hugepage sizes are determined
The hugepage size comes from which level of the page table you stop at when creating a "block mapping":

At PTE level → small page = base page size.

At PMD level → first "huge page" size (block size).

At PUD level → even larger page (gigantic page).

Case 1: 4 KB base page
Base PTE: 4 KB

PMD block: 2 MiB (512 entries × 4 KB)

PUD block: 1 GiB (512 × 2 MiB)

So hugepage sizes = 2 MiB, 1 GiB

Case 2: 64 KB base page
Base PTE: 64 KB

PMD block: 512 MB (8192 entries × 64 KB)

PUD block: 16 GB (32 × 512 MB)

So hugepage sizes = 512 MB, 16 GB

This is why, when 64 KB is the base page size, the first "huge" block mapping jumps to 512 MB, not 2 MiB. The page table walk size multiplies with the base granularity.

3. Default Ranges
Architecture	Base Page Size	Hugepage sizes
x86_64	4 KB	2 MiB, 1 GiB
ARM64 (common Linux distros)	4 KB	2 MiB, 1 GiB
ARM64 (64 KB base)	64 KB	512 MB, 16 GB
ARM64 (16 KB base)	16 KB	32 MB, 1 GB
4. Transparent Huge Pages vs Static Huge Pages
THP (transparent):
Stays limited to the PMD-level huge page.

2 MiB for 4 KB base

512 MB for 64 KB base

Static hugetlbfs:
Can reserve both PMD and PUD levels —
e.g., 1 GiB pages on x86, or 16 GB pages on ARM64 (rare, high-end systems).

5. Why this matters
For 64 KB base kernels, hugepages are much bigger.

Pro: Fewer TLB entries → great performance.

Con: More internal fragmentation and harder to allocate under fragmented memory pressure.

Con: Not friendly for workloads needing smaller hugepages (like 2 MiB-sized THP in databases).

6. Interaction with mTHP
mTHP tries to bridge this gap by introducing intermediate hugepage sizes using the folio mechanism and order- allocations even if the hardware block size jumps from 64 KB → 512 MB.

Example:

On 64 KB base page system:

mTHP may use 64 KB × 8 = 512 KB or 64 KB × 32 = 2 MB folios internally.

Hardware still maps them as 4 KB entries, but reduces kernel overhead and page cache pressure.

Got it — you’re referring to the CONT (Contiguous) bit in the ARMv8 page table descriptors that is used for contiguous mappings, especially with MTHP (Multi-Size Transparent Huge Pages) and other optimizations in the Linux memory management subsystem.

Here’s a detailed breakdown:

1️⃣ What the CONT bit is
In ARMv8-A page tables, there is a CONT (contiguous) bit in Page Table Entries (PTEs, PMDs, PUDs).

This bit indicates that a set of adjacent entries (usually 16) map physically contiguous memory pages.

It enables hardware-level TLB optimizations, meaning the TLB can treat multiple adjacent pages as a single larger block, reducing TLB pressure.

2️⃣ Why it’s used
The ARM architecture has limited TLB entry counts, so reducing TLB misses is critical.

By grouping adjacent mappings together (via CONT), you get:

Fewer TLB entries consumed

Lower TLB miss rates

Performance boost for workloads with large contiguous memory access patterns.

3️⃣ CONT in MTHP (Multi-size Transparent Huge Pages)
MTHP allows Linux to manage huge pages of multiple sizes, e.g., 64K, 128K, 512K, 1M, 2M, etc., dynamically.

On ARM:

CONT is used when allocating contiguous physical pages to form these mid-sized transparent hugepages.

Without the CONT bit, the hardware treats them as separate pages, losing the TLB optimization.

4️⃣ Relationship with struct page and Buddy Allocator
These contiguous blocks still come from the buddy allocator.

When Linux allocates such contiguous pages:

It marks each page’s struct page properly (head/tail for compound pages).

Maps them with the CONT bit set in the PTE.

5️⃣ Memory pressure, fragmentation, and splitting
Splitting: Pages with the CONT bit can be split back into base pages if:

Memory pressure rises.

Migration or compaction requires breaking the contiguous block.

Fragmentation: Over time, high fragmentation reduces the ability to find large contiguous blocks, making CONT mappings harder to create.

Compaction in Linux helps mitigate this by rearranging pages to create contiguous free ranges.

6️⃣ Swap and ZRAM behavior
CONT-bit pages, like other huge pages:

Can be split into base pages and then migrated/swapped.

Cannot be swapped as a single contiguous block.

7️⃣ Zone and cache relationship
These pages typically come from the ZONE_NORMAL or ZONE_DMA32, depending on the platform.

They are not directly related to VFS cache (page cache) unless they are mapping file-backed pages that are promoted to huge mappings.

8️⃣ Relation to malloc/vmalloc/kmalloc
malloc() in user-space:

Goes through brk/mmap → triggers page faults → base pages allocated first.

If THP or MTHP is enabled, the kernel may promote these regions into contiguous pages (with CONT bit set) for performance.

kmalloc/vmalloc:

Can allocate contiguous physical pages (kmalloc up to a limit), but typically do not directly use CONT unless explicitly designed for DMA or performance-critical paths.

9️⃣ Why first hugepage size is large
On ARM64:

Base page size often 64KB.

PMD (level-2 page table entry) covers 512 entries × 64KB = 32MB, but for contiguous mappings with CONT bit (16 pages combined):

16 × 64KB = 1MB contiguous block.

For higher levels like PUD, the sizes grow (e.g., 512MB if mapped as a single block).

1️⃣ struct page vs struct folio
struct page
Represents a single physical page frame in memory (base unit).

Used historically for everything: anonymous pages, file-backed pages, cache pages, compound (huge) pages, etc.

Problems with struct page:

Hard to handle multi-page blocks (like THP or MTHP) because the kernel still treated each page individually.

Performance issues in page cache and I/O.

struct folio
Introduced to represent a contiguous block of pages as one logical unit.

Key goals:

Reduce overhead when accessing page cache (one lock for multiple pages in a folio).

Make THP and MTHP integration cleaner.

Every folio still has a struct page for the head and tail pages internally.

Used in:

File page cache

Anonymous pages

Swap and reclaim

Relation to THP/MTHP:
THP and MTHP are just special types of compound folios. The folio abstraction simplifies managing these multi-page units without looping over individual struct pages.

2️⃣ Relation to rw_semaphore
The rw_semaphore (read-write semaphore) is heavily used in:

Memory management (like mmap_sem / mm->mmap_lock)

Protecting VMAs (Virtual Memory Areas) during:

Page faults

THP/MTHP splitting

Migration

Swap-in/swap-out

For example:

A write lock might be taken during unmapping or remapping operations.

A read lock is enough during page fault handling when the VMA is not being modified.

3️⃣ LRU Lists (Least Recently Used)
Linux uses multiple LRU lists to manage pages for reclaim and swap:

LRU List	Description
Active file	Frequently accessed file-backed pages
Inactive file	Cold file-backed pages (reclaim candidate)
Active anon	Frequently accessed anonymous pages
Inactive anon	Cold anonymous pages (can be swapped out)
Unevictable	Pages pinned by mlock or other reasons
For swap:

Anonymous pages (non-file-backed) are moved from inactive anon → swap when reclaiming memory.

For zram:

Works as a compressed swap device, so pages moved to swap LRU are compressed and stored in zram instead of disk.

4️⃣ Swap vs ZRAM
Feature	Swap Space (Disk/SSD)	ZRAM (RAM Compression)
Location	Disk or NVMe/SSD	RAM (compressed)
Performance	Slower (I/O-bound)	Faster (CPU-bound compression)
Use case	Large swap space	Faster reclaim, embedded/low-memory systems
Page types	Anonymous pages (non-file-backed)	Same (anonymous pages)
THP/MTHP support	THP must be split before swapping	Same: split, compress
Important:

File-backed pages rarely use swap; instead, they are dropped and reloaded from the file system if needed.

Anonymous pages (heap, stack, malloc'd memory) are what go to swap/zram.

So:

Swap and zram handle anonymous pages.

File-backed pages → reclaimed from cache and reloaded on demand instead of using swap.

5️⃣ Summary of relationships
Concept	Purpose	Relation
struct page	Core descriptor of each physical page	Every folio is made up of struct pages
struct folio	Logical unit for page cache (multi-page aware)	THP, MTHP are compound folios

rw_semaphore	Synchronization for page tables and VMA ops	Critical in page faults, THP split/merge
LRU lists	Track active/inactive pages	Used during reclaim/swap/zram
Swap	Offload cold anonymous pages to disk	Slower but large capacity
ZRAM	Compressed swap in RAM	Faster but consumes RAM
6️⃣ Answering your assumptions
“Is swap space for file-backed pages and zram for non-file-backed?”
❌ No. Both swap and zram are for anonymous pages only.

File-backed pages (page cache) can just be evicted since they can be read again from disk.

Anonymous pages (stack, heap, malloc, etc.) must be preserved somewhere → swap/zram.

7️⃣ User-space malloc and kernel memory
When you do malloc() in user space:

It reserves virtual memory first.

Physical pages are faulted in lazily → initially anonymous pages.

If THP/MTHP is enabled, these can be promoted into compound folios.

kmalloc/vmalloc in kernel-space are unrelated, though they may use buddy allocations that overlap physically.

What is migration vs ksamepagemerging ?
ChatGPT said:
Let’s break down Page Migration and KSM (Kernel Samepage Merging), because both deal with moving or sharing physical pages in Linux, but they serve very different purposes.

1️⃣ Page Migration
Page migration is the process of moving a page from one physical location to another while preserving its virtual mapping.
It’s often used in:

Scenario	Why Migration Happens
NUMA balancing	Move hot pages closer to the CPU accessing them (NUMA locality).
Memory compaction	Rearrange pages to create contiguous free memory blocks for THP, CMA, or device DMA.
Hot-remove memory	When offlining a memory block (like removing a DIMM).
Tiered memory systems	Move pages between fast DRAM and slower persistent memory tiers.
Mechanism:

Uses migrate_pages() internally.

Migrated page retains the same virtual address and page->mapping association.

Page locks and reference counts ensure consistency during migration.

Migratable pages:

Anonymous pages

File-backed page cache pages

HugePages (static and THP, though THPs are first split)

ZRAM-backed anonymous pages (indirectly when swapped in/out)

2️⃣ Kernel Samepage Merging (KSM)
KSM is deduplication, not migration.
It scans for anonymous pages with identical content across processes and maps them to the same physical page in a Copy-On-Write (COW) manner.

Scenario	Why KSM Helps
Virtual Machines (KVM/QEMU)	Many guest VMs load identical OS images → saves RAM.
Forked processes (after fork())	Many identical anonymous regions exist until they diverge.
Memory deduplication in containers	Reduce footprint when running many similar workloads.
Mechanism:

Background thread ksmd scans memory regions marked MADV_MERGEABLE.

Identifies pages with same checksum → replaces duplicates with a shared read-only page.

On write, a new private copy is allocated (COW fault).

3️⃣ Migration vs KSM — Key Differences
Feature	Migration	KSM (Samepage Merging)
Goal	Relocate page in physical memory (better locality, compaction, tiering)	Deduplicate identical pages to save memory
Virtual Address	Unchanged	Unchanged
Physical Page	Changes to a new location	Becomes shared (same physical page mapped in multiple places)
Trigger	NUMA balancing, compaction, memory hotplug, etc.	Periodic scanning of MADV_MERGEABLE regions
Write Behavior	No special handling (same writable page)	Triggers Copy-On-Write fault to unshare page
Involves Swap/ZRAM	Yes, during migration under memory pressure	No direct swap interaction
Overhead	Migration latency during move	CPU time in scanning and hashing for duplicates
Use Case	Performance optimization	Memory footprint reduction
4️⃣ Relation with THP and MTHP
Page Migration

Can move THPs and MTHPs but often splits them to 4K base pages first.

Needed for compaction to allocate contiguous space for new THPs.

KSM

Works primarily on 4K anonymous pages.

Rarely effective with THPs unless THPs are split.

5️⃣ LRU and Swap Context
Migrated pages stay on their LRU (active/inactive) list.

KSM-shared pages are also on LRU lists but marked as KSM pages for tracking.

Both mechanisms integrate with the kernel’s reclaim logic:

Migrated pages can still be reclaimed/swapped if anonymous.

KSM pages, if shared, will unshare or split before swap-out.

6️⃣ Example Analogy
Migration: Moving a book from one shelf to another to keep it closer to where it’s often read.

KSM: Having multiple readers share the same copy of the book until someone needs to make personal notes (then they get their own copy).

7️⃣ Quick Code References
Migration: mm/migrate.c — migrate_pages(), migrate_page_move_mapping()

KSM: mm/ksm.c — ksm_do_scan(), cmp_and_merge_page()

2️⃣ What is eBPF
eBPF (extended Berkeley Packet Filter) is a safe, in-kernel virtual machine that allows you to load and run small programs in kernel space without writing or modifying kernel modules.

Runs sandboxed programs inside the kernel.

Ease of use	Easier to deploy (no kernel changes)	Requires tuning, NIC support, and userspace driver binding

eBPF: A programmable, safe in-kernel VM for networking, tracing, and observability — complements but does not replace DPDK.

VFIO: Hardware access layer to enable user-space drivers, often used alongside DPDK for high-performance networking or virtualization.

Let’s break this down clearly. Understanding linear mapping, vmalloc, and the kernel virtual address (VA) space is key to Linux kernel memory management.

1️⃣ Kernel Virtual Address (VA) Space Overview
On 64-bit Linux, the virtual address space is divided into two parts:

Region	Purpose
User Space (lower half, e.g., 0x0000000000000000 – 0x00007fffffffffff)	Memory for user applications, managed via mmap(), brk(), etc.
Kernel Space (upper half, e.g., ffff800000000000 – ffffffffffffffff)	Kernel linear mapping, vmalloc regions, fixmap, module space, etc.
2️⃣ Linear Mapping (Direct Mapping)
Definition
The linear map (also called the direct map) is a 1:1 mapping of all physical RAM into a contiguous range of kernel virtual addresses.

Implemented in PAGE_OFFSET region.

Uses page tables but simple offset arithmetic for translation.

Characteristics

Covers all physical RAM.

Allows kernel to access any physical address quickly.

Allocations from buddy allocator (e.g., alloc_pages(), __get_free_pages()) live here.

Example

void *addr = page_address(page);  // Directly translates to kernel VA
3️⃣ vmalloc Area
Definition
vmalloc provides virtually contiguous memory to the kernel, but not physically contiguous.

It creates separate page table mappings for each page, unlike the linear map where physical pages are contiguous.

Characteristics

Feature	Linear Map	vmalloc
Physical Contiguity	Yes	No
Virtual Contiguity	Yes	Yes
TLB Pressure	Low	Higher (extra page table walks)
Use Case	DMA buffers, page cache, slab allocs	Large allocations for kernel modules, stacks, etc.
Example

void *buf = vmalloc(10 * 1024 * 1024); // 10 MB contiguous in virtual space
4️⃣ Kernel Virtual Address Space Layout
Typical regions in kernel VA space:

Region	Purpose
Linear map	Maps all RAM, direct offset mapping.
vmalloc	For virtually contiguous, non-physically-contiguous allocations.
Fixmap	Fixed virtual addresses for hardware or special mappings.
Module space	Memory for loadable kernel modules.
vmap	Similar to vmalloc but used for mapping arbitrary pages.
5️⃣ Differences in Usage
Use Case	Preferred Mapping
High-speed DMA, page cache, slab allocator	Linear map
Allocations needing virtually contiguous memory but scattered physical pages (e.g., ioremap, kernel stacks, vmalloc)	vmalloc
IO Remapping (PCI, MMIO registers)	vmap/ioremap
6️⃣ Relation to Memory Management
Linear Map

Backed by the buddy allocator.

Physically contiguous → Good for performance, DMA-friendly.

vmalloc

Allocates pages separately and maps them virtually.

Slight overhead due to non-linear mapping and TLB misses.

7️⃣ Interaction with User Space
malloc() in user-space does not interact directly with the kernel's linear map or vmalloc — instead, it uses brk()/mmap() to request memory, managed by the page tables for that process.

Kernel-space allocations (kmalloc, vmalloc) are independent but may eventually back user-space mappings for file-backed or shared regions (e.g., page cache).

8️⃣ Quick Summary
Aspect	Linear Map	vmalloc
Physical Contiguity	Yes	No
Performance	High	Moderate
Use Cases	Page cache, slab cache, DMA buffers	Kernel stacks, module allocations, sparse mappings
Source	Buddy allocator	Page allocator + virtual mapping
Relation to THP	THP can collapse linear map pages	Rare with vmalloc due to non-contiguous physical layout

What is config unmap kernel at el0 ? Can user application see kernel mapping and kernel bindings ? What is vdso ? Apart from that can kernel va space be mapped for user space ? If not, what process kallsyms is then ?
ChatGPT said:
Let’s break this step by step, because this question spans security, kernel virtual address space, and user-kernel interaction in Linux.

1️⃣ CONFIG_UNMAP_KERNEL_AT_EL0
This is a kernel configuration option (CONFIG_UNMAP_KERNEL_AT_EL0) mainly for ARM64 (AArch64) architecture.

It unmaps the kernel's virtual address space when running at EL0 (user mode) to mitigate security vulnerabilities like Meltdown or speculative execution attacks.

How it works
When a process is running in user mode (EL0), the kernel's linear map and kernel VA space are not visible.

When a syscall, exception, or interrupt occurs (switching to EL1), the kernel mapping is temporarily remapped for handling the event, then unmapped again when returning to user space.

2️⃣ Can a user application see kernel mappings?
Before CONFIG_UNMAP_KERNEL_AT_EL0:

Kernel virtual addresses were mapped but protected by permission bits (cannot read/write from EL0).

This allowed speculative execution vulnerabilities to leak data.

After CONFIG_UNMAP_KERNEL_AT_EL0 (and KPTI on x86):

The entire kernel VA space is unmapped while in user mode.

A user process cannot see or guess kernel addresses via normal means.

3️⃣ vDSO (Virtual Dynamic Shared Object)
vDSO is a small shared library mapped into every user process.

Purpose: To let user-space execute certain system calls in user space without a full context switch.

Examples of vDSO usage
gettimeofday()

clock_gettime()

getcpu()

Instead of switching to kernel mode for every call, the kernel maps a read-only page with relevant code/data at a fixed user VA, improving performance.

4️⃣ Can kernel VA space be mapped into user space?
Generally, No, for security and isolation reasons:

Kernel memory is privileged and not directly accessible from EL0.

The kernel enforces strict page table separation (especially with CONFIG_UNMAP_KERNEL_AT_EL0 and KASLR).

Exceptions
Shared memory mechanisms like:

mmap() with /dev/mem, /proc/kcore, or character devices (if allowed — often restricted)

DPDK or VFIO can map DMA buffers from kernel to user, but those are controlled, isolated mappings, not arbitrary kernel space.

5️⃣ Relation to kallsyms
/proc/kallsyms lists kernel symbols and their addresses.

Used for debugging, profiling, or kernel module development.

However:

With kptr_restrict=1 or 2, non-root users see 0x00000000... instead of actual addresses for security.

Even if you see the symbol, you cannot dereference kernel addresses from user space because the mappings are inaccessible under EL0.

6️⃣ Summary Table
Feature	Description
CONFIG_UNMAP_KERNEL_AT_EL0	Unmaps kernel VA space from user mode to prevent Meltdown-style leaks
User-space view of kernel mapping	Not possible after KPTI and ARM64 unmap features
vDSO	Small shared library in user VA for fast syscalls (time, CPU, etc.)
Mapping kernel VA to user	Not allowed except via controlled interfaces (VFIO, /dev/mem, special drivers)
/proc/kallsyms	Shows kernel symbols for debugging; addresses may be hidden or restricted
7️⃣ Security & Performance Trade-off
Security Gain: Prevents side-channel attacks by hiding kernel memory.

Performance Cost: Slight overhead due to remapping during syscalls and interrupts.

Optimizations: Some frequently accessed kernel mappings remain (like vDSO pages or trampolines).

Example Scenario
User program:

#include <time.h>
clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC, &ts);
→ Executes entirely in user space via vDSO mapping for speed.

Accessing kernel:

int fd = open("/proc/kallsyms", O_RDONLY);
→ Requires root to see real kernel symbol addresses.

Alright — let’s dive into KASLR (Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization) and how it interacts with kernel mappings, vDSO, and security in Linux.

1️⃣ What is KASLR
KASLR (Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization) is a security feature that randomizes the location of the kernel and its key structures in virtual memory at boot time.
It’s like ASLR for user-space programs but applied to the kernel.

Enabled by default on modern Linux (both x86_64 and ARM64).

Randomizes:

The kernel text/code base

Modules

Kernel stacks

Some key static mappings.

2️⃣ Why KASLR Exists
Without randomization:

Kernel addresses are predictable.

Exploits like ROP (Return-Oriented Programming) or privilege escalation attacks can jump to known kernel addresses.

With KASLR:

Attackers cannot reliably guess addresses without leaking info first.

3️⃣ How KASLR Interacts with CONFIG_UNMAP_KERNEL_AT_EL0
Feature	Before Meltdown (No Unmap)	After Meltdown (Unmap Kernel at EL0)
KASLR	Randomized addresses, but still mapped into user space → could be leaked via side channels.	Randomized addresses not mapped at EL0, eliminating info leaks.
Security Level	Lower	Higher
4️⃣ vDSO and KASLR
The vDSO mapping is not randomized the same way as the kernel linear map, but it changes location per process for added ASLR in user space.

The vDSO itself is user-facing and does not reveal sensitive kernel addresses.

5️⃣ Kernel VA Mapping & KASLR
The virtual address layout with KASLR (x86_64 example):

Region	Example VA (w/o KASLR)	With KASLR
Kernel text/code	ffffffff81000000	ffffffff82xxxxxx (random offset)
Modules	ffffffffa0000000	ffffffffa2xxxxxx (random offset)
vmalloc area	ffffc90000000000	ffffc900xxxxxx
vDSO (user)	0x7fff...	0x7fff... (random per process)
6️⃣ Kernel Symbol Leaks and /proc/kallsyms
/proc/kallsyms still lists kernel symbols.

But kptr_restrict=1 or 2 (default) masks the real addresses:

ffffffff81000000 T _stext
ffffffff810001f0 T startup_64
→ Non-root users see:

0000000000000000 T _stext
0000000000000000 T startup_64
This prevents attackers from bypassing KASLR via easy symbol leaks.

7️⃣ Interaction with Debugging
Root users can still inspect symbol addresses for debugging or profiling.

Crash dumps (like kdump) save physical addresses; tools like gdb vmlinux still work by correlating random offsets.

8️⃣ Impact on Performance
Minimal overhead, since randomization happens at boot time only.

No runtime penalty except in debugging workflows.

9️⃣ Summary
Feature	Purpose	Relation to Security
KASLR	Randomizes kernel memory addresses at boot	Makes exploits harder
Unmap at EL0	Removes kernel VA mapping in user mode	Stops side-channel info leaks
vDSO	Fast syscall page mapped in user mode	Safe to expose; unrelated to kernel code
kallsyms	Symbol table for debugging	Restricted to prevent leaks
10️⃣ Key Points
Kernel mappings cannot be accessed from user mode.

KASLR and Unmap at EL0 together make kernel address leaks much harder.

vDSO provides optimized syscalls, not a direct kernel address map.

Tools like /proc/kallsyms are controlled to prevent leaks, unless root explicitly allows it.

What is thb shrinker ? What is pmd thb and does it register with shrinker ? How it works internally with processes ? How is it different than OOM ?
ChatGPT said:
Alright, let’s break this down carefully — THP shrinker, PMD THP, how they interact with the memory reclaim path, and how this differs from OOM handling.

1️⃣ Background — THP and PMD THP
THP (Transparent Huge Pages)
Linux automatically backs user memory with huge pages (usually 2 MB) when possible, improving TLB hit rate and performance.

PMD THP

Refers to 2 MB huge pages mapped at the Page Middle Directory (PMD) level in the page table hierarchy.

PMD THPs are the default size for transparent huge pages.

2️⃣ What is the THP Shrinker
A shrinker in the kernel is a mechanism used by the memory reclaim subsystem (via shrink_slab() and related APIs) to reclaim memory from caches or subsystems when memory pressure occurs.

THP shrinker is a specialized shrinker that:

Scans memory to find idle or underused PMD-sized THPs.

Splits them into base 4 KB pages when needed.

Returns those base pages to the buddy allocator for other allocations.

Location in code:
mm/huge_memory.c → split_huge_page_to_list() and mm/huge_memory.c → deferred_split_huge_page()

3️⃣ How THP Shrinker Works
Flow:
Memory pressure detected by page reclaim (kswapd, direct reclaim, etc.).

Shrinkers are called via the shrinker API registered by the THP subsystem.

The THP shrinker:

Walks through a list of deferred split THPs maintained by the kernel.

For each candidate:

Unmaps the huge page temporarily.

Splits the page into 512 × 4 KB base pages.

Updates the reverse mapping (rmap) for each process using that page.

Pages are then reinserted into the LRU lists for reclaim by the usual page reclaim code.

4️⃣ Why THP Shrinker is Needed
Under memory pressure, holding memory in huge pages can lead to:

Fragmentation.

Wasted memory (unused portions of a 2 MB page remain reserved).

Shrinking avoids premature OOM kills by freeing memory earlier.

5️⃣ Interaction with Processes
When a huge page is split:

Page table entries of the process are updated to point to base pages.

No visible effect in user space except a slight latency.

Process continues to run without knowing its THP was downgraded.

6️⃣ PMD THP and Shrinker Registration
Yes, PMD-level THPs register with the shrinker:

The deferred split queue keeps track of PMD THPs that can be split.

khugepaged may also trigger collapses or deferred splits depending on activity.

7️⃣ Difference Between THP Shrinker and OOM
Aspect	THP Shrinker	OOM (Out of Memory)
Trigger	Memory pressure during reclaim	Extreme exhaustion — no reclaimable memory
Action	Splits THPs → frees base pages	Kills a process to free memory
Goal	Reclaim efficiently without killing	Survival by freeing a big chunk
User Impact	Usually none, transparent	Process crash or termination
Latency	Low, safe	High, disruptive
8️⃣ Zones, LRU, and Migratability
Zones: THPs are typically allocated from ZONE_NORMAL or ZONE_DMA32 depending on NUMA and architecture.

LRU lists: Once split, base pages rejoin the LRU inactive or active lists.

Migration: Split base pages can be migrated like normal pages; PMD THPs need special handling for migration.

9️⃣ Fragmentation Handling
PMD THPs rely on contiguous physical memory (512 contiguous base pages).

Shrinking and splitting under pressure reduce fragmentation risk and help the buddy allocator satisfy small-page requests.

🔟 Summary
Concept	Description
THP Shrinker	Reclaims memory by splitting huge pages back to 4 KB pages during memory pressure.
PMD THP	Transparent huge pages mapped at the PMD level (~2 MB).
Process Effect	No visible effect; only internal remapping latency.
Difference vs OOM	Shrinker reclaims silently; OOM kills processes.
Allocator Relation	THPs allocated via buddy allocator, shrinker returns base pages back to it.

You said:
Are swapping and zram complimentary or orthogonal? Do they serve same purpose?
ChatGPT said:
Swapping and zram are complementary, not exactly the same thing — they serve similar goals (freeing physical memory) but in different ways, and they can even be used together in a Linux system.

Here’s a deep dive:

1️⃣ Swapping – The Classic Mechanism
Purpose: Free up physical RAM by moving inactive pages to swap space on storage (HDD/SSD).

How it works:

When RAM pressure increases, kswapd or direct reclaim moves pages to the swap area.

When a process accesses a swapped-out page, it causes a major page fault, and the page is brought back to RAM.

Characteristics:

Slow (limited by storage latency, especially on HDDs).

Can handle large datasets if enough disk space is available.

Swapped pages are stored uncompressed unless combined with compression tools.

2️⃣ ZRAM – Compressed In-Memory Swap
Purpose: Create a compressed swap device in RAM to reduce pressure without using disk I/O.

How it works:

ZRAM creates a block device in RAM.

Pages are compressed (using algorithms like LZO, LZ4, ZSTD) and stored there.

When accessed, they are decompressed back into RAM.

Characteristics:

Much faster than disk-based swap.

Reduces pressure but still uses some physical memory for the compressed pages.

Great for systems without a fast swap disk (like embedded devices, phones, or VMs).

3️⃣ Complementary vs Orthogonal
Feature	Swap (Disk)	ZRAM (RAM-based)	Relation
Storage Location	HDD/SSD	RAM (compressed)	Different
Speed	Slow (I/O bound)	Fast (CPU bound, compression/decompression)	Complementary
Goal	Free RAM	Free effective RAM by compression	Same goal
Persistence	Survives reboot (if file-based swap)	Lost on reboot	Orthogonal
Use Together	✅ Yes, zram first, then swap to disk	✅ Yes, common in Linux	
4️⃣ Practical Use-Cases
Desktop/server with SSD
Use zram first for fast compressed swap → fallback to disk swap for large workloads.

Embedded or mobile device
Use zram only, since there is often no swap partition or disk.

Low-RAM virtual machines
ZRAM helps compress idle pages and avoid OOM situations efficiently.

5️⃣ Integration with Memory Management
Both swap and zram interact with:

kswapd for reclaim.

Page fault handler for bringing back pages.

LRU lists to decide which pages are least active.

ZRAM can also be tuned via sysfs (e.g., /sys/block/zram0/disksize, /sys/block/zram0/max_comp_streams).

6️⃣ Summary
Aspect	Swapping	ZRAM
Mechanism	Write inactive pages to disk	Compress inactive pages in RAM
Latency	High	Low
Capacity	Limited by disk size	Limited by RAM size (compression helps)
Persistence	Yes (swapfile/partition)	No
Best for	Large servers, workloads with big memory but slow access patterns	Low-memory devices, fast reclaim needs
7️⃣ Answer to Your Question
They are complementary, not purely orthogonal.

Both reduce physical RAM usage.

ZRAM is like a fast compressed swap in RAM, while swap space is usually on storage.

Many modern Linux systems combine both:

Use zram as primary swap.

Spill over to disk-based swap if memory pressure continues.

Why zram is block driver ? Why mthb has better compressibility ratio compared to breaking down ? What is difference between zram and zswap ? What is zswap cache vs page cache vs VFs cache ? Does zram and swap support thp, static hugepage and mthp ?
ChatGPT said:
Let’s break this into clear sections because there are multiple concepts here — zram, zswap, compression behavior, caching layers, and hugepage compatibility.

1️⃣ Why ZRAM is a Block Driver
ZRAM exposes itself as a /dev/zramX block device because the Linux swap subsystem only works on block devices.

It is a pseudo-block device driver in RAM:

Data written to it is compressed and stored in RAM.

Reads from it decompress and return the data.

Being a block device also allows using zram for other purposes like:

/tmp storage

Fast scratch partitions

Internally, it uses genhd block layer API and hooks into the swap layer through swapon.

2️⃣ MTHP (Multi-size Transparent Hugepages) & Better Compressibility
Reason for better compression:

Larger pages (64K, 2M, etc.) are often more uniform in content (zeroed ranges, repetitive data, etc.).

Compression algorithms (LZO, LZ4, ZSTD) achieve better ratios on larger contiguous memory compared to compressing multiple fragmented 4K pages separately.

Metadata overhead also reduces when you compress one 64KB page vs sixteen 4KB pages.

Example:

Compressing 16×4KB scattered pages → ~50% saving.

Compressing 1×64KB hugepage → ~65–70% saving due to better pattern detection.

3️⃣ ZRAM vs ZSWAP
Feature	ZRAM	ZSWAP
Location	RAM-only compressed block device	In-RAM compression front-end to disk swap
Usage	Acts as full swap device	Cache for swap pages before writing to disk
Persistence	Volatile (lost on reboot)	Also volatile
Speed	Faster (no disk I/O)	Slower if fallback to disk triggers
Best Use Case	Embedded devices, VMs, low-RAM systems without disk swap	Systems with disk swap that want compression first
Implementation	Separate device /dev/zramX	Built into swap layer
Memory Pressure	Eviction drops data (if no backing store)	Eviction writes compressed pages to disk swap
4️⃣ ZSWAP Cache vs Page Cache vs VFS Cache
Type	What it Holds	Where Used	Key Difference
Zswap Cache	Compressed swap pages before being written to disk	Swap subsystem	Memory-saving cache to reduce disk writes
Page Cache	Cached file data (file-backed pages)	FS read/write operations	Speeds up I/O by keeping file data in RAM
VFS Cache (dentry/inode cache)	Metadata (directory entries, inode structs)	Virtual File System layer	Speeds up path lookups and metadata access
Important Distinction:

Page cache is about actual file content.

VFS cache is about filesystem metadata.

Zswap cache is about compressed anonymous or file-backed pages waiting for eviction.

5️⃣ THP, Static Hugepages, and MTHP with Swap and ZRAM
Feature	Swap	ZRAM	Notes
THP (2M default)	Split into 4K pages before swapping	Split into 4K pages before compression	Native swap/zram don't manage THP as huge chunks
Static Hugepages	Not swappable (used for pinned buffers, DPDK, etc.)	Not usable (not pageable)	Used for pinned allocations, so not reclaimable
MTHP (multi-size)	Will be split before writing to swap or zram	Split into base units for compression	Same reason — compression and swap I/O work at base-page granularity
Why split happens:
Swap and zram are designed around base page sizes (4K, 64K), not large compound pages, for simplicity and to avoid fragmentation during reclaim.

6️⃣ Interaction with Memory Management
Under Memory Pressure:

Page allocator decides LRU victims.

Anonymous pages → first try zram/zswap (if configured).

File-backed pages → dropped if clean (since they can be reloaded from storage).

If zram fills, system either evicts (discard compressed pages) or falls back to disk swap if configured.

With Hugepages:

Compound pages are split during reclaim.

No native support for keeping them as hugepages inside zram/zswap because compression and swap APIs work at the base page granularity.

7️⃣ Summary
ZRAM is a block driver because swap requires a block device, even if it’s in RAM.

MTHP compresses better due to larger, contiguous memory and reduced metadata overhead.

Zswap is not a block device — it’s a swap cache layer inside the kernel.

Caches:

Page Cache = file content.

VFS Cache = filesystem metadata.

Zswap Cache = compressed swap cache.

Hugepages & Swap:

THP, static hugepages, and MTHP must split before swap/zram compression.

Static hugepages cannot be swapped at all since they are pinned.

Zones:

Allocations for zram/zswap usually come from ZONE_NORMAL or ZONE_MOVABLE.

   └─ Page faults handled transparently
9️⃣ Integration with Networking and I/O
[ High-Performance I/O ]
   ├─ DPDK
   │     • User-space packet processing
   │     • Bypasses kernel networking stack
   │
   ├─ VFIO
   │     • Direct device access from user space
   │     • Uses IOMMU isolation
   │
   └─ eBPF
         • In-kernel programmable hooks
         • Observability, security, acceleration
🔍 Key Relationships
Page → Folio: Folios represent one or multiple pages for better efficiency in the kernel.

THP/MTHP ↔ khugepaged: Collapses base pages into huge pages dynamically.

LRU ↔ Swap/Zram: Only anonymous pages are compressed or swapped. File-backed pages rely on page cache instead.

Shrinkers ↔ OOM: Shrinkers reclaim first; OOM is the last resort.

Kernel Mapping ↔ Security: CONFIG_UNMAP_KERNEL_AT_EL0 prevents user-level access to kernel VA.
