Alright — let’s connect CMA and DMA-BUF to the entire memory subsystem we’ve been discussing so far, so you see where they fit in alongside THP, ZRAM, migration, page cache, shrinkers, etc.

1️⃣ CMA — Contiguous Memory Allocator
[ CMA in Memory Management ]
   ├─ Purpose:
   │    • Provides large physically-contiguous regions of memory.
   │    • Needed for DMA-capable hardware (GPU, DSP, multimedia engines).
   │
   ├─ How It Works:
   │    • At boot, reserves a big physically-contiguous memory region
   │      (e.g., 256MB reserved for graphics or camera).
   │    • Pages inside this region can be used by the kernel for normal
   │      allocations **until** a DMA request needs them.
   │    • Uses page migration to free up and compact that region when needed.
   │
   ├─ Relation to Page Types:
   │    • Allocates base pages, but may coalesce into larger compound pages.
   │    • Doesn't directly create THP or static hugepages but can allocate
   │      huge contiguous areas if fragmentation is low.
   │
   ├─ Connection to Migration:
   │    • Relies on the **page migration framework** to move movable pages
   │      out of the reserved CMA region on demand.
   │
   ├─ Connection to Shrinker/OOM:
   │    • If CMA region is fragmented and migration fails → allocation fails.
   │    • Doesn't directly trigger OOM, but failed CMA allocations can
   │      propagate errors to drivers needing contiguous buffers.
Example Use Cases:

GPU framebuffers

Multimedia codecs (video encode/decode)

DMA engines for networking or ISP pipelines

2️⃣ DMA-BUF — Shared Buffer Framework
[ DMA-BUF in Kernel Memory Sharing ]
   ├─ Purpose:
   │    • Framework to share **physically-backed buffers** across multiple
   │      drivers or subsystems (GPU, display, camera, video, etc.)
   │
   ├─ How It Works:
   │    • One driver allocates a buffer (often from CMA or ION).
   │    • Exports a "file descriptor" for that buffer to user space.
   │    • Another driver (e.g., GPU) imports the buffer using the FD.
   │    • Reference counting ensures safe sharing and cleanup.
   │
   ├─ Relationship to CMA:
   │    • Buffers for DMA-BUF often come from CMA because hardware usually
   │      needs contiguous physical memory.
   │
   ├─ Interaction with Page Management:
   │    • The underlying pages can still be migrated **if not pinned**.
   │    • When pinned (for DMA), pages are locked and exempt from reclaim,
   │      compaction, or THP collapse.
   │
   ├─ Performance:
   │    • Avoids expensive copies between subsystems.
   │    • Enables zero-copy pipelines (e.g., camera → ISP → GPU → display).
3️⃣ Integration with Topics in This Thread
Feature	Relation with CMA	Relation with DMA-BUF
THP (Transparent Huge Pages)	CMA usually avoids THP regions, but contiguous blocks from CMA can be mapped as huge pages for performance.	DMA-BUF buffers are fixed-size and pinned, so THP promotion/demotion is not applicable.
MTHP (Multi-size THP)	Not typically combined with CMA.	Same as THP — no dynamic remapping.
Page Migration	Actively used to free up CMA region when needed.	Migration blocked if buffer is pinned for DMA.
Shrinker & OOM	CMA allocations fail gracefully → driver decides fallback; doesn’t trigger OOM unless app retries uncontrollably.	DMA-BUF itself doesn’t reclaim memory; buffers stay until explicitly released.
ZRAM/ZSWAP	CMA pages are not compressed/swapped while pinned.	DMA-BUF pages are also not swappable because they are device-critical.
Page Cache	CMA is not related to page cache directly; used for anonymous driver allocations.	DMA-BUF buffers are not part of page cache but are reference-counted like file-backed pages.
Linear Map & VA Space	CMA regions live in the linear mapping, ensuring physical ↔ virtual translation is straightforward for DMA.	DMA-BUF buffers also appear in kernel VA but protected from user-space mapping unless specifically mmap’d.

5️⃣ Key Points to Remember
CMA is about physical contiguity. It ensures drivers can always get physically contiguous memory regions even under fragmentation by migrating pages out of reserved regions.

DMA-BUF is about buffer sharing. It provides an efficient mechanism for zero-copy sharing between different subsystems, often using CMA-backed memory.

Pinned pages are special. They bypass reclaim, migration, THP collapse, zswap/zram compression, and normal shrinker logic until released.

Security and Mapping: User-space apps can mmap a DMA-BUF FD into their space, but only for that buffer — not arbitrary kernel VA (CONFIG_UNMAP_KERNEL_AT_EL0 still applies).

What is external and internal fragmentation and connect it with whatever we have discussed so far
ChatGPT said:
Let’s deep dive into fragmentation in Linux memory management — internal vs external fragmentation — and connect it with THP, MTHP, CMA, DMA-BUF, ZRAM, page cache, migration, shrinkers, and OOM, as we’ve discussed so far.

1️⃣ What is Fragmentation
Fragmentation happens when memory is not efficiently utilized due to the way pages are allocated and freed.

Type	Definition	Example
Internal Fragmentation	Wasted space inside an allocated block due to allocation granularity not matching the request size.	If an app needs 6 KB but the kernel allocates a 4 KB page, it wastes 2 KB.
External Fragmentation	Memory is available but scattered into smaller chunks that are not contiguous, preventing allocation of a larger block.	Need 2 MB contiguous for THP, but memory is scattered into many 4 KB pages across the zone.
2️⃣ Fragmentation Across Kernel Subsystems
🔹 Transparent Huge Pages (THP)
Goal: Map 2 MB pages instead of 4 KB for performance (TLB efficiency).

Issue: Needs physically contiguous memory.

Fragmentation Effects:

Internal: Each THP is a fixed 2 MB block. If a process only uses 1.2 MB, the rest 0.8 MB is wasted.

External: After uptime or memory churn, fewer contiguous 2 MB blocks are available, causing THP fallback to small pages.

Mitigation:

khugepaged tries to collapse scattered 4 KB pages into THPs if virtual contiguity is there, relying on migration and compaction to fight external fragmentation.

🔹 Multi-size THP (MTHP)
Supports smaller hugepages (e.g., 64 KB, 128 KB, 512 KB).

Advantage: Reduces external fragmentation because allocations are more flexible in size.

Compressibility: Larger, uniform chunks compress better (as we discussed earlier).

🔹 CMA (Contiguous Memory Allocator)
Requires physically contiguous pages for DMA devices.

External Fragmentation Problem:

If the CMA region is fragmented by movable kernel allocations, requests for contiguous buffers can fail.

Solution:

Uses page migration and compaction to free up the region dynamically.

🔹 DMA-BUF (Shared Buffers)
Uses contiguous memory (often CMA).

No Internal Fragmentation: Buffers are allocated per exact size required.

External Fragmentation:

If many buffers are pinned for DMA, fewer movable pages remain for THP or CMA reallocation.

🔹 ZRAM and ZSWAP
ZRAM compresses pages in a block-device-like region.

Internal Fragmentation: Slight, due to compression metadata overhead per page.

External Fragmentation: None, because ZRAM is virtualized and does not rely on contiguous physical memory.

🔹 Page Cache / VFS Cache
Fragmentation mainly affects memory reclaim and compaction.

Heavy cache pressure can scatter pages, worsening external fragmentation for THP and CMA allocations.

3️⃣ Role of Migration, Compaction, and Shrinkers
Mechanism	Helps With	Notes
Page Migration	Moves movable pages to defragment physical space.	Key for CMA and THP allocations.
Memory Compaction	Actively rearranges free pages to create large contiguous regions.	Works in background or on-demand for allocations.
Shrinkers	Frees cache or slab pages to make room.	Can release pressure but does not solve fragmentation if pinned pages block movement.
OOM Killer	Only invoked when free memory is exhausted, not just fragmented.	Fragmentation can cause allocation failure before OOM in some cases.

THP	Wasted space inside 2 MB if underutilized	Needs contiguous 2 MB, fails under fragmentation
MTHP	Less wasted space due to smaller page sizes	Still depends on contiguous blocks but more flexible
CMA	Low, as buffers match request	High if region is fragmented and migration fails
DMA-BUF	Low, buffers are exact size	Pinned buffers can fragment physical memory
ZRAM/ZSWAP	Slight overhead for metadata	No external fragmentation
Page Cache	Depends on object size alignment	Can scatter physical pages, worsening external fragmentation

1️⃣ What is GEM
GEM stands for Graphics Execution Manager, a memory management subsystem in the Linux Direct Rendering Manager (DRM) stack.

It was introduced by Intel but is now a generic framework used by GPU drivers (including KGSL, where you’re moving now).

GEM’s role is to manage graphics buffer objects (BOs) for:

GPU rendering

Compute workloads

Display scan-out (framebuffers)

Sharing buffers between CPU, GPU, and other devices

2️⃣ GEM in the Kernel Memory Landscape
Here’s how GEM fits with what we’ve discussed:

Concept	GEM Relation	Why It Matters
Page Allocations	GEM allocates pages (4K or larger chunks) for GPU buffers.	Ties into internal/external fragmentation depending on buffer alignment and size.
THP / MTHP	GEM buffers can benefit from THP/MTHP if mapped contiguously in userspace, reducing TLB pressure.	However, GPU memory often requires contiguous IOVAs, which makes MTHP helpful but not always guaranteed.
CMA	If GPU needs physically contiguous memory (like display scan-out buffers), GEM may request memory from the CMA pool.	Similar to how DMA-BUF works for multimedia pipelines.
DMA-BUF	GEM buffers can be exported/imported as DMA-BUFs for sharing with other drivers (e.g., camera, display).	Enables zero-copy buffer sharing.
Page Migration & Compaction	When large contiguous buffers are needed, GEM may trigger migration or fallback to scattered allocations with remapping.	Fragmentation affects performance here.
Shrinkers	GEM drivers often register shrinkers to free unused GPU buffers under memory pressure.	Prevents premature OOM kills when VRAM-backed or shmem-backed buffers are idle.
3️⃣ GEM Workflow in Practice
Here’s the lifecycle of a GEM buffer in a typical workload:

[User Space]
  |
  |---> ioctl(DRM_IOCTL_GEM_CREATE)
  |
[Kernel - DRM Driver (GEM Layer)]
  |
  |---> Allocate pages (buddy allocator, shmem, or CMA)
  |---> Map pages into GPU IOMMU space (via SMMU if present)
  |
  |---> Expose fd for user mapping
  |
[User Space]
  |
  |---> mmap(fd) → Direct CPU access
  |
  +---> Submit command buffer → GPU executes using GEM BO
4️⃣ GEM + Fragmentation
Scenario	Impact	Mitigation
Internal Fragmentation	If a GEM buffer is allocated in fixed chunks (e.g., 2 MB) but app only uses 1.5 MB, the extra is wasted.	Drivers often align sizes to page size or MTHP sizes to reduce waste.
External Fragmentation	Over time, large contiguous allocations (for scanout buffers) may fail due to physical page scattering.	Page migration, CMA compaction, or fallback to scattered mappings via GPU MMUs.
5️⃣ GEM and ZRAM/ZSWAP
No direct relation to GEM, but:

Under heavy pressure, system swap (via ZRAM/ZSWAP) may start paging out user-space memory, not GEM GPU buffers (these are usually pinned).

If GEM buffers are not actively pinned, shrinkers may evict or compact them first.

6️⃣ GEM, SMMU, and VFIO
On SoCs with SMMU (IOMMU):

GEM buffers are often mapped into GPU’s IOVA space using page tables.

This reduces the requirement for physically contiguous memory, relying instead on virtual contiguity.

For VFIO-based passthrough, GEM is bypassed, as user-space frameworks like DPDK or CUDA directly map DMA regions.

ChatGPT said:
This paragraph is describing how CMA (Contiguous Memory Allocator) pages are intended to be used in the Linux memory management subsystem and the trade-offs when overusing or underusing them.
Let’s break it down deeply and connect it with our previous discussions on GEM, DMA-BUF, migration, fragmentation, THP, etc.

1️⃣ Key Idea of CMA Pages
CMA reserves a physically contiguous region of memory at boot.

This region is movable-only:

Pages allocated from CMA must be migratable, meaning they can be relocated elsewhere if needed (e.g., via page migration or compaction).

Non-movable allocations (like kernel stacks, page tables, pinned buffers) cannot use CMA memory.

2️⃣ Why Overusing CMA is Dangerous
If CMA pages are over-utilized or allocated for non-movable workloads, two problems occur:

Problem	Explanation
Starvation of Non-Movable Allocations	If the system uses too much CMA for buffers (e.g., pinned GEM buffers, large VRAM allocations), the buddy allocator runs out of regular movable pages, starving other parts of the kernel that need non-contiguous memory.
Performance Degradation	Always using CMA as the first choice can add unnecessary overhead due to compaction/migration pressure when the system tries to reclaim CMA pages for other high-priority allocations.
3️⃣ The "Midway Alternative" (Balanced Usage)
The recommended approach is controlled allocation:

Use CMA pages for allocations that are:

From userspace processes
(e.g., GEM buffers, Android SurfaceFlinger buffers, camera buffers)

Easily migratable or drop-able
(e.g., cached textures, streaming buffers)

Avoid using CMA for:

Kernel pinned pages
(e.g., page tables, DMA mappings that cannot be unmapped)

Structures critical to kernel operation

This balance ensures:

Efficient CMA usage (no idle reserved memory)

No starvation for essential non-movable allocations

Good performance during compaction and migration events

4️⃣ Connection to Previous Topics
Concept	How It Relates to CMA
GEM Buffers	When GPUs or display pipelines request contiguous memory (e.g., for scanout or tiler), CMA provides it. If pinned buffers are allocated without care, they may lead to CMA starvation.
DMA-BUF	Shared buffers (camera → GPU → display) often rely on CMA for contiguous mappings. Proper migration handling keeps these flows efficient.
Page Migration / Compaction	CMA regions are movable by design, allowing pages to be relocated during memory pressure or when defragmentation is triggered.
Internal & External Fragmentation	CMA reduces external fragmentation by reserving a contiguous range upfront. However, if poorly used, it creates internal fragmentation, leaving large reserved areas underutilized.
THP / MTHP	CMA is typically unrelated to THP, but in some workloads (e.g., GPU compute), hugepage-backed buffers can reduce TLB pressure. If CMA memory is blocked by pinned allocations, THP allocations might also get indirectly affected.
ZRAM / ZSWAP	If CMA is fully used and system pressure rises, shrinkers will try to migrate pages out of CMA. Unmovable pages lead to system swap activity, potentially degrading performance.

Drivers should balance allocations between CMA and regular movable memory.

Proper handling avoids performance bottlenecks during high memory pressure.

ChatGPT said:
Great — you’ve asked three very important MM (memory management) topics: PSI pressure, anon vs file memory, and CONFIG_IDLE_PAGE_TRACKING. Let’s go one by one and then connect them with all the subsystems we’ve been discussing (THP, ZRAM, swap, CMA, GEM, DMA-BUF, etc.).

1️⃣ PSI (Pressure Stall Information)
What it is:
PSI = Pressure Stall Information, a kernel feature that measures how much time tasks spend stalled waiting on CPU, memory, or I/O resources.

Introduced in Linux 4.20.

Exposed under /proc/pressure/.

Why:
Not just how much memory/CPU is used, but how much stalling it causes for workloads.

Files:

/proc/pressure/cpu
/proc/pressure/memory
/proc/pressure/io
Example (memory PSI):

some avg10=0.50 avg60=0.25 avg300=0.10 total=200000
full avg10=0.20 avg60=0.10 avg300=0.05 total=100000
some → At least one task is stalled.

full → All tasks are stalled.

avg10/avg60/avg300 → % of time stalled in last 10s/60s/300s.

Relation to earlier topics:

ZRAM/ZSWAP/Swap: High PSI memory values mean tasks are blocked waiting on reclaim/swap-in.

THP/MTHP: Collapse/compaction overhead increases PSI stalls if fragmentation is high.

CMA/GEM/DMA-BUF: If large contiguous allocations fail, drivers may stall waiting for migration/compaction → visible in PSI.

2️⃣ Anonymous (anon) vs File Memory
Anonymous memory (anon):

Memory not backed by a file.

Examples: heap (malloc), stack, mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS).

Lives on the anonymous LRU lists.

Can be swapped out (to disk swap or ZRAM).

File memory (file-backed):

Memory backed by a file or filesystem.

Examples: program text segments (.text), mapped shared libraries, page cache.

Lives on the file LRU lists.

Clean file pages can be dropped (since they can be reloaded). Dirty ones must be written back first.

Relation to topics so far:

Anon pages → candidates for swap/zram/zswap.

File pages → handled via page cache and writeback.

KSM only deduplicates anonymous memory.

THP/MTHP work for both anon and file (file-THP for tmpfs, shmem).

OOM killer prefers killing processes consuming lots of anonymous memory.

3️⃣ CONFIG_IDLE_PAGE_TRACKING
What it is:
A kernel config option (CONFIG_IDLE_PAGE_TRACKING) that allows the kernel to track which pages are accessed/idle.

Useful for performance tuning, NUMA balancing, memory hotplug, and memory tiering (DRAM vs PMEM).

How it works:

Provides /sys/kernel/mm/page_idle/bitmap interface.

Each physical page frame has a bit indicating idle (not accessed recently) or young (accessed).

User-space tools (e.g., migrate_pages, NUMA balancer, Android LMKD) can query and decide which pages to reclaim or migrate.

Use cases:

NUMA balancing: Move hot (frequently accessed) pages closer to CPUs.

Tiered memory systems: Place cold/idle pages on slower memory (NVDIMM/PMEM).

Page reclamation: Evict idle pages first to minimize performance impact.

CMA/DMA-BUF interaction: Idle page tracking helps migration by picking pages less likely to be touched during compaction.

4️⃣ Connecting the Three
                         MEMORY MANAGEMENT
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                                                                 │
 │  PSI Pressure  → tells us when processes are stalling due to    │
 │                   reclaim, compaction, swap/zram/zswap I/O.     │
 │                                                                 │
 │  Anon vs File  → determines which pages can go to swap/zram     │
 │                   (anon), and which can just be dropped (file). │
 │                                                                 │
 │  Idle Page Tracking → lets kernel/userspace know which pages    │
 │                       are active vs idle, guiding migration,    │
 │                       reclaim, or NUMA/tiering decisions.       │
 │                                                                 │
 └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
5️⃣ Example Flow (Camera + GPU Workload)
Camera driver allocates CMA buffers (movable pages).

GEM exports those as DMA-BUF to GPU/display.

If memory pressure rises:

Anon pages (apps heap) → may go to ZRAM/ZSWAP → PSI memory pressure rises.

File pages (code, libraries) → dropped from page cache.

Idle pages detected via idle page tracking → migrated/evicted first.

If CMA region fragmented → compaction triggers migration, stalls show in PSI.

If pressure persists → shrinkers run, then OOM if nothing helps.

✅ Summary

PSI: How bad are stalls from memory/CPU/IO pressure?

Anon vs File: Which pages can swap (anon) vs drop (file)?

Idle Page Tracking: Which pages are idle vs active → informs reclaim/migration/tiering.

┌─────────────┐  [stack]                → anonymous, grows down, guard pages
│   STACK     │  ... argv/envp/auxv, TLS TCB mirror, redzones
└─────────────┘
┌─────────────┐  [vvar / vdso]          → file-like kernel pages for time syscalls
│ VVAR / VDSO │
└─────────────┘
┌─────────────┐  [shared libraries]     → file-backed (page cache), RX .text, RO .rodata, RW .data/.bss
│  lib*.so    │
└─────────────┘
┌─────────────┐  [heap / brk segment]   → anonymous; malloc small/medium via brk arenas
│    HEAP     │  grows up; guarded by ASLR
└─────────────┘
┌─────────────┐  [mmap() area]          → anonymous or file-backed (JIT, arenas, stacks, files, SHM)
│  MMAP AREA  │  glibc uses mmap for large allocations, file maps, stacks for threads
└─────────────┘
┌─────────────┐  [binary text+data]     → file-backed executable: RX .text, RO .rodata, RW .data, zero-fill .bss
│   a.out     │
└─────────────┘
LOW  ADDRS
2) ELF sections → VMAs → Linux mm
Program piece (ELF)	Examples / content	VMA perms	Backing	Page type @fault	Notes in Linux mm
.text	compiled code	r-xp	File-backed	file page	Demand paged from page cache; executable mapping; subject to I/D cache coherency rules.
.rodata	const strings, vtables	r--p	File-backed	file page	Clean pages can be dropped; COW not needed.
.data	initialized globals	rw-p	File-backed initially	file → anon (COW)	First write triggers COW: becomes anonymous.
.bss	zero-initialized globals	rw-p	Zero-fill-on-demand	anonymous	Minor fault allocates zero page → private anon.
Heap (brk)	malloc small/med	rw-p	Anonymous	anonymous	Created by brk(). First touch = minor fault; can be THP/MTHP-promoted.
mmap anon	mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS)	rw-p	Anonymous	anonymous	Used for large malloc, stacks, JIT, arenas; THP/MTHP eligible.
mmap file	mmap("file",…)	r--/rw-/rx	File-backed	file page	Reads/writes hit page cache + writeback.
Thread stacks	pthread stacks	rw-p	Anonymous	anonymous	Guard pages at ends; minor/major faults like heap.
TLS	thread-local storage	mixed	File→COW→Anon	file→anon	Loader sets up TLS images; per-thread.
vDSO / vvar	fast time syscalls	r-xp/r--p	Kernel-provided	special	Mapped by kernel; not swappable.
shared mem	shm, memfd	rw-p	tmpfs/shmem	file( tmpfs )	Lives in shmem page cache; can be swap’d.
Mapping rules & faults

Demand paging: first access causes minor (if page cached) or major fault (needs I/O).

COW: writing to a file-backed private mapping or fork-shared page triggers COW → anonymous.

Swap: only anonymous pages (heap/stack/COW) are swap/zram candidates.

3) Toolchain details you actually see at runtime
PIE + ASLR: randomizes base addresses for binary, libs, heap, stack → mitigates exploits; affects /proc/<pid>/maps order.

GOT/PLT, relocations: live in .got/.plt (file-backed RO/RX) and related fixups; reloc writes trigger COW → anon in data segments.

Dynamic linker (ld.so): itself a mapped ELF with its own .text/.data/.bss VMAs.

Guard pages: no-access pages around stack/threads/JIT regions prevent overflow.

4) How malloc maps to mm (glibc default)
Small/medium allocs: carve from brk heap arenas (anonymous).

Large allocs (≥ threshold, e.g., 128–256 KiB): individual mmap anon regions.

THP/MTHP: kernel may promote long-lived, hot anon regions (heap/mmap) to THP (2 MiB) or MTHP (multi-size) via fault-time alloc or khugepaged collapse.

Under pressure: anon pages → zswap/zram/disk swap; file pages → drop/writeback.

5) Page types & kernel data structures (what the kernel tracks)
Every physical page → a struct page (metadata).

Kernel prefers folios for multi-page units (page cache, THP/MTHP) to reduce locking/overheads.

Anonymous pages: have anon_vma rmap; eligible for KSM (dedup) if MADV_MERGEABLE.

File pages: belong to an address_space (page cache) of an inode; writeback via filesystem ops.

LRU lists (per-node): active/inactive file and anon, plus unevictable (mlock).

6) Fault taxonomy applied to your program
Minor fault (fast): page already in RAM (e.g., page cache hit, zero page); just map PTE.

Major fault (slow): needs I/O (read file page, read from swap/zram).

COW fault: write on shared/private file map or forked anon → allocate new anon page, copy data, update PTE.

7) Huge pages in this layout
Mechanism	Where it applies in a C program	Behavior under pressure
THP (2 MiB)	anon heap, anon mmap, sometimes shmem/tmpfs (file-THP)	Can split to 4 KiB for reclaim/swap
MTHP	anon/file (large folios) for finer granularity hugepages	Splits step-wise; better success under fragmentation
Static HugeTLB	only if you explicitly mmap(MAP_HUGETLB)	Not swappable; outside normal reclaim
8) Reclaim, compaction, migration touches your program
kswapd/direct reclaim: evicts cold anon (→ zswap/zram/disk) or file (drop/writeback).

THP shrinker: splits THPs to base pages first.

Compaction/migration: moves movable pages to create contiguous space (helps THP, CMA).

PSI: memory stalls visible in /proc/pressure/memory during heavy reclaim/compaction.

9) How file I/O ties in (page cache path)
read() → fills page cache pages for that file; next reads are minor faults into your VMA (or copy into your buffer).

mmap(file) → your VMA directly maps those page cache pages; fault populates PTEs to existing cache pages.

Dirty file pages → writeback to storage; clean file pages → drop on reclaim (no swap).

10) Special mappings relevant to C programs
vDSO/vvar: kernel maps read-only pages so clock_gettime() can run in user mode (no syscall).

TLS: per-thread images mapped and then mostly private/anon after reloc/COW.

Shared memory (POSIX shm, SysV shm, memfd_create) via tmpfs/shmem: file-like, but swappable.

11) Security & kernel visibility
KASLR + CONFIG_UNMAP_KERNEL_AT_EL0: kernel VA unmapped at EL0; user cannot see kernel linear map.

/proc/kallsyms: symbol addresses restricted unless permitted; not a mapping the process can access.

12) Quick “/proc/<pid>/maps” cheat (typical)
00400000-00600000 r-xp  a.out      (.text)
00600000-00602000 r--p  a.out      (.rodata)
00602000-0062a000 rw-p  a.out      (.data/.bss → COW to anon on write)
00700000-00f00000 rw-p  [heap]     (brk anonymous)
7f2a00000000-7f2a10000000 rw-p     (mmap anon arenas, JIT, etc.)
7f2a4c000000-7f2a4c200000 r-xp  libm.so
7f2a4c200000-7f2a4c400000 r--p  libm.so
7f2a4c400000-7f2a4c600000 rw-p  libm.so (COW)
7fff5f000000-7fff60000000 rw-p  [stack]
7fff60001000-7fff60005000 r--p  [vvar]
7fff60005000-7fff60007000 r-xp  [vdso]
TL;DR mapping rules
File-backed regions (.text/.rodata/.data, libs, file mmaps) → page cache; COW turns writable parts into anonymous.

Heap/stack/anon mmaps → anonymous; candidates for THP/MTHP, swap/zram under pressure; subject to KSM if enabled.

Reclaim path: file pages drop/writeback; anon pages swap (zswap/zram/disk); THP can split; migration/compaction maintain large-page availability.

Everything physical is tracked by struct page/folios, placed on LRUs, and protected by VM locks (mmap_lock, rwsem) during faults and map changes.

Perfect — this is a core Linux MM concept. Let’s go through slab, slub, slob, how they sit on top of the buddy allocator, and their internal algorithms. I’ll keep this structured so you can see the internals clearly.

1️⃣ Buddy Allocator Recap (Base Layer)
Unit: works in powers-of-2 blocks of pages (2^order, order = 0..MAX_ORDER).

Goal: satisfy requests for physically contiguous pages.

Free lists: per-order, per-zone.

Algorithm:

Alloc:

Round request up to nearest power-of-2 block.

If free list empty at that order, split higher-order block into halves (buddies).

Return one, keep the other.

Free:

Check if buddy block free.

If so, merge into higher-order block.

Repeat until no merge possible.

👉 Provides page-level allocation, but inefficient for small objects (structs, kmalloc, kernel objects).

2️⃣ Slab Allocator Family (Built on Buddy)
Why Slab Layers?
Kernel allocates lots of small objects (inodes, dentries, task_struct, sk_buff, etc).

Buddy gives pages; slab breaks them into caches of fixed-size objects.

Avoids internal fragmentation and speeds up object reuse (less init/teardown).

A. Slab (Original)
Idea: allocate a page (or multiple pages) from buddy, carve into objects.

Data structures:

kmem_cache: describes a cache for a specific object type.

Each cache has slabs: contiguous pages split into equal objects.

Each slab has 3 lists: full, partial, empty.

Algorithm:

Alloc:

Find a cache for requested size.

If a partial slab exists → use free object.

Else, allocate new slab (from buddy), carve into objects.

Free:

Return object to slab’s free list.

If slab empty → return to buddy (optional).

Pros: object coloring, cache hotness, great for SMP.

Cons: high metadata overhead, complexity.

B. SLUB (Default in modern kernels)
Simplification of SLAB (no queues of slabs).

Each kmem_cache holds objects directly inside pages.

Data structures:

struct kmem_cache: describes object size, alignment, flags.

Each CPU has per-CPU freelist for fast allocation.

Pages contain metadata (struct page) describing used/free objects.

Algorithm:

Alloc:

Check per-CPU freelist → O(1).

If empty, fetch a new page from buddy, split into objects, refill freelist.

Free:

Return object to freelist.

If whole page free → return to buddy.

Pros: less fragmentation, lockless fast path, simpler.

Cons: no object coloring, but mitigated with cache alignment.

C. SLOB (Embedded/Minimal Systems)
Simplest slab allocator, optimized for low-memory embedded.

Works like a simple linked-list allocator (like malloc).

Data structures:

slob_block: header with size, next pointer.

Free list: singly linked, first-fit allocation.

Algorithm:

Alloc:

Walk free list.

If block big enough, split and return.

If none found, allocate a new page from buddy.

Free:

Insert block back into free list.

Merge adjacent blocks if possible.

Pros: tiny overhead, simple.

Cons: fragmentation, poor scalability, slower.

3️⃣ Layering with Buddy
[ Buddy Allocator ]
    └── Allocates pages (2^order)
        ├── SLAB → per-cache object slabs, full/partial/empty lists
        ├── SLUB → per-CPU freelists, object metadata in struct page
        └── SLOB → first-fit heap within pages
Buddy ensures physical contiguity and merges/freeing.

Slab family ensures efficient small-object allocation.

Interaction with migration/fragmentation:

Slab/SLUB objects are marked movable/unmovable to allow page migration/compaction (important for THP, CMA).

CMA cannot use unmovable slab pages (like pinned kernel objects).

4️⃣ Example: Allocating task_struct
fork() → kernel calls kmem_cache_alloc(task_struct_cachep).

SLUB:

Check per-CPU freelist for a free task_struct object.

If empty, allocate a new page from buddy.

Carve page into task_struct objects, return one.

Buddy ensures the page is from the right zone (e.g., ZONE_NORMAL).

5️⃣ Comparison Table
Feature	SLAB	SLUB	SLOB
Use	Servers, old	Default general-purpose	Embedded, tiny
Lists	Full/partial/empty slab lists	None, uses per-CPU freelists	Single free-list
Metadata	Per-slab headers	Metadata in struct page	Minimal
Alloc algo	Find slab with free object	Grab from per-CPU freelist	First-fit in free list
Speed	Good	Best (O(1) fast path)	Worst
Memory efficiency	Moderate	High	Low (fragmentation)
6️⃣ Connection to Everything Else We Discussed
Anon/File Pages vs Slab: slab allocators are for kernel objects, not user pages. User anon/file memory still goes via buddy + page cache.

Fragmentation:

Internal: slab/SLUB alignments waste some bytes per object.

External: SLOB worst, SLUB better.

CMA: slab pages are non-movable → CMA cannot reclaim them.

Migration/Compaction: only movable slab caches can be relocated; pinned slab objects block THP/contiguous allocations.

Shrinkers: slab caches register shrinkers (e.g., dentry_cache, inode_cache) → free objects back to buddy under memory pressure.

✅ Summary

Buddy: coarse-grained, contiguous pages in powers of 2.

Slab/SLUB/SLOB: fine-grained, object-level allocators layered on buddy.

SLAB: complex, metadata-heavy.

SLUB: modern default, fast, simple.

SLOB: embedded, minimal.

Integration: They work with shrinkers, migration, CMA, THP, zram/zswap indirectly by controlling what pages are movable.

Awesome—let’s walk through SLAB vs SLUB vs SLOB internals and how they sit on top of the buddy allocator, using a step-by-step kmalloc(128) example, plus ASCII flow diagrams and all the common caveats.

Quick map: where each allocator fits
User/kernel ask for objects (kmalloc/kzalloc/kmem_cache_alloc)
        │
        ▼
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │            Small-object allocators (slab layer)        │
 │  • SLUB (modern default)  • SLAB (classic)  • SLOB     │
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        │            request pages when they run out
        ▼
 ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │                   Buddy allocator                       │
 │  Power-of-2 page blocks (order-0,1,2,...) per zone/node │
 │  Split/merge buddies; honors GFP flags/NUMA policy      │
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
1) Buddy allocator (base layer)
What it does: hands out physically contiguous blocks of 2^order pages from per-zone, per-order free lists.

Allocate

Round up to nearest order

If that free list empty, split a higher order block

Return block

Free

Find buddy of returned block

If free, merge upward and repeat

Why slab needs it: slab/SLUB/SLOB all grab pages from buddy to carve into objects.

2) SLUB internals (default on most modern kernels)
Data structures (simplified)
struct kmem_cache — describes an object type/size (e.g., kmalloc-128 cache)

Per-CPU state:

c->freelist — single-linked list of free objects for the current CPU

c->page — the current slab page source for this CPU

c->partial — small per-CPU cache of partially used pages (optional)

Per-node:

n->partial — node-wide list of partially used pages (shared)

Freelist encoding: SLUB stores the next-pointer inside the freed object itself (tiny header) to avoid extra metadata.

Allocation fast path (O(1), no locks)
kmalloc(128)  →  pick kmalloc-128 cache  →  per-CPU freelist ?
    yes → pop one pointer → return
    no  → slowpath
Slowpath (high level)
If c->page exists but freelist empty → refill from that page’s free objects

Else try per-CPU partial → install as c->page

Else try node partial list (locked)

Else allocate new slab page(s) from buddy (order chosen by SLUB for packing)

Carve into objects, build freelist, return one

Free path
If freed on the same CPU and page is c->page → push into c->freelist (lockless)

If different CPU or page not current → put object back in page freelist with minimal locking; if page becomes empty, it may be returned to buddy

Debug / features that change behavior
slub_debug (redzones, poisoning, sanity checks)

SLAB_TYPESAFE_BY_RCU (RCU rules for reuse)

memcg slab accounting (per-cgroup caches)

cpu_partial: batching of partial pages to avoid contention

3) SLAB internals (classic)
Data structures
kmem_cache: object type/size

Per-CPU magazine (kmem_cache_cpu): a small array of free objects for fast, lockless alloc/free

Per-node (kmem_cache_node) lists of slab pages:

full — no free objects

partial— some free

free/empty — all free

Allocation
kmalloc(128) → find size cache
  per-CPU magazine has free? → pop → return
  else: refill magazine from node’s partial list (lock)
        if none: allocate new slab from buddy, carve objects,
                 move to partial, fill magazine, return
Free
If per-CPU magazine not full → push there (lockless)

Else return object to its slab’s free list (lock); move slab between lists if state changes; if slab empty, may return pages to buddy

Pros/cons: good scalability in its time; more metadata and list management than SLUB, more locks on hot paths.

4) SLOB internals (tiny systems)
Treats each page as a mini-heap with a first-fit free list (slob_block)

Allocate: walk list, split block if large enough; O(N)

Free: insert back; coalesce adjacent free blocks

Requests new page from buddy if no fit

Smallest overhead, worst scalability/fragmentation; used mainly on very small embedded builds

5) What happens on kmalloc(128, GFP_KERNEL) — practical step-by-step
Assume SLUB, CPU 3, NUMA node 0:

A) Warm fast path

The request is mapped to kmalloc-128 cache (power-of-two size class, alignment guaranteed)

SLUB checks per-CPU freelist → has entries

Pops one pointer, returns object (no locks, no IRQ disable)

B) Cold path (no freelist)

No freelist; check c->page → if present, rebuild freelist from that page

If not, try per-CPU partial; if empty, try node partial (take lock)

If none: ask buddy for a new page (often order-0 or order-1 for 128-byte objects)

SLUB carves the page into 128-byte objects, builds freelist

Returns one object; keeps the rest on c->freelist

C) Freeing

Caller kfree(ptr)

If its page == c->page and same CPU → push to per-CPU freelist (lockless)

If that page becomes entirely free, depending on cache policy, it may be put on node partial or returned to buddy

Under pressure

A shrinker (for caches that register one) may reclaim unused slabs, moving them to empty and returning pages to buddy.

Compaction/migration: slab pages are usually unmovable; kernel avoids placing unmovable slabs in movable pageblocks to protect CMA/THP.

6) ASCII flows
SLUB allocate (fast & slow)
kmalloc(128)
  ↓
find kmalloc-128 cache
  ↓
per-CPU freelist ?
  ├─ yes → pop → return
  └─ no  → c->page ?  → rebuild freelist → return
            │
            ├─ if none → per-CPU partial ? → install as c->page → return
            │
            ├─ node partial ? (lock) → install as c->page → return
            │
            └─ buddy alloc new page(s) → carve → set c->page → return
SLAB allocate
kmalloc(128)
  ↓
per-CPU magazine ?
  ├─ yes → pop → return
  └─ no  → refill from node partial (lock)
           ├─ success → pop → return
           └─ else → buddy alloc slab page(s) → carve → add to partial
                     → refill magazine → return
SLOB allocate
kmalloc(128)
  ↓
walk free list (first-fit)
  ├─ found big block → split → return
  ├─ found exact fit → return
  └─ none → buddy alloc new page → add to free list → retry
7) Caveats & “gotchas” with real examples
(1) Context & GFP flags
IRQ/softirq context must use GFP_ATOMIC (cannot sleep). If per-CPU freelist empty and buddy cannot instantly satisfy, allocation may fail.

Example: NAPI RX path: use small kmalloc with GFP_ATOMIC. If you accidentally use GFP_KERNEL, it may sleep → BUG.

(2) NUMA locality
kmalloc_node(size, GFP_KERNEL, nid) sticks to a node.

If node 0 low on memory, SLUB/buddy may fallback to remote node, hurting latency. Watch with perf/numa stats.

(3) Large kmalloc sizes
Beyond cache sizes, SLUB calls kmalloc_large/kmalloc_order → buddy high-order pages.

High order fails under external fragmentation. Prefer kv*alloc (e.g., kvmalloc) which falls back to vmalloc safely.

(4) Debug options change behavior
slub_debug=FZP (Free-poison, Redzone, Poison) adds canaries/fills; slows fast path and increases memory footprint—great for catching overflows/use-after-free but not for production perf.

(5) False sharing & alignment
Objects that multiple CPUs touch should be __cacheline_aligned/SMP_CACHE_BYTES to avoid ping-pong.

Misaligned caches can cripple scalability (e.g., per-CPU stats structs).

(6) Reclaimability
Many slab caches are unreclaimable; they don’t sit on LRUs. If you over-allocate kmalloc memory, zram/swap won’t help; you can hit OOM even with big file cache available.

Use shrinkers (e.g., for dentries/inodes) for reclaimable kernel objects.

(7) CMA/THP interference
Slab pages are generally unmovable, so if the kernel places too many slab pages in movable pageblocks, later CMA/THP allocations can fail. This is why pageblock migration types matter.

(8) Remote free contention (SLUB)
Freeing objects from a CPU different than the one that owns the page induces locking. Hot cross-CPU frees (e.g., networking RX/TX recycling) can cause contention; batching helps.

(9) Constructors & cache init
kmem_cache_create(..., ctor) runs a ctor per object when a slab is first created (not per allocation). Don’t put runtime state there; it’s for one-time layout/init only.

(10) Zeroing vs non-zeroing
kzalloc zeroes the object (costly). Prefer kmem_cache_zalloc for a dedicated cache that expects zeroed objects, or avoid zeroing if you overwrite fully.

8) How SLAB/SLUB/SLOB interact with the rest we discussed
They serve kernel objects only. User memory (heap, stacks, file maps) is managed as anonymous/file pages, not via slab.

Under pressure: shrinkers may free slab caches (dentry/inode/skbuff), returning pages to buddy; only then can THP/CMA allocations succeed.

Not on LRU / not swappable. Slab pages don’t go to zram/zswap; they must be freed by their owners.

Fragmentation: SLUB’s order choice and packing reduce external frag; SLOB is most susceptible; SLAB sits between.

TL;DR cheatsheet
Buddy: page granularity, split/merge, honors zones/NUMA/GFP.

SLUB (default): per-CPU freelist, minimal metadata, lockless fast path; slowpath dips into node partial or buddy.

SLAB: per-CPU magazines + node full/partial/empty lists; a bit heavier.

SLOB: tiny first-fit heap inside pages—simple but slow/fragmented.

kmalloc(128): hits kmalloc-128 cache; SLUB pops from per-CPU freelist; if empty, pulls a page from buddy, carves objects, returns one.

Caveats: GFP flags, NUMA fallback, large size → high-order pages, debug flags impact perf, slab is unreclaimable unless shrinker-managed, alignment to avoid false sharing.

Linux Kernel Allocator Decision Tree (buddy/slub/slab/slob)

Linux Kernel Allocator Decision Tree (Buddy / SLUB / SLAB / SLOB)
Goal: Pick the right allocator + flags fast, avoid stalls/fragmentation, and know your fallbacks.

Quick Picks (90% cases)
kmalloc() / kzalloc() for ≤ PAGE_SIZE-ish objects (use cache sizes: 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1K, 2K, 4K, 8K, …)

kmem_cache_* for hot-path, frequent, same-size objects (create a dedicated cache)

kv*alloc() (kvzalloc/kvmalloc) for potentially large, variable-size buffers (falls back to vmalloc if high-order fails)

vmalloc() / vzalloc() for big, virtually-contiguous, not DMA’d buffers

dma_alloc_*() or CMA for device DMA (physically contiguous)

Decision Tree (ASCII)
Need kernel memory → size S, context C, use U
|
|-- Is this DMA to a device / requires physical contiguity?
|     |-- Yes → dma_alloc_*() (coherent/attrs) or CMA (movable-only)
|     |      ↳ If fails: try smaller buffers, ensure pages movable, free pins
|     |-- No →
|
|-- Is S very large (could exceed order-3 under pressure)?
|     |-- Yes → kvmalloc()/kvzalloc()  (alloc_pages first, fallback to vmalloc)
|     |      ↳ If DMA to device later → map via IOMMU, avoid needing contig
|     |-- No →
|
|-- Is this a frequently-used fixed-size object type?
|     |-- Yes → kmem_cache_create() → kmem_cache_alloc()
|     |      ↳ Add ctor only for one-time init, consider SLAB_TYPESAFE_BY_RCU
|     |-- No →
|
|-- Context allows sleeping?
|     |-- No (IRQ/NAPI/softirq) → use GFP_ATOMIC with kmalloc()
|     |      ↳ Keep sizes small; pre-warm caches; avoid vmalloc()
|     |-- Yes → kmalloc() with GFP_KERNEL
|
|-- NUMA sensitive?
      |-- Yes → kmalloc_node()/alloc_pages_node() with policy; monitor fallback
      |-- No  → default node ok
GFP Flag Cheatsheet
GFP_KERNEL: default, may sleep. Use in process context.

GFP_ATOMIC: non-sleeping (IRQ/softirq/NAPI). Smaller success window.

GFP_NOWAIT: do not sleep; fail fast.

GFP_HIGHUSER/GFP_HIGHUSER_MOVABLE: user pages, movable preferred.

__GFP_ZERO: zero-fill pages (use kzalloc/vzalloc).

__GFP_NOFAIL: avoid if possible; must handle stalls. Prefer retries/backoff.

__GFP_COMP: create compound page for higher-order allocations.

Tips:

For hot RX/TX paths → GFP_ATOMIC + pre-alloc pools.

For movable caches → include __GFP_MOVABLE to help compaction/CMA.

NUMA & Locality
Prefer kmalloc_node() / alloc_pages_node() on the accessing CPU’s node.

Watch /proc/zoneinfo & perf NUMA stats for fallback to remote nodes.

Use mempolicy/set_mempolicy() for users that back user mappings.

Large Alloc Strategy (avoid high-order stalls)
Try kvmalloc() (alloc_pages → fallback to vmalloc)

If DMA later, rely on IOMMU mapping (avoid physical contiguity)

If physical contig truly required → CMA with pages movable; free pins

Consider chunking + scatter-gather lists

SLUB / SLAB / SLOB at a glance
SLUB (default): per-CPU freelists, minimal metadata, O(1) fast path.

SLAB: per-CPU magazines + node full/partial/empty lists; more metadata.

SLOB: first-fit within pages; tiny footprint; fragmentation-prone.

When to create a cache: hot objects, frequent alloc/free, special ctor, alignment needs.

Debug & Hardening (dev/test only on hot paths)
Boot slub_debug=FZP (Free poison / Redzones / Poisoning)

KASAN, KFENCE, KMSAN for memory bugs

__alloc_size, __counted_by, __user annotations

Align hot structs: __cacheline_aligned

Reclaim, Compaction, CMA
Slab pages often unmovable → don’t pollute movable pageblocks; set correct flags

Register shrinkers for caches that can be dropped (dentry/inode/skbuff)

Compaction creates contiguous ranges for THP/CMA; movable pages help

CMA is movable-only; don’t pin long-term in CMA regions

Common Pitfalls & Remedies
IRQ path uses GFP_KERNEL → may sleep → BUG → use GFP_ATOMIC

Large kmalloc stalls → switch to kvmalloc / chunk allocations

Cacheline bouncing → add padding/alignment; per-CPU objects

Leaky slab caches → add shrinker; instrument with perf kmem, slabinfo

CMA alloc failures → free pins, ensure pages movable, compact; reserve enough CMA at boot

High PSI memory stalls → reduce THP collapse on hot paths, tune reclaim, use zswap/zram

Example Flows
A) kmalloc(128, GFP_KERNEL) (SLUB)
Map to kmalloc-128 cache → per-CPU freelist pop (O(1))

Empty? Refill from c->page / per-CPU partial → node partial → buddy allocate

Free: push back to freelist; empty page may return to buddy

B) kvmalloc(200KB, GFP_KERNEL)
Try alloc_pages (order-5) → may fail under fragmentation

Fallback to vmalloc (virtually contig, phys non-contig)

If device needs it: map via IOMMU (avoid contig requirement)

C) DMA buffer for camera (needs contig)
dma_alloc_coherent() or CMA alloc (movable-only region)

If busy: compaction/migration frees CMA area

Export buffer via DMA-BUF; avoid long-term pinning where possible

Handy Commands
cat /proc/slabinfo · slabtop

cat /proc/zoneinfo · cat /proc/pagetypeinfo

echo 1 > /proc/sys/vm/compact_memory (test compaction)

echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches (cache drop test; not for prod)

Print this page and keep it next to your dev box. Adjust thresholds to your workload.

1️⃣ Transparent Huge Pages (THP) vs Hugepages (HugeTLBFS)
THP (Transparent Huge Pages / THB as you wrote)

Automatic promotion of base pages (4 KB) into huge pages (default 2 MB, PMD-mapped).

Works for anonymous mappings (heap, stack) and tmpfs/shmem.

Managed by khugepaged + page fault handler.

Splittable under memory pressure.

Goal: performance via TLB efficiency, transparent to apps.

Hugepages (HugeTLB / Static Hugepages)

Explicit mechanism: reserve a pool at boot (/proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages) or mount hugetlbfs.

User apps must request them (e.g., mmap(MAP_HUGETLB) or libhugetlbfs).

Hugepages = explicit, reserved, pinned

2️⃣ Slab vs Slab Cache
Slab allocator = the mechanism (family: SLAB, SLUB, SLOB) that carves buddy pages into fixed-size objects.

Slab cache = a specific cache for one object type.

Example: kmem_cache_create("task_struct", sizeof(struct task_struct), …)

Each kmalloc-size class (kmalloc-128, kmalloc-256) is itself a slab cache.

👉 Think of slab allocator = factory, slab cache = per-object production line.

3️⃣ Page Cache and File-Backed Memory
Page cache stores file contents (file-backed pages) in memory.

If a process mmaps or reads a file, it uses the page cache → reduces disk I/O.

If memory pressure hits, page cache pages are evicted (dropped) — not written to swap, since they can be reloaded from disk.

Important:

Page cache does not keep "objects evicted to disk".

It’s always a cache of file data to speed I/O.

Point of duplication:

File in page cache (for all processes to share).

Process’s private writable copy (via COW → anonymous page).

👉 So the cache avoids duplicate disk reads/writes; it doesn’t duplicate uselessly.

4️⃣ HWPoison
HWPoison = hardware memory error handling.

When ECC detects an uncorrectable error in a RAM page → kernel marks it poisoned (PG_hwpoison).

That page is offlined: unmapped from processes, migrated/reclaimed, never reused.

Exposed via /sys/devices/system/memory/hwpoison/ and madvise(MADV_HWPOISON).

Used in RAS (Reliability, Availability, Serviceability) subsystems.

5️⃣ KASAN (Kernel Address Sanitizer)
A runtime memory error detector for the kernel.

Instruments memory allocations to catch:

Use-after-free

Out-of-bounds

Invalid free

Implemented by poisoning shadow memory + redzones.

Variants: KASAN inline, outline, hardware-assisted (HWASAN).

Heavy overhead; mostly used in debugging builds.

6️⃣ ftrace
Function Tracer framework in Linux.

Hooks into almost any kernel function entry/exit.

Provides APIs (trace_printk, tracepoints, perf, bpf) to trace kernel execution in real time.

Used for:

Latency tracking

Syscall monitoring

Scheduler tracing

Lock contention debugging

Files: /sys/kernel/debug/tracing/*

7️⃣ kernel_panic_notifier and Callbacks
Kernel has a notifier chain mechanism: modules can register callbacks for events.

panic_notifier_list = chain for panic events.

Example: crash dump, watchdog, reboot manager may register.

Mechanism:

static int my_panic_cb(struct notifier_block *nb, unsigned long event, void *ptr) {
    printk("panic detected: taking action\n");
    return NOTIFY_DONE;
}
static struct notifier_block my_block = { .notifier_call = my_panic_cb };
register_panic_notifier(&my_block);
Other notifier chains exist: cpu_notifier, die_notifier, reboot_notifier, etc.

Helps in custom error handling, logging, failover actions.

User C program
  |
  v
┌───────────────┐
| ELF Sections  | → file-backed (page cache, COW anon)
| Heap/Stack    | → anonymous (swap/zram under pressure)
└───────────────┘
  |
  v
[ Kernel Memory Mgmt ]
  - THP/MTHP: merge anon/file into 2M+ pages
  - Hugepages: explicit reserved
  - Slab/SLUB: kernel object caches (kmalloc, task_struct, inodes)

  - CMA/DMA-BUF: contiguous movable allocations for devices
  - Migration/compaction/shrinkers to maintain balance
  - PSI shows stalls if reclaim/swap causes delays
  |
  v
[ Reliability / Debugging ]
  - HWPoison: retire bad pages
  - KASAN: catch memory bugs
  - ftrace: live tracing/debugging
  - Panic notifiers: custom crash handlers

Slab ≠ Slab cache: allocator vs per-object cache.

Page cache ≠ swap cache: page cache = file data in memory, never swap.

HWPoison = hardware fault isolation,

KASAN = memory bug detector,

ftrace = live tracer,

panic notifiers = callback chains for crash handling.

1️⃣ Anonymous mapping
Created by:

mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS | MAP_PRIVATE, …)

brk() (via malloc, heap growth)

Thread stacks

No file backing → pages are “anonymous” (not tied to an inode).

On first access (fault), they are allocated as zeroed pages.

If swapped, they go to swap/zram, not to disk file.

Eligible for THP/MTHP promotion.

2️⃣ File-backed mapping
Created by:

mmap(fd, …) on a real file

ELF program text/data (mapped by loader)

Backed by page cache of the file.

Clean file pages can be dropped and reloaded from storage.

Dirty pages → written back to file before eviction.

Sharing across processes is easy: same file mapping → same page cache pages.

3️⃣ tmpfs
A special filesystem: “temporary file storage in RAM”.

Mounted usually on /dev/shm, /tmp (depending on distro).

Backing:

Uses shmem (shared memory) API in kernel.

Backed by swap for overflow — so data persists until swap runs out.

Behavior:

Files look like real files (open, read, write).

Contents live in RAM (page cache), but evict to swap when needed.

Use cases:

Fast temporary files

IPC (via memfd_create, shm_open)

Backing store for posix_shm and /dev/shm

4️⃣ shmem (shared memory filesystem API)
shmem = the internal kernel implementation that powers tmpfs.

tmpfs is essentially a user-visible mount of shmem.

Key details:

Each file in tmpfs → inode → address_space → page cache pages.

If memory pressure hits → shmem pages can go to swap/zram.

Used for:

IPC (shmget, shm_open)

Anonymous memfd_create() buffers

Backing store for System V shared memory

👉 tmpfs vs shmem:

tmpfs = filesystem wrapper you mount.

shmem = kernel’s memory-backed file subsystem that tmpfs uses.

5️⃣ Hugepages: reserved vs transparent
Reserved Hugepages (HugeTLB)
Reserved at boot (hugepages=N) or dynamically via /proc/sys/vm/nr_hugepages.

Allocated from buddy at boot time → guarantees large contiguous memory exists.

User must explicitly map them with mmap(MAP_HUGETLB).

Pinned, not swappable, not splittable.

Good for databases, DPDK, HPC needing guaranteed performance.

THP (Transparent Huge Pages)
Not reserved. Kernel promotes anon/file pages into hugepages (2M) on fault or by khugepaged.

Can be split back into base pages under pressure.

Flexible but can fail if system is fragmented.

Transparent: applications don’t need to request them.

6️⃣ CMA vs Hugepages
CMA (Contiguous Memory Allocator):

At boot: reserves a movable memory region.

Used for DMA / device buffers that need physical contiguity.

Pages in CMA pool are movable so kernel can migrate them out when DMA requests memory.

Allocations can be of arbitrary size (not just hugepage multiples).

Hugepages (HugeTLB):

At boot: reserves a pool of fixed-size large pages (2 MB, 1 GB).

For user mappings that request MAP_HUGETLB.

Pinned, not swappable, not migratable.

👉 Difference:

CMA = “flexible, migratable pool” for DMA buffers.

HugeTLB = “fixed, non-movable pool” for app-visible large mappings.

7️⃣ Why Hugepages ≠ THP
Both give you large pages, but:

HugeTLB (explicit hugepages): reserved pool, user must request, pinned, not splittable.

THP: opportunistic, automatic, splittable, fallback to 4K pages if fragmented.

👉 If you mmap(MAP_HUGETLB) → you get explicit reserved hugepages (not THP).
👉 If you just malloc → kernel may back it with THP if available.

Anonymous mapping = no file, swappable (heap/stack).

File-backed mapping = page cache, reloadable from disk.

tmpfs = shmem filesystem → memory-backed, can swap, IPC-friendly.

HugeTLB = reserved pool, explicit, pinned.

CMA = flexible pool for device DMA, migratable.

You said:
what migratable and flexible CMA pool meaning ? where can it get migrated ? are pinned and not swappble terms complimentory ?
ChatGPT said:
Very good Q 👍 — these words “migratable”, “flexible CMA pool”, “pinned”, “swappable” are loaded terms in Linux MM. Let’s carefully untangle them and connect to everything we discussed.

1️⃣ CMA pool: “migratable” and “flexible”
CMA (Contiguous Memory Allocator) reserves a region of RAM at boot.

This region is not permanently locked; instead:

It is marked for movable allocations only (i.e., pages that can be migrated).

Until a driver requests contiguous memory, CMA’s region can be used temporarily for movable pages (like page cache, anon).

👉 Migratable here means:

If a driver suddenly needs N MB contiguous memory from CMA, the kernel can:

Migrate those temporary pages (file cache → drop, anon → swap/zram).

Compact the region, freeing physically contiguous pages.

Thus, CMA memory is flexible:

In idle times, it’s used like normal RAM (but only for movable pages).

When a device (GPU, ISP, V4L2 camera, etc.) asks, CMA can reclaim it for contiguous allocations.

Where can they get migrated?

To any other free page frames outside CMA in the same NUMA node/zone, provided the target pages are available.

If anon → might be swapped/zram’d.

If file-backed → can be dropped and reloaded from disk.

2️⃣ Pinned vs Swappable
Let’s break down the terminology:

Pinned page
A page that cannot be moved or reclaimed while in use.

Example: DMA buffers handed directly to hardware, mlock’ed memory, kernel pages with direct hardware mappings.

Pinned ≠ swappable, because if a page can’t even move, it obviously can’t be swapped.

Pinned = non-migratable + non-swappable.

Swappable page
A page that can be evicted to swap/zram if memory pressure rises.

Typical: anonymous pages (heap, stack).

Swappable pages must be migratable first, because swapping out is just a form of migration (from RAM → swap disk/zram).

👉 So yes, pinned and swappable are complementary in practice:

Pinned page = stuck in RAM, not swappable, not migratable.

Swappable page = migratable (either to another RAM PFN or to swap).

3️⃣ Mapping these back to earlier concepts
Concept	Movable / Migratable	Pinned?	Swappable?
Anon page (heap/stack)	Yes (can migrate)	No	Yes
File-backed page	Yes (drop or reload)	No	Not swapped, but reclaimable
Page cache	Yes	No	Not swapped, but can drop
CMA temporary page	Yes (movable)	No	If anon → swappable
DMA buffer in CMA	Allocated as pinned	Yes	No
HugeTLB (static hugepage)	Not movable (pinned)	Yes	No
THP (transparent hugepage)	Migratable, splittable	No	Yes
Slab (most kernel objects)	Often unmovable	Yes	No
ZRAM/ZSWAP pages	Migrated from anon	No (once inside comp storage)	N/A (already evicted)
4️⃣ Why CMA needs movable-only pages
CMA’s magic is possible only if all pages inside its pool are reclaimable/migratable.

If pinned pages or non-movable kernel slabs ever leak into CMA → compaction fails → devices requesting contiguous DMA buffers fail.

That’s why kernel carefully enforces:

No permanent allocations in CMA except movable ones.

Drivers must free CMA allocations after DMA done, otherwise CMA starves.

5️⃣ Example Scenarios
Camera buffer (DMA-BUF in CMA):

Allocated from CMA → pinned until frame capture is done.

After release → pages go back to CMA pool → may host movable page cache again.

Database with HugeTLB pages:

Uses boot-reserved hugepages → pinned forever.

These pages never migrate, never swap, unlike CMA.

Anonymous heap with THP:

THP is migratable (can be split into base 4K and moved).

If pressure high, anon THPs can even be swapped out.

✅ Key Takeaways
CMA pool = “flexible contiguous region” used as movable-only memory until devices need it.

Migratable = page can be moved to another PFN or evicted to swap.

Pinned = page is locked in RAM (not movable, not swappable).

Swappable requires migratability, so pinned pages are never swappable.

Hugepages vs CMA:

HugeTLB = pinned, reserved, unmovable.

CMA = movable, migratable, reclaimable pool → only pinned when device actively uses it.

I still don't get what is page cache. If we need any file lets say .so from disk, will it be loaded in memory ram as page cache and then get used by cpu from there or two copies onwe having actual content from disk will be loaded in ram and another same copy will be created in ram as page cahec ?
ChatGPT said:
Excellent Q 🙌 — this is a very common confusion. Let’s clear it up with precision:

What is Page Cache?
The page cache is simply the in-memory representation of file contents.

When you read or mmap a file (like a .so), the kernel does not create two copies in RAM.

Instead:

The kernel allocates physical pages in RAM.

These pages are filled with file data from disk.

They are stored in the page cache (tied to the inode of the file).

Processes map/use those very same pages.

👉 The page cache is the actual data in RAM. There’s no “duplicate” copy of the file unless you explicitly copy it (e.g., memcpy into a buffer).

Step-by-step with your .so example
Say process loads libm.so:

Page fault occurs on first access.

Kernel sees mapping → it’s file-backed.

Kernel checks page cache:

If not present, allocate a physical page from buddy → read file block from disk into that page.

Insert it into the file’s page cache (address_space mapping).

Process PTE now points to this page.

CPU executes directly from this page in RAM.

So:

Disk copy = permanent storage on SSD/HDD.

Page cache = in-RAM copy of only the parts you’ve touched (demand paging).

No extra hidden duplicate — page cache is the working copy in RAM.

Why does confusion happen?
Because:

People imagine the kernel loads file into some “page cache” buffer, and then again into process memory.

In reality: the same physical page is used both as the page cache entry and as the process’s mapped page.

Think of it like:

Disk block <-> Page cache page in RAM <-> Process PTE mapping
(only one RAM page, multiple PTEs may point to it).

Writable mappings
If you map a file read/write shared:

Process writes go to page cache page → later written back to disk.

If you map a file read/write private (COW):

First write faults → kernel allocates a new anonymous page, copies data, process writes to that page (not page cache).

Original file page stays untouched in page cache.

Eviction
When RAM is low:

Clean page cache pages → simply dropped (reloaded from disk later if needed).

Dirty page cache pages → written back, then dropped.

Connection to tmpfs/shmem
tmpfs/shmem also uses page cache pages, but instead of being tied to a disk file, they are tied to an in-RAM pseudo-file.

That’s why tmpfs files can swap: the page cache entries are backed by swap when evicted.

✅ Key Takeaway
Page cache is the actual in-RAM copy of file contents.

When you load libm.so, the CPU executes directly from those page cache pages.

No duplicate “shadow copy” exists unless:

You copy data explicitly (e.g., read() into a buffer).

Or you trigger COW with a private writable mapping.

apart from mmap from user space, which calls or apis can directly create anonymous or file backked mappings
ChatGPT said:
Excellent question 🙌 — you’re basically asking: “Besides mmap() that userspace can call, what kernel/user APIs actually create VMAs for anonymous or file-backed mappings?”

Let’s break it down systematically.

1️⃣ Anonymous Mappings (no file backing)
These are memory regions not associated with any file/inode. They come from zero-fill-on-demand pages, and can be swapped.

APIs that create anon mappings:

User space → Kernel:

brk() → extends heap (used by malloc internally).

mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS, …) → explicit anonymous region.

mmap(..., MAP_PRIVATE | PROT_WRITE) of a file → writes trigger COW, creating anonymous pages.

shm_open() + ftruncate() on tmpfs-backed shm → creates pages that behave like anon (backed by shmem, but swap eligible).

memfd_create() → returns an FD backed by shmem/tmpfs (anonymous-like).

Kernel internals:

Stack allocation: new thread (via clone(), pthread_create()) → kernel creates a new anonymous stack VMA.

VDSO mappings may copy pages that become anon (if patched by process).

fork() → child inherits all parent mappings as COW anon (until touched).

2️⃣ File-backed Mappings (tied to a file/inode)
These VMAs are associated with a file in the page cache.

APIs that create file-backed mappings:

User space → Kernel:

mmap(fd, …, MAP_SHARED) → file-backed mapping (shared, changes visible in file).

Executing a binary (execve()) → loader maps ELF sections (text, data, rodata) from the file into memory.

Dynamic linker (ld.so) loads .so files → file-backed mappings.

dlopen() internally → triggers mmap() on the .so.

shm_open() / open("/dev/shm/…") → file-backed (but shmem/tmpfs file).

Kernel internals:

Page cache for file I/O:

read() / write() don’t create mappings, but they populate page cache pages, which are the same pages used by mmap() if later mapped.

tmpfs/shmem: every file in tmpfs/shmem has file-backed VMAs (backed by swap, not disk).

procfs/sysfs/debugfs: files can be mmap’d → file-backed but special.

3️⃣ tmpfs / shmem (special hybrid)
They look file-backed, but the file is in RAM, not on disk.

Created by:

shm_open()

memfd_create()

/dev/shm usage

tmpfs mounts (/tmp, /dev/shm)

Pages are file-backed (inode exists), but since there’s no disk, they go to swap if evicted.

4️⃣ Kernel-only Allocations (not exposed to userland but create mappings)
These don’t use mmap from userspace, but they still create VMAs internally:

vmalloc() / vmap() (kernel allocs non-contiguous memory, maps virtually contiguous).

ioremap() (map device MMIO into kernel VA space → file-backed in a sense, but by device memory).

remap_pfn_range() (used by drivers to mmap device memory into user space, e.g., /dev/fb0).

5️⃣ Table Summary
Type	How Created (User)	How Created (Kernel)	Swappable?
Anonymous	brk(), mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS), COW on write	Thread stacks, fork() COW	✅ Yes
File-backed	mmap(fd), execve ELF load, dlopen()	Page cache, ELF loader	Clean pages: drop; Dirty: writeback
tmpfs/shmem	shm_open, memfd_create, /dev/shm	tmpfs mounts	✅ Yes (swap)
Kernel-only (no user VMA)	N/A	vmalloc, ioremap, driver remap_pfn_range	❌ No
✅ Key Insights
Anonymous mappings come from brk, MAP_ANONYMOUS, stacks, or COW after fork/write.

File-backed mappings come from mmap(fd), ELF loading, shared libs, tmpfs/shmem.

tmpfs/shmem is “file-backed but swap-backed,” a hybrid.

Kernel allocations also use mapping APIs (vmalloc/ioremap), but these are kernel-only.

Perfect 👌 — now we’ll tie Linux memory zones into everything we’ve discussed (THP, HugeTLB, CMA, anon/file, swap/zram, page cache, slabs, etc.).

1️⃣ What are zones?
Zones = logical subdivisions of physical memory in Linux.
Why? Because not all physical memory is equal:

Some devices need DMA-able memory (low PFNs).

Some allocations must be contiguous (CMA, hugepages).

Some allocations must be movable for compaction.

So the kernel splits RAM into zones with different constraints.

2️⃣ Exhaustive List of Linux Memory Zones
Names vary across architectures (x86, ARM, ARM64, PowerPC, etc.), but here’s the superset:

Zone	Purpose
ZONE_DMA	Low PFN memory reserved for devices with old DMA addressing limits (e.g., <16MB on x86, <32-bit addressable range on ARM).
ZONE_DMA32	(On x86-64/ARM64) memory below 4GB, usable by 32-bit PCI devices needing DMA.
ZONE_NORMAL	Main region for kernel allocations, page cache, slabs. Directly mapped in kernel linear map.
ZONE_HIGHMEM	(x86 32-bit only) Memory above 896MB, not permanently mapped into kernel VA. Rare now.
ZONE_MOVABLE	Region reserved for migratable pages only (anon, file cache). Used by compaction, CMA, THP to keep fragmentation low.
ZONE_DEVICE	For device memory managed like RAM via devm_memremap_pages() (e.g., persistent memory, HMM for GPUs). Not swappable.
3️⃣ How Each Zone Connects to What We Discussed
ZONE_DMA / ZONE_DMA32
Used when drivers call dma_alloc_*().

Related to CMA: CMA pools usually carved out of low memory so devices can DMA into it.

Pinned pages for device buffers (DMA-BUF, camera/GPU) often must come from DMA zones.

ZONE_NORMAL
Default zone for almost everything:

Page cache

Slab/SLUB/SLOB caches

Anonymous memory (heap/stack)

File-backed mappings

THP/MTHP promotion: buddy compaction happens here to form contiguous 2M (or other order) chunks.

HugeTLB pages: reserved hugepages usually carved out of ZONE_NORMAL.

ZONE_HIGHMEM (only x86 32-bit)
Not directly mapped in kernel linear address space → must kmap temporarily.

Mostly historical, but influences why zones exist.

THP/HugeTLB not usually placed here.

ZONE_MOVABLE
Special pageblock type for migratable pages only:

Anonymous memory

File cache pages

Unmovable allocations (slab, kernel stacks, pinned DMA pages) cannot go here.

Critical for:

CMA: CMA pools often come from movable blocks.

THP: compaction prefers migrating pages from movable zones.

Page migration: used to free space for large allocations.

👉 This zone is why we earlier said: “CMA pages must be migratable, otherwise contiguous allocations fail.”

ZONE_DEVICE
Added for persistent memory (NVDIMM/pmem) or device-managed RAM (GPUs via HMM).

Shows up as a zone but doesn’t behave like regular DRAM:

Not swappable

May not be on LRU

Used via special APIs (mmap of DAX, HMM for GPU).

4️⃣ Zone ↔ Concepts Table
Concept	Zone relevance
Page cache	ZONE_NORMAL (or MOVABLE if migratable)
Anon pages	ZONE_NORMAL / ZONE_MOVABLE
Swap/ZRAM	Not a zone (side storage), anon pages from NORMAL/MOVABLE get evicted there
THP	Needs contiguous 2M from ZONE_NORMAL/MOVABLE
MTHP	Needs contiguous blocks (order depends) from ZONE_NORMAL/MOVABLE
HugeTLB	Reserved at boot, usually from ZONE_NORMAL
CMA	Carved out of ZONE_MOVABLE so allocations can migrate out
Slab caches	Usually ZONE_NORMAL; often unmovable so they avoid MOVABLE
Pinned DMA pages	From ZONE_DMA/DMA32/NORMAL depending on device addressing
HWPoison	Any zone page can be poisoned; kernel must migrate if movable
NUMA nodes	Each node has its own set of these zones (e.g., Node0: DMA, DMA32, NORMAL, MOVABLE)
5️⃣ Visual Textual Map
[ Physical Memory Layout per NUMA node ]
 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │  ZONE_DMA     (lowest PFNs, for legacy DMA)  │
 │  ZONE_DMA32   (below 4GB, PCI DMA devices)   │
 │  ZONE_NORMAL  (main RAM, page cache, slabs)  │
 │  ZONE_MOVABLE (only migratable pages, CMA,THP│
 │  ZONE_DEVICE  (pmem/HMM device memory)       │
 └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

- Page cache & slabs live mostly in NORMAL
- Anon/file cache can live in MOVABLE (reclaimable/migratable)
- CMA comes out of MOVABLE to ensure contiguous DMA buffers
- THP/MTHP allocations compact within NORMAL/MOVABLE
- HugeTLB pool reserved from NORMAL at boot
- Swap/ZRAM are not zones, but evict anon pages from NORMAL/MOVABLE
✅ Key Takeaways
Zones split physical memory by constraints (DMA, migratable, persistent).

ZONE_NORMAL = the default playground (page cache, anon, slabs).

ZONE_MOVABLE = ensures CMA/THP can find contiguous memory by excluding pinned/unmovable allocations.

Pinned vs swappable: pinned (DMA, kernel objects) → avoid MOVABLE; swappable anon/file pages → preferred in MOVABLE.

Hugepages vs CMA: both pre-reserve, but HugeTLB is pinned (NORMAL), CMA is migratable (MOVABLE).

Each NUMA node has its own copy of these zones.

Annotations

👉 So:

Page cache = active_file + inactive_file.

Anonymous (swap-eligible) = active_anon + inactive_anon.

CMA pool = nr_free_cma.

Pinned kernel/DMA = unevictable.

2️⃣ HMM (Heterogeneous Memory Management for GPUs)
Problem
Modern GPUs (NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm Adreno with SVM) want to share memory with the CPU:

Unified Virtual Addressing (CPU+GPU see same pointers).

GPU can directly access system RAM pages.

Need page faulting on GPU side if a page is missing.

HMM Solution
HMM = Heterogeneous Memory Management, part of Linux MM.

Allows GPU drivers to:

Mirror CPU page tables into GPU’s MMU (via SVM = Shared Virtual Memory).

Handle GPU page faults by calling into the Linux MM to migrate pages if necessary.

Support memory migration between device memory (VRAM) and system DRAM.

Flow:

Process allocates memory (anon/file-backed).

HMM lets GPU page tables map those same pages.

If GPU touches a page not resident → HMM triggers CPU page fault handling → allocate/migrate page → update GPU PTE.

👉 This is how modern APIs (CUDA UM, ROCm SVM, OpenCL SVM) work under Linux.

3️⃣ devm_memremap_pages() vs ioremap()
Both are about mapping physical addresses into the kernel virtual address space, but they’re very different in intent.

ioremap()
Used for device MMIO (memory-mapped registers, framebuffers).

Creates non-cacheable, strongly ordered mappings.

Doesn’t treat the range as normal RAM.

Example: map PCI BAR registers or GPU command buffer space.

devm_memremap_pages()
Used for device memory that behaves like RAM (e.g., NVDIMM persistent memory, HMM GPU VRAM).

Returns an array of struct pages → the memory becomes part of the page allocator.

Can be used with normal kernel allocators (page cache, anon pages).

Supports ZONE_DEVICE.

Integrated with migration, compaction, and LRU if applicable.

👉 Key difference:

ioremap() = just map device space for MMIO, no struct page, not on LRU, not swappable.

devm_memremap_pages() = register memory with Linux MM as managed pages (like DRAM/ZONE_DEVICE).

4️⃣ How this ties together
/proc/zoneinfo shows the health of each zone (Normal, Movable, CMA pool, etc.).

Page cache/anon balance shows how much RAM is used for code/data vs heap/swap.

CMA free indicates how much contiguous space remains for DMA.

THP allocations consume large chunks from Normal/Movable, compaction tries to migrate anon/file pages out.

HMM introduces ZONE_DEVICE memory for GPUs/accelerators, letting them share pages with CPU (migratable if needed).

ioremap vs memremap_pages → pure MMIO vs treat-as-RAM.

✅ Summary

Zones: DMA/DMA32 (low addressable), Normal (main), Movable (migratable-only), Device (HMM/pmem).

/proc/zoneinfo: shows anon/file/unevictable/CMA distribution.

HMM: lets GPUs share CPU memory, handle GPU page faults, migrate between DRAM and VRAM.

ioremap = MMIO registers; devm_memremap_pages = managed device memory as pages.
