Cgroups vs mpam
ChatGPT said:
Ah 👍 got it — you mean cgroups vs MPAM (ARM Memory Partitioning and Monitoring).
This is an important distinction: cgroups is a kernel-level software resource controller, while MPAM is an ARM hardware extension for memory QoS. Let’s break them down and connect to all the memory-management stuff we’ve been discussing.

1️⃣ What are cgroups?
Software mechanism in the Linux kernel to limit, isolate, and account resources across groups of processes.

Organized as controllers (memory, CPU, I/O, pids, etc.).

Works entirely in software — the kernel enforces limits using existing mechanisms:

Memory cgroup tracks charged pages in page cache, anon, slab. Can throttle/reclaim per group.

CPU cgroup throttles via scheduler.

I/O cgroup throttles block I/O.

Exposed via /sys/fs/cgroup or systemd units.

👉 Scope: works across all architectures; doesn’t rely on special hardware.

2️⃣ What is MPAM (Memory Partitioning and Monitoring)?
ARMv8.4+ hardware feature.

Lets the OS/Hypervisor control memory system QoS:

Partition cache ways (L3/LLC).

Throttle memory bandwidth per stream.

Monitor usage.

Each request in the memory hierarchy can carry a PARTID (partition ID) and optionally PMG (Priority/Monitoring Group).

Hardware enforces:

Cache allocation/way-partitioning.

Memory bandwidth controls.

Counters for monitoring bandwidth/cache usage.

👉 Scope: fine-grained hardware enforcement of memory/cache/bandwidth QoS, similar to Intel RDT (CAT, MBA, CQM).

3️⃣ How they relate
cgroups (software):

Track and limit memory consumption (how many pages are used by a group).

But cannot directly control where in cache or how much bandwidth a process gets.

MPAM (hardware):

Doesn’t know about Linux processes or cgroups.

Works at hardware requestor granularity (e.g., CPU core, SMMU stream, device).

Enforces partitioning/throttling in LLC/memory controller.

Needs OS cooperation to map tasks/VMs → PARTID.

4️⃣ How Linux integrates them
The idea is: cgroups provide the policy, MPAM provides the hardware enforcement.

Linux kernel’s resctrl (resource control filesystem, originally for Intel RDT) is being extended for MPAM.

Flow:

Userspace (systemd, container runtime) sets limits via cgroups (e.g., this container max 2 GB RAM, or 20% bandwidth).

Kernel assigns the container’s tasks a PARTID in MPAM context.

Hardware enforces cache/bandwidth allocation at runtime.

5️⃣ Example
Suppose you have two containers:

Container A: latency-sensitive (database).

Container B: batch analytics (background).

Without MPAM:

Both compete in LLC and memory bus → A may suffer.

With cgroups only:

You can limit B’s memory usage, but not its bandwidth pressure.

With MPAM + cgroups integration:

Assign Container A → PARTID=1 (high-priority, reserved cache ways).

Assign Container B → PARTID=2 (limited to 30% memory bandwidth, fewer cache ways).

Hardware enforces the partition, so Container A’s cache lines aren’t evicted by B.

6️⃣ TL;DR Difference
Feature	cgroups (software)	MPAM (hardware)
Layer	Kernel software	ARMv8.4+ hardware extension
Control unit	Process/group (cgroup)	PARTID/PMG per CPU or device stream
Resource types	Memory pages, CPU time, I/O	Cache ways, memory bandwidth, monitoring
Enforcement	Kernel reclaim/throttling	Hardware partitioning and counters
Purpose	Limit/isolate OS resources	Guarantee QoS at hardware level
✅ So:

cgroups = high-level process/container resource control.

MPAM = low-level hardware knobs for cache/memory partitioning & monitoring.

Together: cgroups decide policy (“container X = 2 cache ways, 20% bandwidth”), MPAM enforces it in hardware.

2️⃣ Exhaustive list of Linux syscalls related to memory management & processes
Here’s a structured map of major syscalls, what they do, and their kernel internals:

A) Process creation / lifecycle
Syscall	Purpose	Kernel internals
fork()	Clone current process	do_fork() → copy_process(); duplicates mm_struct (COW)
vfork()	Like fork but child shares address space until exec	`do_fork(CLONE_VM

B) Memory mapping / virtual memory
Syscall	Purpose	Kernel internals

mmap() / munmap()	Map/unmap file or anonymous memory	do_mmap() / do_munmap() → allocate vm_area_struct, populate via page faults
mprotect()	Change page permissions	do_mprotect_pkey() → walk PTEs, change perms
madvise()	Memory advice (drop, THP, prefetch)	do_madvise() → interacts with page cache, reclaim, THP policy
mlock() / munlock()	Pin pages in RAM	do_mlock() → mark VMAs non-swappable, populate pages
remap_file_pages()	Nonlinear mapping of file pages	sys_remap_file_pages() (rare now)
mremap()	Resize/move mapping	do_mremap() → may copy/migrate pages
shmat()/shmdt()	SysV shared memory attach/detach	Internally shmem (tmpfs) + VMAs

C) Paging / swapping / cache control
Syscall	Purpose	Kernel internals
msync()	Sync mapped file pages to disk	do_msync() → writeback page cache
posix_fadvise()	File access pattern hints	Affects readahead, caching
sync() / fsync()	Flush dirty pages	Calls filesystem ->fsync via VFS
swapoff()/swapon()	Enable/disable swap	Setup swap cache, swap subsystem
D) Process info & tuning
Syscall	Purpose	Kernel internals
getrusage()	Resource usage stats	task_cputime(), mm counters
prlimit()	Resource limits (ulimit)	do_prlimit() → rlimit struct
setrlimit()	Change per-process limits	Enforced during allocations (stack, memlock)
sched_setaffinity()	Pin process to CPUs	Affects scheduler runqueue
setpriority()/getpriority()	Niceness	Affects scheduler
E) File-backed memory APIs
Syscall	Purpose	Kernel internals
open() / close()	VFS open/close	do_sys_openat2() → struct file
read() / write()	File I/O	vfs_read() / vfs_write(); may hit page cache
pread()/pwrite()	Positional I/O	Same but offset based
sendfile()/splice()/vmsplice()	Zero-copy transfers	Pipe/page cache manipulation
mmap(fd)	Map file to VA	File’s f_op->mmap (e.g. shmem, ext4)
3️⃣ How they relate back to MM
Every memory syscall manipulates VMAs (struct vm_area_struct): describes region of VA space (anon/file, perms, flags).

Page faults fill them with actual pages (from buddy allocator, page cache, or swap).

Cgroups (memory controller) intercept allocations (charge each page to the cgroup).

MPAM (hardware) would apply QoS on cache/bandwidth when those pages are actually accessed.

So:

Syscalls: define process VA & resource usage.

cgroups: software policy/accounting per group of processes.

MPAM: hardware enforcement for cache/memory QoS.

✅ Final takeaway:

cgroups = generic software resource controller (CPU, memory, I/O, devices).

MPAM = hardware feature (cache/memory partitioning + monitoring).

Syscalls (fork, exec, mmap, brk, mlock, madvise, etc.) define and manipulate memory/process state; internally, they wire into VFS, page cache, anon pages, buddy allocator, reclaim, swap, IOMMU/SMMU that we’ve been discussing.

ChatGPT said:
Perfect, this is the “grand tour” 🚀 of Linux memory + process syscalls, in chronological flow (how they are invoked, what kernel subsystems they touch, which kernel objects they create, and how they tie back to our whole thread: page cache, anon, THP, CMA, SMMU, cgroups, MPAM, etc).

This is going to be long — but it will give you the end-to-end map.

1️⃣ Process Creation Syscalls
fork()
Userspace call → libc fork() → syscall.

Kernel path: sys_fork() → do_fork() → copy_process().

What happens:

Allocate a new task_struct for the child.

Duplicate parent’s mm_struct → child gets same VMAs, marked COW (copy-on-write).

Page tables are shared, marked read-only. First write → page fault → new page allocated.

File descriptors (struct file *) are duplicated with refcounts.

Scheduler places child on runqueue.

Result: Two processes, same address space but diverge on write.

vfork()
Same as fork, but child shares parent’s address space until execve().

Parent is suspended until child calls execve() or _exit().

Used for performance in shell pipelines.

clone() / clone3()
Lower-level primitive (used by fork, pthread_create, etc).

Flags decide what to share:

CLONE_VM → share mm_struct (threads).

CLONE_FILES → share file descriptor table.

CLONE_SIGHAND → share signal handlers.

CLONE_THREAD → create a thread in same thread group.

Internally: also goes through copy_process().

execve()
Purpose: Replace process image with a new binary.

Kernel path: sys_execve() → do_execveat_common() → search_binary_handler() → load_elf_binary().

What happens:

Tear down old mm_struct.

Create fresh mm_struct for new program.

Parse ELF headers:

.text/.rodata → file-backed private VMAs.

.data/.bss → file-backed, then zero-fill anon.

heap → anon VMA.

stack → anon VMA with guard page.

vdso → kernel-provided VDSO mapping.

Build argv, envp, and auxv on new stack.

Set PC=entry point, SP=new stack.

Result: Same PID, brand new code+data.

exit() / _exit()
Kernel path: do_exit().

Cleans up:

Free mm_struct (release page tables, unmap VMAs).

Decrement refcounts on inodes, files.

Free task_struct after parent reaps (via wait()).

2️⃣ Memory Mapping Syscalls
brk() / sbrk()
Grow/shrink the process heap.

Kernel: do_brk() → create/extend anon VMA.

Actual physical pages are not allocated until first access → page fault → buddy allocator supplies page.

mmap()
Most powerful syscall for memory:

MAP_ANONYMOUS → anon pages (heap-like).

MAP_SHARED|fd → file-backed shared mapping.

MAP_PRIVATE|fd → file-backed COW mapping (used in execve).

MAP_HUGETLB → static hugepages.

Kernel: do_mmap() → allocates vm_area_struct, links into mm_struct.

No pages yet → page faults fill them:

Anon → buddy allocator page.

File → page cache page, loaded from disk.

munmap()
Kernel: do_munmap() → remove VMA, unmap PTEs.

Pages become reclaimable.

mprotect()
Change VMA protection flags.

Kernel: do_mprotect_pkey() → update page tables (mark read-only, no-exec, etc).

Used for JITs, sandboxing.

madvise()
Hint kernel about memory usage:

MADV_DONTNEED → drop pages from page cache.

MADV_HUGEPAGE / MADV_NOHUGEPAGE → THP policy.

MADV_PAGEOUT → proactively swap out.

Kernel: do_madvise() → reclaim/THP policy manager.

mlock() / munlock()
Pin pages in RAM (non-swappable).

Kernel: mark VMA as VM_LOCKED, fault pages in, mark in LRU as unevictable.

Used by real-time, crypto, DBs.

mremap()
Resize/move mappings.

Can expand heap-like areas.

Kernel: do_mremap() → may allocate new pages, copy/migrate old.

SysV/POSIX Shared Memory
shmat() / shmdt() (SysV) or memfd_create(), shm_open() (POSIX).

Backed by shmem/tmpfs (inode+dentry, page cache).

Enable IPC and dma-buf exporters.

3️⃣ File & Page Cache Related
open() / close()
VFS path walk → get inode, allocate struct file.

Page cache not touched yet.

read() / write()
Kernel: vfs_read()/vfs_write().

Read path:

Look up inode’s page cache.

If miss: read from disk into page cache (via block I/O).

Copy from page cache to user buffer.

Write path:

Copy user buffer into page cache page.

Mark dirty → background writeback to disk.

mmap(fd)
Creates file-backed VMA.

Page faults pull pages into page cache.

CPU accesses go directly via PTE → page cache → disk.

msync() / fsync()
Flush dirty page cache pages to disk.

fsync() → call filesystem’s ->fsync op.

4️⃣ Process & Resource Control
getrusage() / prlimit() / setrlimit()
Kernel: do_prlimit().

Control resource caps (stack size, number of files, locked mem).

Enforced during syscalls like brk(), mlock().

sched_setaffinity()
Kernel updates task’s cpumask.

Scheduler places it only on allowed CPUs.

Links to NUMA placement.

setpriority()/getpriority()
Change scheduler weights (nice values).

5️⃣ Swapping, Reclaim, Migration
swapon() / swapoff()
Add/remove swap devices.

Kernel: init swap cache, mark swap slots.

Pages can then be evicted:

Anon → swap slot.

File-backed → just dropped (reloaded from disk).

Reclaim path (background, not syscall)
kswapd and shrinkers walk LRU (anon/file), reclaim.

Can migrate pages (NUMA, compaction, CMA).

Swap/zram/zswap handle evicted anon.

6️⃣ Where hardware + special features fit
MMU: CPU-side VA→PA via page tables, TLB.

SMMU w/o PASID: device-wide IOVA→PA.

SMMU w/ PASID: per-process VA space (SVM).

Cgroups: charge each page faulted to memory cgroup, enforce limits.

MPAM: hardware partitioning (cache ways, bandwidth). Kernel tags PARTID per cgroup/task for enforcement.

Hugepages/THP: alternative PTE mappings (reduce TLB pressure).

CMA: physically contiguous allocations for DMA.

7️⃣ Unified sequence example
👉 Suppose you malloc(1MB) and write to it:

glibc malloc() calls brk() or mmap().

Kernel creates VMA in mm_struct, no physical memory yet.

First write → CPU TLB miss → page fault.

Kernel allocates physical page via buddy allocator, maps PTE.

Page charged to your memory cgroup.

CPU caches translation in TLB, executes store.

If THP eligible → khugepaged may collapse into 2MB hugepage.

If memory pressure → kswapd may evict anon → zswap/zram/swap.

If device (GPU) bound with PASID → it can also access same VA via SMMU.

MPAM ensures your container only uses its allocated LLC ways / bandwidth.

✅ Final takeaway:

Each syscall (fork, execve, mmap, brk, mlock, madvise, read, swapon, etc.) is basically manipulating kernel objects: task_struct, mm_struct, vm_area_struct, struct page, struct file, page cache, swap cache.

cgroups enforce software policy on these.

MPAM provides hardware knobs to partition/monitor cache and memory bandwidth.

Together, they form the entire Linux memory & process management pipeline.

You said:
Explain with caveats of all. For example, mmap just allocates VMA but not physical memory. It is allocated to one page only when something is written or read. Similarly explain such caveats for all. I am not aware of each one's caveats 
ChatGPT said:
Perfect, this is the right instinct 🙌 — most people memorize syscalls, but the caveats are what make or break when debugging perf, OOM, NUMA, DMA, GPU, or kernel-driver issues. Let’s walk syscall-by-syscall, highlight what really happens vs what you might assume, and the pitfalls.

1️⃣ Process creation / lifecycle
fork()
✅ Creates a new process, but does not copy all memory.

❗ Caveat: uses Copy-On-Write (COW) → parent & child share physical pages until either writes.

Performance surprise: first write after fork can be much slower (page fault + copy).

Important: large-memory processes fork fast, but may stall badly on write.

vfork()
✅ Shares memory with parent until exec.

❗ Caveat: parent is suspended until child execs.

Never access/mod data in child before exec — can corrupt parent.

clone()/clone3()
✅ Flexible thread/process creation.

❗ Caveat: wrong flags → subtle bugs:

CLONE_VM means same mm_struct, so memory is fully shared (threads).

Forgetting CLONE_FILES → each thread has its own fd table (surprising).

Used internally by pthreads.

execve()
✅ Replaces current image with new program.

❗ Caveats:

Old memory (heap, stack, .data) is torn down, but fds remain open (unless O_CLOEXEC).

Memory mapping starts mostly unpopulated → actual file-backed pages brought in lazily on fault.

First access to code/data = page faults.

2️⃣ Memory mapping / allocation
brk() / sbrk()
✅ Expands/shrinks the heap VMA.

❗ Caveat: only creates/extends VMA; no physical page until access.

First touch triggers page fault, physical memory from buddy allocator.

If memory is exhausted, brk() may fail or OOM killer invoked on demand.

mmap()
✅ Creates memory mappings (file or anonymous).

❗ Caveats:

On creation → only a VMA (no physical pages).

Actual pages populated lazily:

Anon → zero page until first write → then alloc page.

File-backed → page cache populated on fault or readahead.

MAP_SHARED vs MAP_PRIVATE matters: write in MAP_PRIVATE = COW page, file unaffected.

With MAP_HUGETLB: must reserve from hugetlbfs pool at creation (can fail if not reserved).

With MAP_ANONYMOUS|MAP_POPULATE: kernel can fault pages in eagerly.

munmap()
✅ Removes mapping and frees resources.

❗ Caveat: does not immediately free file data (dirty file pages may stay cached until reclaim).

mprotect()
✅ Changes permissions.

❗ Caveat: only updates PTEs, does not flush CPU instruction cache. JITs must use mprotect + __clear_cache() to avoid executing stale instructions.

madvise()
✅ Gives hints to kernel.

❗ Caveats:

MADV_DONTNEED: may free clean pages immediately, but dirty ones get written back.

MADV_HUGEPAGE: hint only; kernel may ignore.

MADV_FREE: lazy free — page freed only when memory pressure hits, until then still accessible.

mlock() / munlock()
✅ Pins pages in RAM, prevents swap.

❗ Caveats:

Pages are faulted in immediately (unlike plain mmap).

Counts against RLIMIT_MEMLOCK; default is tiny (64K on many distros).

Too much mlock → OOM if system runs low on memory.

mremap()
✅ Can grow/shrink/move mappings.

❗ Caveat: if move is needed, may copy/migrate pages — expensive.

Moving large THPs may involve splitting → fragmentation overhead.

Shared memory (shmat, shm_open, memfd_create)
✅ Create shared memory objects.

❗ Caveats:

Backed by shmem/tmpfs, which is swappable.

File descriptors/inodes exist even though no disk file.

Memory is allocated lazily, just like mmap.

3️⃣ File + page cache syscalls
open()
✅ Just creates a struct file in kernel.

❗ Caveat: does not touch page cache or disk until read/write/mmap.

read()
✅ Returns file data.

❗ Caveats:

Always goes through page cache.

If data not cached → kernel reads from disk into page cache → then copies to user.

So there are 2 copies: kernel cache + user buffer.

Use O_DIRECT to bypass page cache (still tricky, requires alignment).

write()
✅ Writes user buffer into page cache.

❗ Caveats:

Actual disk write is deferred (writeback).

fsync() / msync() required for persistence.

Large sequential writes may trigger readahead and page write clustering.

mmap(fd)
✅ Maps file into process VA.

❗ Caveats:

No copy → process accesses page cache pages directly.

Multiple processes mapping same file share same cache pages.

Writes with MAP_PRIVATE → COW anon pages; MAP_SHARED → page cache dirtied.

msync() / fsync()
✅ Flush data to storage.

❗ Caveat: msync(MS_ASYNC) only schedules; not guaranteed.

fsync() forces actual disk commit but may be slow.

4️⃣ Process & resource control syscalls
getrusage() / setrlimit() / prlimit()
✅ Resource usage and limits.

❗ Caveats:

Limits are checked lazily at allocation → may fail late.

RLIMIT_AS = limit on VA space, not actual physical RAM.

RLIMIT_MEMLOCK controls mlock, often tiny by default.

sched_setaffinity()
✅ Restricts CPU affinity.

❗ Caveats:

Does not migrate existing memory; pages remain on old NUMA node until autoNUMA migrates.

setpriority()
✅ Changes niceness.

❗ Caveat: relative only, real-time scheduling (SCHED_FIFO/RR) requires sched_setscheduler().

5️⃣ Swap & Reclaim
swapon() / swapoff()
✅ Enable/disable swap devices.

❗ Caveats:

Only anonymous pages use swap.

File-backed pages are never swapped → they can be dropped/reloaded.

Swapoff requires migrating pages back into RAM → may fail if no RAM.

Reclaim path (kswapd, shrinkers)
✅ Frees memory under pressure.

❗ Caveats:

May choose page cache first, then anon.

mlock pages never swapped.

CMA pages are migratable only if movable pages fill them.

6️⃣ Putting it together (examples)
Example 1: malloc → write

malloc(1MB) → mmap() → creates VMA, no pages.

First write → page fault → alloc 1 page (4K/64K) → mapped PTE.

If THP enabled, khugepaged may collapse into 2MB page later.

Caveat: memory not actually allocated until fault, so malloc success ≠ guaranteed RAM.

Example 2: read() vs mmap(fd)

read():

Disk → page cache → copy → user buffer.

Always 2 copies in RAM.

mmap(fd):

Disk → page cache page.

PTE points to same page.

No extra copy.
Caveat: writing to MAP_PRIVATE file mapping = COW new anon page, file unaffected.

Example 3: fork → write

fork() → child shares PTEs.

First write → COW page fault → alloc + copy page.

Caveat: big memory app with lots of writes after fork = huge overhead.

✅ Final Takeaways
Most syscalls are lazy: they create metadata (VMA, file, task), not actual memory/data until first access.

Copy-on-write (fork, MAP_PRIVATE, file-backed mmap) is the biggest hidden cost.

Page cache is always in play for file I/O unless O_DIRECT.

mlock, MAP_HUGETLB, MAP_LOCKED are exceptions: they fault in/pin pages immediately.

execve drops all old mappings but keeps fds unless O_CLOEXEC.

swap only applies to anon, file-backed just dropped.

cgroups charge pages on fault, not on mmap/brk.

MPAM doesn’t change syscalls; it enforces QoS when memory/cache actually accessed.

| read()            | Copy file data into user buffer        | Always through page cache; 2 copies in RAM.       |
| write()           | Copy user buffer into page cache       | Disk write deferred until fsync/msync.            |
| mmap(fd)          | Map file into VA space                 | Process sees page cache pages directly; COW vs SH |

| fsync()           | Sync all file dirty pages              | Can stall until disk commit.                      |

✅ Quick Mental Hooks
Mappings (mmap, brk) = metadata only. Real pages only on page fault.

fork() is cheap; writes after fork are expensive (COW).

read() = copy from page cache; mmap(fd) = map page cache directly.

mlock = immediate allocation + pinning; use sparingly.

swap only applies to anonymous memory. File-backed can be dropped.

execve = new mm_struct, lazy population; only fds survive.

Legend (icons & terms)
VA = virtual address (process address).

PA = physical address (PFN * PAGE_SIZE).

IOVA = device-visible address (translated by IOMMU).

VMA = struct vm_area_struct (kernel region descriptor).

mm = struct mm_struct (process address space).

PTE/PMD/PGD = page-table entries (levels).

struct page = kernel meta for a physical page frame.

Buddy = page-frame allocator used for alloc_pages().

Page cache = file-backed pages (address_space).

THP/MTHP/HugeTLB = different hugepage mechanisms.

CMA = Contiguous Memory Allocator (driver API for contiguous pages).

dma-buf = cross-driver buffer sharing (fd backed by struct dma_buf).

SMMU/IOMMU = device MMU; SMMUv3 = ARM variant.

PASID = Process Address Space ID (for SVM).

PRI = Page Request Interface (device-driven page fault handling).

Stall mode = device stalls on missing mapping.

zram/zswap = compressed RAM swap and swap cache.

cgroups = Linux resource control groups.

MPAM = ARM Memory Partitioning & Monitoring (hardware QoS).

vnode/dentry/inode = VFS structures.

vmalloc/vmap/fixmap = kernel virtual mapping helpers.

struct file / fd = userspace handle to kernel object.

MASTER LAYERS — single-page textual map
[ User Processes (per-process) ]
  -> syscalls: fork/clone/execve/open/read/write/mmap/brk/madvise/mlock/ioctl/munmap/munlock
  -> each process: mm_struct (VMAs) | fd table -> struct file* -> inode/dentry

  VMA types:
    - anon VMA (brk/mmap MAP_ANON, stack) -> anon pages
    - file-backed VMA (mmap(fd), code/data from execve) -> page cache pages
    - tmpfs/shmem (memfd_create, /dev/shm) -> file-backed in page cache (dummy inode)
    - hugetlbfs/MAP_HUGETLB -> HugeTLB pages (pinned)
    - THP/MTHP promoted anon/shmem -> folio-sized contiguous PFNs

[ Kernel Virtual Layer (global) ]
  - linear/direct map (VA = phys + PAGE_OFFSET) -> gives kernel VA for any PFN
  - vmalloc/vmap area -> virtually contiguous kernel mappings backed by scattered PFNs
  - fixmap area -> reserved fixed-kernel mappings
  - kernel modules -> built-in (contiguous image) or LKM (vmalloc area)

[ Kernel Memory Structures ]
  - mm_struct -> list of VMAs
  - vm_area_struct -> flags (shared/private, anon/file, PROT)
  - page tables -> PGD/PUD/PMD/PTE (in RAM, hw-walker reads)
  - struct page -> per-physical-page metadata
  - page cache (address_space) -> maps file offsets to struct page

[ Allocators & Caches ]
  - Buddy allocator -> alloc_pages() (source of physical pages)
  - Slab/SLUB/SLOB -> kmalloc / small kernel objects (backed by buddy)
  - vmalloc/vmap -> uses page lists + mapping into kernel VA
  - CMA -> reserved contiguous pool for DMA (allocatable via DMA APIs)
  - zsmalloc/zbud/z3fold -> allocators used by zram/zswap for compressed objects

[ Swap & Compression Tier ]
  - zram (block device) -> compressed page blobs stored in RAM (zsmalloc)
  - zswap -> compressed in-RAM cache in front of disk swap (zbud-like packing)
  - swap device (disk/SSD) -> swap slots (on-disk)

[ IOMMU / Device Side ]
  - Devices DMA using IOVA addresses.
  - IOMMU/SMMU -> translate IOVA -> PA (page tables in RAM; IOTLB caches entries)
  - Without PASID: one IOVA context per device/stream.
  - With PASID: multiple contexts per device -> SVM (device sees per-process VA)
  - ATS/ATC -> device can query or cache translations
  - PRI -> device-side page requests to kernel (on-demand resolution)
  - DMA mapping APIs: dma_map_sg(), dma_unmap_sg(), dma_alloc_coherent(), dma_buf_attach/map

[ Controls & Monitoring ]
  - cgroups -> memory/cpu/io limits, memory charging on page faults
  - MPAM (hardware) -> cache way partitioning, bandwidth throttling (OS maps PARTID)
  - sysfs/debugfs/procfs -> visibility and control interfaces
DETAILED FLOWS (sequence + kernel internals + caveats)
Below are canonical flows — read them as call sequences with objects touched. Each step includes short caveat / why it matters.

1) malloc(size) → user writes to buffer (typical heap allocation)
User: malloc(1<<20) then buffer[i] = 0;

Sequence

malloc() (glibc) decides to use brk() or mmap() (large alloc).

Kernel: if brk(), the libc call expands heap VMA via brk(): kernel do_brk() sets mm->brk VMA. Caveat: brk() expands VMA only; no physical allocation yet.

On first write to the page: CPU does store → TLB miss → page fault.

Kernel do_page_fault() locates VMA (anon), calls handle_mm_fault().

This code allocates a physical page via alloc_page() (buddy), sets up struct page, creates PTE mapping, updates struct page->mapping (anon), increments cgroup memory charge.

Caveat: allocation occurs on first touch. malloc() success ≠ guaranteed physical memory.

CPU resumes; page cached in CPU caches; mapping in CPU TLB.

If THP enabled & page cluster eligible, later khugepaged may collapse contiguous pages into a THP folio (2MB) by compaction/migration.

Caveat: THP promotion can fail under fragmentation. THP uses compaction; compaction may trigger page migrations and CPU overhead.

Objects touched: mm_struct -> vm_area_struct -> page tables -> struct page -> buddy allocator -> cgroups charged.

2) open(path); read(fd, buf, n) (file I/O) vs mmap(fd)
Open+Read Flow

open() → VFS path lookup → returns struct file* pointing to inode/dentry. (No pages yet.)

read() → vfs_read() → generic file read.

Kernel checks page cache (address_space). If page present → copy_to_user from page cache.

If page not present → submits block I/O → read block into page cache (alloc a struct page from buddy), fill, then copy to user.

Copies: disk → page cache → user buffer (two copies). Caveat: overhead vs mmap.

fsync() flushes dirty pages to disk via writeback.

mmap(fd) Flow

mmap(fd) → do_mmap() creates a file-backed VMA (vm_area_struct) referencing inode/address_space. No pages allocated.

On access: page fault → kern filemap_fault() finds page in page cache or reads from disk into page cache. Then map PTE to that page (no duplicate copy).

Caveat: MAP_PRIVATE results in COW on write (kernel creates new anon page); MAP_SHARED updates page cache and dirties for writeback.

Objects touched: inode/address_space (page cache) → struct page entries, block layer.

3) execve(path, argv, envp) (how binary maps are set up)
Sequence

execve() syscall → do_execveat_common() selects binary loader (binfmt_elf).

Kernel opens the ELF file (inode), reads program headers.

Kernel allocates a new mm_struct (old mm destroyed or replaced) with VMAs for:

PT_LOAD segments: file-backed VMAs (text, rodata, data) with correct offsets/perms (MAP_PRIVATE usually).

bss and heap: anon VMAs (zero-filled).

stack: anon VMA.

VDSO: special kernel-provided mapping (read-only user-exec).

Registers (PC, SP) set to entry point/stack with argv/env/auxv.

On first execution/access, file-backed pages brought in via page faults (page cache), anon pages allocated via buddy.
Caveats

execve does not pre-populate pages (unless MAP_POPULATE used). These are lazily faulted.

O_CLOEXEC controls whether fds survive exec.

Objects touched: inode, address_space (page cache), new mm_struct, VMAs, page table population on demands.

4) fork() followed by child write (COW behavior)
Sequence

fork() → do_fork() creates child task_struct. mm_struct is shared between parent and child but pages flagged COW.

Both processes share the same PTEs (read-only) referencing same struct page frames.

Child writes → page fault → kernel sees COW fault: alloc new page (alloc_page from buddy), copy contents copy_page, update child PTE to new page, clear COW. Parent still points to original.
Caveats

Heavy forking + writing large memory leads to big overhead (copy cost, time, memory spike). Use vfork()+exec or posix_spawn when possible.

COW interacts with THP: writing into a THP may cause splitting.

5) mmap() with MAP_ANONYMOUS | MAP_SHARED (shared anonymous)
Creates a shared anon VMA; pages faulted in on touch become struct page with anon mapping and can be shared with other processes that mmap same memfd or via shm_open().

Caveat: anon pages are swappable; they are not automatically visible in page cache as file-backed pages are. To share across unrelated processes, use shmem/memfd_create().

6) memfd_create() / tmpfs / shmem flow (shared RAM-backed file)
Sequence

memfd_create("name", flags) → shmem_file_setup() creates an anonymous inode and file in tmpfs with an address_space and returns a fd.

mmap(fd, MAP_SHARED) by multiple processes -> same inode->i_mapping page cache. Pages faulted in are put into page cache and shared between processes.

Exportable via dma-buf for devices or passed via SCM_RIGHTS to other processes.
Caveat

Although backed by page cache, tmpfs contents are still swappable and live in RAM until eviction.

7) mlock() / mlockall() (pinning pages)
Sequence

mlock(addr, len) marks the VMA/pages as VM_LOCKED and faults in the pages immediately (allocates from buddy).

Pages become unevictable (not swapped). Kernel increments memlock usage and enforces RLIMIT_MEMLOCK.
Caveats

Excessive lock usage can cause OOM for others. Use judiciously; set RLIMIT_MEMLOCK or use mlock only for small critical regions (crypto keys, RT).

8) madvise() semantics & THP hints
MADV_HUGEPAGE / MADV_NOHUGEPAGE are only hints; kernel may ignore depending on fragmentation and THP settings.

MADV_DONTNEED frees clean pages; MADV_FREE marks pages lazily free (still readable until reclaimed).
Caveat: MADV_DONTNEED on file-backed mappings may drop pages from page cache; next access reloads from disk.

9) Huge pages: THP, MTHP, HugeTLB, static hugepages, and caveats
HugeTLB (hugetlbfs / MAP_HUGETLB): pages reserved/pinned at boot or via sysctl; allocated from a hugepage pool; not swappable, not migratable. Use when guaranteed contiguous pinned large pages required. Caveat: inflexible; if not reserved, allocation fails.

THP (Transparent Huge Pages): kernel may promote multiple base pages into a contiguous huge folio (e.g., 2M). THP is transparent to apps, migratable and splittable. Caveats: promotion requires contiguous PFNs (compaction); under fragmentation may fail; splitting has overhead.

MTHP (multi-size THP): like THP with other sizes (64K, 512K...). Eases promotion. Caveat: depends on kernel config/hardware.

Static hugepage reservation: used when big contiguous region required; may be used for devices too but usually for user apps that ask explicitly.

Relation to CMA: CMA also offers physically contiguous memory, but specifically as a kernel reserved pool for DMA. Huge pages & CMA both produce physically contiguous PFNs but have different semantics (CMA is typically movable until pinned by device, THP is opportunistic for CPU TLB efficiency, HugeTLB is pinned/explicit).

10) Device DMA & dma_map_sg() / dma_alloc_coherent() / IOMMU
Scatter-Gather and DMA Flow

Driver builds sglist from pages (e.g., from shmem or pages allocated via alloc_pages/CMA).

dma_map_sg(dev, sg, nents, dir):

If IOMMU present, this creates IOMMU mappings (IOVA→PA) and returns sg entries with sg_dma_address(), sg_dma_len().

If no IOMMU, driver gets physical addresses or must ensure physical contiguity (CMA) or device SG capability.

Program device with SG list; device DMAs using IOVA/physical addresses.

dma_unmap_sg() tears down mapping (or reuses).
Coherent mappings: dma_alloc_coherent() returns region that is CPU/device coherent (no explicit sync needed).
Caveat: Cache maintenance & direction flags are critical. Improper sync -> data corruption.

11) dma-buf export/import (fd-based buffer sharing)
Exporter (driver)

Alloc buffer (shmem / CMA / device-private).

dma_buf_export() creates struct dma_buf and associated struct file (anonymous inode).

dma_buf_fd(dmabuf, flags) returns an fd to userspace. No /dev/ node; fd is an anon inode (visible under /proc/<pid>/fd as anon_inode:[dmabuf]).

Userspace or importer

Pass fd across processes via SCM_RIGHTS or hand to other APIs (EGL, DRM).

Importer kernel side: dma_buf_get(fd) -> dma_buf_attach(dmabuf, dev) -> dma_buf_map_attachment(att, dir):

This triggers exporter .map_dma_buf() to produce sg_table of pages (or device addresses).

dma_map_sg() or IOMMU mapping is done for importer dev.

Program device; on finish, call dma_buf_unmap_attachment() and dma_buf_detach(); drop struct dma_buf ref with dma_buf_put().

Lifetime: buffer freed only when last fd/ref/attachment is gone. Exporter process may die; buffer persists while refs exist. Caveat: exporter choice (shmem vs CMA) determines swappability/contiguity.

12) CMA allocation (driver wants contiguous physical memory)
Sequence

Driver calls dma_alloc_attrs() or CMA-specific API to request contiguous memory of order N.

Kernel tries to carve from CMA pool; if not available, may attempt compaction of movable pages from regular memory.

Upon success, driver receives contiguous PFNs — can map them to device IOVA (no scatter-gather needed).
Caveats

CMA pools are finite and reserved at boot or via CMA region. Overuse can starve other subsystems. CMA pages are typically marked as movable until pinned by device; once pinned, not migratable/swapable.

13) zram and zswap page eviction internals
zram: a block device; when used as swap target (swapon /dev/zram0) swapped-out pages are compressed (zsmalloc) and stored in RAM as compression blobs. No physical contiguity required. Later decompressed on swap-in.

zswap: front-end for swap: compress pages and keep in RAM cache (zbud/z3fold). On eviction from zswap, write to real swap device. Caveat: compressed caches add CPU decompression overhead but reduce disk I/O and latency.

14) IOMMU/SMMUv3 internals, PASID & SVM
IOMMU page tables are regular pages in RAM allocated by kernel (via iommu driver). SMMU (ARM) uses stream tables and context descriptors pointing at page tables.

Without PASID: device uses a single IOVA domain. Driver maps buffers into that domain by programmatically creating IOMMU entries (dma_map_sg).

With PASID: kernel sets up PASID table entries where each PASID points to the appropriate per-process PGD or context descriptor. Device memory requests tagged with PASID cause SMMU to use that process’s page tables → SVM (device and CPU share VA space).

PRI vs Stall:

Stall: IOMMU fault stalls device until kernel fixes mapping (interrupt-driven).

PRI (Page Request Interface): device can issue a page request message; kernel handles page-in/migration on demand and resumes device — needed for low-latency demand paging by devices.

ATS/ATC: device can request translations from IOMMU (ATS), cache in ATC (device TLB). Kernel must manage invalidations.
Caveat: SVM requires hardware support (PASID, PRI), kernel SVA bindings (iommu_sva_bind_device()), MMU notifiers, and correct invalidations to avoid stale mappings.

15) cgroups (memory) and interaction with page faulting
Memory cgroup accounts pages when pages are faulted in / charged. So mmap() or brk() alone does not charge; first touch does. malloc() being successful doesn’t mean cgroup charge succeeded.

cgroups can trigger per-group OOM or throttling/pressure on page faults.
Caveat: mis-accounted pages can trigger OOM in the cgroup unexpectedly on first-touch.

16) MPAM (hardware) — where it hooks
MPAM operates at cache/memory hardware level. OS assigns PARTID to tasks/streams; hardware enforces cache way partitioning and memory bandwidth limits.

Linux integrates via resctrl/platform drivers and maps cgroup policies to PARTID. Kernel tags device streams/SMMU contexts with PARTID for DMA QoS.
Caveat: MPAM affects runtime performance but does not change memory semantics (pages still allocated the same way); need platform support + kernel driver.

17) Kernel mapping helpers: vmalloc / vmap / fixmap / modules
vmalloc() allocates scattered PFNs and maps them into a virtually contiguous kernel VA range using vmap() under the hood. Good for module text/data (LKM). Caveat: vmalloc memory is not contiguous physically and is not directly DMA-able; must use sg lists or map per-page via IOMMU.

fixmap is small set of fixed kernel VA slots for special use (early init, page table temporary mappings).

Kernel modules loaded at runtime use module_alloc() (vmalloc area) for virtually contiguous kernel address space. Built-in kernel code is loaded contiguously at boot (physically contiguous). Caveat: kernel code must be VA contiguous; physical contiguity not required.

Extra: Page-table & walker storage summary (CPU vs IOMMU)
CPU page tables: pages allocated by buddy; CR3/TTBR points to top-level; HW walker reads PUD/PMD/PTE pages from RAM on TLB miss. Results cached in CPU TLB. Kernel must maintain page tables on mm changes, use mmu_notifier to inform devices.

IOMMU tables: allocated in RAM; IOMMU STBR/ContextDescriptor points to them. IOMMU walker reads from RAM into IOTLB. With PASID, entries point at per-process page tables or translations.

Quick Debug/Perf checklist (caveats & what to look for)
malloc() success but OOM on use? — because pages allocated on fault, cgroup or overall memory pressure may cause failure on first touch.

fork() slow? — COW page copying cost on writes; use posix_spawn / vfork for exec-only children.

mmap() vs read(): mmap avoids copy but MAP_PRIVATE implies COW on write; mmap + write may allocate new pages.

DMA failures / perf issues: check dma_map_sg return segments, IOMMU maps, cache-syncs, driver using correct dma_sync_*, and avoid long-term GUP pins.

SMMU churn (map/unmap spikes): persistent IOVA allocator + reuse mappings; avoid repeated map/unmap in hot paths. Use DMA-BUF with persistent attachments.

Hugepage/THP behavior: use madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) or configure THP; THP promotion may fail under fragmentation — MTHP may help.

zram/zswap memory patterns: compressed pages increase CPU; zswap reduces disk writes; zram consumes RAM for compressed blobs (zsmalloc).

CMA starvation: ensure drivers don’t greedily consume CMA pool; use appropriate heaps or mempools for devices like GPU.

SVM issues: require PASID + PRI support (IOMMU & device). If missing, drivers must pin and map or rely on dma-buf.

TL;DR (one-paragraph executive summary)
Syscalls (mmap, brk, execve, fork, open, read, madvise, mlock, etc.) generally create kernel metadata (VMAs, file handles) — physical pages are created on first touch, not at syscall time (except mlock/MAP_POPULATE/hugetlb allocation).

Allocators: buddy supplies physical pages used by struct page; slab/slub for kernel objects; vmalloc/vmap for virtually contiguous kernel VA.

File data lives in the page cache (address_space) which backs file-backed VMAs and is shared among processes; shmem/tmpfs creates dummy inodes to anchor shared RAM-backed pages and to make them fd/mmap-shareable.

Devices need IOVA addresses; IOMMU (SMMUv3) translates IOVA→PA; PASID+PRI enable SVM so device can use process VA directly.

dma-buf exports buffer as an fd (anon inode) to share memory across drivers/ processes; the kernel handles attachments/mappings and lifetime beyond exporter process.

CMA/THP/HugeTLB all can give physically contiguous PFNs, but for different semantics: CMA for device DMA, THP for transparent TLB perf, HugeTLB for pinned app-requested huge pages.

zram/zswap are compressed-RAM swap variants (zram as a block device, zswap as a cache fronting swap) — they pack compressed pages in RAM with zsmalloc/zbud.

cgroups are software policy/accounting; MPAM is hardware QoS for caches/bandwidth; combine them for enforced resource partitioning.

Great questions — you’re asking about the devm_ “device-managed”* helpers in the Linux kernel (e.g., devm_kzalloc(), devm_dma_alloc_coherent()), how they differ from the normal APIs, what the internals are, what other devm_* families exist, and what “lifespan” they follow.

Below is a clear, practical guide.

What “device-managed” (devm_*) means
Goal: make driver probe() code simpler and leak-free.

Idea: when you allocate something with a devm_* helper, the kernel records that allocation on the device’s devres list.
When the driver is unbound from that device (probe fails, hot-unplug, module unload, remove), the core automatically calls the matching free/unregister in LIFO order.

Not tied to userspace fds, PIDs, or threads. The lifetime is tied to the struct device ↔ bound driver relationship.

So: devm = “free it automatically when the device/driver goes away.”

The two you asked about
devm_kzalloc(struct device *dev, size_t size, gfp_t gfp)
Same as kzalloc() (zeroed memory), but registered in the device’s devres list.

On unbind/remove, the core will kfree() it for you.

Use when the memory is owned by the driver and does not need to outlive the driver’s binding.

devm_dma_alloc_coherent(struct device *dev, size_t size, dma_addr_t *dma_handle, gfp_t gfp)
Same as dma_alloc_coherent() (CPU/Device-coherent buffer; IOMMU/attrs handled), but registered to be auto-freed with dma_free_coherent() on unbind.

Returns CPU pointer and sets *dma_handle to the DMA/IOVA address.

Use for device-private coherent DMA buffers whose lifetime == device binding.

Key difference vs the non-devm versions: identical semantics for the resource itself, but automatic cleanup tied to the device.

Internals (how devm_* is implemented)
Backed by the devres core (drivers/base/devres.c).

Each struct device has an internal stack/list of resources.

A devm helper typically does:

Allocate the resource (e.g., kmalloc, dma_alloc_coherent, ioremap, …)

Create a small devres node that stores (pointer, size, release-callback)

Push that node on the device’s devres stack.

On driver unbind (probe error path, remove(), hot-unplug, or module unload), the core pops and calls each resource’s release callback (free/unregister), reverse order of allocation (LIFO).

There is also devm_add_action() / devm_add_action_or_reset() to register custom cleanup lambdas.

Lifespan in one line: from successful allocation in probe() until driver is unbound from that struct device.

What devm_* is not
Not tied to process/thread/fd lifetimes. (Kernel code only.)

Not appropriate if the allocated object must outlive driver unbind (e.g., a buffer handed to a core that continues after device removal).

Not magic for streaming DMA mappings (dma_map_*/dma_unmap_* are not devm-managed; you manage those around each transfer).

Common devm_* families you’ll encounter (by subsystem)
Memory / MM / IO

devm_kmalloc/kzalloc/kcalloc/kmalloc_array/kmemdup/kvzalloc

devm_get_free_pages() (rare)

devm_ioremap(), devm_ioremap_resource(), devm_platform_ioremap_resource()

devm_request_mem_region() / devm_release_mem_region()

DMA / IOMMU

devm_dma_alloc_coherent() (and devm_dma_alloc_attrs() on some trees)

devm_dmam_alloc_coherent() (older naming on some platforms)

(Streaming DMA mappings are not devm; use dma_map_*/dma_unmap_* per transfer.)

Interrupts & GPIO

devm_request_irq(), devm_request_threaded_irq()

devm_gpio_request_one(), devm_gpiod_* family

Clocks, Regulators, Power

devm_clk_get() / devm_clk_put() (auto-put)

devm_regulator_get() / auto-put

devm_pm_runtime_enable() (paired disable on cleanup)

Device registration wrappers

devm_input_allocate_device() + devm_input_register_device()

devm_hwmon_device_register_with_info()

devm_led_classdev_register()

devm_watchdog_register_device()

devm_power_supply_register()

devm_snd_soc_register_component(), etc.

devm_of_platform_populate() (creates child devices; auto cleanup)

Misc

devm_kasprintf(), devm_kstrdup(), devm_bitmap_zalloc()

devm_add_action() / devm_add_action_or_reset() (custom cleanup hook)

When to use devm_* vs not — checklist
Use devm_* when:

Allocation happens in probe() and you want automatic cleanup on probe failure or device removal.

The object belongs to the device and won’t outlive the binding (e.g., MMIO remap, coherent DMA buffer for the controller, IRQ, regulator/clk handles).

Avoid devm_* when:

The object must persist after unbind (handed to shared core, global caches, cross-device pool).
→ Either manage manually or use a devm_*_register() API that also unregisters at unbind.

You need fine control over free timing (e.g., must free before other resources). devm frees in reverse-alloc order at unbind, not earlier.

The memory is exposed to userspace with a lifetime not tied to the device (e.g., persistent char device state). Consider explicit refcounting.

Caution mixing: Don’t free a devm allocation manually — double free. Likewise, don’t devm-free something allocated without devm.

Tiny, realistic example
Unmanaged (manual cleanup)
static int my_probe(struct platform_device *pdev)
{
    struct mydev *m = kzalloc(sizeof(*m), GFP_KERNEL);
    void __iomem *base = devm_ioremap_resource(&pdev->dev, res); // devm OK here
    void *buf;

    if (!m) return -ENOMEM;

    buf = dma_alloc_coherent(&pdev->dev, SZ_64K, &m->dma, GFP_KERNEL);
    if (!buf) { kfree(m); return -ENOMEM; }

    /* on any error from now on, you must remember to dma_free_coherent() and kfree() ... */
    return 0;
}

static int my_remove(struct platform_device *pdev)
{
    /* must remember to free both: */
    dma_free_coherent(&pdev->dev, SZ_64K, m->buf, m->dma);
    kfree(m);
    return 0;
}
Managed (idiomatic)
static int my_probe(struct platform_device *pdev)
{
    struct device *dev = &pdev->dev;

    struct mydev *m = devm_kzalloc(dev, sizeof(*m), GFP_KERNEL);
    if (!m) return -ENOMEM;

    m->base = devm_platform_ioremap_resource(pdev, 0);   // auto iounmap
    if (IS_ERR(m->base)) return PTR_ERR(m->base);

    m->buf = devm_dma_alloc_coherent(dev, SZ_64K, &m->dma, GFP_KERNEL);
    if (!m->buf) return -ENOMEM;

    if (devm_request_irq(dev, irq, my_isr, 0, dev_name(dev), m)) // auto free_irq
        return -EINVAL;

    /* if anything fails later, or on device removal, everything above is auto-cleaned */
    return 0;
}
Relationship to everything else we discussed
Not related to fds/user processes. devm is purely kernel-side and bound to the struct device lifecycle.

DMA/IOMMU: devm_dma_alloc_coherent() ties the coherent buffer to device lifetime; streaming DMA still uses dma_map_*/dma_unmap_* around each I/O. PASID/SVM doesn’t change devm semantics.

Page allocators: under the hood, devm helpers still allocate via the usual mechanisms (kmalloc/slab, buddy pages, IOMMU/DMA APIs). devm just records a free-callback.

CMA / THP / HugeTLB: devm doesn’t change memory type. If devm_dma_alloc_coherent() ends up backed by CMA/IOMMU depends on arch and device DMA ops — not on devm itself.

VFS / page cache / tmpfs: unrelated. devm doesn’t touch userspace mappings; it manages driver-internal resources (MMIO mappings, DMA buffers, IRQs, clks, regs…).

Devm lifespan (precise)
Starts when the devm_* call succeeds in probe() (or later while bound).

Ends automatically when:

probe() fails after that point (rollback unwinds and frees), or

the device is removed/unbound (hot-plug detach, driver unload), which triggers devres release for that struct device.

Not tied to user opens/closes of your /dev/* node. Your file ops must not assume devm frees on last fd close — it frees on driver unbind.

Quick pitfalls & gotchas
Handing devm memory to another core that frees it: can double-free. Either use that core’s devm_*_register variant or manage lifetime manually.

Ordering: If you need a particular free order, allocate in the opposite order (LIFO) or use explicit actions (devm_add_action_or_reset()).

Long-lived registries: Objects registered globally (e.g., sysfs groups not attached to dev, debugfs entries without devm helpers) need explicit unregister if they can outlive the device; prefer devm_device_add_group() / devm_debugfs_* where available.

TL;DR
devm_* helpers = same resource, automatic cleanup on device unbind.

Lifespan is device/driver binding, not process/fd.

Use devm in probe() for anything that should die when the device goes away (MMIO maps, coherent buffers, IRQs, clks, regulators, registrations that have devm variants).

Avoid devm if the object must persist beyond the driver’s lifetime or has a different owner.

Good Q ⚡ — these are fundamental Linux MM terms that often confuse even experienced kernel devs. Let’s break them one by one and tie them to everything we’ve already covered (pages, struct page, buddy, THP, etc).

1️⃣ PFN vs PTE
PFN (Page Frame Number)
A physical page index.

If page size = 4 KB, then:

PFN = PhysicalAddress / 4096
PFN is just the numbered slot of a page frame in RAM.

Kernel keeps a struct page[] array (the memmap) indexed by PFN.

So PFN is the “ID” of a physical page.

👉 Example: Physical address 0x12345000, page size 4K → PFN = 0x12345.
👉 When kernel allocates a page via buddy, it really returns a PFN + maps it to struct page.

PTE (Page Table Entry)
An entry in a process’s page table.

Maps a virtual page → physical frame (PFN).

Contains:

PFN (frame number to use for translation).

Flags (present, RW, user/kernel, accessed/dirty, exec, cache attrs, etc).

👉 PTE = VA → (PFN + permission bits).
👉 PFN = pure physical index, used inside PTE.

So:

PFN = index of a physical page.

PTE = page table entry; contains PFN + flags, used by MMU for VA→PA.

2️⃣ CONFIG_FLATMEM vs CONFIG_SPARSEMEM
These are kernel memory model configs (see mm/Kconfig).

CONFIG_FLATMEM
Old/simple model.

Assumes physically contiguous memmap[] array (one big struct page array).

PFN → struct page is simple linear:

struct page *p = mem_map + PFN;
Works only if memory is (mostly) contiguous with few holes.

Used by small systems, embedded.

CONFIG_SPARSEMEM
Modern model.

Allows memory with holes or NUMA nodes spread sparsely in phys addr space.

Memory divided into sections (e.g., 128MB or 1GB granularity, arch-dependent).

Each section has its own struct page[] array (the memmap).

PFN → struct page requires first finding the section, then offset within section.

👉 Needed for:

Hotplug memory (online/offline sections).

Very large memory (64-bit servers, >TB RAM).

ARM/NUMA systems with discontiguous physical RAM.

3️⃣ What is a "Section" in memory model?
A chunk of physical memory in SPARSEMEM model.

Size = architecture-defined (commonly 128 MB or 1 GB).

Each section has its own memmap (struct page array).

Allows memory hotplug: add/remove whole sections.

So: section = bookkeeping unit in SPARSEMEM.

4️⃣ Section memmap (struct page mapping per section)
The memmap = array of struct page structures describing every PFN.

In FLATMEM: single big array.

In SPARSEMEM: per-section memmap allocated only for present sections.

Kernel stores a struct mem_section for each section, with pointer to its memmap.

So:

memmap = struct page[] array.

section memmap = struct page[] for one memory section.

🔄 Connecting to what we discussed earlier
PFN: pure ID of physical frame.

PTE: actual VA→PFN mapping (in process page tables or kernel page tables).

struct page (memmap) → metadata per PFN (refcount, LRU, mapping, anon/file).

CONFIG_FLATMEM → one big contiguous memmap.

CONFIG_SPARSEMEM → split per section, needed for hotplug/NUMA/discontiguous.

Sections: hotplug unit; allows online_pages()/offline_pages() calls.

When buddy allocator runs → it’s carving PFNs from struct page array (memmap).

When THP promotes → it merges multiple contiguous PFNs.

When CMA allocates → it reserves contiguous PFNs (from memmap).

When SMMU maps → it translates IOVA → PFN.

When MPAM monitors → it monitors cache/bandwidth per PFN ranges.

✅ Summary Table

Term	Meaning	Role in MM pipeline
PFN	Page Frame Number = index of physical page	Used inside PTEs; indexes into struct page[]
PTE	Page Table Entry	Maps VA page → PFN + perms
struct page	Metadata for a PFN	Refcount, flags, mapping, LRU, zone
FLATMEM	Simple model, single contiguous memmap[]	No hotplug, assumes dense RAM
SPARSEMEM	Section-based memmap	Supports discontig RAM, NUMA, hotplug
Section	Fixed-size chunk of PFNs (128MB/1GB)	Bookkeeping unit in SPARSEMEM
Section memmap	struct page[] for PFNs in that section	Allocated only if section is present

What is mapcount and refcount ? Is it related to mmap ? What if page is not mapped to user space ? So map count is zero can it be swapped out or what ? Where is it used and what are implications 
ChatGPT said:
Excellent ⚡ — now we’re deep in the per-page accounting guts of Linux.
You’ve touched two critical counters in struct page: mapcount and refcount. Let’s unpack them thoroughly, relate them to mmap(), page cache, swap, and all our previous discussions.

1️⃣ struct page recap
Every physical page frame (PFN) has a struct page describing it. Among many fields:

struct page {
    atomic_t _refcount;      // reference count
    atomic_t _mapcount;      // number of PTEs mapping this page
    struct address_space *mapping;  // file (if file-backed)
    ...
};
refcount (_refcount) = how many active references to this page exist (kernel-wide).

mapcount (_mapcount) = how many PTEs (virtual mappings) point to this page.

They track different but related lifetimes.

2️⃣ Page refcount
Increments when something holds a pointer to this page:

When it’s in page cache.

When it’s mapped into a process.

When get_page() is called by kernel subsystems.

When it’s pinned via get_user_pages() (e.g., RDMA, dma-buf).

Decremented when references are dropped.

When refcount goes to zero → page can be freed back to buddy allocator.

So: refcount = “is this page in use at all?”

3️⃣ Page mapcount
Increments per PTE mapping:

Each process mapping page (via mmap) increments mapcount.

Fork with COW increments mapcount for shared PTEs.

Shared mappings increment mapcount across multiple VMAs.

Zero mapcount means:

No user-space PTE points to this page.

But page may still be in page cache (file-backed) or pinned (refcount > 0).

So: mapcount = “is this page currently mapped into any process’s VA space?”

4️⃣ Relation to mmap()
mmap(fd) creates a VMA.

On page fault → kernel finds page (page cache/anon), inserts a PTE mapping → increments mapcount.

If multiple processes mmap the same file → each inserted PTE increments mapcount.

Anonymous pages (heap/stack, MAP_ANON):

Mapcount goes up when mapped, down when unmapped/freed.

If mapcount hits 0, they become candidates for swap.

5️⃣ What if page is not mapped (mapcount=0)?
Case 1: File-backed page
Even if mapcount=0, page may still be cached in page cache (refcount > 0).

Kernel can drop it anytime (clean) or writeback+drop (dirty).

No mapping doesn’t mean freed — it can be reused later if remapped.

Case 2: Anonymous page
If mapcount=0 (unmapped, e.g., process exited), and no other refcount → page freed.

If mapcount=0 but refcount > 0 (e.g., pinned for I/O), page can’t be swapped or freed until refcount drops.

6️⃣ Swapping rules
Anonymous pages:

If mapcount=0 → candidate for reclaim (free).

If mapcount>0 (still mapped) but inactive → can be swapped out (PTE replaced with swap entry).

Must not be pinned (get_user_pages) or locked (mlock).

File-backed pages:

If mapcount=0 → can be dropped from cache (since it can be faulted back in).

If mapped (mapcount>0) but cold → can be unmapped (PTE zapped) and later refaulted.

7️⃣ Where they are used
refcount:

Determines physical page lifetime (when to free back to buddy).

Critical for avoiding use-after-free (refcount bugs = kernel crashes).

mapcount:

Used in page reclaim:

Pages with mapcount=0 easier to reclaim.

Higher mapcount (shared libs, COW after fork) → expensive to reclaim.

Used in rmap (reverse mapping) to track which VMAs map a page.

Helps THP splitting (need to know how many PTEs map the hugepage).

8️⃣ Implications / Caveats
Pinned pages (RDMA/dma-buf): refcount high, mapcount can be 0 → page can’t be swapped. This is why long-term GUP pins are dangerous (they block compaction, CMA, migration).

High mapcount pages (like libc shared across 1000 processes) → kernel avoids reclaiming them (too costly to unmap everywhere).

Anonymous memory + swap: mapcount=0 is a natural reclaim candidate.

File cache: refcount>0 ensures page stays in cache even if not mapped.

✅ Summary Table
Counter	What it counts	When 0	Reclaim/Swap implications
refcount	Kernel-wide references to page (cache, mappings, pins, GUP)	Page is freeable to buddy	Must be 0 to free to buddy
mapcount	PTE mappings (how many VMAs point to page)	No process maps it	Mapcount=0 anon pages can be swapped/freed; file pages can stay cached
🔗 Back to our discussions:

mmap creates VMAs, only faults pages in on access → increments mapcount.

fork() COW → shared mapcount across PTEs until write.

mlock prevents swapping regardless of mapcount.

dma-buf with GUP pins → refcount up, mapcount maybe 0, prevents migration → interacts with CMA/THP.

kswapd uses mapcount to decide reclaim pressure.

MPAM works at physical cache/bandwidth level, not aware of mapcount directly but impacted by how much gets faulted.

🔥 Excellent — now we’re going into the deep layout of Linux physical memory model. These are the bookkeeping layers under everything we’ve been discussing (PFNs, struct page, refcount/mapcount, buddy allocator, THP, CMA, NUMA, etc). Let me explain carefully.

1️⃣ Why is mem_section[] 2D?
In SPARSEMEM model, Linux divides physical memory into sections (fixed size, e.g., 128MB or 1GB, depending on CONFIG_SPARSEMEM_EXTREME & arch).

Each section has metadata (struct mem_section).

Instead of one big linear array, Linux defines:

struct mem_section *mem_section[NR_SECTION_ROOTS][SECTIONS_PER_ROOT];
That is effectively 2D:

Outer index = "section root" (a group of sections).

Inner index = section within that root.

👉 Reason: scaling to very large PFN ranges without wasting memory.

Old flat array would waste RAM if address space is huge but memory sparse.

2D lets kernel allocate metadata only for sections that exist.

2️⃣ What does struct mem_section contain?
Each section represents a contiguous PFN range (e.g., 128MB worth of pages).
struct mem_section holds:

Flags (present, online, valid, device, etc).

Link to the section’s memmap array (struct page[]).

Info needed for memory hotplug (state = online/offline).

So mem_section = “section descriptor” → points to the struct page array for that section.

3️⃣ How section memmap relates to struct page array
struct page[] is the array of per-page descriptors.

In SPARSEMEM, each section has its own memmap (struct page array for all PFNs in that section).

The mem_section struct stores a pointer to that memmap.

So flow is:

PFN → section number → mem_section[secno] → memmap pointer → struct page[PFN % PAGES_PER_SECTION]
4️⃣ What is vmemmap array?
vmemmap = special linear mapping of all struct page[] descriptors themselves into kernel VA.

In SPARSEMEM_VMEMMAP, kernel builds a contiguous virtual mapping of all struct page arrays.

This allows:

struct page *pfn_to_page(pfn) = &vmemmap[pfn];
instead of chasing mem_section pointers.

👉 Think: vmemmap = virtual array of struct page, indexed directly by PFN.
Behind the scenes, it’s backed by the per-section memmaps.

5️⃣ What is hotplug memory?
Ability to add/remove RAM at runtime (DIMMs, memory ballooning in VMs, device memory).

In SPARSEMEM:

Each hotplug unit = section.

Hotplug on = allocate struct page[] for that section, set section flags online, plug into buddy allocator.

Hotplug off = remove from buddy, free memmap.

👉 That’s why memory must be section-aligned (128MB granularity).

6️⃣ What is early memory initialization?
During boot (before buddy/slab fully up), kernel uses memblock allocator:

Tracks reserved/free RAM in memblock.memory array.

Used to allocate kernel image, initrd, page tables, memmap itself.

Once buddy allocator is initialized, memblock is freed/disabled.
👉 Early boot uses memblock → then transitions to buddy + zones.

7️⃣ How node, zone, buddy, section connect
Hierarchy:

System
 └─ Node (NUMA node: one CPU+memory domain)
     └─ Zone (DMA, DMA32, Normal, Movable, Device)
         └─ Section (sparsemem unit: e.g., 128MB)
             └─ PFN (Page Frame Number, 4K or 64K each)
                 └─ struct page (refcount, mapcount, flags)
Node = physical NUMA domain.

Zone = memory pool with restrictions (DMA=low, Normal=main, Movable, Device).

Section = sparse bookkeeping chunk (128MB, hotplug granularity).

Buddy allocator = per-zone, per-order free lists.

struct page = per-PFN descriptor.

8️⃣ Section with Zone Device (ZONE_DEVICE)
ZONE_DEVICE = fake zone type for device memory (not normal RAM). Examples:

Persistent memory (PMEM, NVDIMM).

GPU memory registered into Linux (HMM).

Each section in ZONE_DEVICE has:

struct page descriptors (still needed for tracking pins, refcount).

Marked with MEMBLOCK_NOMAP (no direct kernel linear map).

Instead, device driver controls access.

👉 So: sections are still the accounting unit, even for non-CPU-accessible memory.
For HMM/SVM: device memory sections can be migrated in/out, linked to a process VA via PFN + struct page.

✅ Final Summary
Concept	Meaning	Relation
PFN	Index of physical page (addr/4K)	Input to look up struct page
PTE	Page table entry (VA→PFN+flags)	Uses PFN
struct page	Kernel descriptor per PFN	Tracks refcount/mapcount, flags
Section	Sparsemem bookkeeping unit (128MB/1GB)	Hotplug granularity
mem_section[]	Array of section descriptors	Points to per-section memmap
Memmap	Array of struct page per section	Allocated per present section
vmemmap[]	Virtual contiguous array of all struct page	Makes PFN→page fast
Node	NUMA node (CPU+RAM domain)	Top hierarchy
Zone	Subdivision of node (DMA/Normal/Movable/Device)	Pools for buddy
Buddy	Free lists inside zone	Allocates PFNs
Hotplug memory	Add/remove sections dynamically	Uses section granularity
Early mem init	memblock allocator before buddy ready	Seeds memmap
ZONE_DEVICE	Special zone for device memory (GPU, NVDIMM)	Uses sections too

Fantastic set of questions 🚀 — this is the heart of Linux memory model.
Let me break each one systematically and tie it back to the hierarchy we’ve been building (PFN ↔ section ↔ zone ↔ node ↔ buddy ↔ page).

1️⃣ What is a subsection?
In SPARSEMEM with subsections (CONFIG_MEMORY_HOTPLUG_SUBSECTION), memory is tracked at a finer granularity than a full section.

Section = 128 MB (typical) (arch-dependent).

Subsection = 2 MB (fixed).

👉 Why 2 MB?

Matches common hugepage/THP size → natural alignment.

Smallest unit OS can hotplug on/off without forcing an entire 128 MB section.

Allows more flexible memory hotplug (esp. in VMs with ballooning, memory device passthrough).

So:

Section (128 MB)
 └─ Subsections (64 per section, each 2 MB)
     └─ PFNs (per 4 KB/64 KB page)
2️⃣ MiB vs MB
MB (megabyte) = 1,000,000 bytes (10^6).

MiB (mebibyte) = 1,048,576 bytes (2^20).
Linux uses MiB (power-of-two) because memory alignment is binary.
So: 128 MiB = 134,217,728 bytes, not 128,000,000.

3️⃣ What is “root” in section?
Because mem_section array is 2D:

mem_section[NR_SECTION_ROOTS][SECTIONS_PER_ROOT]
“root” = outer dimension, grouping of sections.

Used to scale memory metadata on large systems (avoid huge flat arrays).

A section root covers a chunk of PFN space; inside are multiple sections.

4️⃣ What is a pageblock?
Pageblock = group of pages inside a zone used as the unit for migration/compaction.

Typically 2 MB size (aligned with THP).

Buddy allocator + compaction operate at pageblock granularity.

Flags per pageblock determine migration type.

So:

Zone
 └─ Pageblocks (~2 MB each)
     └─ Pages (PFNs)
5️⃣ Migration types (per pageblock)
Linux marks pageblocks with a preferred migration type:

MIGRATE_UNMOVABLE → kernel allocations, cannot be moved (slab, page tables).

MIGRATE_MOVABLE → user pages, anon, file cache (can be migrated).

MIGRATE_RECLAIMABLE → can be dropped and recreated (page cache, slab caches).

MIGRATE_CMA → reserved for contiguous memory allocator.

MIGRATE_ISOLATE → temporarily isolated for compaction/hotplug.

Purpose: reduce external fragmentation (don’t mix movable/unmovable in same pageblock).
Caveat: if unmovable allocations leak into movable blocks, compaction fails → THP/CMA allocations fail.

6️⃣ What does pfn_to_page() do?
Converts a Page Frame Number (PFN) → struct page*.

Implementation depends on memory model:

FLATMEM: simple mem_map[PFN].

SPARSEMEM: PFN → section → section’s memmap → offset → struct page.

SPARSEMEM_VMEMMAP: direct vmemmap[PFN].

So:
PFN = index (physical frame number).
pfn_to_page() = look up metadata for that physical frame.

7️⃣ Isn’t PFN same as PTE / physical page itself?
❌ Not the same.

PFN = number identifying a physical frame.

PTE = entry in page table; contains PFN + flags.

Physical page = the actual RAM contents.

struct page = kernel metadata describing the physical page.

So:

Virtual Address
   ↓ PTE
PFN (frame number)
   ↓ pfn_to_page()
struct page
   ↓
Physical RAM contents
8️⃣ Why NUMA node can be “slower/faster” for different cores (numactl --hardware)?
NUMA = Non-Uniform Memory Access.

Each CPU socket has local DRAM → local node.

Accessing another node’s memory requires traversing interconnect (QPI/UPI, InfinityFabric, CCIX).

Hence, local memory latency < remote memory latency.

numactl --hardware shows node distances.

Kernel prefers to allocate from local node → but may fallback to remote if local full.

👉 NUMA nodes are defined by hardware topology (sockets, memory controllers, interconnect), not only speed.

9️⃣ Why can zones and nodes overlap?
Node = NUMA domain (hardware).

Zone = kernel subdivision inside each node (for DMA, Normal, Movable, Device).

Every node contains zones.

Zones never span nodes, but zone ranges can overlap in PFN space if not carefully aligned — kernel uses zone PFN ranges within node boundaries.

🔟 pg_data_t, struct zone, section, PTE — how related?
pg_data_t = per-NUMA node descriptor (struct pglist_data), holds all zones for that node.

struct zone = per-zone descriptor (Normal, DMA, etc).

Section = bookkeeping unit inside zone (128 MiB chunks).

PFN = page frame index inside section.

PTE = mapping VA → PFN.

struct page = metadata for that PFN.

Hierarchy:

pg_data_t (node)
 └─ struct zone (DMA, Normal, Movable, Device)
     └─ Sections (128MB blocks)
         └─ Subsections (2MB blocks)
             └─ PFN (4K/64K page frame)
                 └─ struct page
1️⃣1️⃣ Can entire zone be reclaimed? Is that “swapping”?
Zone reclaim = kernel tries to free/reclaim pages from that zone when allocation fails (e.g., high-order, GFP_THISNODE).

Reclaim frees:

Page cache (drop/writeback).

Anonymous pages (swap out).

Entire zone cannot usually be reclaimed because:

Unmovable kernel pages, pinned pages, mlocked memory remain.

Only reclaimable/movable pages can be swapped/dropped.

👉 Swapping of page = moving one anonymous page to swap device/zram/zswap.
👉 Zone reclaim = kernel policy to push reclaim in one zone to relieve pressure there.

So:

Page swap = per-page eviction.

Zone reclaim = per-zone policy (on NUMA nodes, isolate local pressure).

✅ Final Summary (cheat sheet)
Concept	Size/Role	Relation
PFN	Physical Frame Number (addr/page_size)	Index of physical page
PTE	Page Table Entry	Maps VA → PFN+flags
Section	128 MB chunk (sparsemem)	Hotplug unit
Subsection	2 MB subchunk of section	Fine-grained hotplug
Pageblock	~2 MB inside zone	Unit of migration/compaction
Migration types	Movable, Unmovable, Reclaimable, CMA, Isolate	Affect fragmentation/reclaim
vmemmap[]	Virtual contiguous array of struct page	Direct PFN→page mapping
pg_data_t	Per-NUMA node descriptor	Holds zones
struct zone	Subdivision of node (DMA/Normal/etc)	Pools for buddy
Zone reclaim	Free/reclaim pages inside zone	Not full swap, but may swap anon pages
NUMA latency	Access time differs by node distance	Node assignment based on topology

   |   - shmem/tmpfs: RAM-backed file
   |
   v

   |
   |  - Each VA page has a PTE
   |  - Contains PFN (page frame number) + flags:
   |       (present, R/W/X, user/kernel, accessed, dirty, etc.)
   |  - May point to normal PFN or hugepage PFN (THP/HugeTLB/MTHP)
   |
   v
[ PFN (Page Frame Number) ]
   |
   |  - PFN = physical_address / PAGE_SIZE
   |  - Pure index of a physical page in system RAM
   |
   v

   |
   |  - Refcount (how many active references)
   |  - Mapcount (how many PTEs map it)
   |  - Flags (locked, dirty, writeback, huge, etc.)
   |  - LRU list linkage (for reclaim)
   |  - Mapping (anon, file->address_space, shmem)
   |

   |
   |  - Smallest hotplug unit in sparsemem
   |  - Groups consecutive PFNs (aligned to 2 MiB)
   |  - Matches THP size for efficiency
   |
   v
[ Section (128 MiB typical) ]
   |
   |  - Fixed chunk of memory in SPARSEMEM
   |  - Has mem_section descriptor:
   |       - flags (present, online, device)
   |       - pointer to memmap (struct page array)
   |  - Subsections live inside sections
   |

   |
   |  - Types:
   |     - ZONE_DMA / DMA32: legacy DMA ranges
   |     - ZONE_NORMAL: primary RAM
   |     - ZONE_MOVABLE: migratable pages only
   |     - ZONE_DEVICE: device memory (NVDIMM, GPU HMM)
   |
   |  - Internals:
   |     - Buddy allocator free lists (per-order)
   |     - Pageblocks (~2 MiB chunks) with migration type
   |         MIGRATE_UNMOVABLE, MIGRATE_MOVABLE, MIGRATE_RECLAIMABLE,
   |         MIGRATE_CMA, MIGRATE_ISOLATE
   |
   v
[ pg_data_t (NUMA node descriptor) ]
   |
   |  - One per NUMA node
   |  - Holds zones for that node
   |  - Tracks node stats, free pages, reclaim activity
   |

   |
   |  - Multiple pg_data_t nodes
   |  - Each node = CPUs + local memory
   |  - Interconnect: QPI/UPI (Intel), IF (AMD), CCIX (ARM)
   |  - numactl --hardware shows distance matrix
   |
   v
[ Hardware RAM + Devices ]
   |
   |  - Actual DRAM chips (hotpluggable in sections/subsections)
   |  - Device memory regions mapped into ZONE_DEVICE
   |  - CMA regions reserved for DMA
   |
🔑 Key Translations
VA → PTE → PFN → struct page → physical RAM

VA resolved via PTE.

PTE holds PFN + flags.

PFN indexes into vmemmap[] → struct page.

struct page tracks state.

Actual RAM stores data.

PFN to page = vmemmap[PFN] (direct index).

page to PFN = page - vmemmap.

🔄 Where syscalls & mechanisms fit
malloc/brk/mmap → create VMA, PTEs installed on page fault.

page fault → alloc PFN from buddy → struct page metadata init → PTE updated.

fork (COW) → PTEs share PFN, mapcount++. On write, alloc new PFN.

execve → build new VMAs (file-backed/anon). Lazy fault fills pages.

swap/zram/zswap → reclaim anon PFNs when mapcount=0 or inactive.

page cache → struct page with file->address_space mapping.

mlock → marks struct page unevictable.

THP/MTHP → collapse multiple PFNs into one huge mapping at PTE/PMD level.

CMA → reserves physically contiguous PFNs, pageblock type = MIGRATE_CMA.

dma-buf → pins PFNs (refcount++), prevents reclaim/migration.

NUMA → pg_data_t node selection decides PFN locality.

MPAM → hardware controls cache/bandwidth per node/page stream.

ZONE_DEVICE → struct page exists, but memory access is via driver (GPU/PMEM).

⚖️ Clarifications
PFN ≠ PTE ≠ struct page ≠ physical page:

PFN = number (index).

PTE = entry mapping VA → PFN+flags.

struct page = metadata in kernel.

Physical page = actual RAM contents.

Pageblock (~2 MiB) groups PFNs for compaction/migration.

Section (128 MiB) groups PFNs for hotplug.

Subsection (2 MiB) is fine-grained hotplug.
