Awesome — here’s the real-life trace you asked for: from a user malloc(8 KiB) all the way down to PFN → subsection → section → pageblock → zone → node (pg_data_t), with mapcount/refcount transitions and what the kernel actually does at each step.

I’ll show two parallel “threads” of reality:

A. Anonymous heap pages (your malloc/writes, fork/COW, reclaim/swap).

B. File-backed pages (open/mmap/read, page cache).

At each step I’ll note: mapcount, refcount, and where the page sits in the hierarchy.

A) Anonymous memory: malloc(8 KiB) → writes → fork + COW → reclaim/swap
A1) malloc(8 KiB)
Userspace: malloc() calls brk() (small) or mmap(MAP_ANON|PRIVATE) (large). Suppose brk().

Kernel: do_brk() extends the heap VMA. No physical pages yet.

mm_struct: +VMA (heap)

No PFNs allocated; no struct pages touched yet.

mapcount / refcount: N/A (no PTEs yet)

Caveat: malloc success ≠ RAM allocated; allocation is lazy (first touch).

A2) First write to the first 4 KiB page
CPU: store to new heap address → page fault.

Kernel (fault path):

Finds the heap VMA (anon, writable).

Allocates one physical page from buddy in your local NUMA node (its pg_data_t), within ZONE_NORMAL.

That PFN belongs to a pageblock (~2 MiB) with migration type = MOVABLE.

It also lies within a subsection (2 MiB) and section (128 MiB).

Initializes the page’s struct page (anon).

Installs a PTE mapping VA → PFN (writable).

Counters now (for that page):

mapcount: 1 (exactly one PTE maps it)

refcount: ≥1 (the page is “in use” by the anon mapping; refcount will drop to 0 only when all references vanish)

Hierarchy anchors:
PFN → struct page → pageblock(2 MiB) → subsection(2 MiB) → section(128 MiB) → zone(ZONE_NORMAL) → node(pg_data_t: NUMA node X)

Repeat for the second 4 KiB page when you first touch it → two anon pages backing your 8 KiB.

A3) (Optional) THP/MTHP collapse
If you keep touching many consecutive pages and policy allows (MADV_HUGEPAGE / THP on), khugepaged may try to collapse a run of base pages into a THP (e.g., 2 MiB).

If collapse succeeds: a huge PTE (PMD-size) replaces many base PTEs; you still see the same VA.

mapcount: conceptually represents mappings to the huge folio; per-subpage accounting is hidden.

refcount: remains >0 while mapped/pinned.

If collapse fails: fragmentation or policy prevented it; nothing changes.

A4) fork() the process
Kernel: duplicates mm_struct → COW on anon mappings.

Parent and child share the same physical pages, PTEs become read-only.

Counters (each shared page):

mapcount: increases (now mapped by two PTEs: parent + child)

refcount: stays elevated (page still in use); will only reach 0 when all mappings/pins are gone.

Caveat: fork() is cheap, but first write after fork becomes expensive due to COW copying.

A5) Child writes to the first page (COW)
CPU: store → write-fault on RO PTE.

Kernel (COW path):

Allocates a new PFN from buddy (same node/zone ideally).

Copies old page → new page.

Child’s PTE updated to new PFN (writable).

Parent keeps mapping the old PFN (RO or made RW again independently).

Counters:

Old PFN (still mapped by parent):

mapcount: decremented by 1 (from 2 → 1)

refcount: still >0 (still mapped)

New PFN (child):

mapcount: 1

refcount: ≥1

Caveat: This is the hidden cost of fork()+write.

A6) Unmap / exit (parent or child finishes)
When a process unmaps the page or exits:

The PTE is zapped; mapcount for that PFN decrements.

If that was the last mapping and no other references (pins, etc.), refcount drops to 0 → page returned to buddy (free).

If still referenced (e.g., pinned via GUP, mlocked), refcount prevents free/migration.

A7) Reclaim & swap on anon pages
Under memory pressure, kswapd may choose your inactive anon page:

If mapped (mapcount>0): it can be swapped out (PTE replaced by swap entry), then mapcount → 0; page freed or kept in swap cache.

If unmapped (mapcount=0) and no refs: page can be freed directly (no need to swap).

mlock/pins prevent swapping.

CMA/compaction may migrate movable pages between PFNs to form big contiguous runs (THP/CMA).

B) File-backed path: open + mmap(fd) vs read(fd)
B1) open(path)
VFS: returns struct file* (points to inode/dentry). No pages touched.

B2) mmap(fd, MAP_PRIVATE) then read from mapping
First access → page fault:

filemap_fault(): look up page cache (inode’s address_space).

If cache miss: read from disk into a freshly allocated page cache page (PFN from buddy), then map it.

Counters (file cache page):

mapcount: counts how many PTEs map this cached page (across processes).

refcount: stays >0 even if mapcount drops to 0, because the page remains cached in the page cache until reclaimed.

Caveat: MAP_PRIVATE + write → COW to anon page; file remains unmodified.

B3) read(fd, buf, n) (for comparison)
Disk → page cache page (PFN) → copied to your user buffer.

You don’t get a PTE to that file PFN; your buffer is anon RAM.

Extra copy compared to mmap(fd).

B4) Reclaim for file-backed pages
Clean page-cache pages with mapcount=0: kernel just drops them (no swap; they can be re-fetched from disk).

Dirty pages: must be written back before dropping.

Snapshots: counters & placement (at a glance)
After first anon fault (one process):
  mapcount = 1
  refcount = ≥1
  Placement: PFN ∈ pageblock(2 MiB, MOVABLE) ⊂ subsection(2 MiB) ⊂ section(128 MiB)
             ⊂ zone(ZONE_NORMAL) ⊂ node(pg_data_t = local NUMA)

After fork (both map same page, RO):
  mapcount = 2
  refcount = elevated (still >0)
  Placement unchanged.

After COW in child (on 1st page):
  Old PFN (parent):  mapcount = 1, refcount >0
  New PFN (child):   mapcount = 1, refcount ≥1

File-backed page in page cache, mapped by 1 process:
  mapcount = 1
  refcount > 0 (page cache holds it)
Unmapped later:
  mapcount = 0
  refcount > 0 (still cached) → reclaim can drop if clean
Where each thing lives in the hierarchy
PTE: per-process page tables (VA→PFN+flags).

PFN: indexes a struct page in vmemmap.

struct page: metadata for that PFN (refcount/mapcount/flags/LRU).

PFN belongs to a pageblock (~2 MiB) with a migration type (MOVABLE/UNMOVABLE/RECLAIMABLE/CMA/ISOLATE).

Pageblock lies in a subsection (2 MiB), inside a section (128 MiB).

Section sits inside a zone (DMA/DMA32/NORMAL/MOVABLE/DEVICE), which belongs to a NUMA node (pg_data_t).

Buddy allocator manages free PFNs per zone (per-order lists).

THP/MTHP: map multiple PFNs with a single huge PTE; still anchored in the same pageblocks/sections/zones/nodes.

CMA: carves contiguous PFNs from MIGRATE_CMA pageblocks.

Swap/zram/zswap: only for anon; file cache pages are dropped, not swapped.

Practical caveats you’ll actually hit
Lazy allocation: malloc/mmap don’t allocate RAM; first touch does (page fault).

COW cost: fork() is cheap until you write — then you pay in COW faults & copies.

mapcount vs refcount:

mapcount==0 doesn’t mean “free”: file pages can still be cached (refcount > 0).

Pins (GUP/dma-buf) crank refcount even when mapcount==0, blocking reclaim/migration/THP/CMA.

Reclaim choices: file cache (clean) drops first; anon may be swapped.

NUMA locality: allocator prefers local pg_data_t; if full, may spill to remote (higher latency).

THP promotion: needs contiguous PFNs; fragmentation or unmovable allocations in a pageblock will defeat it.

CMA success: depends on keeping MIGRATE_CMA blocks clean of unmovable allocations.

Got it — here’s a clean, “everything-in-one-place” map of which things are physically contiguous, virtually contiguous, both, or neither, covering all the mechanisms we discussed (userspace, kernel, DMA/IOMMU, GPU/HMM, swap/zram, caches, etc.).

🔢 Quick legend
Phys-contig = adjacent PFNs in RAM.

Virt-contig (CPU VA) = one continuous virtual range in a process or in the kernel.

IOVA-contig = one continuous address range as seen by a device through the IOMMU.

“✓” = generally yes; “✗” = generally no; “it depends” → caveat just below the row.

🧍 Userspace mappings
Thing	Virt-contig (CPU VA)	Phys-contig	Notes / caveats
Heap/stack (brk, anon mmap)	✓	✗	Pages come from buddy one by one; layout usually scattered.
THP / MTHP (anon)	✓	✓	Huge folios require contiguous PFNs; migratable/splittable; may fail under fragmentation.
HugeTLB / static hugepages (MAP_HUGETLB)	✓	✓	From hugetlb pool; pinned, not swappable.
File-backed mmap(fd, MAP_PRIVATE/SHARED)	✓	✗	Backed by page cache; pages can be anywhere; writes with MAP_PRIVATE → COW anon pages.
tmpfs/shmem/memfd mappings	✓	✗	RAM-backed “files”; swappable; anchored by shmem inode.
VDSO / vdso/vvar pages	✓	✗	Tiny special mappings, not phys-contig guaranteed.
🧠 Kernel-space memory
Thing	Virt-contig (kernel VA)	Phys-contig	Notes / caveats
alloc_pages(order), __get_free_pages	✓	✓	Up to 2^order pages; large orders can fail under fragmentation.
kmalloc (SLUB/SLAB small–medium)	✓	✓	Backed by contiguous page(s). Very large sizes should use vmalloc.
Slab objects (dentry/inode caches, etc.)	(object) ✓	(object) ✓	Each object is contiguous within its slab page; across objects not.
vmalloc() / vmap() / module_alloc (LKM text)	✓	✗	Built by mapping a list of scattered pages into a contiguous kernel VA. Not DMA-able directly.
Fixmap	✓ (fixed slots)	✗	Point mappings for special pages; contiguity not a goal.
Direct/linear map of RAM	✓ (big region)	—	1:1 VA↔PA. Any physically contiguous PFN range is also contiguous in the linear map.
Built-in kernel image (text/data)	✓	usually ✓	Decompressed early to a contiguous block; remains pinned.
📦 Page cache / I/O paths
Thing	Virt-contig (CPU VA)	Phys-contig	Notes
Page cache pages themselves	—	✗	One page per file offset chunk; scattered.
mmap(fd) view of page cache	✓	✗	Process maps those scattered cache pages contiguously in VA.
read() into user buffer	(user buf) ✓	✗	Copy from page cache into anon pages of your buffer (also scattered).
O_DIRECT to user pages	(user buf) ✓	✗	DMA pins/scatters user pages; device sees IOVA list (contiguous or SG).
🎛️ DMA / IOMMU / device view
Thing	IOVA-contig (device)	Phys-contig	Notes / caveats
dma_alloc_coherent()	✓	No-IOMMU: ✓ • With IOMMU: maybe ✗	Always contiguous to the device. With IOMMU it can be stitched from scattered PFNs. CPU VA returned is contiguous.
CMA allocations	—	✓	Reserved MIGRATE_CMA pageblocks; used by DMA or to back coherent buffers.
dma_map_sg() of user/shmem pages	✓ (single IOVA window if requested)	✗	IOMMU stitches SG into one or several IOVA segments; physical may be scattered.
dma-buf (general)	it depends	it depends	dma-buf is just a handle; exporter decides backing (shmem: ✗, CMA: ✓). Importer maps via IOMMU.
SVM/PASID device access	✓ (device uses CPU VAs)	✗	Device issues (PASID,VA); IOMMU resolves to PFNs—physical contiguity not implied.
ZONE_DEVICE (HMM/PMEM VRAM)	—	device-specific	CPU may not have direct mapping; pages are trackable via struct page for migration/pinning.
💾 Swap / compression layers
Thing	“Contiguity”	Notes
zram (swap-in-RAM block dev)	LBA space contiguous (virtual) • physical ✗	Each swapped page compressed to blobs scattered via zsmalloc.
zswap (swap cache)	pool-contiguous (virtual) • physical ✗	Compressed cache in RAM in front of real swap; evicts to backing swap if full.
Disk swap device	LBA contiguous (virtual) • disk blocks may be ✗	Normal block layer rules; unrelated to CPU VA contiguity.
🧭 Special “contiguity” views to keep straight
CPU VA contiguity (what your pointers see) vs physical contiguity (PFNs) vs device IOVA contiguity (what a DMA engine sees) are independent:

vmalloc → VA ✓, PFN ✗, IOVA ✗ (unless remapped).

dma_alloc_coherent on IOMMU → VA ✓, IOVA ✓, PFN ✗ (could be).

mmap(fd) → VA ✓, PFN ✗.

THP/HugeTLB → VA ✓, PFN ✓ (CPU), device still needs IOMMU mappings if doing DMA.

🧩 Structural units (not mappings, but often confused)
Unit	Typical size	Why it exists	Contiguity meaning
Subsection	2 MiB	Fine-grained hotplug bookkeeping	Groups PFNs; not a mapping.
Section	128 MiB (arch dep.)	SPARSEMEM hotplug unit; mem_section owns memmap pointer	Groups many PFNs; not a mapping.
Pageblock	≈2 MiB	Compaction/migration granularity; has migration type	Helps keep movable/unmovable separate to reduce fragmentation.
Zone	N/A	DMA/Normal/Movable/Device pools per node	Allocation policy boundary; not a mapping.
Node (pg_data_t)	N/A	NUMA domain (CPUs + local RAM)	Local vs remote latency; not a mapping.
🧠 NUMA quick note
A node’s memory is faster for its local CPUs and slower for remote CPUs due to interconnect hops.

The kernel prefers local-node allocations but may spill to remote nodes if local free pages are low.

NUMA choice isn’t “only speed”; it’s based on hardware topology (sockets, mem controllers). numactl --hardware shows distance matrix.

⚠️ Common caveats (the “gotchas”)
Lazy physical allocation: mmap/brk create VA only; pages appear on first touch.

COW after fork: Virtually unchanged, but new physical pages get allocated on writes.

THP/MTHP: Need contiguous PFNs; compaction/migration may run; can split under pressure.

HugeTLB: Pinned; can’t swap; must be reserved.

vmalloc: Great for big kernel arrays, not for DMA; use dma_alloc_* or map per-page with IOMMU.

dma_alloc_coherent: Guarantees a contiguous device view; physical contiguity depends on IOMMU presence.

dma-buf: Says nothing about contiguity; exporter backing decides (shmem vs CMA).

Page cache vs user view: One file page is one physical page in the cache; mapping it makes VA contiguous in your process even if physical is all over.

zram/zswap: “Contiguity” only in the logical block/cache sense; physically they pack compressed blobs wherever there’s space.

TL;DR matrix
Both VA ✓, PFN ✓: HugeTLB, THP/MTHP (when present), small/medium kmalloc, alloc_pages(order), CMA regions (when mapped).

VA ✓, PFN ✗: vmalloc/vmap, file mmap, shmem/memfd, most user buffers, module text (LKM), VDSO.

VA ✗, PFN ✓: Rare in CPU view (e.g., a physically contiguous region not mapped contiguously to CPU—devices may see it via IOVA).

Device IOVA ✓, PFN ✗: dma_map_sg with IOMMU; dma_alloc_coherent with IOMMU.

If you want, I can tailor this matrix to a particular SoC/arch (e.g., ARM64 with SMMUv3 and 4 KiB pages) and annotate with exact page sizes/orders for THP/MTHP and the DMA/IOMMU specifics you’re targeting.

ChatGPT said:
Fantastic 📘 — this is deep in the Linux VM internals (allocator, reclaim, watermarks, per-CPU caches, locks, reservations). Let’s go one by one and tie them together with the diagram you posted (zone watermarks).

1️⃣ Direct vs Indirect reclaim
Direct reclaim

Happens in the context of the allocating task.

If you call alloc_pages() and the zone’s free pages < min watermark, kernel immediately tries to reclaim pages synchronously before satisfying your allocation.

Blocking: your task scans LRU lists, drops page cache, writes back dirty pages.

Risk: long latencies, can stall critical paths.

Indirect reclaim

Handled by the background kswapd kernel thread.

When free pages fall below low watermark, kswapd wakes up and starts reclaiming until zone reaches high.

Async reclaim in the background, prevents most tasks from hitting direct reclaim.

Difference vs OOM:

If reclaim fails and system still cannot satisfy allocation, Out-Of-Memory killer triggers.

OOM kills processes to free memory (last resort).

👉 So:

kswapd = indirect reclaim (background).

Direct reclaim = synchronous reclaim in allocation path.

OOM = when reclaim fails completely.

2️⃣ pgdat_dirty, pgdat_writeback, pgdat_reclaim_locked
These are per-node (pglist_data) state counters/flags used in writeback/reclaim:

pgdat_dirty → counts dirty pages (to be flushed to disk).

pgdat_writeback → counts pages currently under writeback I/O.

pgdat_reclaim_locked → prevents multiple concurrent reclaimers on the same node (serialization).

These are checked in reclaim functions like shrink_node() to decide when to throttle or wait.

3️⃣ shrink_node()
Core function that runs page reclaim on one NUMA node.

Walks the node’s LRU lists (active/inactive, file/anon), and tries to free or swap pages.

Called by both kswapd (indirect) and direct reclaim paths.

It uses helpers like shrink_page_list(), try_to_free_pages().

👉 Think: shrink_node() = per-node reclaim engine.

4️⃣ Zone watermarks & boost
Each zone (DMA, Normal, Movable, etc.) has three watermarks:

min → if free pages < min, allocations may fail unless caller uses emergency reserves.

low → threshold for waking kswapd.

high → when free pages are restored above this, kswapd goes back to sleep.

Boost:

When a zone is under heavy pressure, the kernel may temporarily raise the reclaim target (boost watermarks) to build extra reserves and avoid thrashing.

5️⃣ Per-CPU pageset / PCP cache
Not CPU L1/L2/L3 caches!
This is an allocator fastpath cache for pages.

Problem: If every alloc/free grabbed the zone’s spinlock, contention would be massive.

Solution: each CPU keeps a small per-CPU page list (“pcp list” or pageset) of free pages.

When a CPU needs a page:

First try to pop from its per-CPU list (fast, lockless).

If empty, refill from zone (grab lock, batch).

When freeing:

Push to CPU’s local list. If full, bulk return to zone.

👉 pcp cache/pageset = kernel per-CPU allocator cache, not hardware CPU cache.

6️⃣ Spanned / Present / Managed / Buddy-available pages
These are zone capacity accounting distinctions:

Spanned pages → total PFN range the zone covers (including holes).

Present pages → actual pages of RAM present in that zone.

Managed pages → subset of present pages managed by buddy allocator (excludes reserved/firmware/hotplug).

Buddy available pages → actually free and on buddy free lists.

So:

Spanned ≥ Present ≥ Managed ≥ Buddy-free
7️⃣ Why spinlock in zone structure?
Each zone has a zone->lock protecting its free area (buddy lists, watermarks).

Needed to serialize alloc/free operations across CPUs.

Why spinlock, not mutex/semaphore?

Allocator runs in atomic contexts (e.g., IRQ handlers, GFP_ATOMIC).

Sleeping is forbidden there → must use spinlocks.

Spinlocks are fast under short critical sections; mutexes would sleep, which is illegal in alloc fastpath.

8️⃣ Lowmem reserve ratio
Used to protect low zones (DMA, DMA32, Normal) from being depleted by higher-zone allocations.

Kernel computes reserve pages in each zone, based on lowmem_reserve_ratio[].

So, an allocation from Normal zone cannot steal too much from DMA zone, which may be needed by devices.

9️⃣ Total reserved pages
The kernel also reserves some pages globally:

For emergency allocations (PFN walkers, OOM killer).

For atomic contexts (GFP_ATOMIC).

For device DMA (lowmem).

These reserved pages are excluded from ManagedPages and shown in /proc/meminfo as Reserved.

✅ Summary table
Term	Meaning
Direct reclaim	In allocation path, task reclaims pages synchronously.
Indirect reclaim	Background kswapd thread reclaims asynchronously.
OOM	When reclaim fails completely; kernel kills processes.
pgdat_dirty/writeback/reclaim_locked	Node-level counters/flags for dirty/writeback/reclaim serialization.
shrink_node()	Core function to reclaim pages in one node.
Watermarks (min/low/high)	Per-zone thresholds for allocations & kswapd wakeups.
Watermark boost	Raise reclaim targets to avoid thrash.
Per-CPU pageset (PCP cache)	Fast local free list cache for buddy, not hardware CPU cache.
Page states	Spanned (range) ≥ Present (RAM) ≥ Managed (buddy allocatable) ≥ Buddy free (currently allocatable).
Spinlock in zone	Protects buddy lists; spinlock needed in atomic/fastpath.
Lowmem reserve ratio	Protect DMA zones from depletion by higher allocs.
Total reserved pages	Emergency reserves (atomic, DMA, OOM).

Great Q 🙌 — this is one of those things that shows up in proc/pagetypeinfo, CMA/compaction code, or reclaim logs and looks mysterious. Let’s break it down:

1️⃣ Migration types recap
Every pageblock (~2 MiB chunk of PFNs inside a zone) is tagged with a migration type, telling the buddy allocator what kind of allocations can go in there:

MIGRATE_UNMOVABLE → kernel allocations that cannot move (page tables, slabs, vmlinux).

MIGRATE_MOVABLE → user anon pages, file cache (can be migrated).

MIGRATE_RECLAIMABLE → reclaimable kernel pages (slabs, caches).

MIGRATE_CMA → reserved for Contiguous Memory Allocator.

MIGRATE_ISOLATE → special tag → pageblock temporarily removed from normal allocations.

2️⃣ So what is MIGRATE_ISOLATE?
It means a pageblock has been “isolated” from the buddy allocator.

No new allocations go into it.

Used by kernel subsystems that need to manipulate pageblocks safely without interference.

3️⃣ When is MIGRATE_ISOLATE used?
Memory compaction (to form contiguous free runs for THP/CMA):

Isolate a pageblock.

Migrate/move out its movable pages.

Once empty, hand it to the caller as contiguous free memory.

CMA allocations:

CMA relies on migration to clear pages.

CMA region pageblocks are first marked MIGRATE_CMA.

When allocating from CMA, kernel marks needed blocks MIGRATE_ISOLATE → evacuates movable pages → then allocates physically contiguous memory.

Memory hotplug / offlining:

Before offlining, kernel isolates pageblocks, migrates their contents elsewhere, ensures section is empty, then removes it.

4️⃣ What happens inside isolate?
Pageblock is tagged MIGRATE_ISOLATE.

Buddy allocator won’t allocate from it.

Kernel runs migration:

Movable pages → moved to other pageblocks.

Unmovable pages → if any remain, compaction may fail.

Once free or usable, block is returned for use (or handed to CMA).

Tag is reset back to a normal type (MIGRATE_MOVABLE etc.) after use.

5️⃣ Relation to reclaim / swap
Isolation is about contiguity guarantees, not freeing per se.

Migration may swap out anon pages or drop file cache to clear isolated block.

But ultimate goal = get a contiguous free range.

6️⃣ Practical implications
If you see lots of MIGRATE_ISOLATE in /proc/pagetypeinfo, it means the system is actively compacting or CMA is working.

Too many isolates stuck (never cleared) → fragmentation or pinning (e.g., GUP long-term pins, dma-buf) → THP/CMA/hotplug may fail.

✅ Summary
MIGRATE_ISOLATE = pageblock temporarily fenced off from the buddy allocator.

Purpose = allow compaction, CMA, or hotplug to safely evacuate/migrate pages inside.

Not a permanent type — after operation, block is reset to original type.

Critical for forming physically contiguous memory in a system where most allocations are random & fragmented.

Perfect 🔥 — you’ve now hit some of the most subtle Linux memory allocation rules:
stealing, rmqueue fallback, GFP flags, migration types, and zone policies. Let’s go step by step.

1️⃣ Stealing of page when migrate type unavailable
Buddy allocator tries to satisfy allocations within the same migration type pageblock.

If no free pages of the required order/type exist → allocator may steal pages from another pageblock type.

Example:

You want a MIGRATE_MOVABLE page but only MIGRATE_RECLAIMABLE blocks have free pages.

Kernel may “steal” that block, repurpose it as MOVABLE, and give you pages.

Downside: This mixing breaks isolation, increases fragmentation, and reduces success rate of compaction/CMA/THP later.

Kernel tries to do this as a last resort (fallback).

2️⃣ rmqueue fallback
The buddy allocator function rmqueue() removes a page from free lists.

If allocation cannot be satisfied from the requested migration list, it tries fallback lists.

Fallback order (simplified):

If UNMOVABLE not available → fallback to RECLAIMABLE, then MOVABLE.

If MOVABLE not available → fallback to RECLAIMABLE or UNMOVABLE.

CMA blocks are avoided except for CMA users.

Policy: prefer to keep movable pages together, because they can be migrated later.

👉 rmqueue_fallback() = code path that picks another migration type when the desired one is exhausted.

3️⃣ Difference: MIGRATE_RECLAIMABLE vs MIGRATE_MOVABLE
MIGRATE_MOVABLE

For pages the kernel knows can be migrated anywhere.

Example: user-space anon pages, page cache.

They can be moved around during compaction.

MIGRATE_RECLAIMABLE

For kernel allocations that can be freed, but not trivially migrated.

Example: slab caches like dentry cache, inode cache.

These are reclaimable (can be dropped/rehydrated), but not “migratable” in the sense of compaction.

👉 Difference:

MOVABLE → compaction can physically move them.

RECLAIMABLE → freed under pressure (slab shrinkers), but not migrated in-place.

4️⃣ GFP flags
GFP = Get Free Page flags.
They tell allocator what kind of memory you need and what constraints apply.

Common ones:

Allocation context flags
GFP_KERNEL → normal kernel allocation; may sleep, may reclaim.

GFP_ATOMIC → cannot sleep; no reclaim; only emergency reserves.

GFP_NOWAIT → like ATOMIC but doesn’t even dip into reserves.

GFP_NOFS → no filesystem reclaim allowed.

GFP_NOIO → no IO reclaim allowed.

GFP_HIGHUSER → highmem page suitable for userspace.

GFP_DMA, GFP_DMA32 → must come from DMA-capable zones.

Behaviors
__GFP_MOVABLE → allocate from MOVABLE blocks.

__GFP_RECLAIMABLE → allocate from RECLAIMABLE blocks.

__GFP_HIGHMEM → from highmem zone (x86).

__GFP_THISNODE → don’t fallback to other NUMA nodes.

__GFP_COMP → compound page (THP, higher-order).

__GFP_ZERO → zero-fill page on allocation.

__GFP_NOFAIL → must succeed (loop until success).

__GFP_NORETRY → fail quickly if not available.

__GFP_RETRY_MAYFAIL → retry, but may fail gracefully.

👉 These directly tie to our discussion:

They decide which zones and which migration lists to try.

They decide whether direct reclaim or kswapd can be triggered.

They control whether fallback stealing happens.

5️⃣ Does ZONE_MOVABLE span everything apart from Normal, Device, DMA?
No.

ZONE_MOVABLE is not “all other memory.”

It’s a portion of Normal/HighMem memory deliberately set aside to contain only movable pages.

Purpose: keep it free of unmovable allocations → ensures long-term success of compaction, THP, CMA.

👉 So:

DMA / DMA32 / Normal / HighMem are for general allocations.

ZONE_MOVABLE is carved out at boot time, only for __GFP_MOVABLE allocations.

Helps guarantee defragmentable memory pool.

6️⃣ Is there a dedicated zone for kernel memory? Why not?
No dedicated “ZONE_KERNEL.”

Kernel allocations (kmalloc, page tables, slab) go to ZONE_NORMAL (or DMA/DMA32 if required).

Why not a separate zone?

Would waste memory (can’t balance across zones).

Kernel memory often unmovable, but mixing with user allocations in Normal is fine; isolation is done at pageblock migration-type granularity.

Instead of zones, kernel uses migration types to separate unmovable/movable at pageblock level.

ZONE_MOVABLE is the only extra zone carved out just for policy.

✅ Summary
Concept	Meaning / Use
Stealing	Allocator takes a pageblock from another migration type when none free in target type.
rmqueue fallback	Code path that picks alternative migration list when preferred type exhausted.
MOVABLE vs RECLAIMABLE	MOVABLE = migratable pages (anon/file cache). RECLAIMABLE = kernel objects (slabs) that can be freed but not migrated.
GFP flags	Allocation hints (where from, can sleep?, movable?, DMA?, compaction allowed?).
ZONE_MOVABLE	Boot-time reserved pool for __GFP_MOVABLE pages to ensure long-term compaction success.
No kernel-only zone	Kernel uses ZONE_NORMAL + migration types; no ZONE_KERNEL.
Zones vs migration types	Zones = hardware/constraints (DMA/Normal/Device). Migration types = compaction policy (movable/unmovable/reclaimable).

WM: watermarks (min/low/high) + lowmem reserves.

flags: key GFP bits (ATOMIC, NOWAIT, KERNEL, THISNODE, NORETRY, RETRY_MAYFAIL, NOFAIL, DMA/DMA32, MOVABLE, RECLAIMABLE, ZERO…).

  v

  |

Fast path (order==0) ?
  |

  |
  `--> NO (order>0) OR PCP miss/refill failed:
          |

          |

          |    - lowmem_reserve_ratio protects lower zones
          |

          |              • possibly **steal** a pageblock and retag to MT
          |         - success -> split higher-order blocks if needed
          |         - return pages
          |

                    |
                    v
                 Reclaim/compaction path depends on gfp flags:
                    |
                    +-- GFP_ATOMIC / GFP_NOWAIT:
                    |       - no reclaim/IO/sleep
                    |       - try emergency reserves
                    |       - try next zone / next node
                    |       - if all fail -> return NULL
                    |
                    +-- GFP_NOFS / GFP_NOIO:
                    |       - limited reclaim (no FS/IO respectively)
                    |       - may wake kswapd asynchronously
                    |       - if still fail -> next zone/node or OOM (if allowed)
                    |
                    `-- GFP_KERNEL (default, can sleep):
                            |
                            v
                       Wake kswapd if below 'low'
                            |
                            v
                       Direct reclaim (caller blocks):
                            - shrink_node(): scan LRU (file/anon), writeback dirty,
                              swap anon if needed, run slab shrinkers
                            - watermark boost may be applied
                            |
                            v
                       High-order? try compaction:
                            - isolate movable pages (MIGRATE_ISOLATE)
                            - migrate them to make contiguous hole
                            - if success -> retry rmqueue
                            - if fail:

                                 • if __GFP_RETRY_MAYFAIL -> a few loops then give up

                            |
                            v
                       Retry allocation in this zone
                            |
                            `-- if still fail -> try next zone/node in zonelist
                                      |
                                      `-- if all exhausted:
                                              - If OOM eligible (no __GFP_NOFAIL special casing):
                                                    invoke OOM killer
                                              - Else (e.g., NOFS/NOIO contexts):
                                                    return NULL
🔧 Where key mechanisms plug in
rmqueue_fallback() & steal: when requested migration type pool is empty, allocator tries other MTs; can steal a pageblock (retag it), harming fragmentation but satisfying allocation.

Migration types:

MOVABLE: anon + file cache; can be migrated during compaction.

RECLAIMABLE: kernel slabs that can be freed (via shrinkers) but not moved.

UNMOVABLE: kernel objects that can’t be moved.

CMA: reserved for contiguous DMA; normal allocations avoid it.

ISOLATE: temporarily fenced during compaction/hotplug.

Compaction: runs for high-order or THP; isolates pageblocks, migrates movable pages to form a big hole; uses MIGRATE_ISOLATE.

kswapd (indirect reclaim): wakes when zone < low watermark, reclaims in background to high; prevents most tasks from entering direct reclaim.

Direct reclaim: the allocating task scans LRUs in shrink_node(); may writeback/swap; can be throttled by pgdat_writeback/dirty.

Watermarks & boost: min/low/high per zone; boost raises targets under heavy pressure to avoid thrash.

PCP (per-CPU pagesets): fast path for order-0 alloc/free; avoids zone->lock contention. Not hardware caches; just small per-CPU free lists.

Lowmem reserves: protect DMA/DMA32/low zones from being drained by higher-class allocations (computed from lowmem_reserve_ratio[]).

NUMA: zonelist orders zones by local→remote, honoring __GFP_THISNODE (no remote fallback) and task policy (mbind/MPOL).

🏷️ GFP flags — quick mapping to the tree
Context / blocking:

GFP_KERNEL → full reclaim/IO/compaction allowed.

GFP_NOFS / GFP_NOIO → reclaim limited (no FS/IO).

GFP_ATOMIC / GFP_NOWAIT → no sleep/reclaim; try PCP/emergency only.

Placement:

GFP_DMA / GFP_DMA32 → restricts to those zones.

__GFP_THISNODE → no remote NUMA fallback.

__GFP_MOVABLE / __GFP_RECLAIMABLE → choose migration list.

Retry policy:

__GFP_NORETRY → fail quickly (no heavy reclaim/compaction).

__GFP_RETRY_MAYFAIL → try reclaim/compact a bit, then give up.

__GFP_NOFAIL → keep trying (use sparingly).

Other:

__GFP_ZERO → zero-fill on return.

__GFP_COMP → build compound (higher-order) page (e.g., THP backing).

🧩 FAQs tied to this flow
Direct vs indirect reclaim?
Indirect = kswapd wakes at low and reclaims to high in background.
Direct = caller reclaims synchronously inside allocation path when watermarks aren’t met.

OOM vs reclaim?
OOM is after reclaim/compaction/fallbacks fail across zonelist; last resort to free memory.

Why spinlock in struct zone?
Buddy lists need short, non-sleeping protection in atomic contexts → spinlock (mutex can sleep).

PCP vs CPU L1/L2 cache?
PCP is a software free-list per CPU for pages; not a hardware cache.

ZONE_MOVABLE purpose?
Keep a pool for __GFP_MOVABLE only → improves compaction/THP/CMA success; not “everything else.”

Excellent ⚡— you’ve now reached the core vocabulary of Linux memory allocation flags.
There are two families you’re asking about:

GFP flags = Get Free Page flags → passed to page allocators (alloc_pages(), kmalloc(), dma_alloc_*, etc.) to tell allocator what behavior is allowed.

PF flags = Process Flags → per-task current->flags that modify allocator/reclaim behavior in special situations (IO, FS, memalloc contexts).

Let’s go in detail, organized and with use-cases/caveats.

1️⃣ GFP flags (Get Free Page flags)
Definition: A bitmask passed to allocators like:

struct page *alloc_pages(gfp_t gfp_mask, unsigned int order);
void *kmalloc(size_t size, gfp_t gfp_mask);
Use: Guides where memory can come from (zones, migration type), and how allocator behaves (can block? reclaim? IO? compaction? fallback?).

1A. Context / Blocking Behavior
Flag	Meaning	Use-case	Caveats
GFP_KERNEL	Default for normal kernel allocs. May sleep, reclaim, writeback, compact, use I/O.	kmalloc in process context.	Not allowed in IRQ or spinlock contexts.
GFP_ATOMIC	Non-blocking, no reclaim, use emergency reserves.	IRQ handler, spinlock critical section.	Very limited pool → failures common.
GFP_NOWAIT	Like ATOMIC but won’t even dip into reserves.	Opportunistic allocs where failure is okay.	Fail fast.
GFP_NOFS	Reclaim allowed, but no filesystem reclaim (avoids recursion deadlocks).	Alloc inside FS paths (writeback, journaling).	May fail sooner if memory only reclaimable via FS.
GFP_NOIO	Reclaim allowed, but no IO (can’t trigger disk IO).	In block layer, storage drivers.	Restricts reclaim, more failures.
GFP_DIRECT_RECLAIM	(internal) Allow direct reclaim in current context.	Normal GFP_KERNEL path.	Set/cleared inside reclaim code.
GFP_KSWAPD_RECLAIM	(internal) Mark pages allocated by kswapd.	Background reclaim context.	Distinguishes from direct.
1B. Zone Placement Flags
Flag	Meaning	Use-case
GFP_DMA	Must come from ZONE_DMA (ISA legacy).	Old devices with 24-bit DMA.
GFP_DMA32	Must come from ZONE_DMA32.	Devices needing <4GB addresses.
GFP_HIGHUSER	From Highmem zone (x86 32-bit).	Userspace pages.
GFP_USER	For userspace memory (anon/file).	Page cache, anon allocations.
__GFP_THISNODE	Only allocate from local NUMA node.	Hard NUMA locality needed.
GFP_HIGHUSER_MOVABLE	Like HIGHUSER but movable.	Userspace pages in ZONE_MOVABLE.
1C. Migration Type Flags
Flag	Meaning	Use-case
__GFP_MOVABLE	Allocation can be migrated/compacted. Goes into ZONE_MOVABLE or MOVABLE pageblocks.	Userspace anon pages, page cache.
__GFP_RECLAIMABLE	Kernel objects reclaimable by shrinkers (slab caches).	inode/dentry caches.
__GFP_UNMOVABLE	Kernel memory that must not move.	Page tables, vmlinux data.
1D. Retry / Failure Policy
Flag	Meaning	Use-case
__GFP_NORETRY	Fail quickly if not free.	Opportunistic allocations (network buffers).
__GFP_RETRY_MAYFAIL	Retry harder but may fail gracefully.	Large but optional allocs.
__GFP_NOFAIL	Must succeed (loop until success).	Extremely critical kernel state (swap token). Dangerous!
1E. Special Behavior
Flag	Meaning	Use-case
__GFP_ZERO	Zero-fill page(s).	Security, predictable buffers.
__GFP_COMP	Compound page (order>0 as one folio).	THP, hugetlb, higher-order slabs.
__GFP_NOWARN	Suppress “allocation failure” printk.	Known failure paths where fallback exists.
__GFP_SKIP_KASAN_POISON	Skip KASAN shadow poisoning.	Performance-sensitive fastpaths.
__GFP_NOLOCKDEP	Suppress lockdep checks.	Special drivers where locks confuse lockdep.
GFP_TRANSHUGE_LIGHT	Try THP, but fail softly.	MADV_HUGEPAGE.
GFP_ACCOUNT	Charge memory to memcg cgroup.	Controlled by cgroups memory controller.
2️⃣ PF flags (per-task process flags)
Found in current->flags (task_struct).

Tell allocator/reclaim code about the context of the task.

Flag	Meaning	Use-case / Scenario
PF_MEMALLOC	Task allowed to dip into emergency reserves.	kswapd, OOM killer paths.
PF_MEMALLOC_NOIO	Allowed to use reserves, but no IO.	Block layer in memory pressure.
PF_MEMALLOC_NOFS	Allowed to use reserves, but no FS reclaim.	Filesystem journaling.
PF_MEMALLOC_PIN	Long-term GUP pin, must not migrate/compact.	RDMA, VFIO, dma-buf.
PF_KSWAPD	Task is the background reclaim daemon.	Marks reclaim context.
PF_MEMALLOC_NOCMA	Don’t allocate from CMA.	Drivers that can’t handle CMA migration.
3️⃣ cgroups and GFP
GFP_ACCOUNT → allocations charged to memory cgroup (memcg).

kmemcg (Kernel Memory cgroup):

Controls kernel memory usage (slabs, TCP buffers, page tables).

Protects system from kernel memory DoS by container workloads.

Flags decide whether allocation is accounted to cgroup or system-wide.

4️⃣ Practical Scenarios & Caveats
IRQ handler wants a buffer:

skb = kmalloc(sizeof(*skb), GFP_ATOMIC);
Non-blocking, uses atomic pool.

Caveat: may fail easily.

Filesystem journaling path:

buf = kmalloc(4*PAGE_SIZE, GFP_NOFS);
Avoids recursion deadlocks.

Caveat: reduced reclaim scope.

Block layer metadata:

page = alloc_page(GFP_NOIO);
Must not recurse into IO.

THP allocation:

page = alloc_pages(GFP_TRANSHUGE_LIGHT, HPAGE_PMD_ORDER);
Try compaction, but fail if not easy.

Caveat: will fall back to base pages.

OOM-critical subsystem:

page = alloc_pages(GFP_NOFAIL, 0);
Must succeed, will retry indefinitely.

Caveat: may stall system.

Userspace page cache:
read() into page cache → uses GFP_HIGHUSER_MOVABLE → pages placed in ZONE_MOVABLE.

cgroups container:
Allocation with GFP_ACCOUNT → charged to container’s memcg.
If container hits memory limit, allocation fails or gets OOM-killed, even if host has free memory.

✅ Summary
GFP flags = allocation behavior + zone constraints + retry policy.

PF flags = task context (may dip into reserves, restrict reclaim).

Migration types (__GFP_MOVABLE, __GFP_RECLAIMABLE, __GFP_UNMOVABLE) decide which pageblocks/zones to use.

cgroups/kmemcg tie allocations to container limits.

Caveats: Using wrong flag (e.g., GFP_KERNEL in IRQ) → deadlocks; using NOFAIL too loosely → stalls entire system; ATOMIC can fail often.

Great, you’ve captured the core trick of the buddy allocator 📖 — the binary buddy system. Let’s go step by step with explanation + a practical example so you can visualize how Linux allocates and frees physical pages.

1️⃣ The Idea of Buddy Allocator
Physical memory is divided into blocks of size 2^order pages (order = 0 means 1 page, order = 1 means 2 pages, etc.).

Free lists are maintained for each order in each zone (Normal, DMA, etc).

On allocation:

If exact block size is unavailable, a higher-order block is split into “buddies”.

On freeing:

Allocator tries to merge (coalesce) a block with its buddy into a higher-order block.

Key trick:
The buddy of a block can be found by flipping a single bit in the PFN (Page Frame Number).

2️⃣ Why flipping a bit works
Every block is aligned to its own size.

Example: order-3 block = 2^3 = 8 pages.
→ Aligned to multiples of 8 PFNs.

So, given PFN = 0b01011000 (PFN 88 decimal):

It represents the base of an order-3 block (8 pages).

Its buddies when split are:

Block 1: PFNs 0b01011000 to 0b01011011 (88–91)

Block 2: PFNs 0b01011100 to 0b01011111 (92–95)

How to find buddy of a given block?

Just flip the bit at the position = order.

E.g. for order-2 block at PFN 0b01011000, flip bit 2:

0b01011000 ^ (1 << 2) = 0b01011100.

So 88 (0x58) and 92 (0x5C) are buddies at order-2.

3️⃣ Coalescing on free
When freeing:

Look at freed block’s PFN.

Compute buddy PFN by flipping the order bit.

If buddy is also free (in the same order’s freelist), remove both and merge into order+1 block.

Repeat recursively up to MAX_ORDER.

So allocation splits downward, freeing merges upward.

4️⃣ Practical Example
Say memory zone starts with 64 free pages (order=6 block).

Step A: Allocate 8 pages (order=3)
Buddy allocator doesn’t have an order-3 block → splits:

Order-6 (64p) → two order-5 (32p).

Take one order-5, split → two order-4 (16p).

Take one order-4, split → two order-3 (8p).

Return PFN=0 (pages 0–7).

Free lists now:

Order-6: 0

Order-5: 1 block (pages 32–63)

Order-4: 1 block (pages 16–31)

Order-3: 1 block (pages 8–15)

Step B: Free PFN=0 (8p, order=3)
Buddy = PFN=8 (flip bit 3).

PFN=8–15 is free (in freelist).

Merge → new block at PFN=0, order=4 (16 pages).

Now order-4 freelist has two blocks (0–15 and 16–31).

Kernel may later merge these into an order-5 (0–31).

5️⃣ Metadata organization (last photo explanation)
Each pg_data_t = one NUMA node.

Contains node_zones[MAX_NR_ZONES].

Each zone (Normal/DMA/Movable) has:

zone->free_area[MAX_ORDER].

Each free_area[order] has a list of free blocks of size 2^order.

Protected by zone->lock (a spinlock, because allocations can happen in IRQ/atomic context → can’t sleep).

So memory allocator = hierarchy:

Node (pg_data_t)
 └─ Zone (Normal/DMA/etc)
     └─ free_area[MAX_ORDER]
         └─ freelist of blocks of 2^order pages
6️⃣ Why this is efficient
Finding buddy = O(1) (flip one bit).

Splitting/merging = logarithmic in order (MAX_ORDER steps max).

Linux MAX_ORDER ~11 (so max block ~4 MB on 4K pages).

Thus both allocation & free are extremely fast.

7️⃣ Practical Caveats
Internal fragmentation: If you need 5 pages, buddy alloc gives 8 (order-3). Wastes 3.

External fragmentation: Long uptime with random alloc/free → blocks scattered → high-order requests (e.g., THP 2M) fail even though total free memory is high.

Compaction: Kernel migrates pages to restore big contiguous runs.

CMA: Reserves special regions for guaranteed contiguous allocations.

✅ In short:

Buddy allocator: keeps memory in power-of-two blocks.

Buddy found by bit flip of PFN.

Free merges upward, alloc splits downward.

Managed per zone with free_area[] lists.

1️⃣ First picture (NR_PCP_LISTS / PCP structure)
This explains the per-CPU pageset (PCP):

What it is:
Each CPU keeps a small cache of free pages, organized by migration type (MOVABLE, RECLAIMABLE, UNMOVABLE, CMA, ISOLATE) and by order (block size).

Why:
To avoid global spinlock contention on the zone’s buddy allocator for every alloc/free.
→ Most allocations are order-0 (single pages), so keeping per-CPU freelists avoids locking.

Key fields:
lock → spinlock to protect PCP list when bulk draining/refilling.

IRQ-save variant (pcp_spin_lock_irqsave) is used because alloc/free can happen in IRQ context.

We disable IRQs locally so that the same CPU cannot deadlock itself if an IRQ handler tries to allocate/frees while holding the lock.

count → number of base pages currently cached in PCP.

Each alloc/free updates this.

high → high watermark.

If PCP exceeds this many pages, extra pages are drained back to the zone buddy free lists.

Keeps caches bounded.

batch → how many pages to transfer between PCP and zone buddy lists at once.

Example: If PCP empty, refill a “batch” from zone buddy.

If PCP > high, drain a batch back.

Tuned by zone_batchsize(), default is min(1MB, 0.1% of zone).

free_factor → modifies how aggressively to free back larger order pages.

Avoids PCP hoarding higher-order blocks that fragment memory.

Implements exponential back-off: the larger the block, the more quickly it is freed back.

expire → PCPs are per-CPU but memory can belong to other NUMA nodes.

This field is used by refresh_cpu_vm_stats() to expire PCP pages for remote zones after a delay, to rebalance across CPUs.

lists[] → actual linked lists of pages, separated by migrate type and order.

2️⃣ Second picture (alloc path diagram)
This is the allocator call graph:

alloc_page(), get_zeroed_page(), __get_free_pages(), kmalloc_order() all funnel into → alloc_pages().

alloc_pages() picks correct NUMA node → _alloc_pages().

_alloc_pages() first tries fastpath PCP → if fails, calls slowpath buddy allocator.

If still fails, _alloc_pages_bulk() can batch allocate for efficiency.

This is the flow from API to buddy.

3️⃣ Page alloc costly order
Defined as PAGE_ALLOC_COSTLY_ORDER (currently 3, i.e. 8 contiguous pages).

Meaning:

For orders ≤ 3, PCP caching is used.

For orders > 3 (like huge pages), PCP caching is bypassed → allocations go straight to buddy.

Why?

Large allocations are rare and need true contiguity.

Caching large blocks in PCP would fragment memory and quickly drain buddy lists.

So PCP is optimized only for small orders (≤ 3 pages = 32 KB on 4K base pages).

4️⃣ Relation of PCP to costly order
PCP lists exist for orders 0..PAGE_ALLOC_COSTLY_ORDER.

Each CPU will cache only small/medium pages; larger requests bypass PCP → go to buddy with locks.

Transparent Huge Pages (THP) add an extra PCP order (NR_PCP_THp) if configured.

5️⃣ Why IRQ-save variant is used
Per-CPU allocator lock protects PCP lists.

Alloc/free can be called in hard IRQ context (e.g. networking, block I/O).

If an IRQ handler ran in the middle of holding the PCP lock and also tried to take it → deadlock.

Solution:

Use spin_lock_irqsave() → disables local IRQs while lock held.

Prevents re-entrancy on the same CPU.

After unlocking, IRQ state restored.

✅ Putting it together (Practical Scenario)
A process calls kmalloc(128, GFP_KERNEL).

This uses alloc_pages(order=0).

_alloc_pages() first looks in the current CPU’s PCP freelist (order 0, MIGRATE_UNMOVABLE).

If present → take a page, count--, return.

Fast, no global lock.

If PCP empty:

Grab a batch (say 30 pages) from zone buddy → fill PCP → satisfy request.

If PCP count > high:

Drain extra pages back to zone buddy list in bulk.

If request was order=4 (16 pages > costly order):

Skip PCP → go straight to buddy allocator.

🔑 Key Takeaways
PCP pagesets = per-CPU page caches, not CPU hardware caches.

Optimized for small, frequent alloc/free (order 0–3).

PAGE_ALLOC_COSTLY_ORDER = cutoff for PCP caching.

irqsave spinlocks prevent deadlocks in IRQ contexts.

PCP keeps alloc/free fast and reduces spinlock contention on zones.

Batching avoids thrashing zone buddy lists.

Perfect ✅ These diagrams you shared are essentially the allocation path internals of the Linux memory subsystem — how the kernel goes from a kmalloc() or alloc_pages() request → checking PCP caches → buddy allocator → reclaim/compaction → fallback/OOM.

I’ll break it down step by step, layer by layer, so it’s clear in your head and you can confidently explain in an interview.

1️⃣ Big Picture
When kernel needs pages (via alloc_pages()), the flow is:

Fast path → Per-CPU Page Lists (PCP).

Cheap, no global locking.

Slow path → Zone’s buddy allocator.

Splitting/coalescing, fallback across migration types.

Slowest path → Reclaim / Compaction / kswapd / OOM.

Only if memory pressure.

2️⃣ First diagram (PCP vs Buddy)
Check if order <= PAGE_ALLOC_COSTLY_ORDER
        |
        +-- yes → use PCP list (rmqueue_pcplist)
        |
        +-- no → go directly to buddy (rmqueue_buddy)
PCP (Per-CPU Pageset): for small orders (0–3). Fastpath.

Buddy Allocator: for large orders or PCP miss.

Then:

If zone below watermarks → wake kswapd.

Else return page.

Interview point:
PCP = fast freelist for small allocations. Buddy = fallback general allocator. kswapd = background cleaner if pressure.

3️⃣ Second diagram (rmqueue flow)
This is the allocator inside a zone (rmqueue()):

Acquire zone->lock (spinlock, IRQ-safe).

If higher-order available & ALLOC_HARDER flag set → try that.

Example: atomic context may dip into reserved MIGRATE_HIGHATOMIC.

Try alloc from rmqueue().

If success → update zone stats → return page.

If fail → maybe try rmqueue_smallest() fallback.

Release lock.

Key:
This ensures atomicity when multiple CPUs allocate from the same zone.

4️⃣ Third diagram (rmqueue_fallback)
This is when buddy runs out of the exact migrate type or order:

If ALLOC_NOFRAGMENT set → stricter min order to avoid breaking blocks.

Otherwise, set current order = requested.

Loop downwards from MAX_ORDER-1 to min order:

If free list found → success.

If not → find suitable fallback.

Fallback rules:

If MIGRATE_MOVABLE unavailable → fallback to RECLAIMABLE/UNMOVABLE.

Steal pageblock if needed.

Edge case: choose smallest stealable page if nothing else.

Interview point:
Fallback = stealing from other migration lists → causes fragmentation. Last resort to avoid OOM.

5️⃣ Fourth diagram (rmqueue_buddy)
Core buddy allocator logic:

Set current_order = requested.

While current_order < MAX_ORDER:

Try to remove page from free_area list.

If found → split higher blocks down via expand().

Return page.

If not → increment current_order (search bigger block).

This is where the binary buddy splitting happens:

Large block found → split into smaller until reaching requested order.

Fast because buddy math = just bit flips.

6️⃣ Fifth diagram (get_page_from_freelist)
This is zone iteration:

Pick zones from zonelist (based on GFP mask, NUMA policy).

If cpusets enabled → check cgroup/cpuset permissions.

Check dirty page spread limits.

If ALLOC_NOFALLBACK → restrict to preferred node.

Check watermarks (min/low/high).

If zone passes watermark:

Try rmqueue() from that zone.

If success → return page.

If fail → maybe reclaim.

If all zones fail → go to reclaim/slowpath.

7️⃣ Sixth diagram (alloc_pages_slowpath)
Final safety net:

Initialize GFP + alloc flags.

Try get_page_from_freelist().

If success → return.

Else → reset GFP/nodemask/spread flags.

Try again via __alloc_pages_slowpath().

This triggers:

Direct reclaim (shrink_node)

Compaction (migrate pages, isolate)

Waking kswapd

Possibly OOM if everything fails

8️⃣ How to explain in interview (summary story)
Imagine I get asked: “Explain Linux page allocation internals.”
Here’s how you can say it smoothly:

"When the kernel needs pages, it first tries the per-CPU pageset (PCP) fast path. These are small freelists cached per CPU for order-0–3 allocations. If the page is found there, allocation succeeds without taking global locks.

If PCP is empty, or allocation is larger, the kernel calls into the buddy allocator via rmqueue_buddy. This maintains free lists of blocks in powers of two, per zone and per migration type. If the exact block isn’t found, the allocator may fallback to other migration types, or steal a pageblock, though that can cause fragmentation.

If even buddy can’t satisfy the allocation because the zone is below its watermarks, the kernel either wakes up kswapd (background reclaim) or enters direct reclaim in the calling thread. If reclaim and compaction both fail, eventually the OOM killer is triggered.

So in short: allocation is PCP → buddy → reclaim/compaction → OOM, with migration types and watermarks deciding the exact path.”

9️⃣ Sticky memory anchors (to always remember)
PCP = “my CPU’s pocket money for pages” (fast, no lock).

Buddy = “bank” (big allocator, slower, locks).

Fallback/steal = “borrowing from other buckets” → fragmentation.

Reclaim = “selling old stuff” (LRU shrink).

Compaction = “rearranging house to make one big free room”.

kswapd = “janitor cleaning in background”.

OOM killer = “evicting someone from house when no space left”.

Perfect 👍 — this last diagram you’ve shared is the freeing side of the Linux page allocator (the reverse of allocation that we discussed earlier). This is just as important in interviews because allocation and freeing together demonstrate understanding of lifetime of a page.

Let’s break this down carefully so you will always remember and can explain to an interviewer.

1️⃣ Big Picture of Page Freeing
When you call __free_pages(page, order) or indirectly free via kfree():

Decrement reference count (put_page()).

If refcount reaches zero → page is truly free.

If compound page (THP/hugetlb) → handled specially.

Page is returned either to:

Per-CPU Pageset (PCP) cache (fast path), or

Zone buddy allocator free list (slow path).

2️⃣ Walking through the Diagram
Step A: Entry
You free a page → call chain looks like:

kfree() → free_pages() → __free_pages() → __free_pages_ok()
First step is checking if the page is compound (THP/hugetlb).

Step B: Is page compound?
If compound page:

Might be a Transparent Huge Page (THP), hugetlb, or higher-order alloc.

Then call:

folio_put() (newer API)

destroy_compound_page() for teardown.

Each tail page references the head, so head cleanup tears down the structure.

If not compound:

Go to normal free path.

Step C: Reference counting
put_page() / page_ref_dec():

Each struct page has a refcount (how many users still map it).

Example: a page might be in page cache + mapped in 2 processes → refcount=2.

Freeing decrements → when 0, the page can actually be released.

Practical anchor:
Think of refcount as “how many people still have the key to this hotel room.” Only when last person leaves → housekeeping can clean and put room back to available list.

Step D: Fast path → Per-CPU Pageset (PCP)
If order ≤ PAGE_ALLOC_COSTLY_ORDER (small pages), free path tries to put the page into PCP freelist.

This is lockless per-CPU, so very fast.

But:

If PCP count > high watermark → batch drain to buddy allocator.

Uses flags PCP_CLEAR_BATCH etc.

Step E: Slow path → Buddy allocator
If PCP cannot take it (too big, or PCP full):

Acquire zone->lock (spinlock IRQ-safe).

Add page block to zone’s free_area[order] list.

Try coalescing with buddy → merge upwards into larger block.

Release lock.

Key:
This is symmetric with allocation:

Allocation splits downwards.

Freeing merges upwards.

3️⃣ Internal Free Page Flags
When freeing a page, kernel looks at internal flags in struct page:

PG_reserved → Reserved by kernel (not freed to buddy). Example: kernel image text/data.

PG_slab → Page belongs to slab allocator, goes back to slab cache not buddy.

PG_compound → Marks head of compound page (THP/huge). Tail pages have PG_tail.

PG_locked → Page is under writeback, cannot free.

PG_dirty → Page dirty (modified) → must be written back before reclaim.

PG_swapcache → Page is in swap cache → handled differently.

PG_active/PG_inactive → Page is on LRU list, freed via shrinkers.

So not every page goes directly to buddy!
Depending on flags, free path diverts:

Page cache page → drop from radix tree + LRU.

Slab page → back to slab.

Compound → special teardown.

4️⃣ Practical Example
👉 Suppose process frees a 4K heap page (free(ptr)):

User calls free() → libc eventually calls munmap() or returns chunk to kernel.

Kernel does __free_pages(page, 0).

Refcount hits 0.

Page not compound.

Goes into CPU’s PCP freelist. Count++.

If PCP count > high watermark → drain batch back to zone buddy.

👉 Suppose process unmaps a Transparent Huge Page (THP, 2MB):

Refcount of THP head page goes 0.

Tail pages are still marked PG_tail, but they point back to head.

destroy_compound_page() clears tail states.

Whole 2MB freed back to buddy in one go.

👉 Suppose freeing a page cache page:

Page is file-backed, PG_dirty set.

Cannot directly free — must go via writeback and LRU shrinker.

After written back and unmapped → PG_dirty cleared → goes to buddy.

5️⃣ Interview-Style Summary Answer
If asked: “Explain how Linux frees pages internally.”

You can say:

"When a page is freed, the kernel decrements its reference count. If the count is nonzero, the page is still in use somewhere and isn’t actually freed. If it hits zero, the kernel checks the page type. Slab pages go back to slab caches, page cache pages may need writeback, and compound pages like THPs need special teardown.

For normal pages, freeing first tries to put them in the per-CPU page freelist (PCP) for fast reuse. If PCP is full, or the page is a larger order, it goes to the buddy allocator. There, the allocator merges it with its buddy if free, recursively coalescing into larger blocks.

This makes freeing O(logN), but in practice very fast due to PCP caches and batching."

6️⃣ Memory Anchor (to never forget)
Think of freeing as returning a book to a library:

First, check if anyone else still has the book reserved (refcount).

If it’s a normal paperback, put it into the small shelf near the desk (PCP cache).

If shelf too full, push a bunch of books back into the main archive room (buddy).

If it’s a special edition (compound/slab), send it to the special collections desk.

Excellent 🙌 — this is the heart of the buddy allocator free path. Let’s walk through it as if we’re the kernel, freeing an actual physical page frame, checking migration type, and coalescing it back into larger blocks in the zone’s buddy pool.

1️⃣ Setup: Buddy System Recap
Memory managed in zones (DMA, Normal, Movable).

Each zone has free_area[MAX_ORDER].

order = 0: single 4K pages.

order = 1: 2 contiguous pages.

order = 2: 4 contiguous pages …

Up to MAX_ORDER (~2MB–4MB block).

Free lists are segregated by migration type:

MIGRATE_UNMOVABLE → kernel objects, not migratable.

MIGRATE_MOVABLE → user anon/file cache, migratable.

MIGRATE_RECLAIMABLE → slabs that can be dropped.

MIGRATE_CMA → reserved contiguous DMA region.

MIGRATE_ISOLATE → temp for compaction.

2️⃣ Example Scenario
Assume base page size = 4KB.
Zone Normal has some fragmented memory.

We’re freeing PFN = 20, order = 0.
(Physical frame 20 = address 20 * 4KB = 80KB.)

3️⃣ Step-by-Step Free Path
Step A: Reference counting
Kernel decrements page->_refcount.

If not zero → still in use (mapped somewhere). Stop.

If zero → page is really free. Continue.

Step B: Identify migration type
From page->flags and page->alloc_flags:

Anon/file → MIGRATE_MOVABLE.

Slab cache → MIGRATE_RECLAIMABLE.

DMA buffer → MIGRATE_CMA.

Suppose our page is anon → MIGRATE_MOVABLE.

Step C: Insert into buddy free_area
We free PFN=20 into free_area[0][MIGRATE_MOVABLE].

The buddy of PFN=20 is PFN=21 (flip lowest bit).

Buddy math:

buddy_pfn = pfn ^ (1 << order)
= 20 ^ (1 << 0)
= 20 ^ 1
= 21
Check if PFN=21 is free in same order/migrate list.

Step D: Coalesce if possible
Suppose PFN=21 is also free (in free_area[0]).

Remove both PFN=20 and PFN=21.

Combine into block [20–21], order=1.

Insert into free_area[1][MIGRATE_MOVABLE].

Now check buddy at order=1:

buddy_pfn = 20 ^ (1 << 1)
= 20 ^ 2
= 22
So our block [20–21] buddy is [22–23].

If [22–23] is also free → merge into order=2 block [20–23].

Repeat upward until MAX_ORDER or no buddy free.

Step E: Final Insertion
Suppose [22–23] was allocated → cannot merge further.

So block [20–21] stays in free_area[1][MIGRATE_MOVABLE].

4️⃣ Practical Flow (PFN Example)
Let’s say initially free lists look like this:

free_area[0][MOVABLE] = { pfn=5, pfn=7, pfn=21 }
free_area[1][MOVABLE] = { }
Now freeing PFN=20:

Insert 20 into order=0. Now {5,7,20,21}.

Buddy(20) = 21 → found in list. Merge.

Remove 20+21 → add block [20–21] at order=1.
→ free_area[1] = {[20–21]}.

Buddy([20–21]) = [22–23] → not free. Stop.

Final state:

free_area[0][MOVABLE] = {5,7}
free_area[1][MOVABLE] = {[20–21]}
5️⃣ Migration Types in Coalescing
Page freed goes back into the same migrate type freelist it was allocated from.

Example: freeing anon page → goes to MOVABLE lists.

CMA pages → only to CMA pool.

Exception: stealing in fallback during allocation — pageblocks can be retagged, so freed page might go into a different migration list (if the pageblock’s migrate type was changed).

6️⃣ Important Internal Flags During Free
PG_compound → if THP → free entire compound at once.

PG_slab → goes to slab allocator, not buddy.

PG_reserved → never freed to buddy.

PG_locked / PG_writeback → reclaim cannot free until I/O done.

PG_lru → pages must be dequeued from LRU before free.

7️⃣ Interview-Style 1-Minute Summary
"When freeing a page, the kernel first decrements its refcount. If it drops to zero, the page is put into the appropriate per-CPU list or zone buddy list based on its migration type. The buddy of a page is found by XOR’ing its PFN with 1 << order. If that buddy is also free, both are removed and coalesced into the next higher order block. This repeats recursively up to the largest order possible. Finally, the resulting block is inserted into the zone’s free_area[order]. This ensures fast merging and reduces fragmentation. Special pages like THPs, slabs, or CMA have their own free paths but ultimately large allocators still rely on buddy coalescing."

Buddy found with bit flip,

Freed into migrate type list,

Coalesced upwards.

1️⃣ The Key Structures
mm_struct
→ Represents the memory layout of a process.
→ Each process has one (shared between threads).
→ Important fields:

pgd → pointer to Page Global Directory (root of page tables).

mmap → linked list of VMAs (vm_area_struct).

mm_users, mm_count → refcounts.

→ Each contiguous VA range with same properties (anon/file, read/write, etc).
→ Example: heap, stack, mmap’d file.

Page tables (pgd_t, p4d_t, pud_t, pmd_t, pte_t)
→ Multi-level radix tree mapping Virtual → Physical.

2️⃣ 5-Level Page Tables on x86-64
Normally x86-64 uses 4-level paging (48-bit VA).
With 5-level paging (LA57) → up to 57-bit VA.

Levels:

PGD (Page Global Directory)

P4D (Page Upper Directory, only used if 5-level)

PUD (Page Middle Directory)

PMD (Page Table Directory)

PTE (Page Table Entry, points to actual PFN + flags)

3️⃣ First Diagram (4KB page, 5-level walk)
👉 Each VA is split into fields:

VA[56:48] → PGD index  
VA[47:39] → P4D index  
VA[38:30] → PUD index  
VA[29:21] → PMD index  
VA[20:12] → PTE index  
VA[11:0]  → Offset within 4KB page
Walk:

CPU starts from mm_struct->pgd.

Extract top bits (PGD index), find entry.

Follow down through P4D → PUD → PMD.

At PTE, you get PFN + flags.

Add VA offset → physical address.

💡 This is the slow path. Fast path uses TLB cache.

4️⃣ Second Diagram (2MB Huge Page)
Here PMD entry has a "hugepage" bit set.

Instead of pointing to a PTE table, PMD maps directly a 2MB contiguous range.

VA split:

VA[56:48] → PGD
VA[47:39] → P4D
VA[38:30] → PUD
VA[29:21] → PMD
VA[20:0]  → Offset within 2MB page
Result:
→ Skips the PTE level entirely.
→ Saves one indirection, fewer TLB entries.

5️⃣ Third Diagram (1GB Huge Page)
Here PUD entry has hugepage bit set.

Maps 1GB contiguous block directly.

VA split:

VA[56:48] → PGD
VA[47:39] → P4D
VA[38:30] → PUD (huge page!)
VA[29:0]  → Offset within 1GB page
6️⃣ Fourth Diagram (4-level, 4KB page)
Same concept, but without P4D (legacy x86-64).

VA split:

VA[47:39] → PGD
VA[38:30] → PUD
VA[29:21] → PMD
VA[20:12] → PTE
VA[11:0]  → Offset
This is the most common Linux config today (48-bit VA).

7️⃣ Fifth Diagram (1GB Huge Page, 4-level)
Skips PTE + PMD levels.

PUD entry itself maps 1GB.

8️⃣ Relating to mm_struct
Let’s walk through malloc + access example:

Process malloc(4KB)

libc malloc → brk or mmap.

Kernel updates mm_struct->mmap (new VMA).

No physical page yet → just VA reserved.

First write (page fault)

Page fault handler (handle_mm_fault).

Allocates physical page from buddy.

Updates page tables:

Walk mm_struct->pgd.

Create intermediate P4D/PUD/PMD if needed.

Allocate PTE table if not present.

Fill PTE → PFN + present bit.

Access again

TLB caches VA→PA, no page table walk.

If THP enabled:

Kernel may allocate a 2MB contiguous block and set PMD huge bit.

Then one entry maps 2MB of VA → PA.

If hugetlbfs:

mmap() with MAP_HUGETLB reserves pre-allocated hugetlb pages.

Then PUD/PMD entries map them.

9️⃣ Tie-In with What We Discussed Earlier
Anonymous pages (heap, stack) → mapped via PTEs (normal 4KB).

File-backed (ELF text, mmap files) → mapped via PTEs or THPs if eligible.

THP → collapses multiple PTEs into one PMD hugepage.

Hugetlb → user explicitly requests, kernel installs at PUD/PMD level.

CMA → used to ensure physical contiguity if device DMA requires it.

SMMU/IOMMU → does a second VA→PA translation for devices, but concept is same.

🔟 Interview 60-sec Summary
“Each process has an mm_struct, which points to the root of its page tables (pgd) and describes its VMAs. On x86-64, virtual addresses are translated by a 4 or 5-level page table walk: PGD → P4D → PUD → PMD → PTE → PFN. Normally PTEs point to 4KB pages. But if the hugepage bit is set in PMD or PUD, the walk stops early, mapping a 2MB or 1GB hugepage. Transparent Huge Pages (THP) optimize anonymous memory to use PMD-level hugepages, while hugetlbfs allows explicit user control. This whole structure is managed per-process in mm_struct, but backed by the global buddy allocator that provides the physical frames.”

1️⃣ What is mm_struct?
mm_struct = “Memory descriptor” of a process.

Every userspace process in Linux has exactly one.

It describes:

Virtual Address Space layout (via VMAs).

Page tables (root PGD).

Accounting (RSS, swap, NUMA policy).

Locks (semaphores, spinlocks).

Think of it as the master memory context for a process.

2️⃣ Kernel Code: Definition
(from include/linux/mm_types.h)

struct mm_struct {
    struct vm_area_struct *mmap;     /* List of VMAs */
    struct rb_root mm_rb;            /* RB-tree of VMAs */
    u64 mmap_base;                   /* Base addr for mmap */
    unsigned long task_size;         /* Size of userspace */
    pgd_t *pgd;                      /* Root of page tables */
    atomic_t mm_users;               /* User space threads using this mm */
    atomic_t mm_count;               /* Reference count */
    spinlock_t page_table_lock;      /* Protects page tables */
    struct rw_semaphore mmap_lock;   /* Protects mmap list/tree */
    unsigned long total_vm;          /* Total VM size in pages */
    unsigned long locked_vm;         /* Locked (mlock’d) VM */
    struct mm_rss_stat rss_stat;     /* Resident Set Size */
    struct list_head mmlist;         /* List of all mm’s */
    ...
};
3️⃣ Key Fields
mmap → linked list of all VMAs (struct vm_area_struct).

mm_rb → VMAs also stored in an RB-tree for fast lookup.

pgd → pointer to root page table of this process.

mmap_lock → read/write semaphore for VMA operations (mmap(), munmap(), brk()).

rss_stat → counts how many physical pages are resident (anon/file-backed).

mm_users → #threads sharing the same mm (thread group).

4️⃣ Example: Process Creation
Let’s walk through fork() → exec() using mm_struct:

Fork()
do_fork() → copy_process().

dup_mm() is called.

struct mm_struct *dup_mm(struct task_struct *tsk) {
    struct mm_struct *mm, *oldmm = current->mm;
    mm = allocate_mm();              // allocate new mm_struct
    memcpy(mm, oldmm, sizeof(*mm));  // copy fields
    mm->pgd = pgd_alloc(mm);         // allocate new top-level page table
    dup_mmap(mm, oldmm);             // copy VMAs
    return mm;
}
Creates a new mm_struct.

Copies VMA list from parent.

Copies PGD entries (page tables shared CoW until write).

Exec()
do_execve() → exec_mmap() → mm_init().

Old mm_struct is dropped.

New mm_struct created:

VMAs for ELF segments (text, data, bss).

Heap via brk.

Stack VMA.

pgd set up empty.

5️⃣ Example: malloc()
When you do:

char *buf = malloc(4096);
glibc malloc may call brk() or mmap().

Kernel takes mmap_lock and extends/creates a new VMA in mm_struct->mmap.

No physical page yet.

On first access → page fault → handled via handle_mm_fault().

handle_mm_fault(vma, address, flags):
    pte = get_locked_pte(mm, address);
    if (!pte_present) {
        page = alloc_page();             // buddy allocator
        set_pte_at(mm, address, pte, page_to_pte(page));
    }
6️⃣ Example Code: Inspecting mm_struct in Kernel Module
You can introspect in kernel:

#include <linux/module.h>
#include <linux/init.h>
#include <linux/sched.h>
#include <linux/mm.h>

static int __init mm_demo_init(void) {
    struct mm_struct *mm = current->mm;  // current process’s mm
    printk("Process: %s (pid=%d)\n", current->comm, current->pid);
    printk("  pgd: %px\n", mm->pgd);
    printk("  total_vm: %lu pages\n", mm->total_vm);

    return 0;
}
module_init(mm_demo_init);
When you insmod this module inside a process context (say insmod from a shell), you’ll see:

Root PGD address.

Total VM size.

Resident Set Size (how many pages in RAM).

7️⃣ Tie to Our Previous Discussions
Anon pages (heap/stack) → created in mm_struct->mmap as VMAs with no file backing.

File-backed pages (ELF, mmap) → VMAs with vm_file != NULL.

THP → page fault handler may install PMD-mapped pages in page table under this mm.

Hugetlb → special VMAs created with MAP_HUGETLB, tracked in mm_struct.

Cgroups → memory usage accounted per mm_struct.

SMMU/IOVA → devices DMA into PFNs that belong to a process mm_struct if SVM enabled.

8️⃣ Interview 60-sec Summary
“mm_struct is the per-process memory descriptor in Linux. It contains the process’s VMAs (describing virtual address ranges), a pointer to the root of its page tables (PGD), and accounting like RSS and total_vm. On fork, the child gets a new mm_struct with copied VMAs and shared page tables via CoW. On exec, a fresh mm_struct is created with new VMAs for the binary’s text, data, heap, and stack. During malloc, a new VMA is created in mm_struct, but physical memory is only allocated on the first page fault, when the fault handler walks the page tables under mm_struct->pgd and installs a PTE mapping to a physical page.”

Explain pgprot_t type, and all these flags, their use, practical scenario and caveats 
ChatGPT said:
Perfect question 🚀 — these diagrams are about page table entry (PTE/PMD/PUD/PGD) flags, i.e. the control bits in the hardware page table entries.
Let’s go step by step.

1️⃣ What is pgprot_t?
In Linux, pgprot_t is an abstraction for the protection and attribute bits of a page table entry.

Defined in arch/x86/include/asm/pgtable_types.h:

typedef struct { unsigned long pgprot; } pgprot_t;
It wraps the low-order bits of a PTE/PMD that encode access rights, caching, hugepage, dirty/accessed bits, NX, etc.

Kernel functions like pgprot_writecombine(), pgprot_noncached(), pgprot_kernel help construct these bits.

So → address + pgprot = complete PTE entry.

2️⃣ x86-64 Page Table Flags (from your images)
Key Bits:
Bit	Flag	Meaning	Practical Use	Caveats
0	_PAGE_PRESENT	Is the mapping valid (VA→PA)?	If 0, page fault triggered.	Swapped-out pages have P=0 but info in PTE for swap.
1	_PAGE_RW	Writable if set.	Kernel/user writes.	If 0, write → protection fault. Used for CoW.
2	_PAGE_USER	Accessible from user mode.	Distinguishes kernel-only vs userspace mappings.	Kernel addresses usually have U=0.
3	_PAGE_PWT	Page Write-Through cache policy.	Used for device memory requiring write-through.	Rare in normal RAM.
4	_PAGE_PCD	Page Cache Disable.	For MMIO, memory-mapped devices.	Shouldn’t be set for normal RAM (perf hit).
5	_PAGE_ACCESSED	Hardware sets on first access (R/W/X).	Used by Linux page reclaim (LRU).	Must be cleared by kernel to detect future use.
6	_PAGE_DIRTY	Hardware sets on write.	Used for deciding which pages need writeback.	Cleared by kernel after flush.
7	_PAGE_PSE	Page Size Extension (hugepage indicator).	At PMD: 2 MiB pages. At PUD: 1 GiB pages.	Requires contiguous physical memory.
8	_PAGE_PAT	Page Attribute Table (caching policy).	Controls WC/UC memory (graphics, MMIO).	Works with MTRRs.
9	_PAGE_GLOBAL	Mapping survives TLB flush on CR3 reload.	Kernel linear mapping.	Dangerous if misused in userspace.
10–11	_PAGE_SOFTW1-2	Software defined bits.	Used by Linux: _PAGE_PROTNONE, swap encoding.	Not visible to hardware.
12	_PAGE_PAT_LARGE	PAT flag for hugepages.	Cache policy for large pages.	Specific to PSE entries.
59–62	Protection Keys (PKEY)	Per-page protection keys (user-mode).	Fine-grained memory isolation (Intel MPK).	Only in newer CPUs.
63	_PAGE_NX	No Execute.	W^X policy, prevents code execution.	Security feature (DEP).
3️⃣ Relationship to Kernel / mm_struct
Each VMA (struct vm_area_struct) has vm_page_prot (a pgprot_t).

When Linux installs PTEs in page fault handler, it combines:

VMA flags (VM_READ/WRITE/EXEC).

Architecture default protections.

Then sets the final PTE bits accordingly.

Example:

pte_t pte = mk_pte(page, vma->vm_page_prot);
4️⃣ Practical Scenarios
Anonymous page (heap/stack): _PAGE_PRESENT | _PAGE_RW | _PAGE_USER | _PAGE_ACCESSED.

File-backed clean page (mapped from disk): _PAGE_PRESENT | _PAGE_USER | _PAGE_ACCESSED. (No _PAGE_DIRTY until written).

Kernel linear map: _PAGE_PRESENT | _PAGE_RW | _PAGE_GLOBAL.

Device MMIO: _PAGE_PRESENT | _PAGE_RW | _PAGE_PCD.

NX enforced heap: _PAGE_PRESENT | _PAGE_RW | _PAGE_NX.

5️⃣ Caveats
Accessed/Dirty: Only hardware updates them; kernel must clear to “monitor.”

Global: If wrongly used in user mappings → stale TLB leaks.

NX: Not available on old CPUs (pre-AMD64/NX-bit era).

PCD/PWT: If wrongly set on DRAM, performance tanks.

Soft bits: Kernel-specific encoding (e.g., swap entry encoding) → non-portable.

6️⃣ Interview 60s Answer
“On x86, every page table entry has address bits and attribute bits packed together. Linux abstracts the attributes as pgprot_t. These include present, writable, user/supervisor, cache policy (PWT/PCD/PAT), Accessed/Dirty for page reclaim, PSE/PAT for hugepages, Global for kernel mappings, NX for security, and software bits for swap/protnone. For example, an anonymous heap page is present, RW, user, accessed, NX; a kernel linear mapping adds Global; and device memory disables caching. These flags tie directly to VMAs in mm_struct via vm_page_prot and are installed by the page fault handler when building PTEs.”

What are software defined page, global page, cache disabled, protection key, devpage, soft dirty, uffd wp, no struct page, cpa test, prot none mapped page
ChatGPT said:
Excellent — you’re now asking about the “non-obvious” page types and flags that Linux attaches to PTEs, some hardware-defined, some software-only. Let’s unpack each one in detail, linking back to everything we discussed.

1️⃣ Software-defined page
These are PTE bits that hardware ignores, but Linux uses for its own bookkeeping.

Examples:

_PAGE_SOFT_DIRTY (soft-dirty tracking for mprotect(PROT_WRITE) + checkpointing).

_PAGE_PROTNONE (used to mark “present but inaccessible” → allows NUMA migration, swap-out tracking).

Swap encoding: PTEs with !present encode swap entry indexes in the “address” field.

✅ Use: Efficient kernel tricks without extra metadata structures.

⚠️ Caveat: Must not conflict with hardware-reserved bits.

2️⃣ Global page
Hardware flag: _PAGE_GLOBAL.

Means: This mapping isn’t flushed from TLB on context switch (CR3 reload).

✅ Use: Kernel’s linear/direct map (low-level identity mapping of RAM) stays always in TLB for performance.

⚠️ Caveat: Should not be set for user pages (stale TLB leaks across processes → security risk).

3️⃣ Cache disabled page
Flags: _PAGE_PCD (Page Cache Disable), _PAGE_PWT (Write-Through).

Means: CPU won’t cache accesses; all reads/writes go to memory or bus.

✅ Use:

MMIO (memory-mapped registers of devices).

Framebuffers where caching would cause coherency issues.

⚠️ Caveat: Never use on normal RAM → kills performance.

4️⃣ Protection Key (PKEY) pages
Hardware support: Intel MPK (Memory Protection Keys).

Uses bits 59–62 in PTE.

Each page gets a “protection domain.”

User process can change access rights to domains via WRPKRU instruction without kernel involvement.

✅ Use: Fast per-thread isolation inside same address space (e.g. JIT sandboxing).

⚠️ Caveat: Only available on modern x86 CPUs; adds complexity.

5️⃣ Devmap (device-mapped page)
Linux internal concept → _PAGE_DEVMAP.

Means: Page belongs to device memory (like persistent memory / DAX).

In this case, there may be no real struct page backing or it’s special.

✅ Use: Direct access (DAX), GPU device memory.

⚠️ Caveat: Not swappable; page refcounting different.

6️⃣ Soft-dirty page
Software-defined PTE flag (_PAGE_SOFT_DIRTY).

Kernel sets it when a page is written to after being marked clean.

Used by:

CRIU (Checkpoint/Restore In Userspace).

Userfaultfd + live migration (track which pages changed).

✅ Use: Track incremental changes without kernel overhead.

⚠️ Caveat: Needs explicit reset by prctl() or clear_refs.

7️⃣ UFFD-WP (Userfaultfd Write Protect) page
Flag: _PAGE_UFFD_WP.

Means: Userfaultfd is monitoring this page; writes will trap into userfaultfd handler.

✅ Use: Live migration, VM snapshotting, demand paging in userspace.

⚠️ Caveat: Slows down writes; must be managed carefully.

8️⃣ No struct page
Linux normally has a struct page for each physical page frame (PFN).

But for device memory, persistent memory, or some huge mappings, no struct page exists.

Kernel marks it with _PAGE_SPECIAL / _PAGE_DEVMAP → means “don’t try to refcount this.”

✅ Use: NVDIMM DAX (direct access storage) — bypass page cache, access persistent memory directly.

⚠️ Caveat: Normal kernel subsystems (LRU, swap) can’t handle these.

9️⃣ CPA test pages
CPA = Change Page Attributes (kernel API for changing caching attributes at runtime).

Example: set_memory_uc(), set_memory_wc().

CPA test mappings are temporary test PTEs set up while verifying attribute transitions.

✅ Use: Debugging, architecture verification.

⚠️ Caveat: Not used in normal runtime.

🔟 PROT_NONE mapped page
Linux trick:

Mark a VMA with PROT_NONE → user cannot access, but VMA still reserves VA range.

Implemented with _PAGE_PROTNONE bit (software-defined).

✅ Uses:

NUMA balancing: migrate page to another node while keeping VA stable.

Guard pages in stacks.

⚠️ Caveat: Still “present” in VMA, but any access faults into kernel.

🔄 How These Fit Into Our Thread
Anon pages: Present, RW, USER, DIRTY when written.

File-backed pages: Present, USER, may drop P=0 if evicted.

Tmpfs/shmem: File-backed but anonymous-like → can be soft-dirty tracked.

ZRAM/swap: Non-present PTE encodes swap slot instead of PA.

THP/MTHP: Use _PAGE_PSE (2MB PMD) or PUD (1GB).

CMA/hugetlb: Physically contiguous, still use normal PTE flags.

GPU/HMM: Device pages may be _PAGE_DEVMAP or _PAGE_SPECIAL.

Reclaim/migration: Use _PAGE_PROTNONE and soft-dirty bits to detect and track activity.

✅ Interview-ready 60s Summary:

“Linux uses both hardware-defined and software-defined PTE bits. Hardware ones include Present, RW, User, Global, Cache Disable, PAT, NX, PSE for hugepages, and PKEY for memory protection keys. Software ones include soft-dirty for CRIU, uffd-wp for live migration, prot-none for NUMA balancing, devmap for device memory, and no-struct-page for DAX memory. Together, they let Linux distinguish normal RAM, device memory, swappable vs pinned, and track dirtying/migration. For example, a GPU buffer may be marked _PAGE_DEVMAP and unswappable, while a migrating anonymous page is temporarily _PAGE_PROTNONE to fault back in.”
