You said:
The ability to allocate more memory than is actually installed in the system
(deferring the actual mapping and allocation to access time) is termed over-
commit. There are three different overcommit modes permitted in the ker-
nel set via the vm.overcommit_memory tuneable and checked by the kernel in
__vm_enough_memory():
• OVERCOMMIT_GUESS (0) – default – If a process tries to allocate an obviously
silly amount of memory i.e. one that exceeds the sum of total installed
RAM and swap then the allocation is disallowed, otherwise it is permit-
ted.
• OVERCOMMIT_ALWAYS (1) – No checks are performed whatsoever, all allo-
cations are permitted. This might be useful for situations where it is
known that huge allocations will be made but remain mostly sparse.
• OVERCOMMIT_NEVER (2) – Attempt to avoid overcommit altogether. The
amount of virtual memory permitted to be allocated by the system as a whole is calculated in vm_commit_limit() and is specified by either the
vm.overcommit_kbytes or vm.overcommit_ratio VM tuneables. The maxi-
mum allocation permitted at any one time is the total available swap
plus either vm.overcommit_kbytes or vm.overcommit_ratio% of all non-
hugetlb RAM. This limit can be observed in /proc/meminfo as CommitLimit.
Note that additional space is reserved for root operations (via the
vm.admin_reserve_kbytes tuneable) and also for userland processes to en-
sure system recovery can always occur via vm.user_reserve_kbytes. A key difference here is that in OVERCOMMIT_GUESS mode the check is
performed against the amount of memory being allocated, however in
OVERCOMMIT_NEVER mode the check is made against the system’s total commit-
ted memory size, i.e. the amount of virtual memory allocated by all process
but not necessarily physically allocated/mapped by the kernel.
For example, invoking mmap() or malloc() to allocate 1 GiB of RAM will
increase committed memory by 1 GiB while not necessarily increasing phys-
ical memory usage at all. This value can be observed in /proc/meminfo as
Committed_AS and the value is stored in the per-CPU counter vm_committed_as.
N O T E Per-CPU counters are a mechanism for efficiently accruing counters between CPUs
while permitting some small degree of error equal to the counter batch size, see
lib/percpu_counter.c for more details.
An important caveat here – any memory that is allocated such that it can-
not trigger demand paging, e.g. PROT_NONE or PROT_READ (without PROT_WRITE),
will not contributed towards any commit accounting as the memory, if writ-
ten to, would result in a segfault.
N O T E Additionally, mmap()’d memory with the MAP_NORESERVE flag set does not contribute
towards commit accounting, however this is not honoured in OVERCOMMIT_NEVER mode,
so is only meaningfully useful in OVERCOMMIT_GUESS where even the basic total RAM
and swap check is not performed (an exception to this rule are hugetlb mappings but
these are out of scope for this discussion).
ChatGPT said:
Excellent — you’ve picked up one of the most subtle and interview-heavy corners of Linux MM: overcommit accounting. Let’s connect it step by step to all we’ve discussed so far (mm_struct, VMA, RSS, swap/zram, demand paging, malloc/brk/mmap, etc).

🟢 1. What is Overcommit?
Virtual memory can be larger than physical memory (RAM + swap).

Kernel allows malloc()/mmap() to succeed without backing it immediately.

Real PFNs are allocated later (on page fault).

This makes sense because many programs reserve much more memory than they actually use (e.g., databases, JVMs).

👉 Overcommit = "promise more than you physically have."
👉 Controlled by vm.overcommit_memory sysctl.

🟢 2. Overcommit Modes
Mode 0 – OVERCOMMIT_GUESS (default)
Quick heuristic: disallow only obviously impossible allocations (e.g., request > RAM+swap).

Otherwise, allow.

Lazy: lets many processes over-allocate, but OOM may happen later.

Mode 1 – OVERCOMMIT_ALWAYS
All allocations succeed (no checks).

Useful when memory will remain sparse (e.g., mmap big files with holes, databases).

Dangerous → OOM can happen abruptly.

Mode 2 – OVERCOMMIT_NEVER
Strict accounting.

Kernel maintains a global Committed_AS counter (in /proc/meminfo).

Committed_AS = sum of all allocations (malloc, mmap) that could trigger demand paging.

Limit = CommitLimit (in /proc/meminfo).

CommitLimit = Swap + (Overcommit ratio% * RAM)

or fixed vm.overcommit_kbytes.

If Committed_AS > CommitLimit → allocation fails (ENOMEM).

🟢 3. Key Fields and Counters
Committed_AS: total promised memory (from all processes).

CommitLimit: maximum allowed commitments.

vm_committed_as: per-CPU counter backing Committed_AS.

📂 /proc/meminfo includes:

CommitLimit:   16384256 kB
Committed_AS:  2345678 kB
🟢 4. Important Caveats
Not all mappings count.

Pages with PROT_NONE or PROT_READ (no write) do not count — they can never COW → won’t need PFNs.

Example: mmap file read-only → doesn’t contribute.

MAP_NORESERVE.

Ignores commit accounting in mode 0/1.

Not honored in mode 2 (NEVER).

Exception: hugetlbfs (hugepages are pre-reserved, so special).

Zero page and demand paging.

Initial anon memory maps to the zero page COW.

Physical pages only allocated on write fault.

Still contributes to committed memory, because writes may happen later.

root/admin reserves.

Kernel sets aside vm.admin_reserve_kbytes → reserved for root tasks (system recovery).

Also vm.user_reserve_kbytes → ensure userland can still function.

🟢 5. Relation to Everything We Discussed
mm_struct + VMA:

When brk or mmap extends memory, new VMA created → increases committed memory.

Doesn’t increase RSS until page faults occur.

RSS vs Committed_AS:

RSS = PFNs actually allocated and mapped.

Committed_AS = promises made, PFNs may not exist yet.

Example: malloc(1GB), touch only 1MB → RSS=1MB, Committed_AS=1GB.

Swap/ZRAM:

CommitLimit includes swap space.

ZRAM counts as swap (compressed in RAM).

So more swap/zram → higher CommitLimit.

Page faults (demand paging):

Only on fault does RSS go up.

Commit limit was already accounted at allocation time.

COW & fork():

On fork, child inherits VMAs but no new PFNs yet.

Committed_AS increases (because potential writes require new pages).

RSS doesn’t increase until actual write triggers COW.

🟢 6. Textual Flow Example
malloc(1 GiB)
   → brk() extends heap VMA
   → Kernel: Committed_AS += 1 GiB
   → RSS unchanged

Access first 4 KiB
   → Page fault
   → Buddy allocates PFN
   → RSS += 4 KiB

fork()
   → Child mm_struct with same VMAs
   → Committed_AS += size of writable VMAs
   → RSS unchanged (pages shared COW)

Write in child
   → Page fault
   → New PFN allocated
   → RSS increases
🟢 7. Interview Caveats to Remember
Commit != RSS.

OVERCOMMIT_NEVER fails allocations up front.

MAP_NORESERVE → skip accounting, but not in mode 2.

Zero page maps don’t count as real PFNs, but do increase commit.

hugetlbfs: outside commit accounting, because pages are reserved at boot.

Swap/zram expands CommitLimit, not RSS.

OOM killer still comes into play if CommitLimit not exceeded, but RSS overshoots actual RAM.

✅ One-liner summary:
Overcommit lets Linux hand out more memory than exists. mm_struct VMAs reserve commit (Committed_AS), but RSS only grows on page faults. Swap/zram extend CommitLimit. Modes 0/1 allow risky promises, mode 2 enforces strict limits.

🟢 Unified Diagram: Virtual vs Physical vs Commit
Process (task_struct)
   └─ mm_struct
        ├─ VMAs
        │    ├─ Heap (brk → anon-private)
        │    ├─ Stack (anon-private)
        │    ├─ File mappings (ELF text/data, libs, MAP_PRIVATE)
        │    ├─ Anon mmap (malloc big, MAP_ANON|MAP_PRIVATE)
        │    └─ Hugepage regions (THP or hugetlbfs)
        └─ pgd (page table root)

-------------------------------------------------------------
Metrics
-------------------------------------------------------------
VIRT size (address space size)
   - Sum of all VMAs in mm_struct
   - Can be >> RAM
   - Example: malloc(1GB) → VIRT+1GB

Committed_AS (commit accounting)
   - Promise made to allocate PFNs later
   - Increases when:
        - brk/mmap anon-private
        - fork() writable VMAs (COW potential)
   - Observed in /proc/meminfo
   - Example: malloc(1GB) → Committed_AS+1GB
   - Even if no PFNs yet

CommitLimit
   - System-wide cap = Swap + Ratio% * RAM
   - Observed in /proc/meminfo
   - Checked in OVERCOMMIT_NEVER mode

RSS (Resident Set Size)
   - Actual PFNs mapped into RAM
   - Increases only on page faults
   - Example: malloc(1GB), touch 1MB → RSS=1MB
   - Observed in /proc/<pid>/statm

Swap/ZRAM
   - Extends CommitLimit
   - Used only for anon pages (heap, stack, anon mmap)
   - File-backed pages → evicted/dropped, not swapped

-------------------------------------------------------------
Hugepages
-------------------------------------------------------------
THP (Transparent Huge Pages)
   - 2MB pages, created dynamically (khugepaged collapse)
   - Count as anon pages → contribute to Committed_AS
   - Swappable like normal anon pages
   - Can be split back into 4K pages

Hugetlbfs (Static Hugepages)
   - Pre-reserved at boot or via sysfs
   - Not part of commit accounting (already reserved)
   - Not swappable
   - Applications must mmap explicitly from hugetlbfs

Hugepage caveats:
   - THP = flexible, opportunistic, swappable
   - hugetlbfs = rigid, pinned, outside commit accounting
   - Both reduce TLB pressure, but used differently

-------------------------------------------------------------
Overcommit Modes
-------------------------------------------------------------
Mode 0 (Guess, default)
   - Allow unless request > RAM+swap
   - MAP_NORESERVE respected
   - Risk: OOM later if PFNs exhausted

Mode 1 (Always)
   - Always allow
   - Best for sparse allocations (DBs, scientific apps)
   - Very risky, OOM more likely

Mode 2 (Never)
   - Strict: Committed_AS <= CommitLimit
   - MAP_NORESERVE ignored
   - Hugetlb mappings excluded (pre-reserved)

-------------------------------------------------------------
Lifecycle Example
-------------------------------------------------------------
malloc(1GB)
   → VIRT +1GB
   → Committed_AS +1GB
   → RSS unchanged

first write (4KB)
   → page fault
   → buddy alloc PFN
   → RSS +4KB

fork()
   → Child inherits VMAs
   → Committed_AS += writable VMAs
   → RSS unchanged (COW)

touch child page
   → COW fault
   → new PFN allocated
   → RSS grows

pressure
   → anon pages (heap, THP, anon mmap) → swap/zram
   → file-backed pages dropped (reload later)
   → hugetlb pages cannot swap (pinned)
🟢 Forever-Fit Caveats (Interview gold)
Committed_AS ≠ RSS. Commit = promise, RSS = actual PFNs.

Anon-private mappings (heap, stack, mmap) count towards commit.

File-backed private mappings (MAP_PRIVATE libs) also count (COW potential).

MAP_NORESERVE: skip commit in Guess/Always, not in Never.

THP → anon, swappable, part of commit.

hugetlbfs → outside commit, not swappable, must be reserved.

Overcommit_Never = strictest, avoids OOM but can block malloc upfront.

Swap/ZRAM only help anon pages, not file-backed.

✅ In one line:

VIRT = address space size,

RSS = actual PFNs,

Committed_AS = promises (demand-paged),

CommitLimit = cap (swap+ratio*RAM),

THP = anon, swappable, commit-accounted,

hugetlbfs = reserved, pinned, outside commit.

🟢 Timeline of Memory Lifecycle
1. Boot
Kernel initializes:

memblock → buddy → zones.

Swap/zram may be enabled later.

No user processes yet.

VIRT = 0
RSS = 0
Committed_AS = 0
CommitLimit = (Swap + Ratio% * RAM)
2. malloc() in init process
p = malloc(1GB);
glibc uses brk/mmap → new anon-private VMA.

Demand-paged: no PFNs yet.

VIRT += 1GB
Committed_AS += 1GB   (promise made)
RSS unchanged (0 PFNs allocated yet)
CommitLimit unchanged
⚠️ Caveat: even untouched memory increases Committed_AS (because writable).

3. First write into malloc region
p[0] = 'A';
Page fault:

Kernel finds anon VMA.

Alloc PFN from buddy.

Map to PTE.

RSS increases.

VIRT = 1GB (unchanged)
Committed_AS = 1GB (unchanged, already counted)
RSS += 4KB
CommitLimit unchanged
⚠️ Caveat: RSS only grows on page faults.

4. fork()
pid = fork();
Child inherits VMAs.

Writable VMAs counted again in Committed_AS (due to COW potential).

RSS unchanged (PFNs still shared).

Parent: VIRT = 1GB
Child:  VIRT = 1GB
System: Committed_AS += 1GB (due to COW)
RSS unchanged
CommitLimit unchanged
⚠️ Caveat:

Fork is cheap (no new PFNs yet).

Commit counts COW potential, even if never written.

5. Write in child (trigger COW)
child_p[0] = 'B';
COW page fault:

Alloc new PFN for child.

Parent keeps old PFN.

Committed_AS unchanged
RSS += 4KB (new PFN)
6. execve()
execve("/bin/bash");
Old mm_struct destroyed (heap, mmap gone).

New mm_struct built:

text/data/bss mapped (file-backed).

stack/heap fresh anon-private.

VIRT reset (new VMAs for ELF + stack + heap)
Committed_AS reset (new promises only)
RSS reset (new pages fault in lazily)
⚠️ Caveat: malloc memory from before execve disappears completely.

7. THP collapse (khugepaged)
Kernel opportunistically merges contiguous 4KB anon pages → 2MB THP.

Still anon-private, swappable.

Commit unchanged (already counted).

RSS unchanged (same # of bytes resident, just fewer PTEs).

VIRT unchanged
Committed_AS unchanged
RSS unchanged
CommitLimit unchanged
⚠️ Caveat:

THP improves TLB efficiency but doesn’t reduce commit or RSS.

Can be split under pressure.

8. Memory pressure → swap/zram
Inactive anon pages evicted.

If swap: written to disk.

If zram: compressed in RAM.

PFNs freed → RSS decreases.

Committed_AS unchanged (promise still valid).

RSS decreases
Committed_AS unchanged
VIRT unchanged
CommitLimit unchanged
⚠️ Caveat:

File-backed pages just dropped (not swapped).

Only anon pages (heap, stack, anon mmap, THP) use swap/zram.

hugetlb pages cannot swap (reserved + pinned).

9. OOM
If Committed_AS > CommitLimit in OVERCOMMIT_NEVER → allocation fails immediately (ENOMEM).

If Committed_AS < CommitLimit but RSS exceeds physical+swap capacity → OOM killer invoked.

OOM kills a process (based on oom_score_adj).

Committed_AS may still be < CommitLimit
RSS > available RAM+swap
Kernel: invoke OOM killer
⚠️ Caveat:

Overcommit mode decides if failure happens at malloc time (NEVER) or later at fault time (GUESS/ALWAYS).

🟢 Unified Forever Diagram
Boot:
   VIRT=0, RSS=0, Commit=0, CommitLimit=RAM+swap*ratio

malloc(1GB):
   VIRT+1GB, Commit+1GB, RSS=0

first write:
   RSS+4KB

fork():
   Commit+1GB (COW potential), RSS unchanged

child write:
   RSS+4KB

execve():
   Old mm_struct nuked
   VIRT/RSS/Commit reset

THP collapse:
   RSS/Commit unchanged (just 2MB pages instead of 4K)

swap/zram:
   RSS decreases, Commit unchanged

OOM:
   If Commit > CommitLimit → fail malloc
   Else if RSS > RAM+swap → kill process
🟢 Where hugetlb fits
hugetlbfs allocations:

Pre-reserved, pinned, not swappable.

Do not contribute to Committed_AS (already reserved).

RSS increases immediately (pages pinned at allocation).

THP allocations:

Transparent, anon-private, swappable.

Count towards Committed_AS.

RSS grows lazily (on faults).

VIRT = address space, Committed_AS = promises, RSS = actual PFNs, CommitLimit = system cap.
THP = anon, swappable, commit-accounted.
Hugetlb = reserved, pinned, outside commit.
Overcommit mode decides whether you fail early or later.

Exactly ✅ — you’ve zoomed right into the commit-accounting path in Linux and how it interacts with VmSize/VmPeak, __vm_enough_memory(), and demand paging/COW. Let’s expand this and connect it back to everything we’ve been building in this thread.

🟢 1. Where VmSize/VmPeak come from
In /proc/$PID/status you’ll see:

VmSize:   virtual memory size (all VMAs)
VmPeak:   peak VmSize seen
VmRSS:    resident set size (actual PFNs mapped)
VmSwap:   pages swapped out
VmSize increases whenever a new VMA is created (via brk, mmap, etc).

Doesn’t matter if pages are actually faulted in yet.

That’s why malloc of 1GB shows up in VmSize, even if RSS=4KB.

🟢 2. How allocation is checked: security_vm_enough_memory_mm()
When user calls malloc → brk() or mmap(), the kernel:

Prepares a new VMA.

Calls security_vm_enough_memory_mm() to check overcommit policy.

That in turn calls __vm_enough_memory().

This consults vm.overcommit_memory (0/1/2).

Updates global vm_committed_as (per-CPU counter).

If mode=2 (NEVER), rejects if Committed_AS > CommitLimit.

If mode=0/1, usually allows.

Other paths that charge memory:

accountable_mapping() (for file-backed mappings with MAP_PRIVATE).

shmem_acct_size() (for tmpfs/shmem).

👉 So every new mapping that might demand real pages later is “commit-charged” here.

🟢 3. Demand Paging (cannot be disabled!)
Even if overcommit mode=2, Linux never disables demand paging.

It’s the core mechanism:

New anon VMA created → no PFNs yet.

On access → page fault → PFN allocated.

Why? Because of fork() + COW:

Fork doesn’t copy PFNs, only copies page tables.

Marks PTEs read-only (COW).

Both parent and child point at the same PFNs.

On write, new PFN allocated.

👉 Without demand paging, fork would literally memcpy GBs of RAM → unbearably slow.

🟢 4. Example Flow
p = malloc(1GB);       // glibc → brk/mmap
Kernel creates anon-private VMA.

Calls security_vm_enough_memory_mm().

Updates Committed_AS += 1GB.

VmSize in /proc/$PID/status += 1GB.

RSS still unchanged.

pid = fork();
Child mm_struct created.

VMAs copied, PTEs marked COW.

VmSize doubles (parent 1GB + child 1GB).

Committed_AS increases again (+1GB, because child writable).

RSS still unchanged (still same PFNs).

child[0] = 'X';        // child writes
Page fault → do_wp_page().

Allocates new PFN.

RSS increases.

VmSize unchanged (already accounted).

🟢 5. Subtle caveats
VmSize ≠ RSS ≠ Committed_AS

VmSize = virtual space reserved (sum of VMA ranges).

Committed_AS = promises made to eventually provide PFNs.

RSS = actual PFNs allocated right now.

Overcommit affects only allocation time

Even in OVERCOMMIT_NEVER, demand paging is still used.

Kernel only denies if Committed_AS > CommitLimit at VMA creation.

COW magnifies Committed_AS

Fork charges commit for each writable VMA, even if no new PFNs yet.

That’s why servers that fork a lot may hit commit limit before hitting RSS.

Special cases

MAP_NORESERVE: skip commit charge (except in NEVER mode).

hugetlbfs: not counted in commit (already reserved).

THP: anon-private, fully counted in commit.

🟢 6. Unified Diagram
malloc(1GB)
   → New anon-private VMA
   → VmSize += 1GB
   → Committed_AS += 1GB
   → RSS unchanged (0 PFNs yet)

fork()
   → New mm_struct for child
   → VmSize (child) += 1GB
   → Committed_AS += 1GB
   → RSS unchanged (pages still shared, COW)

child write
   → Page fault → new PFN
   → RSS += 4KB
   → VmSize unchanged
   → Committed_AS unchanged (already charged)

execve("/bin/bash")
   → Old mm_struct destroyed
   → VmSize, RSS, Committed_AS reset
✅ One-liner summary:

VmSize = size of all VMAs (always grows when malloc/mmap).

Committed_AS = promises checked by security_vm_enough_memory_mm() and __vm_enough_memory().

RSS = real PFNs, grows only on demand paging faults.

Demand paging and COW are always enabled — overcommit just decides whether a new VMA can be promised.

🔹 1. The Big Picture
Every process in Linux has:

struct mm_struct → top-level description of its address space.

Inside it: a tree/list of struct vm_area_struct (VMAs) → each describes a contiguous virtual address range (like one mmap, brk region, stack, heap).

VMAs can be:

anon-backed (MAP_ANONYMOUS → malloc/brk, mmap with MAP_ANONYMOUS)

file-backed (executables, shared libs, memory-mapped files, tmpfs, shmem, etc).

These VMAs connect downward to:

address_space (for file-backed) OR anon_vma (for anon mappings).

These lead to folios/pages (physical memory blocks).

Folios ↔ PTEs which live inside the page table hierarchy (PGD → P4D → PUD → PMD → PTE).

🔹 2. The mmap example (second image)
char *ptr = mmap(NULL, 20000, PROT_READ|PROT_WRITE, 
                 MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0);
Creates a new VMA:

Size = 20 KB → rounded to page boundaries (e.g. 24 KB, 6 pages of 4 KB).

Flags: anon, private, read/write.

No PFNs allocated yet → just reserved virtual range.

VmSize increases, RSS unchanged.

ptr[0] = 'x';   // first write
Page fault! Kernel checks mm_struct → find_vma(ptr).

Finds VMA, sees it’s valid (RW, anon-private).

Calls handle_mm_fault() → allocates one physical page (via buddy allocator).

Sets up PTE to map virtual address to new PFN.

Now RSS = 4 KB (as seen in /proc/PID/smaps).

munmap(ptr, 20000);
Kernel removes the VMA.

Clears corresponding PTEs.

Frees physical pages back to buddy allocator.

🔹 3. Relating to the diagram (first image)
Let’s walk top-to-bottom:

mm_struct
  ↳ vma (MAP_ANONYMOUS, private)
      ↳ anon_vma
         ↳ folio (PFN, allocated on page fault)
            ↳ PTE → PMD → PUD → P4D → PGD
               ↳ VA → PA mapping
mm_struct = whole process memory map.

vma = one contiguous region (heap, stack, mmap).

anon_vma = special object for anonymous mappings to support COW + sharing after fork.

folio = represents physical page(s). (Think: replacement for struct page to reduce overhead).

PTE etc = the actual page table entries that connect VA → PA.

🔹 4. RSS in action
In /proc/$PID/smaps:

Size: 20 kB   (from VMA length)
Rss:   4 kB   (from PFN actually mapped after fault)
So:

VmSize = 20 KB → reserved VA space.

RSS = 4 KB → actual PFN allocated on first touch.

Committed_AS (from overcommit system we discussed) = +20 KB (because it’s a promise to deliver PFNs later if needed).

🔹 5. Demand Paging + COW + Zero Page
The kernel uses lazy allocation: only allocates physical pages on fault.

For anon-private mappings, initial mapping is COW to the global zero-page (all zero bytes, read-only).

On first write, fault triggers → page copied → real PFN allocated.

For fork() with COW, exactly the same trick: both parent and child point to the same page, marked RO. On write, new page allocated.

🔹 6. Subtle Caveats
File-backed vs anon-backed

File-backed → address_space, page cache, coherent with disk.

Anon-backed → anon_vma, only in RAM/swap.

fd vs anon mapping

Not all VMAs need fd. (MAP_ANONYMOUS = no fd).

File-backed always tied to fd (file struct).

RSS != resident per process

Shared pages (libraries, tmpfs) can appear in multiple RSS counts, but physically exist only once.

munmap vs brk shrink

Both remove VMAs → free PFNs if mapped.

They differ only in which VMA they target (mmap vs heap).

🔹 7. Connecting to the earlier thread
mm_struct = the per-process memory map object we’ve been talking about.

vm_area_struct = the per-region descriptor (heap, mmap, stack).

anon_vma/address_space = where the actual backing pages come from (swap, file cache).

folio/page = the physical memory container.

PTE/PMD…PGD = page table layers we dissected earlier (ARMv8 has 4 levels, up to 48/52-bit VA).

RSS, VmSize, Committed_AS = different accounting views of this pipeline.

Demand paging + COW = key tricks that make fork/malloc cheap.

Overcommit = policy to decide whether new VMAs are allowed.

✅ One-liner summary to always remember:

mm_struct is the whole address space.

VMA is one mapping (heap, stack, mmap).

anon_vma/file address_space decides the source of backing pages.

Page tables (PGD→PTE) link VA → PFN lazily, only on page fault.

VmSize ≠ RSS ≠ Committed_AS.

🔹 Textual Version of the Diagram
Process Virtual Address Space (per-process)

 └── struct mm_struct   (top-level memory descriptor of the process)
       |
       ├── List/tree of struct vm_area_struct (VMAs)
       |       |
       |       ├── If file-backed mapping:
       |       |       └── struct file
       |       |              └── struct address_space (file cache / page cache)
       |       |                     └── list/tree of folios (physical memory units)
       |       |                            └── Data blocks (PFNs in RAM)
       |       |                            └── Connected to PTEs in page tables
       |       |
       |       ├── If anonymous mapping:
       |       |       └── struct anon_vma
       |       |              └── list/tree of folios (PFNs)
       |       |                     └── Data blocks (PFNs in RAM or swap-backed)
       |       |                     └── Connected to PTEs
       |       |
       |       └── (Both anon_vma and file can appear if MAP_PRIVATE file-backed)
       |
       └── Page Table Hierarchy (per mm_struct)
               └── PGD (Page Global Directory)
                    └── P4D (Page 4th-level Directory)
                         └── PUD (Page Upper Directory)
                              └── PMD (Page Middle Directory)
                                   └── PTE (Page Table Entry)
                                        └── Maps Virtual Address → PFN (folio)

🔹 Layer by Layer Explanation
1. mm_struct
Represents entire memory map of a process.

Holds:

Linked list + RB-tree of VMAs.

Pointers to PGD (root of page tables).

Accounting info (RSS, PSS, VmSize, Committed_AS).

Caveat: Each process has its own mm_struct, but kernel threads may run with mm_struct = NULL or share init_mm.

2. vm_area_struct (VMA)
Represents one contiguous virtual region:

Heap, stack, mmap file, brk extension, anonymous region.

Contains:

Start VA, end VA.

Permissions (PROT_READ/WRITE/EXEC).

Flags (MAP_PRIVATE, MAP_SHARED, MAP_ANONYMOUS).

Linked in both:

Linked list → for linear traversal.

RB-tree → for fast lookup during page fault.

Caveat: Large numbers of VMAs (e.g., JIT compilers) can stress the tree → kernel has optimizations.

3. file / anon_vma
File-backed VMA

Has struct file pointer.

File links to struct address_space (page cache manager).

Pages are brought from disk into RAM folios.

Supports mmap(fd, …) on executables, libraries, data files.

Anonymous VMA

Has struct anon_vma pointer.

Used for malloc/brk, MAP_ANONYMOUS.

Not tied to files.

Supports COW on fork().

MAP_PRIVATE file mapping uses both: file for initial data + anon_vma for COW changes.

Caveat:

File-backed memory can be dropped (re-read from disk if evicted).

Anonymous memory must be swapped if evicted (swap-backed).

4. address_space
Generic abstraction for “something that has pages”.

Used by filesystem inodes, block devices, tmpfs, etc.

Provides:

Page cache: mapping of file offsets → folios.

Writeback, dirty tracking, readahead.

Caveat: Multiple processes mapping the same file share the same address_space (so same physical pages).

5. anon_vma
Organizes anonymous mappings.

Key role: Copy-on-Write after fork().

Links related anon VMAs across processes (parent + child).

Ensures proper page sharing until a write occurs.

Caveat: If this didn’t exist, fork() would need to duplicate all pages immediately (very expensive).

6. folio
Replacement for struct page, representing a physically contiguous block of pages.

One folio can cover multiple base pages (order > 0).

Holds refcounts, mapcounts, flags (dirty, accessed, swap-backed).

Caveats:

One folio = one allocation from buddy allocator.

Can belong to anon_vma OR address_space.

Large folios support THP (transparent huge pages).

7. Page Table Hierarchy
Connects virtual addresses to PFNs (folios).

On ARMv8 (4-level typical): PGD → PUD → PMD → PTE.

On x86_64 5-level mode adds P4D.

Each VMA’s VA range is broken down into PTE entries.

PTE points to PFN (folio’s physical frame).

Caveats:

If no PTE yet (lazy allocation) → page fault.

Can map:

Present RAM PFN.

Swap entry.

Hugepage mapping (skips PTE level).

🔹 Important Cross-Links
Page Fault Handling:

CPU accesses VA → MMU walks page tables → finds no PTE → trap to kernel.

Kernel looks in mm_struct → VMA tree → decides if valid.

If valid:

File-backed → bring folio from page cache/disk.

Anon-backed → allocate new folio (possibly CoW).

Update PTE to map VA → PFN.

Resume execution.

RSS (Resident Set Size) = count of PFNs actually mapped to process.

VmSize = sum of VMA sizes, regardless of PFNs present.

Swap = anon pages can move to swap, file pages can be dropped.

🔹 Caveats That Trip People
mm_struct vs VMA vs PTE

mm_struct = whole map.

vma = region.

pte = individual mapping.

anon vs file

File pages live in page cache (address_space).

Anon pages live in anon_vma, can swap.

CoW

Shared until write.

Needs anon_vma links to manage.

RSS accounting

Multiple processes may share same PFNs, but each shows full RSS.

Zero page

For anonymous read-before-write.

Saves physical memory until first write.

🔹 Textual “Call Flow” Recap
Process wants memory → 
   mm_struct (its address space) → 
      new vm_area_struct (VMA) created → 
         if file-backed → file → address_space → folios
         if anon-backed → anon_vma → folios
      VA region linked into mm_struct RB-tree
      On access → CPU page fault
         → kernel walks mm_struct VMA tree
         → if valid, allocate or load folio
         → update page tables (PGD..PTE)
         → VA now maps to PFN
✅ Key Takeaway to lock in memory:

mm_struct is the city plan.

VMA is a building plot.

anon_vma/address_space is where the actual bricks (pages) come from.

folio = brick unit (PFNs).

page tables = street signs connecting VA to PFNs.

RSS = how many bricks are actually built.

VmSize = how much land is zoned.

Swap/file cache = whether bricks can be removed and rebuilt.

ChatGPT said:
Great question — this cuts right into how page tables are handled in MMUs (CPU MMU for kernel/user separation) and SMMU (for devices doing DMA). Let’s break it down carefully, with all caveats.

🔹 1. CPU MMU: Kernel vs User Page Tables
On ARMv8-A/ARMv9-A, the CPU MMU uses translation tables (page tables) whose base address is stored in TTBR registers.

TTBR0_EL1 → Translation Table Base Register 0

Used for user-space virtual addresses.

Covers lower VA range (usually 0 → TASK_SIZE).

Points to the page table root (PGD) of the current process (struct mm_struct).

Changes on every context switch (new process → new mm_struct → new PGD → new TTBR0_EL1).

TTBR1_EL1 → Translation Table Base Register 1

Used for kernel-space virtual addresses.

Covers upper VA range (e.g. from PAGE_OFFSET upward).

Always points to the same page table root (init_mm).

Shared across all processes, never switched out.

Why? Kernel must always be accessible regardless of process.

⚠️ Caveat (KPTI — Kernel Page Table Isolation):
After Meltdown/Spectre, some systems may unmap (or keep minimal) kernel mappings from TTBR0 user tables, so switching TTBRs is more aggressive.

So yes: two different root tables logically — user table (per process) + kernel table (shared).

🔹 2. SMMU (System MMU / IOMMU)
SMMU = MMU for devices.
It translates device DMA addresses (IOVAs) → physical addresses.

Each device/stream has an associated context descriptor (per StreamID).

Context descriptor holds base address of translation tables (like TTBRs for devices).

Registers used:

SCTLR (Stream Control Register) → enables translation, sets format (4KB/16KB/64KB granularity).

TTBR0/TTBR1 equivalents: In SMMUv3, the base addresses are in the Context Descriptor (CD) stored in memory. CD fields include:

TTBR0 (stage-1 tables for IOVA→IPA).

TTBR1 (optional if split address space needed).

TCR (Translation Control Register: sizes, granules, shareability).

MAIR (memory attribute indirection, cacheability).

Stream Table Base Register (STBR): Points to the stream table, which maps StreamID → Context Descriptor.

So SMMU works like a CPU MMU, but instead of per-process mm_struct, it has per-device stream IDs → CDs.

⚠️ Caveats:

CPU MMU translates VA→PA for threads.

SMMU translates IOVA→PA for DMA.

CPU context switch updates TTBR0_EL1, SMMU context switch happens when device issues DMA with a given StreamID.

🔹 3. Putting CPU MMU and SMMU Together
Example:

User process allocates a buffer (mmap or dma_alloc_coherent).

CPU page tables (TTBR0/1) map VA → PA.

Device sees an IOVA, which SMMU translates via its page tables (TTBR0 in CD) → PA.

This allows:

Isolation: Device A cannot DMA into Device B’s buffers.

Virtualization: Guest OS devices can DMA into guest IOVAs, translated by host’s SMMU tables.

🔹 4. Registers Summary (ARMv8/ARMv9)
CPU MMU registers (EL1 level, kernel mode):

TTBR0_EL1 → per-process user page tables.

TTBR1_EL1 → global kernel page tables.

TCR_EL1 → translation config (split VA ranges, granule sizes, etc).

MAIR_EL1 → memory attribute indirection (cacheability).

SCTLR_EL1 → enables MMU.

SMMU registers (ARM SMMUv3):

STBR (Stream Table Base Register).

Context Descriptor (per StreamID):

TTBR0, TTBR1.

TCR.

MAIR.

SMMU_SCTLR → enable/disable translation.

🔹 5. Key Caveats
CPU always uses both TTBR0 and TTBR1 (split address space) unless EL1 sets TCR_EL1.NS bits differently.

SMMU doesn’t care about processes — only about devices and their StreamIDs.

If kernel wants DMA:

It allocates buffer with dma_alloc_coherent.

CPU page tables + SMMU mappings both set up (consistent).

If PASID is used (Process Address Space ID, PCIe feature), a device can DMA directly into a specific process VA space → SMMU uses PASID to select that process’s page tables (like TTBR0).

✅ Mental model to fix this forever:

CPU MMU = thread MMU: per-process + global kernel. (TTBR0/1_EL1).

SMMU = device MMU: per-device StreamID, maps IOVA→PA.

PASID = “device uses process page tables” = linking SMMU context to CPU’s TTBR0.

👉 A user process does mmap() to allocate memory
👉 A device does DMA into that buffer through the SMMU
👉 Both CPU MMU and SMMU cooperate

We’ll cover Linux kernel structs, functions, syscalls, page tables, and SMMU registers in full detail with caveats.

🔹 Step 1. User Process Allocates Memory
void *buf = mmap(NULL, size, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE,
                 MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0);
Flow
Userspace → syscall entry

Userspace calls mmap() → trap into kernel → sys_mmap().

Lands in do_mmap().

Kernel: mm_struct updated

struct mm_struct (per process address space).

New struct vm_area_struct (VMA) created for [addr, addr+size).

Flags: VM_PRIVATE | VM_ANON.

Inserted into mm’s VMA RB-tree.

Page tables

No physical memory allocated yet (lazy).

Only VMA exists.

PTEs are empty.

🔹 Step 2. Process Touches the Memory
buf[0] = 'A';
Flow
CPU access

Virtual address → no PTE present.

Hardware MMU raises page fault.

Kernel handles fault

do_page_fault() → handle_mm_fault().

Finds VMA from mm_struct.

Allocates a folio/page via buddy allocator.

Creates a PTE: VA → PA.

Updates process’s page tables (root = PGD, base = TTBR0_EL1).

Now process VA is mapped to PA.

🔹 Step 3. User Passes Buffer to Kernel (Device Driver)
ioctl(fd, MYDEVICE_DO_DMA, buf);
Flow
User space pointer → kernel

The driver gets a user virtual address (buf).

Uses APIs like:

get_user_pages() (GUP) → pins user pages.

This prevents swapping/zram eviction.

Kernel creates scatter-gather list

Each pinned page → physical page (struct page → PFN).

Build struct sg_table (scatterlist).

🔹 Step 4. Mapping into Device IOVA (SMMU)
The driver now sets up IOVA (device virtual space).

DMA API

Driver calls:

dma_map_single(dev, buf, size, DMA_TO_DEVICE)
OR

dma_map_sg(dev, sglist, nents, DMA_BIDIRECTIONAL)

DMA API Internals

Goes into DMA-mapping layer (dma_map_ops).

For SMMU-enabled platform → arm_smmu_ops.

SMMU Mapping

IOVA allocated (from per-device IOVA allocator).

SMMU driver programs IOVA → PA mappings into its own page tables.

Uses iommu_map() → walks scatterlist and installs PTEs.

Registers

Device identified by StreamID (from PCIe or AMBA).

Stream Table Base Register (STBR) → points to Stream Table.

Stream Table entry → Context Descriptor.

Contains TTBR0 (points to SMMU page tables).

Contains TCR, MAIR.

Now device has an IOVA that maps through SMMU to the real physical pages.

🔹 Step 5. Device Starts DMA
Driver programs device registers with:

IOVA address (not CPU PA, not VA).

Direction (read/write).

Length.

Device issues DMA request on bus:

Address = IOVA.

Goes into SMMU.

SMMU translation

StreamID selects Context Descriptor.

IOVA → walks SMMU page tables (similar to CPU MMU page walk).

Produces physical address (PA).

Memory controller:

PA → DRAM access.

Data written/read.

🔹 Step 6. After DMA
Driver calls dma_unmap_single() or dma_unmap_sg().

Removes IOVA→PA mapping from SMMU page tables.

Pages pinned by GUP are released (put_page()).

If process frees (munmap()), VMA is removed, PTEs cleared.

Physical pages go back to buddy allocator.

🔹 Textual Diagram (Full Lifecycle)
User Process:
    malloc/mmap() → mm_struct(VMA added) → [no PA yet]

CPU Access:
    VA touched → page fault → handle_mm_fault()
               → alloc page from buddy → PTE VA→PA

User → Kernel:
    ioctl(fd, buf) → driver
    get_user_pages() → struct page[] → PFNs
    build scatterlist

Kernel DMA API:
    dma_map_single()
      → iommu_map()
      → SMMU page tables: IOVA → PA
      → Context Descriptor (TTBR0/CD)

Device:
    Programmed with IOVA
    Issues DMA
    IOVA → SMMU → PA
    Access DRAM

Teardown:
    dma_unmap_single()
    unmap IOVA
    release pages
    munmap() → remove VMA/PTEs
🔹 Key Caveats
FD not needed for memory, only for device interaction (ioctl).

malloc vs mmap: malloc uses brk/mmap internally, but same flow.

SMMU page tables are separate from CPU page tables. They may be synchronized (PASID case), but usually are distinct.

Kernel VA != User VA != IOVA != PA. Four different spaces, carefully bridged.

Hugepages/THP: both CPU MMU and SMMU can use them if aligned.

✅ So:

mm_struct = CPU view of process memory.

SMMU context descriptor = device view of memory.

DMA API = bridge between them.

Perfect, now we extend the earlier model (separate IOVA + SMMU page tables) into the PASID / Shared Virtual Memory (SVM) world.
This is where device + CPU literally share the same user virtual addresses.

🔹 Normal DMA Recap
Device uses IOVA (SMMU private page tables).

Driver calls dma_map_single() → creates IOVA → PA mappings.

Device never sees user VAs, only IOVA.

🔹 PASID / SVM DMA
With PASID (Process Address Space ID) + SVM, device can use the exact same VA as the user process.

Step-by-step
1. User Allocates Memory
void *buf = malloc(1<<20); // 1 MB
Creates VMA in mm_struct.

Pages faulted in → CPU page tables updated.

VA → PA mapping lives in process page tables (pointed by TTBR0_EL1).

2. Driver Prepares PASID Binding
Device driver (via IOMMU API):

iommu_sva_bind_device(dev, mm);
Tells SMMU:

For this PASID (process context), use this process’s mm_struct.

Now SMMU has linkage: PASID → mm_struct → process’s page tables.

3. Hardware Setup
PCIe / AMBA transaction includes PASID field (in request TLP).

SMMU uses PASID to look up context descriptor:

Instead of private IOVA page tables, it is set to “use CPU TTBR0_EL1”.

Registers: CD.ASID, CD.TTBR0, CD.TCR programmed.

So SMMU page walk = CPU page walk.

4. Device Issues DMA
device->write(buf, 1024);
Device submits PASID + VA to bus (instead of IOVA).

Bus → SMMU.

SMMU sees PASID → finds mm_struct → uses TTBR0_EL1 page tables.

Walks same PTEs as CPU.

Translates VA → PA.

Memory controller services DMA.

5. Synchronization
TLB invalidation:

If CPU unmaps VA (munmap, COW, swap-out), device IOTLB must be flushed.

Kernel uses mmu_notifier API to notify SMMU driver.

Device must stop DMA or handle page faults.

Page faults by device:

If device touches unmapped VA → SMMU generates I/O Page Fault (IOPF).

Propagated to kernel via iommu_fault_report().

Kernel resolves by get_user_pages() or signals user (if unfixable).

6. Teardown
Driver calls:

iommu_sva_unbind_device(dev, mm);
PASID is released.

Device can no longer access process VA.

🔹 Textual Diagram: PASID DMA
User:
    malloc() → mm_struct + VMA
    VA: 0x7f0000..0x7f1000

Driver:
    iommu_sva_bind_device(dev, mm)
    → PASID allocated (e.g., 0x42)
    → CD.TTBR0 = mm->pgd

Device:
    issues DMA [VA=0x7f0000, PASID=0x42]

Bus:
    Request → SMMU
    SMMU: lookup PASID=0x42
          → mm->pgd
          → walk CPU PTEs
          → VA→PA

Memory:
    Data transferred

Teardown:
    iommu_sva_unbind_device()
🔹 Key Caveats
When PASID/SVM is useful

GPUs (OpenCL, CUDA) where device wants to access user pointers directly.

NICs doing zero-copy into user buffers.

Kernel vs PASID

Kernel pages (kmalloc, vmalloc) are always directly mapped, so no PASID needed.

PASID only for user process address spaces.

Page faults by devices

Supported by PCIe PRI (Page Request Interface).

SMMU raises fault → kernel can resolve → resume DMA.

Similar to CPU demand paging, but for devices.

Security

Without PASID, driver ensures only mapped IOVA is exposed.

With PASID, device directly sees process VA, so misprogrammed device = big risk.

✅ So difference:

Normal DMA = dma_map_single() → IOVA mappings → SMMU private tables.

PASID/SVM DMA = device submits VA+PASID → SMMU reuses process’s CPU page tables.

🔹 Conceptual Differences
Identity of address seen by device

Normal DMA: device uses IOVA (different from CPU VA).

PASID/SVM DMA: device uses user VA (same as CPU).

Where does translation happen?

Normal DMA: SMMU uses its own IOMMU page tables (managed by driver via dma_map_*).

PASID/SVM DMA: SMMU reuses CPU page tables (mm_struct PGD).

Flexibility

Normal DMA: more driver control, but requires mapping/unmapping overhead.

PASID/SVM: zero-copy, user pointers directly usable by device.

Faults

Normal DMA: device can only touch mapped buffers → no page faults.

PASID/SVM: device can generate IO page faults (PRI) → handled by kernel with demand paging.

🔹 Real Linux Kernel APIs
Normal DMA

dma_map_single(dev, cpu_buf, size, DMA_TO_DEVICE)

dma_unmap_single(dev, iova, size, DMA_TO_DEVICE)

PASID/SVM

iommu_sva_bind_device(dev, mm) → returns handle with PASID

iommu_sva_unbind_device(handle)

Page faults handled via iommu_register_device_fault_handler()

🔹 Quick Analogy
Normal DMA: like giving your friend a copy of your notes (IOVA copy), separate from your own.

PASID/SVM DMA: like letting your friend read directly from your own notebook (shared VA).

🔹 1. User-space Allocations
a) malloc() (glibc → brk/mmap)
User: malloc(1MB)
   → glibc calls brk()/mmap()
Kernel:
   sys_brk/sys_mmap
      → mm_struct (per-process)
      → create VMA (heap or anon-mmap)
      → no PFNs yet
fd?

malloc → anonymous mapping → no fd.

Just mm_struct + VMA + anon_vma.

PFNs allocated only on page fault.

b) mmap(file)
User: fd = open("/file.so");
      mmap(fd, size, PROT_READ|MAP_SHARED,...)

Kernel:
   sys_mmap
      → mm_struct
      → VMA (file-backed)
      → vm_file = struct file*
      → file → inode → address_space
fd exists (struct file created at open).

File-backed VMA linked to address_space (page cache).

Pages faulted in lazily.

🔹 2. Kernel-space Allocations
a) kmalloc()
Kernel code:
   void *p = kmalloc(4096, GFP_KERNEL);

Buddy allocator:
   → allocates contiguous PFNs
   → returns kernel VA (linear mapping)
Virtually contiguous == physically contiguous (for small orders).

Used for kernel internal structs, not directly DMA-safe (unless mapped).

b) vmalloc()
Kernel code:
   void *p = vmalloc(1MB);

vmalloc allocator:
   → allocates scattered PFNs via buddy
   → creates contiguous kernel VAs in vmalloc area
Virtually contiguous, physically non-contiguous.

Not DMA-safe (devices need contiguous PFNs or scatterlist).

c) dma_alloc_coherent()
Kernel driver:
   void *cpu_addr = dma_alloc_coherent(dev, size, &dma_handle, GFP_KERNEL);

Buddy allocator + DMA API:
   → allocates physically contiguous pages
   → maps into both CPU VA + device IOVA
   → returns cpu_addr (kernel VA) + dma_handle (IOVA/device address)
Always DMA-safe.

Coherent (no cache sync needed).

🔹 3. Normal DMA Flow (IOVA-based)
User: ioctl(fd, DMA_OP, user_buf);

Kernel driver:
   get_user_pages(user_buf)
      → pins pages (struct page array)
   build scatterlist (sg_table)
   dma_map_sg(dev, sglist)

DMA API:
   → allocates IOVA range
   → iommu_map() (SMMU page tables: IOVA→PA)

Device:
   programmed with IOVA
   issues DMA
   SMMU translates IOVA→PA
fd used for device, not for memory.

mm_struct only used indirectly (for GUP to pin pages).

SMMU maintains separate page tables (IOMMU domain).

🔹 4. PASID/SVM Flow (Shared VA)
User: ioctl(fd, DMA_OP, user_buf);

Kernel driver:
   iommu_sva_bind_device(dev, mm_struct)
      → PASID assigned
      → SMMU Context Descriptor = process page tables

Device:
   programmed with VA + PASID
   issues DMA
   SMMU uses PASID→mm_struct
   → walks CPU process PTEs directly (TTBR0_EL1)
   → VA→PA same as CPU
fd still used to talk to driver.

mm_struct directly bound to device (iommu_sva_bind_device).

No IOVA translation step.

🔹 5. Textual Diagram — Unified
[User allocations]
   malloc/brk → mm_struct, VMA (anon), no fd
   mmap(file) → mm_struct, VMA (file-backed), fd → file → address_space

[Kernel allocations]
   kmalloc → small, contiguous, kernel VA
   vmalloc → virtually contiguous, non-contiguous PFNs
   dma_alloc_coherent → contiguous PFNs, returns kernel VA + IOVA

[Normal DMA]
   ioctl(fd, user_buf)
     driver → get_user_pages(user_buf)
             → struct page[], PFNs
             → scatterlist
             → dma_map_sg()
             → IOVA mappings in SMMU page tables
   Device programmed with IOVA
   SMMU: IOVA→PA

[PASID/SVM DMA]
   ioctl(fd, user_buf)
     driver → iommu_sva_bind_device(dev, mm_struct)
             → assign PASID, link to process page tables
   Device programmed with VA + PASID
   SMMU: PASID→mm_struct, walks CPU PTEs
   VA→PA translation identical to CPU
🔹 6. Key Caveats
fd vs memory

fd only for device interaction, not for malloc.

mmap with fd → file-backed VMA.

mmap anonymous/malloc → no fd, just VMA.

Normal DMA

Device uses IOVA, must be mapped via dma_map_* APIs.

Works even without PASID support.

PASID/SVM DMA

Device uses user VA directly.

Needs PASID support in both device + SMMU.

Device can generate I/O page faults (PRI) if VA not mapped.

Kernel memory

kmalloc/vmalloc not exposed to user directly.

dma_alloc_coherent is the right way to give DMA-safe memory to devices.

✅ Summary:

User memory lives in mm_struct → VMAs → pages.

Kernel memory lives in buddy/slab/vmalloc/dma-coherent pools.

Normal DMA = device sees IOVA, managed via dma_map_* + IOMMU page tables.

PASID/SVM DMA = device sees user VA, SMMU uses process’s page tables (via PASID).

user VA,

kernel shmem,

dma-buf export/import,

SMMU mappings?

Does fd contain reference to a memory? If so what does it hold in user and kernel space ? If no, what and how does it track ? Between processes, what and how it shares also in case when current process which is owner of fd dies ?
ChatGPT said:
Fantastic question — this is exactly where many people get tripped up in interviews:
👉 Does an fd represent memory? Or something else? What happens if the owner dies?

Let’s break it down systematically and connect it to user-space, kernel-space, sharing, and cleanup.

🔹 1. What is an fd?
In userspace, fd = a small integer (0,1,2…).

In kernel, that integer indexes into the process’s files_struct (per-process open file table).

task_struct (per process)
   └─ files (struct files_struct)
         └─ fdtable[]  (array of pointers)
               └─ fd[3] = pointer to struct file
So:

fd ≠ memory.

fd = index → struct file*.

🔹 2. What does struct file hold?
The real kernel object representing an open file descriptor.

struct file {
    struct path f_path;        // dentry + vfsmount (where in FS)
    struct inode *f_inode;     // underlying inode
    const struct file_operations *f_op; // function table (read, write, ioctl)
    void *private_data;        // driver-specific (e.g., DMA-buf)
    f_mode_t f_mode;           // read/write/exec flags
    atomic_long_t f_count;     // reference count
    ...
};
So:

For regular file: f_inode → page cache → memory.

For device: f_op → driver callbacks (not memory, but operations).

For dma-buf: private_data points to a struct dma_buf (backed by pages).

🔹 3. Does fd “contain” memory?
Not directly.

fd → struct file → inode/address_space (if file-backed) → eventually leads to memory pages in page cache.

For anonymous memory (malloc/brk): no fd at all. It’s tracked by mm_struct and VMAs, not fd.

For shared memory (shm_open, memfd_create, tmpfs/shmem, dma-buf): fd does exist → underlying object lives in kernel → memory indirectly reachable.

👉 Rule: fd = handle to a kernel object. That object may contain memory mappings (via inode/page cache, shmem, dma-buf), or may represent a device.

🔹 4. Sharing Between Processes
Sharing happens when processes duplicate or send fds.

Mechanisms:

fork() → child inherits parent’s fd table → same struct file *.

dup() → new fd number, same struct file *.

SCM_RIGHTS (Unix socket) → pass fd between processes.

All cases: the same struct file * (same f_count).

So both processes can read/write to the same object, and if it’s memory (e.g., memfd, shmem, dma-buf), they are sharing the same pages.

🔹 5. What happens when owner dies?
If a process exits, its files_struct is destroyed.

For each open fd:

Kernel calls fput(struct file *) → decrements f_count.

If f_count goes to zero:

The underlying object is freed:

If regular file → inode/dentry refcount decremented.

If shmem/memfd → memory released if no one else mapped it.

If dma-buf → pages unpinned, SMMU mappings removed.

If device → driver’s release() called.

⚠️ If other processes still hold a reference (dup, fork, fd passing), the struct file lives on.

So:

fd dies with process,

struct file object lives until last reference gone.

🔹 6. Practical Scenarios
Regular File
fd = open("foo.txt")
   fd=3 → struct file → inode → page cache
   mmap(fd) → VMA mapped to address_space
fd references struct file, not memory directly.

Memory only appears if you mmap or read/write.

Shared Memory (memfd_create)
fd = memfd_create("shm", 0)
   fd=3 → struct file (tmpfs/shmem) → struct address_space
   mmap(fd) → anon-like VMA, swappable
fd holds kernel shmem object → multiple processes can map same memory via fd passing.

dma-buf
fd = dma_buf_fd(dma_buf)
   fd=3 → struct file (f_op = dma_buf_ops)
   file->private_data = struct dma_buf
fd references dma_buf object → contains pinned pages / scatterlist.

Multiple processes can import/export fd to share GPU/accelerator buffers.

🔹 7. Textual Diagram (Full)
Userspace:
   fd = small int
   stored in process fd table (files_struct)

Kernel:
   fdtable[fd] = struct file *
   struct file
      ├─ f_inode (for file-backed)
      │    └─ address_space → page cache → struct page[]
      ├─ f_op (ops for devices, sockets, dma-buf)
      ├─ private_data (driver or dma-buf pointer)
      ├─ f_count (refcount)

Sharing:
   fork/dup/SCM_RIGHTS → multiple fds → same struct file
   refcount++ → stays alive

Exit:
   close(fd) or process exit → fput()
   f_count-- 
   if 0 → cleanup (release memory/device)

Caveat:
   malloc/brk memory → mm_struct + VMAs, not fd
   file-backed/shmem/memfd/dma-buf → tracked via fd
✅ In short:

fd is an index → struct file (kernel object handle).

It doesn’t hold memory directly but may reference objects that back memory (inode page cache, shmem, dma-buf).

Sharing works by refcounting the struct file.

If the owner dies but others still reference → memory/object lives on.

So when fd is shared accross processes and original process does it gets killed what happens ? Explain using mmap, dma-buf and manual way exhaustively with all caveats 
ChatGPT said:

Thought for 1m 21s
Great question — this is all about object lifetimes and who holds the last reference.
Short rule to tattoo on your brain:

An fd is just a handle (an integer) to a kernel object (struct file).
The object stays alive until the last reference drops — not until the process that created it dies.

Below I’ll walk through three sharing styles you asked for — mmap, dma-buf, and a couple of “manual” ways — and spell out exactly what survives when the original process dies.

🔹 Ground rules (apply to every case)
fd ≠ memory. In userspace it’s an int; in kernel it indexes the process’s files_struct to a struct file.

Lifetimes are refcounted. The struct file (and whatever it represents) lives while any of these hold a reference:

another process’s fd (dup/SCM_RIGHTS/fork-inherited),

a VMA mapping (vma->vm_file keeps a ref),

a driver/attachment (e.g., dma-buf import, IOMMU mapping),

page cache / inode refs as appropriate.

When a process exits, the kernel closes all its fds (fput() on each), and unmaps all its VMAs. Only if that drops the last reference does the kernel free the object/memory.

🟢 Scenario A — Regular file (or tmpfs/memfd/shmem) + mmap
How sharing happens
Process A: fd = open(...) (or memfd_create, shm_open) → mmap(fd, ...).

Share fd to Process B via fork/dup/SCM_RIGHTS.
(Or B maps the same pathname; for memfd/tmpfs it still goes through an fd.)

If A dies, but B still has:
1) An open fd
The struct file lives (its f_count > 0).

For a regular file: data is on disk; page cache pages stay while referenced or hot.

For tmpfs/shmem/memfd: the in-memory object persists as long as any fd or mapping exists.

B can keep reading/writing/mmaping as usual.

2) No fd, but still has the mmap mapping
B’s VMA holds a reference (vma->vm_file) to the same struct file.

Mapping remains valid until B unmaps or exits.

Dirty pages (MAP_SHARED) are written back by kernel writeback as usual.

3) Mapping types matter
MAP_SHARED (file-backed):

B sees A’s writes that made it to page cache before A died.

Mapping continues to reflect file contents (disk or tmpfs).

MAP_PRIVATE (COW):

B’s future writes are private; A’s private dirty pages die with A.

B still sees the underlying file content (plus B’s own privates).

4) Unlinked files
If A did unlink() but B still has the fd or mapping:

The file’s name is gone, but the inode + data remain until the last ref drops (classic UNIX semantics).

For memfd there’s never a directory name; the same “live while referenced” rule applies.

Caveats

A mapping outlives the fd used to create it. You can close(fd) and keep using the mapping.

For tmpfs/shmem/memfd, if the last fd and last mapping go away, the memory is freed immediately (there’s no backing disk).

RSS vs commit: mappings count toward VIRT/Committed_AS at creation; actual PFNs (RSS) are only faulted in on access.

🟢 Scenario B — dma-buf (zero-copy sharing between processes/drivers)
How sharing happens
Exporter (often a driver, sometimes userspace via DRM) creates a struct dma_buf backed by pages (shmem/GEM, CMA, etc.).

Export returns an fd whose struct file has f_op = dma_buf_ops and file->private_data = struct dma_buf.

Importers in other processes receive that fd (SCM_RIGHTS), call dma_buf_attach()/dma_buf_map_attachment(), or mmap() it for CPU access.

If the exporter A dies, but:
1) Any importer still holds the dma-buf fd or a mapping
The dma-buf refcount stays > 0 → buffer remains alive.

Device attachments and IOMMU mappings created by importers also keep it alive.

Importers can continue GPU/ISP/… DMA and CPU access as before.

2) No one holds the fd, but an importer still has it mmap’d
The VMA maps the dma-buf file, keeping a ref → still alive.

When importer unmaps/exits, ref drops; if it was last → dma-buf release() runs:

Detach/unmap from devices (IOMMU unmap),

Free backing pages (shmem/CMA/…).

3) All users gone
The final fput() calls dma-buf ->release() → pages freed, SMMU detach, fences cleaned.

Caveats

If a driver pinned userspace pages with GUP (get_user_pages) to export them and then forgets to put_page() on release, those pages remain pinned even after the process dies (nasty leak/“long-term pinning”).

If a device is actively DMAing when the last ref drops, exporters should quiesce/wait on fences before teardown. Good drivers do this; bad ones can crash hardware.

SVM/PASID case: if the dma-buf relies on the exporter’s process address space (rare), then that PASID binding dies with the process; normal dma-bufs are not tied to a process mm and are fine.

🟢 Scenario C — “Manual” ways to share (no dma-buf)
I’ll cover the three common patterns people mean by “manual”:

C1) Anonymous shared memory across fork()
p = mmap(NULL, len, PROT_RW, MAP_SHARED|MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0);
if (fork()==0) { /* child sees same shared anon pages */ }
Parent and child share the same physical pages (MAP_SHARED anon).

If parent (creator) dies, the child’s mapping remains; pages are now “owned” by the child’s mm_struct.

When the last process unmaps/exits, pages are freed (no backing file).

Caveat: MAP_PRIVATE|ANON is not shareable across unrelated processes (only via fork and then it’s COW).

C2) POSIX shared memory (shm_open) / memfd_create (tmpfs/shmem)
This is file-backed memory in tmpfs:

lives in RAM/swap,

referenced via fd and mappings.

If creator dies but others still hold fd or mappings, the object persists.

shm_unlink() removes the name; data persists until last ref drops.

C3) Plain read()/write() IPC
There is no shared memory — you copy bytes between processes.

If the reader/writer dies:

peer sees EOF or EPIPE/SIGPIPE.

Nothing persists in RAM beyond kernel socket/pipe buffers.

🧭 Lifetimes — one compact diagram
        fd table              kernel object           backing memory
     (per process)             (struct file)         (pages / SMMU maps)
A ──► fd:int ──────────┐      f_count=2  ◄─────────────┐
                       ├──► B: fd:int                  │
mmap(fd) in B: VMA ────┘                                │
   (holds vma->vm_file ref)                             │

If A exits:
  - closes A’s fd (f_count--)         (still >0)  → object stays
  - A’s VMAs unmapped (drop refs)

If B later:
  - unmaps last VMA and/or closes fd  (f_count→0) → free pages/unmap SMMU
🧨 Subtle caveats & “gotchas” interviewers love
A mapping can outlive the fd used to create it (VMA holds a ref).

MAP_PRIVATE file mmaps don’t propagate your writes; your dirty private pages die with you.

tmpfs/shmem/memfd live only in RAM/swap; without any fd or mapping they vanish immediately (no disk inode to keep them).

dma-buf lifetimes are independent of the exporter process; the buffer lives until the last fd/mapping/attachment is gone.

GUP pins survive process death until the pin holder (driver) drops them.

With SVM/PASID DMA, if a process dies, its PASID context is torn down; devices must stop using those VAs (the IOMMU will fault).

Closing the last fd to a regular file does not delete its contents — it’s on disk. Unlink removes the name, not the data; the inode persists while open or mapped.

TL;DR
If others still hold an fd or mapping, nothing breaks when the creator dies.

The kernel frees things only when the last reference (fd, VMA, device attachment) disappears.

For dma-buf, importer fds/mappings keep the buffer alive; exporter death doesn’t kill it.

For anonymous or tmpfs mappings, memory disappears immediately once the last fd/mapping is gone (no disk backing).

You said:
So why mmap sharing is dangerous and dma-buf is good ? If fd sharing itself can keep fd available even if original process dies, what is point of having dmabuf
ChatGPT said:
Excellent question ⚡ — you’ve caught the apparent overlap between mmap-based sharing and dma-buf-based sharing. At first glance both use fd → kernel object → shared memory, and both survive the death of the creator. So why is dma-buf “special” and why not just mmap+fd everywhere?

Let’s go deep.

🔹 1. mmap-based sharing (file, shmem, memfd)
How it works

Create file or shmem (open, memfd_create, shm_open).

Share fd with another process (via fork, dup, SCM_RIGHTS).

Both processes mmap(fd) into their VA.

Kernel struct file → inode/address_space → page cache is shared.

Problems / Limitations

CPU-centric: mmap sharing is perfect if only CPU processes need to share data. But devices (GPU, ISP, NIC, etc.) don’t speak “page cache” — they need scatter-gather lists and IOMMU mappings.

Cache coherency: If you hand-shake pages to a device driver via get_user_pages(), you pin them. If the process dies without cleanup, those pages may remain pinned (resource leak).

No unified fencing: Two processes may write/read same mmap region without a proper synchronization primitive (like futex). For devices, there’s no standard fencing mechanism to coordinate when a buffer is ready.

Drivers reimplement wheel: Every driver would have to take a struct file, pin pages, set up IOMMU, handle cache sync. This leads to duplication, bugs, leaks.

Security: With plain mmap + fd sharing, nothing prevents accidental/uncontrolled access. Devices would need to trust user pages they’re given.

🔹 2. dma-buf-based sharing
How it works

A producer (exporter) allocates a buffer (often shmem, GEM, CMA, etc.).

Exports it as a dma-buf fd → kernel struct file with f_op = dma_buf_ops.

Other processes or drivers import that fd via dma_buf_attach().

Kernel tracks all attachments (who has this buffer).

Provides synchronization (dma_fence) so producer/consumer coordinate.

Provides cache maintenance hooks for devices with different cache models.

Advantages

Device-agnostic sharing: Standard API across GPU, camera, display, V4L2, audio, etc. Any driver that understands dma-buf can attach to the same buffer without reinventing mapping/pinning.

Unified lifetime: Buffer lives until the last fd or mapping goes away. Clean release path via dma-buf ->release().

Avoids long-term pin leaks: dma-buf core manages page pinning/unpinning properly. Regular mmap+GUP is prone to “forever pinned pages.”

Synchronization: dma-fence system coordinates producer/consumer (e.g., GPU rendering done → display engine can scanout). mmap gives you none of that.

IOMMU/I/O ready: dma-buf easily integrates with SMMU/IOVA. Normal mmap regions are just VA↔page cache; drivers have to build scatterlists manually.

Security/isolation: Devices only see dma-buf pages; kernel validates attachments. With raw mmap, device drivers might accept arbitrary user pointers (dangerous).

🔹 3. Key Difference in Philosophy
mmap+fd sharing:

General-purpose user-to-user memory sharing.

Kernel doesn’t assume devices are involved.

Lightweight, but dangerous for long-lived zero-copy device buffers.

dma-buf sharing:

Explicit device-to-device and device-to-user buffer sharing framework.

Tracks buffer lifetime, pinning, IOMMU mappings, cache sync, fencing.

Solves the "scatterlist/IOMMU/cache-coherency" nightmare once, in one place.

🔹 4. Why mmap sharing is “dangerous”
Pinning with get_user_pages() can starve the system (pages become unswappable).

No standard cleanup — if a process dies, kernel may not know whether pinned pages can safely be freed.

Different devices have different DMA requirements (contiguous, aligned, uncached) → plain mmap can’t express these.

Multiple drivers duplicating logic → more bugs.

🔹 5. Why dma-buf is “good”
Standard cross-driver interface.

Safe lifetime & cleanup.

Built-in fencing/synchronization.

Designed to work with IOMMUs (SMMU v3, PASID, etc.).

Supports CPU access via mmap of the dma-buf fd, but with controlled lifetime.

🔹 TL;DR
mmap+fd: good for CPU-to-CPU shared memory; dangerous for device buffers (leaks, no sync, no cache mgmt).

dma-buf: purpose-built for cross-device zero-copy sharing; tracks lifetime, pinning, IOMMU mappings, sync.

👉 That’s why graphics stacks (DRM/GEM), multimedia pipelines (V4L2, camera → ISP → GPU → display), and compute offload all standardized on dma-buf, not “just mmap.”

✔ GPU imports and processes,
✔ display imports and scans out,
showing why this works with dma-buf but would be unsafe with just mmap?

You said:
Why spinlock is not advisable on single core ?
ChatGPT said:
This is a classic trap in kernel interviews — let’s unpack it carefully.

🔹 1. What is a spinlock?
A spinlock is a busy-wait lock:

If the lock is free → acquire it.

If the lock is held → spin in a loop, checking repeatedly, until it becomes free.

In multiprocessor (SMP) systems, that makes sense:

If another core holds the lock, you spin while the other finishes.

When it releases, your core grabs it.

No sleeping, no context switch → very fast.

🔹 2. Why spinlocks are bad on single-core
On a single-core CPU, only one thread of execution can run at a time.

Case:

Task A acquires the spinlock.

Gets preempted (voluntarily or by scheduler/IRQ).

Task B tries to acquire the same spinlock.

Task B spins forever…

But Task A (the only one that could release it) never runs, because the CPU is stuck spinning in Task B.

→ Deadlock.

This is why spinlocks are dangerous/useless on UP (uniprocessor) systems.

🔹 3. What happens in Linux?
Linux kernel has a config option:

CONFIG_SMP = multiprocessor: spinlocks are real spinlocks.

!CONFIG_SMP (uniprocessor): spinlocks are compiled down to preemption disabling (preempt_disable()/preempt_enable()) or nothing.

That way, on UP systems, you don’t deadlock.

🔹 4. Practical caveats
Interrupt context: Even on single-core, spinlocks (with irqsave) are used to protect from interrupts on the same CPU.

Example: bottom-half code and interrupt handler could race on same variable.

Spinlock here prevents re-entrancy (with local_irq_disable).

So spinlocks are not totally useless on UP — but they are never used for "wait until another thread on another CPU releases it".

For “sleepable” locks (mutex, semaphore), scheduler can reschedule and let lock owner run → no deadlock.

🔹 5. Rule of thumb
On SMP → spinlocks are great for short critical sections, because another CPU can release it in parallel.

On UP → spinlocks collapse into preemption/IRQ disable (no busy-wait).

Never use a true spinning loop on UP, because you’ll starve the lock owner.

✅ One-liner answer:
On a single core, spinlocks are pointless and dangerous: if you spin, the lock holder can’t run to release it, so you deadlock. That’s why Linux compiles them into preemption/IRQ-disables on UP systems instead of busy-wait loops.

👉 Do you want me to also connect this with zone/buddy allocator locks (like zone->lock using spinlock) and explain how Linux handles them differently on UP vs SMP? That’s a favorite interview deep dive.

You said:
What is user DMA ?
ChatGPT said:
Great question 👍 — “user DMA” (sometimes called uDMA or userspace DMA) is one of those terms that gets tossed around in Linux/SoC/GPU/NIC contexts and can mean slightly different things depending on audience. Let’s pin it down clearly and connect to everything we’ve discussed.

🔹 1. The classic DMA model
Normally:

Kernel driver allocates DMA-safe memory (via dma_alloc_coherent, CMA, or shmem).

Driver maps memory into device’s IOVA via SMMU/IOMMU (dma_map_single, dma_map_sg).

Userspace interacts only via fd/ioctl — it doesn’t directly hand raw pointers to the device.

The kernel is the middleman ensuring safety, pinning, IOMMU setup, cache management.

🔹 2. What “user DMA” means
User DMA = letting user processes directly supply memory buffers for DMA instead of going through only kernel-allocated ones.

That means:

A process calls malloc() or mmap() to allocate memory.

Passes the pointer (VA) or fd to the kernel (via ioctl or write).

Kernel pins those user pages (get_user_pages()).

Maps them into the device’s IOVA via the SMMU.

Device now DMA’s directly into the process’s own memory.

So user DMA = device → user VA (via kernel mediation).

🔹 3. How it is implemented
Pinning user pages

Kernel pins the physical pages backing the user VA (get_user_pages with FOLL_PIN).

Prevents them from being swapped out or migrated.

Scatter-gather setup

Kernel collects PFNs into a struct scatterlist.

IOMMU mapping

If IOMMU/SMMU present:

Maps the pinned pages into device IOVA space.

If no IOMMU: requires contiguous physical pages or bounce buffers.

DMA

Device programmed with IOVA (or VA if PASID/SVM).

DMA goes directly into user pages.

Cleanup

After DMA, driver unmaps/unpins (put_page).

🔹 4. Why “user DMA” is tricky / dangerous
Pinning leaks: if pages stay pinned too long → they are unswappable → can cause memory pressure & OOM.

Security: handing arbitrary user VA to device without checks can let a buggy/malicious app trick a device into DMAing into kernel memory.

Coherency: caches must be flushed/inv’ed properly (if not coherent).

Lifetime mismatch: user could munmap() while DMA is still active → kernel must handle refcounts correctly.

🔹 5. Modern safe solutions
Instead of raw “user DMA” with arbitrary pointers, Linux provides controlled mechanisms:

dma-buf:

User gets an fd that represents a DMA-safe buffer.

Safe sharing across processes/devices.

VFIO + UIO frameworks:

For userspace drivers, VFIO exposes IOMMU mappings safely.

User can control DMA-capable regions, but kernel still pins/validates.

PASID / SVM (Shared Virtual Memory):

Device directly uses user-space VAs (SMMU with PASID).

Page faults handled in kernel (PRI/IOPF).

This is “next-gen user DMA” — safer because the IOMMU enforces isolation.

🔹 6. Practical Examples
Networking (DPDK, RDMA/InfiniBand):

NIC DMA directly into user-space buffers → ultra-low latency.

Kernel pins memory via mlock() or driver APIs.

GPU/Compute (OpenCL, CUDA, KGSL):

User VA shared with GPU via SVM/PASID → GPU does user DMA into process memory.

Storage (SPDK, NVMe):

NVMe controller DMA directly into user-space IO buffers.

🔹 7. Textual Diagram
Userspace:
   buf = malloc(4KB)
   ioctl(fd, START_DMA, buf)

Kernel:
   get_user_pages(buf) → pin PFNs
   build scatterlist
   iommu_map(sglist) → IOVA
   program device registers with IOVA

Device:
   DMA write → IOVA → SMMU → PFN → process’s RAM

After:
   dma_unmap_sg()
   put_page()
   buffer is released
✅ Summary:

User DMA = devices DMA directly into user-space memory.

Kernel still mediates (pinning + mapping).

Dangerous if misused (pin leaks, security holes), which is why frameworks like dma-buf, VFIO, PASID/SVM exist — to make it safe and general.

You said:
What is difference between shmem and tmpfs
ChatGPT said:
Excellent question 🔥 — people often conflate shmem and tmpfs because they are tightly coupled, but they are not identical. Let’s break it down clearly and connect it to all the Linux mm concepts we’ve discussed.

🔹 1. tmpfs
Filesystem:

tmpfs is a RAM-based filesystem.

You mount it with:

mount -t tmpfs none /mnt
Everything created there is stored in volatile memory (RAM, plus swap if allowed).

Supports standard filesystem objects: files, directories, inodes, dentries.

Backed by the generic shmem code in the kernel.

Usage:

/dev/shm is a tmpfs mount, used for POSIX shared memory (shm_open).

Used by memfd_create() to create anonymous in-memory files.

Provides a real filesystem interface (file names, inodes).

🔹 2. shmem
Kernel internal memory manager:

shmem (short for shared memory) is the implementation layer that manages page allocation, swap support, and page cache for anonymous, swappable memory objects.

It provides a backing store for tmpfs files.

It also backs other kernel features that need “anonymous, but swappable” pages.

Used in:

tmpfs (all tmpfs files are internally shmem inodes).

/dev/shm (POSIX shared memory uses tmpfs → shmem).

memfd_create() (anonymous file-like objects backed by shmem).

dma-buf (many exporters use shmem to back buffers).

System V SHM segments (shmget/shmat) use shmem if CONFIG_SHMEM=y (otherwise fall back to hugetlbfs).

🔹 3. Relationship (layering)
Think of it like this:

User process
   │
   ├── open/mmap on tmpfs file (/dev/shm/foo, memfd, POSIX shm)
   │
   └──> tmpfs filesystem layer
             │
             └──> shmem.c (internal implementation)
                        │
                        ├── allocates anonymous pages
                        ├── manages swap-in/swap-out
                        └── integrates with page cache
So:

tmpfs = filesystem front-end.

shmem = memory management back-end.

🔹 4. Differences in Properties
Aspect	tmpfs	shmem
What it is	A filesystem type (mountable)	Kernel’s internal implementation
User-visible	Yes (mount -t tmpfs, /dev/shm)	No direct mount; used indirectly
Objects	Files, dirs, inodes, dentries	Inodes and pages only
Lifetime	As long as filesystem mount exists	As long as an object references it
Swap support	Yes (if system swap enabled)	Yes
Backing	Uses RAM + swap	Same
Usage examples	/dev/shm, memfd, POSIX shm	tmpfs files, dma-buf, SysV shm
🔹 5. Why both exist
tmpfs gives you a filesystem abstraction: files, names, permissions, mount options.

shmem is the mechanism: it manages swappable, page-cache-like anonymous memory.

tmpfs delegates to shmem for all its actual memory handling.

You can’t “mount shmem”; you mount tmpfs. But internally tmpfs is just shmem plus FS glue.

🔹 6. Subtle Caveats
If CONFIG_SHMEM=n, then tmpfs won’t work; SysV SHM segments will use hugetlbfs (no swap, fixed-size hugepages).

shmem pages are swappable (unlike hugetlb).

shmem uses the page cache infrastructure, so a shmem file looks like a regular file in VFS, but its “backing store” is RAM/swap, not disk.

mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS) is not shmem: it uses anonymous VMAs, backed directly by swap, not a file. But if you do shm_open or memfd_create, you are explicitly creating shmem/tmpfs files.

✅ Summary in one-liner:

tmpfs = mountable RAM filesystem (front-end).

shmem = kernel’s internal swappable memory object manager (back-end).

tmpfs files are backed by shmem; many kernel features (POSIX SHM, memfd, dma-buf) use shmem even without you mounting tmpfs manually.

You said:
Why anonymous is backed by swap ? What happenes when mount or unmount happens and connect with everything discussed so far and with all caveats. Why hugetlbfs is not swappable? Also give comparison table which you told
ChatGPT said:
Perfect — this is a deep one 🔥. Let’s go step by step, tie it back to everything we’ve discussed, and finish with the comparison table you asked for.

🔹 1. Why anonymous memory is backed by swap
Anonymous mappings = memory not tied to a file.

Examples: malloc (via brk/mmap), stack, mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS).

These pages have no permanent backing store.

If RAM is full, kernel must evict something.

For file-backed pages:

They can just be dropped (reloaded later from disk).

For anonymous pages:

They must be written somewhere, or the data is lost.

That "somewhere" = swap space (disk, zram).

This is why we say anon memory is swap-backed.

👉 Caveat: If swap is disabled, anon memory still works, but under extreme pressure the kernel hits the OOM killer because it can’t evict.

🔹 2. What happens when you mount or unmount tmpfs
Mounting tmpfs:

Creates a new superblock (filesystem instance).

Root dentry/inode created.

All files under that mount live in RAM+swap (via shmem).

Limitations set by mount -t tmpfs -o size=… (CommitLimit applies).

Unmounting tmpfs:

Kernel destroys dentries/inodes.

All files and their pages are freed (back to buddy allocator).

If data was swapped out, swap slots freed too.

👉 Caveat: tmpfs is volatile: data gone on unmount or reboot.

🔹 3. Why hugetlbfs is not swappable
hugetlbfs = special FS for managing hugetlb pages (reserved at boot or via sysfs).

hugetlb pages are:

Preallocated at boot (or via nr_hugepages).

Physically contiguous.

Reserved only for hugetlbfs use.

They are not part of the normal buddy allocator pool, and swap subsystem doesn’t handle them.

They can’t be evicted, because there’s no mechanism to split and write them out.

Once allocated to a process, they stay resident until freed.

👉 Caveat: This makes hugetlbfs predictable (for DBs, HPC apps needing deterministic latency), but at the cost of flexibility.

🔹 4. Comparison Table
Here’s the big picture comparing anonymous, tmpfs/shmem, and hugetlbfs:

Feature	Anonymous (malloc/stack)	tmpfs/shmem (memfd, /dev/shm)	hugetlbfs (hugepages)
How created	brk, mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS)	shm_open, memfd_create, tmpfs file	mount -t hugetlbfs, mmap
fd required?	❌ No	✅ Yes (file descriptor backing)	✅ Yes (fd from hugetlbfs file)
File visible in VFS?	❌ No	✅ Yes (tmpfs mount or memfd)	✅ Yes (hugetlbfs mount)
Backing	Swap space (if needed)	Swap space (if needed)	Reserved hugepage pool
Swappable	✅ Yes	✅ Yes	❌ No
On unmap/exit	Pages freed back to buddy/swap	Inodes released, pages freed	Hugepages returned to pool
Size granularity	Base page (4K/64K) or THP	Base page or THP	Hugepage size only (2M, 1G…)
Physically contiguous?	❌ No	❌ No (uses normal allocator)	✅ Yes (hugetlb reserved pool)
Zero-copy IPC?	❌ No	✅ Yes (fd-based sharing)	✅ Yes (fd-based sharing)
Common use	malloc/stack/heap	POSIX SHM, memfd, dma-buf backing	Databases, HPC, DPDK
🔹 5. Connecting to earlier discussions
Anonymous pages → managed by mm_struct/VMAs, backed by swap if evicted.

tmpfs/shmem → fd-based, lives in VFS, but uses same swap-backed shmem.c internally.

hugetlbfs → totally separate allocator (not swap, not buddy), ensures large physically contiguous pages.

THP/MTHP (transparent/medium THP) → different: these are anon pages promoted to large folios automatically, but still swappable. Unlike hugetlb.

Mount/unmount: tmpfs integrates with VFS (superblock, inode, dentry) while anon doesn’t — that’s why tmpfs/shmem can be shared with fd.

DMA-buf: often backed by shmem (because fd-based, swappable, kernel can pin pages for DMA). Never by anonymous pages directly. Sometimes by hugetlb if contiguous needed.

✅ In one line:

Anonymous = process-private, swap-backed, no fd.

tmpfs/shmem = swap-backed, fd-based, lives in VFS.

hugetlbfs = huge, reserved, pinned, non-swappable.
