You said:
If driver supports dynamic update, then what is point of having pri ? Also can pri induce access violation because it can demand any page ?
ChatGPT said:
Great question 👍 — this is exactly the subtle design trade-off between “classic IOMMU mapping” and PRI/SVM. Let’s break it down carefully.

🔹 1. If driver already supports dynamic updates, why PRI?
Without PRI/SVM:

Driver workflow today (classic DMA API):

Userspace/driver allocates buffer (malloc, shmem, dma_alloc …).

Driver explicitly pins pages (get_user_pages).

Driver calls iommu_map() to install IOVA→PA mappings into SMMU.

Device can DMA only inside this range.

If device touches outside → abort/stall → kernel bug.

So even with “dynamic update”:

The CPU must anticipate all device needs up front.

If device suddenly needs another page, the CPU must pin/map beforehand.

That means either:

Over-provision mappings in advance, or

Do expensive “stop device → reprogram SMMU → resume”.

👉 PRI removes this anticipation.

Device can directly signal: “I need VA=0x12345000”.

Kernel pins/maps only when needed (just-in-time, demand paging).

This saves memory (no over-provision), and enables large sparse address spaces (e.g. GPU VRAM).

🔹 2. Can PRI induce access violations?
Yes, and this is a key caveat.

Device can theoretically issue a PRI request for any virtual address.

Kernel/IOMMU driver must validate:

Is this VA part of the process’s mm_struct (a valid VMA)?

Does it have the right protections (R/W/X)?

Is this device authorized for this process/PASID?

If invalid → kernel responds with DMA page fault failure:

Device gets error response (like SIGSEGV for DMA).

Access is denied; no mapping is created.

👉 So PRI does not bypass protection. It just extends demand paging to devices.

🔹 3. Where PRI shines vs plain dynamic updates
Fine granularity: driver doesn’t need to map whole 1 GB buffer up front; only pages actually touched by device are mapped.

Lazy migration: HPC/AI workloads can migrate pages CPU↔GPU on demand.

SVM synergy: with PASID, device faults are resolved against the same mm_struct as the process. Device and CPU literally share VA.

Performance: less CPU intervention, fewer TLB shootdowns, less memory pinned unnecessarily.

Without PRI:

Only pre-pinned, pre-mapped DMA.

No on-demand growth/shrink.

Bad for GPUs (sparse textures, pageable memory) and NICs (zero-copy send/recv).

🔹 4. Textual Diagram
[Classic DMA]
Userspace malloc() → anon pages
Driver: pin pages + iommu_map()
Device DMA → IOVA
If device touches unmapped → abort/stall (fatal)

[DMA with PRI]
Userspace malloc() → anon pages
Device DMA → VA 0xABC
SMMU miss → raises PRI
Kernel: check VMA, pin, map IOVA
Device retries → success
If invalid → PRI response = access denied
🔹 5. Caveats
PRI adds latency → device stalls until kernel resolves fault.

If device floods PRIs, CPU may thrash.

Security critical: kernel must not allow device to “probe” arbitrary process VAs.

Only useful when combined with SVM (per-process PASID contexts). Without PASID, PRI just adds complexity.

✅ Interview one-liner:
Dynamic updates require the driver to pre-map memory; PRI lets devices fault in pages on demand, just like CPU demand paging. It saves memory and enables true shared VA (SVM). PRI requests are validated against process VMAs, so they can’t escape protection; invalid requests return access violation instead of mapping.

In mmstruct, what are mmap, mm_rb, vmacache_seqnum, get_unmapped_area, mmap_base, task_size, highest_vm_end, pgd, mm_users, mm_count, pgtables_bytes, map_count, page_table_lock, mmap_lock, mmlist, def_flags, write_protect_seq, flags, owner, cpu_bitmap
ChatGPT said:
Excellent 👌 — this is the deep-dive into struct mm_struct internals.
I’ll go field by field, explain what it means, where it is used, how it relates to everything in our thread (VMAs, task_struct, demand paging, SVM/PRI, swap, etc.), and give caveats.

🔹 struct mm_struct Key Fields
🔸 VMA Management
mmap

Head of the linked list of all struct vm_area_struct for this process.

Example: heap VMA, stack VMA, file-backed VMA.

Demand paging uses this list to check “is the faulting address valid?”.

mm_rb

Red-black tree of VMAs.

Faster lookup than walking linked list.

Used in find_vma() when resolving page faults.

vmacache_seqnum

Optimization. Stores sequence numbers for per-thread VMA cache.

Speeds up repeated lookups of nearby addresses (common during faults).

get_unmapped_area

Function pointer.

Chooses where in VA space to place a new mapping (for mmap()).

Different strategies: arch-dependent, file system–dependent (e.g., hugetlbfs).

🔸 Address Space Layout
mmap_base

Base address where new anonymous mappings via mmap() will start.

Used for ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization).

task_size

Max user virtual address allowed for this process.

On 64-bit ARM, usually 0x0000_ffff_ffff_ffff for user.

Kernel ensures mappings don’t cross into kernel half.

highest_vm_end

Tracks the highest mapped virtual address in this mm.

Used for brk() growth and some memory accounting.

🔸 Page Table Root
pgd

Pointer to root page table for this mm (top-level entry → TTBR0_EL1).

Switched on context switch.

🔸 Reference Counting
mm_users

Count of threads using this mm (task_structs pointing to it).

fork() duplicates mm (new), clone(CLONE_VM) shares mm.

mm_count

Count of kernel references to this mm.

Example: held by active_mm when kernel threads borrow an mm.

Freed only when both mm_users and mm_count reach zero.

🔸 Memory Usage Tracking
pgtables_bytes

Tracks bytes of memory used by page tables themselves.

Important for accounting, since page tables also consume RAM.

map_count

Number of VMAs in this mm.

Example: after 1000 shared libs loaded, map_count = 1000+.

🔸 Synchronization
page_table_lock

Spinlock protecting page table modifications (PTE updates).

Used during faults, CoW, mprotect.

⚠️ Spinlock (not mutex) because faults may happen in interrupt context.

mmap_lock (was mmap_sem)

Read-write semaphore protecting VMA tree (mmap, mm_rb).

Readers for page fault lookup, writer for mmap()/munmap().

⚠️ Contended lock in fork-heavy workloads.

🔸 List & Flags
mmlist

Links all mm_structs into a global list.

Used by memory reclaim (kswapd, shrinkers) to scan processes.

def_flags

Default VMA flags for new mappings.

E.g., VM_MAYREAD | VM_MAYWRITE.

write_protect_seq

Sequence counter for page-table write-protection (used in COW tracking).

Helps synchronize with GUP (get_user_pages) when pages are pinned.

flags

mm-level flags.

Example: MMF_DUMPABLE (can this mm be dumped in core dump?).

🔸 Misc Ownership / CPU Tracking
owner

Pointer back to main task_struct that owns this mm.

Helps in OOM killer to identify victim.

cpu_bitmap

Bitmask of CPUs currently running threads of this mm.

Used for TLB shootdowns (only IPI those CPUs).

🔹 How it ties to our discussion
Page faults: walk mm_rb (or mmap list if cache miss), check VMA validity, allocate pages, install into pgd.

Swap/zram: eviction relies on mmlist to scan mm_structs.

Fork/CoW: mm_users tracks how many tasks share mm; CoW uses write_protect_seq.

SVM/PRI: pgd is what SMMU points to when PASID is bound to a process.

Fd → mmap(fd): creates VMA, linked in mmap, increments map_count.

Lazy TLB (kernel threads): use mm_count so mm_struct isn’t freed while borrowed.

Cgroups: rss counters inside mm_struct are charged to memcg.

🔹 Example Walkthrough: malloc(4KB)
malloc() → glibc calls brk() or mmap().

Kernel:

Acquires mmap_lock.

Allocates new vm_area_struct.

Inserts into mmap linked list + mm_rb.

Updates map_count.

Access → page fault:

Looks up VMA (via vmacache_seqnum, else RB tree).

Acquires page_table_lock.

Allocates page (buddy allocator).

Updates pgd entry.

Increments rss_stat.

🔹 Textual Diagram
task_struct
 └─ mm (struct mm_struct)
       ├─ mmap (linked list of VMAs)
       ├─ mm_rb (red-black tree of VMAs)
       ├─ vmacache_seqnum (fast path cache seq)
       ├─ get_unmapped_area (placement policy)
       ├─ mmap_base / task_size / highest_vm_end
       ├─ pgd (root page table for VA→PA)
       ├─ mm_users / mm_count (refcounts)
       ├─ pgtables_bytes (page tables RAM used)
       ├─ map_count (# of VMAs)
       ├─ page_table_lock / mmap_lock (synchronization)
       ├─ mmlist (global reclaim list)
       ├─ def_flags / flags / write_protect_seq
       ├─ owner (task_struct of main process)
       └─ cpu_bitmap (for TLB shootdown)
✅ Interview one-liner:
mm_struct is the per-process address space descriptor: VMAs in mmap/mm_rb, page tables via pgd, reference counts (mm_users/mm_count), synchronization locks (mmap_lock, page_table_lock), accounting (pgtables_bytes, map_count), and ownership (owner, cpu_bitmap). It is the glue between user VA space, page faults, swap, cgroups, and even device SVM.

You said:
In vma cloning for threads, does stack and registers also get cloned ? Tell me which ones are and which not ?
ChatGPT said:
Excellent question 👍 — this gets right into the difference between fork(), clone(), exec() and threading.
We need to separate VMAs, page tables, stack, and registers because they behave differently.

🔹 What happens during VMA cloning (fork/clone)?
When you call fork() or clone(CLONE_VM):

VMAs

Entire VMA list (mm_struct.mmap) is cloned.

New child mm_struct points to the same physical pages, marked Copy-on-Write (CoW).

Both parent & child see same data until one writes → page fault → private copy allocated.

Page tables

Top-level pgd is copied for the child.

PTEs point to the same PFNs as parent, marked read-only (for CoW).

🔹 Registers and stack
Registers (CPU state)

Registers are not cloned in mm_struct (they live in task_struct->thread / pt_regs).

On fork(), child gets a copy of parent’s register state.

Only difference: return value of fork:

Parent sees child PID.

Child sees 0.

Stack

Two cases:

fork() / clone without CLONE_VM:

Child gets a new stack VMA copied from parent, again CoW pages.

So initially identical, but logically independent.

clone(CLONE_VM | CLONE_THREAD) (pthreads):

Threads share the same mm_struct.

But each thread must have its own user stack.

Kernel enforces this: clone() requires stack argument (new stack pointer).

Otherwise threads would overwrite each other’s local variables.

So:

Processes → separate stack, CoW.

Threads → shared VA space, but separate stack VMAs.

🔹 What is cloned vs what is shared?
| Resource | fork() (new process) | clone(CLONE_VM|CLONE_THREAD) (thread) |
|----------------------------|-------------------------------------|------------------------------------------|
| mm_struct (VMAs, pgd) | New mm_struct, CoW with parent | Shared mm_struct with parent |
| File descriptor table | Shared if CLONE_FILES | Usually shared |
| Signal handlers | Shared if CLONE_SIGHAND | Usually shared |
| Registers | Copied from parent (new thread state)| New thread starts with provided stack ptr|
| User stack | CoW copy (new process stack) | Must supply new stack area |
| Kernel stack (task_struct)| Always new (per task) | Always new (per thread) |

🔹 How mm_struct fields behave
mmap/mm_rb:

fork → duplicated VMAs, new mm_struct.

thread → shared mm_struct, same VMA tree, but new stack VMA created.

pgd:

fork → new page tables allocated, entries CoW.

thread → same pgd (shared).

mm_users:

Increases for each thread sharing mm.

🔹 Caveats
If you fork() and then exec(), all old VMAs are destroyed, and new ones created from ELF binary.

Kernel threads (kthread) don’t use user VMAs → mm=NULL, only active_mm.

Thread-local storage (TLS) is managed by libc, using separate stack/segment.

Registers always get saved/restored by scheduler on context switch; they’re not part of mm_struct or VMA.

🔹 Textual Flow Example: pthread_create()
Parent process task_struct
 ├─ mm → mm_struct
 │     ├─ VMAs (text, data, heap, stack)
 │     └─ pgd (page tables)
 └─ registers (RIP, RSP, general regs)

pthread_create()
 └─ clone(CLONE_VM | CLONE_THREAD | CLONE_SIGHAND …, new_stack_ptr)
      ├─ New task_struct
      │   ├─ mm = same mm_struct
      │   ├─ registers = copy of parent regs
      │   │       RIP = thread start fn
      │   │       RSP = new_stack_ptr
      │   └─ kernel stack = new
      └─ New user stack VMA inserted into mm_struct
✅ Interview one-liner:
In a fork, VMAs and page tables are cloned with CoW, registers are copied, and child gets its own CoW stack. In threads (clone with CLONE_VM), all VMAs and pgd are shared, but each thread has its own user and kernel stack; registers are initialized separately.

You said:
mm_users
Incremented by mmget() (or, if we need to be cautious about whether or not
we have already reached zero users, mmget_not_zero()) and decremented by
mmput() (or, optionally, asynchronously via mmput_async().)
Counts the number of userland references to the process address space.
If this value is non-zero then mm_count will also be non-zero (i.e. userspace as
a whole counts as 1 mm_count).
When this reference count reaches zero, all userland-specific metadata is
torn down as are all userland mappings via __mmput(). Importantly, the kernel
mappings remain and so does the object as a whole, with mm_count simply
being decremented, only if this reaches zero does the object as a whole get
torn down (see below).
Other users which increment this reference counter might include a
forked process (via copy_process() which invokes copy_mm() which invokes
mmget() in turn), the move_pages() syscall for moving pages between nodes via
kernel_move_pages(), among many other users, often via the get_task_mm() and
access_process_vm() functions.
4.3.1.2 mm_count
Incremented by mmgrab() and decremented by mmdrop().
Counts the number of kernel references to the process address space (im-
portantly, including the process itself i.e. its struct task_struct object).
The reference count is incremented when lazy TLB mode is entered, ei-
ther by a kernel process reusing the existing process address space mappings
without swapping out its PGD (which involves expensive TLB invalidation)
or a task such as exiting a process that needs to tear things down but keep
the mm_struct around for a while, e.g. in exit_mm(). See the virtual memory
chapter for more on the TLB. Any non-zero number of mm_users count as 1
mm_count.
If the reference count drops to zero, this invokes __mmdrop() which frees
the mm_struct’s PGD and the mm_struct itself among other housekeeping tasks.
By this point all user mappings will already have been freed.
ChatGPT said:
Perfect 👌 — you’ve pulled out the subtle but critical distinction between mm_users and mm_count inside struct mm_struct.
Let’s walk through it slowly, with practical flow, internals, and caveats so this sticks forever.

🔹 mm_users
Definition: Number of userland tasks (threads) actively using this mm_struct.

Manipulated by:

mmget(), mmget_not_zero() → increment.

mmput(), mmput_async() → decrement.

Usage:

Forked processes increment this (via copy_mm() → mmget()).

Thread groups increment when sharing the same mm.

Syscalls like move_pages() or debugging APIs that temporarily borrow the mm.

When reaches zero:

All user mappings and metadata are torn down in __mmput().

Example: page tables freed, VMAs destroyed, rss stats dropped.

⚠️ BUT the mm_struct object itself still exists until mm_count also drops.

🔹 mm_count
Definition: Number of kernel references to the mm_struct.

Manipulated by:

mmgrab() → increment.

mmdrop() → decrement.

Usage:

Kernel threads using lazy TLB (task->mm = NULL, task->active_mm = prev->mm).

Exiting tasks that still need mm_struct alive until cleanup finishes.

Debuggers, /proc access (get_task_mm()).

When reaches zero:

Invokes __mmdrop().

Frees the pgd and the mm_struct itself.

At this point, everything is gone (both user and kernel refs).

🔹 Relationship Between Them
Invariant:
If mm_users > 0 ⇒ mm_count > 0.

Why? Because userspace counts also imply at least one kernel reference.

Think of it as:

mm_users = “# of living user tasks with this mm”
mm_count = “# of total kernel references (including mm_users)”
So:

mm_users = logical reference from threads.

mm_count = umbrella reference from anyone, kernel included.

🔹 Practical Flow Examples
1. Fork
fork()
 └─ copy_process()
      └─ copy_mm()
           └─ mmget() → increments mm_users
           └─ mmgrab() → increments mm_count
Both parent and child now share mm_struct references.

2. Thread exit
last thread exits
 └─ mmput()
      └─ mm_users → 0
      └─ __mmput()
           ├─ free all VMAs
           ├─ tear down user mappings
           └─ leave mm_struct alive
At this point: no user space, but mm_struct may still be alive if kernel has refs.

3. Lazy TLB (kernel threads)
kthread runs
 └─ task->mm = NULL
 └─ task->active_mm = prev->mm
 └─ mmgrab() ensures mm_count++
So the mm_struct doesn’t vanish while kernel borrows its PGD.

4. Final drop
last kernel reference
 └─ mmdrop()
      └─ mm_count → 0
      └─ __mmdrop()
           ├─ free pgd
           └─ free mm_struct object
Only now is the mm_struct fully destroyed.

🔹 Textual Diagram
struct mm_struct
 ├─ mm_users: # of user tasks using this mm
 │     • Incremented by mmget()
 │     • Decremented by mmput()
 │     • → 0 ⇒ __mmput(): destroy VMAs, free user mappings
 │
 └─ mm_count: total kernel refs (includes mm_users)
       • Incremented by mmgrab()
       • Decremented by mmdrop()
       • → 0 ⇒ __mmdrop(): free pgd + mm_struct itself
🔹 Caveats
mm_users=0 does NOT mean mm_struct is gone — kernel may still need it (e.g. active_mm, debugging).

mm_count=0 = the real death of mm_struct.

This split avoids premature free while kernel threads temporarily borrow someone else’s mm.

Important for /proc, ptrace, lazy TLB, and NUMA page migration (move_pages()).

✅ Interview one-liner:
mm_users counts live userland threads in an mm_struct, torn down at 0 via __mmput(). mm_count counts all kernel refs (including userland), torn down at 0 via __mmdrop(). Thus user mappings die at mm_users=0, but the mm_struct survives until all kernel references drop too.

You said:
Why kernel need to reference mm_struct ? Isn't it user space stuff ?
ChatGPT said:
This is a great catch ⚡ — on the surface, struct mm_struct looks like pure userspace bookkeeping (VMAs, page tables, rss stats).
But the kernel must keep references to it in several situations because the CPU/MMU itself does not distinguish “userland” and “kernelland” page tables cleanly — both interact with it.

Let’s go through why kernel needs mm_struct references.

🔹 1. Lazy TLB for kernel threads
Problem: Kernel threads (kthread) don’t have user VMAs.

If they ran with mm = NULL, CPU would have no valid page tables loaded in TTBR0_EL1 (ARM) or CR3 (x86).

That would force constant TLB invalidations when switching back to user tasks.

Solution:

Kernel threads set task->mm = NULL but task->active_mm = last->mm.

That borrowed mm_struct is kept alive with mmgrab(), so it doesn’t disappear.

👉 Kernel is “borrowing” the user’s mm_struct to keep TLB valid and avoid performance loss.

🔹 2. /proc, ptrace, debugging
Tools like gdb, strace, top, or even reading /proc/$pid/maps need to inspect another process’s memory.

Kernel must pin that process’s mm_struct (get_task_mm()) while walking its VMAs or page tables.

Without kernel refs, the mm_struct could be freed while debugger is using it.

🔹 3. NUMA migration / memory reclaim
Page migration (move_pages()) or reclamation (kswapd) walks a process’s VMAs and page tables.

These kernel threads are not the process itself but still need to hold an mm_struct ref while operating.

🔹 4. Page fault handling with SVM / PRI (IOMMU)
When a device faults via PRI (Page Request Interface) with a PASID, kernel uses the process’s mm_struct to walk its page tables and resolve mapping.

The IOMMU driver increments mm_count to keep that mm_struct alive while handling DMA.

🔹 5. Exit path ordering
When last userspace task exits, mm_users → 0 → __mmput() destroys VMAs + page tables.

But exit path itself still needs mm_struct to clean things up!

So kernel holds mmgrab() until teardown completes, then mmdrop() finally frees the object.

🔹 Textual Diagram
Process exits:
 task->mm->mm_users → 0
 └─ __mmput() tears down VMAs & user mappings
 └─ mm_count still > 0 because:
        - active_mm borrowed by kernel thread
        - /proc reader inspecting maps
        - IOMMU PRI fault handler holding reference
When last kernel reference drops:
 mm_count → 0
 └─ __mmdrop() frees pgd + mm_struct
🔹 Caveats
Kernel threads don’t need VMAs but need valid page tables (active_mm).

Kernel must not free mm_struct while it’s still in use anywhere in kernel subsystems.

That’s why mm_count exists separate from mm_users.

✅ Interview one-liner:
Although mm_struct describes userspace, the kernel must reference it too: for lazy TLB with kernel threads, for /proc and ptrace inspection, for NUMA page migration and IOMMU PRI faults, and during orderly process exit. Hence mm_count tracks kernel refs beyond mm_users, ensuring mm_struct isn’t freed prematurely.

Why mm would be null and why ttbr0_el1 will not have page loaded in kernel thread
ChatGPT said:
Excellent ⚡— this is one of those things that looks odd at first glance but makes perfect sense once you connect TLB, mm_struct, and kernel threads. Let’s go step by step.

🔹 Why mm can be NULL in kernel threads
User processes:

Each task_struct has task->mm pointing to its own mm_struct (VMAs, page tables).

On context switch, kernel loads task->mm->pgd into TTBR0_EL1 (ARM) or CR3 (x86).

This sets up user address space.

Kernel threads (kthread):

They never execute in user mode → no user VMAs, no mm_struct.

If kernel gave them a fake mm_struct, it would waste memory (VMAs, rss stats, etc.).

So: task->mm = NULL for kernel threads.

🔹 What happens to TTBR0_EL1?
On ARMv8/AArch64:

TTBR0_EL1 = translation base for user space.

TTBR1_EL1 = translation base for kernel space.

In kernel mode, CPU always uses TTBR1_EL1 for address translation.

So in theory, a kernel thread doesn’t need TTBR0_EL1 at all.

But:

Hardware caches (TLB, walk caches) still contain entries from TTBR0_EL1.

If you flush TTBR0_EL1 every time you switch into/out of a kernel thread, you’d burn tons of cycles.

🔹 The lazy TLB trick (active_mm)
Instead of leaving TTBR0_EL1 empty:

Kernel thread’s task->active_mm points to the last user task’s mm_struct.

Scheduler loads that mm’s pgd into TTBR0_EL1.

This keeps valid user mappings in TLB (even though the kernel thread won’t use them).

Why?

Saves performance: avoids flushing/reloading TLB every time kernel thread schedules in/out.

Ensures TTBR0_EL1 always has something valid, preventing corner-case faults on CPU speculation.

🔹 Textual Flow Example
User process A runs
 └─ task->mm = mm_A
 └─ TTBR0_EL1 = mm_A->pgd
 └─ TTBR1_EL1 = kernel pgd (global)

Kernel thread K runs
 └─ task->mm = NULL
 └─ task->active_mm = mm_A
 └─ TTBR0_EL1 = mm_A->pgd still loaded
 └─ TTBR1_EL1 = kernel pgd

User process B scheduled
 └─ task->mm = mm_B
 └─ TTBR0_EL1 switched to mm_B->pgd
 └─ TTBR1_EL1 = kernel pgd
So TTBR0_EL1 always has some pgd, even when kernel thread runs.

🔹 Why not just flush TTBR0_EL1 for kernel threads?
Caveats:

Performance: flushing TLB on every context switch kills performance.

Speculative execution: CPU may speculatively fetch using TTBR0_EL1 even in kernel mode. Having a valid mapping avoids spurious faults.

Lazy borrow is simpler: kernel just increments mm_count on the borrowed mm to keep it alive.

🔹 Summary
Kernel threads don’t have user VMAs → task->mm = NULL.

But CPU still needs valid page tables in TTBR0_EL1.

Kernel borrows last used mm (task->active_mm) to keep TTBR0_EL1 valid.

This avoids TLB flush storms and speculative faults.

When all references are done, mm_count ensures mm_struct isn’t freed too early.

✅ Interview one-liner:
Kernel threads have mm=NULL since they never run user code, but CPU’s TTBR0_EL1 still needs a valid pgd for TLB/speculation. So kernel uses active_mm to borrow the last user mm_struct, increments mm_count to pin it, and avoids flushing TTBR0_EL1 on every context switch.

Perfect, you’ve picked up on one of the core tricks in Linux memory management: idle tasks, kernel threads, and init_mm. Let’s tie everything together with all caveats.

🔹 Idle Task and init_task
Each CPU has a special task_struct called the idle task.

Declared statically in kernel (init_task).

Scheduler switches to this when the CPU has nothing else to run.

It is not a real process (no user space, no binary, no mm).

So:

idle_task->mm      = NULL   // no user mm
idle_task->active_mm = &init_mm
🔹 init_mm
init_mm is a global mm_struct object, defined in mm/init-mm.c.

It represents the kernel’s own page tables, built during early boot.

Its .pgd = swapper_pg_dir → the kernel’s master PGD.

All kernel threads and idle tasks reuse init_mm as their active_mm.

That’s why you see in the screenshot:

mm_users = 2 → ensures init_mm never gets freed.

Used as the “backing mm” for kernel-only contexts.

🔹 Why idle tasks use init_mm
Hardware requires some PGD in TTBR0_EL1, even if we don’t run user code.

Flushing the TLB on every idle entry would be expensive.

So kernel sets active_mm = &init_mm.

This way, TLB entries remain valid, and CPU speculation doesn’t fault.

🔹 Relationship: idle task, kernel thread, user process
Task type	task->mm	task->active_mm	TTBR0_EL1	TTBR1_EL1
User process	= user mm_struct	= user mm_struct	user PGD	kernel PGD
Kernel thread	NULL	borrowed mm	borrowed	kernel PGD
Idle task	NULL	init_mm	init_mm	kernel PGD
🔹 Lifecycle Example (ARMv8 / TTBR0_EL1 + TTBR1_EL1)
Boot:

Kernel builds swapper_pg_dir.

Stored in init_mm.pgd.

Loaded into TTBR1_EL1 (kernel space).

TTBR0_EL1 empty (no user yet).

Start first user process (init):

Allocates its own mm_struct.

Kernel loads mm->pgd into TTBR0_EL1.

Now user space is live.

Switch to idle task (CPU idle):

task->mm = NULL, active_mm = init_mm.

Scheduler keeps TTBR0_EL1 pointing to init_mm.

Switch back to user process:

Load that process’s mm->pgd into TTBR0_EL1.

Kernel always keeps TTBR1_EL1 with global kernel mappings.

🔹 Why mm = NULL but active_mm != NULL
mm = NULL → marks it as a kernel-only task (no VMAs, no RSS).

active_mm → ensures TLB/PGD are still consistent with some page tables.

This separation allows scheduler to reuse mappings without flushing.

🔹 Practical caveats
Lazy TLB:
Kernel threads borrow someone else’s mm (via active_mm). Reference counters (mm_count) ensure it isn’t freed too early.

init_mm special cases:

Used for early boot memory mappings (__kernel_physical_mapping_init).

Used for kernel-only operations like pgd_offset_k().

Head of mmlist (swap-related cleanup).

If mm_struct could be NULL in hardware:
The CPU would crash or speculatively access unmapped memory. So active_mm always points to a safe pgd (init_mm).

🔹 Textual Diagram
CPU Boot:
  init_mm.pgd = swapper_pg_dir  ---> TTBR1_EL1 (kernel space)
                                   TTBR0_EL1 empty

Idle task:
  task->mm = NULL
  task->active_mm = &init_mm
  TTBR0_EL1 = init_mm.pgd (safe pgd)
  TTBR1_EL1 = kernel pgd

Kernel thread:
  task->mm = NULL
  task->active_mm = borrowed from last process
  TTBR0_EL1 = borrowed->pgd
  TTBR1_EL1 = kernel pgd

User process:
  task->mm = its mm_struct
  task->active_mm = its mm_struct
  TTBR0_EL1 = user->pgd
  TTBR1_EL1 = kernel pgd
✅ One-liner takeaway:
Idle tasks and kernel threads don’t own an mm_struct, but the CPU always needs a valid PGD in TTBR0_EL1. So Linux uses active_mm, pointing to init_mm or a borrowed mm, while keeping mm=NULL to mark kernel-only tasks.

You said:
Kernel page table mappings are rooted in the PGD defined in swapper_pg_dir
and assigned to the init_mm.
Userland mappings are always present whether in userland or kernel
mode. On x86-64, which kernel mappings are present is dependent on
whether or not an important security mitigation, termed Page Table Isolation
(PTI), is enabled. This was implemented in order to address the ‘meltdown’
security vulnerability (a detailed discussion of which is outside the scope of
this book).
The kernel needs to have userland mappings in place for process-specific
transactions such as system calls in order that it can interact with userland
memory, e.g. to copy memory between kernel and userland so these must
be maintained between each.
When the PTI mitigation is not in place, then the mappings are simple –
both kernel and userland contain kernel and userland mappings, with the
kernel mappings maintaining page flags rendering them unusable in user-
land, and kernel mappings maintained such that the TLB is not flushed be-
tween context switches (see the virtual memory chapter for more on these
flags).
The feature is made available via CONFIG_PAGE_TABLE_ISOLATION but even if
this configuration option is set, the mitigation will only be enabled if the
X86_FEATURE_PTI flag is set, which is only enabled if the CPU is vulnerable to
meltdown, checked in pti_check_boottime_disable().
When PTI is enabled, then PGDs are allocated as order-1, i.e. 8 KiB, fo-
lios and contain two separate PGD tables, one for userland mode and one
for kernel mode.
In kernel mode (the first 4 KiB of the order-1 PGD) all kernel and user-
land mappings are present, however userland mappings are marked non-
executable in order to avoid any mistake in page table assignment in user-
land mode.
In userland mode, however (the last 4 KiB of the order-1 GPD), only a
bare minimum set of kernel mappings are present, the minimum required to permit kernel transition. By using order-1 PGD pages, we need only flip
a bit to switch between the two, which is what kernel_to_user_pgdp() and
user_to_kernel_pgdp() do.
Importantly, note that the struct mm_struct->pgd field is set to the kernel
portion of the order-1 PGD, i.e. the lower portion, with the userland map-
pings kept in the adjacent base page. This means initial transitions to an-
other process address space, performed in the kernel, maintain kernel map-
pings.
When a PGD entry needs to be updated for userland, the function
pti_set_user_pgtbl() is invoked which, if the PTI mitigation is in place, in-
vokes __pti_set_user_pgtbl(). This uses kernel_to_user_pgdp() to update the
userland portion of the PGD, and adds an equivalent in the kernel portion
of the PGD with execution disabled as previously discussed.
Switching between processes is ultimately performed by
switch_mm_irqs_off(), typically on context switch via context_switch() (shown
in listing 4-5) but also in other code paths via switch_mm() or activate_mm().
These functions change the PGD the CPU is currently using in the hard-
ware, which for x86-64 is specified by the cr3 control register whose value is
determined by build_cr3() and set by load_new_mm_cr3()*.
Note however that we remain in kernel mode as other actions need to
be performed before actually switching into user mode if that is what is re-
quired. As a result, as discussed above, we use the struct mm_struct->pgd field
which is pointing at the kernel PGD table, and thus this logic remains largely
unmodified.
The real change arises in the entry code that returns from a sys-
tem call or interrupt (including scheduler interrupts), for example
common_interrupt_return() and entry_SYSCALL_64() which both invoke the
SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3() and SWITCH_TO_USER_CR3_STACK() assembly macros which
fixup the PGDs accordingly before loading them into cr3.
I have focused on the PTI logic in a fair bit of detail here as a result of
it complicating the otherwise fairly clear logic around kernel and userland
page table mappings, which without this mitigation are simply stored in the
same page tables, only with the kernel mappings explicitly made unavailable
to userland.
ChatGPT said:
Great — you’ve just hit the Page Table Isolation (PTI) machinery, which is one of the trickiest but most illuminating pieces of Linux VM internals. Let me unpack this in plain but detailed terms, connect it to our earlier mm_struct/pgd/vma discussion, and highlight the caveats.

🔹 Normal (non-PTI) world
On x86-64 before meltdown/PTI, a single PGD (Page Global Directory) per process contains both:

User mappings (lower half of VA)

Kernel mappings (upper half of VA)

These kernel mappings are marked as:

present but only accessible in ring 0 (CPL=0)

so if userland tries to touch them, → #GP (fault).

Advantage:

When switching processes, kernel does not flush kernel mappings from TLB → huge perf win.

CPU sees same kernel VA everywhere, only the user VA portion changes.

🔹 PTI (Page Table Isolation)
Meltdown broke this model: speculative execution could peek at those kernel mappings from userland.

Fix = PTI:

Linux now splits PGD into two halves (an order-1 allocation = 8 KB = two PGDs side-by-side):

Kernel PGD (first 4 KB):

Kernel mappings + user mappings

But user mappings are NX (non-executable) for safety

User PGD (second 4 KB):

User mappings

Only minimal kernel trampoline mappings (just enough to get into kernel and switch to kernel PGD)

🔹 Switching between the two
mm_struct->pgd points at the kernel portion of this dual PGD.

When entering kernel mode (syscall, interrupt):

CPU loads the kernel PGD (SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3)

Now kernel and userland VAs are both mapped → safe for copy_to_user() etc.

When returning to user mode:

CPU switches to the user PGD (SWITCH_TO_USER_CR3_STACK)

Kernel mappings disappear (except the trampoline).

This flip is cheap → just a CR3 write with a bit toggle (kernel_to_user_pgdp(), user_to_kernel_pgdp()).

🔹 Internals + Key Functions
pti_set_user_pgtbl()

Ensures any change to user PGD is also reflected in kernel PGD (but NX).

switch_mm_irqs_off() / context_switch()

Classic context switch path, sets mm->pgd into CR3 (with kernel portion).

entry_SYSCALL_64(), common_interrupt_return()

Low-level entry code macros do the actual flip back to user CR3.

🔹 Where mm_struct fits
mm_struct->pgd

For PTI: points to the kernel half of dual PGD.

For non-PTI: points to the single shared PGD.

TLB behavior:

Non-PTI: kernel mappings persist in TLB across switches.

PTI: user PGD does not cache kernel mappings, so flip → kernel reloads needed.

🔹 ARMv8/v9 caveat
ARM wasn’t hit by meltdown the same way, but similar concepts apply:

TTBR0_EL1 = user space page table root.

TTBR1_EL1 = kernel space page table root (always mapped).

That’s effectively PTI by design → no meltdown risk.

So PTI is really an x86-64 specific hack.

On ARM, mm_struct->pgd is used to program TTBR0_EL1; kernel mappings live permanently in TTBR1_EL1.

🔹 Why kernel still maps userland pages
Because:

syscalls like read() or write() need to copy data between kernel and user space.

That means kernel must see userland VA → must maintain user mappings even while in kernel mode.

So PTI doesn’t delete user mappings from kernel PGD, it just enforces NX on them.

🔹 Textual Flow
User process runs:
    CR3 → user PGD (user mappings + minimal kernel trampoline)
    TTBR0_EL1 (ARM) or CR3 (x86-64)

Syscall entry:
    Save state
    SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3()
    CR3 → kernel PGD (kernel mappings + user mappings NX)
    Execute syscall
    Possibly copy_from_user() using those mappings

Syscall exit:
    SWITCH_TO_USER_CR3_STACK()
    CR3 → user PGD
    Resume in userland
🔹 Caveats
Performance hit:

PTI costs ~5–30% perf depending on syscall-heavy workloads (extra CR3 flush).

On ARM → no such overhead thanks to TTBR split.

init_mm:

Kernel’s own mm, with swapper_pg_dir.

Always present in TTBR1_EL1 (ARM) or in kernel PGD (x86).

Security:

With PTI, user can’t speculatively touch kernel mappings.

But still possible to pass kernel pointers to syscalls → kernel must validate every pointer.

✅ Summary one-liner:
Without PTI, both kernel and user mappings coexist in the same PGD, with kernel made inaccessible via flags. PTI splits them into dual PGDs, flipping CR3 on syscall/interrupt entry/exit. On ARM, this separation is built-in with TTBR0/TTBR1, so meltdown didn’t bite.

ChatGPT said:
Perfect — you’ve landed on the fork() vs execve() lifecycle and how kernel mappings propagate. Let’s break it down carefully and connect it to everything we’ve discussed so far (mm_struct, init_mm, PGD, PTI/TTBR split, etc.), with the right caveats.

🔹 Step 1: Kernel mappings established early
During early boot, the kernel:

Initializes swapper_pg_dir (the kernel’s master PGD).

Populates direct map (linear PA→VA mapping for all RAM).

Populates vmalloc area, fixmaps, kernel text/data, etc.

All this is anchored in init_mm (struct mm_struct for the kernel).

👉 So from the beginning, all kernel threads and all user processes share the same kernel VA mappings.
This is why a copy_page_range() or mm_init() always includes kernel portions.

🔹 Step 2: fork() path
When a process forks:

Call chain:
kernel_clone() → copy_process() → copy_mm() → dup_mm() → dup_mmap() → copy_page_range()

What happens:

A new mm_struct is created for the child.

Kernel mappings (from swapper_pg_dir/init_mm) are reused (not duplicated).

On x86 non-PTI: copied straight into new PGD.

On x86 PTI: user + kernel halves are prepared accordingly.

On ARM: TTBR1_EL1 (kernel half) is shared, TTBR0_EL1 (user half) is duplicated.

User mappings are copied Copy-on-Write (CoW):

Instead of duplicating all pages, PTEs are marked read-only.

Both parent & child PGDs point to the same physical pages.

On write, a page fault triggers a private copy.

👉 Result: fast fork, kernel mappings are inherited wholesale, user pages deferred via CoW.

🔹 Step 3: execve() path
When a process calls execve():

Call chain:
sys_execve() → do_execveat_common() → exec_mmap() → mm_alloc() → mm_init()

What happens:

A new mm_struct is allocated from scratch.

A new PGD is allocated (pgd_alloc() → arch-specific pgd_alloc()).

Kernel mappings (direct map, vmalloc, fixmap, etc.) are cloned in from init_mm.
(i.e., only kernel part is reused, user part is blank slate).

Old VMAs are destroyed, new VMAs are created to load the binary (ELF interpreter, stack, heap).

👉 Result: process loses all its old user mappings but retains kernel mappings.
That’s why fork + exec is the standard model: fork copies context, exec resets userland.

🔹 Why both paths preserve kernel mappings?
Kernel mappings must always exist in every process:

Syscalls need to copy_to_user()/copy_from_user().

Interrupts/exceptions can occur at any time.

Device DMA may need to resolve kernel VA → PA.

Without shared kernel VA space:

Every syscall would require switching the kernel’s own PGD (expensive TLB flush).

That’s why Linux design is:
all tasks share kernel half of the PGD, but each has private user half.

🔹 How this looks (ARM vs x86)
On ARM (built-in PTI via TTBRs):
TTBR1_EL1 → Kernel PGD (same for all processes)
TTBR0_EL1 → User PGD (per process, from mm_struct->pgd)
On x86 (no PTI):
CR3 → One PGD containing both kernel + user mappings
switch_mm() just swaps user part, keeps kernel part identical
On x86 (PTI enabled):
CR3 → Flips between two PGDs per process:
       - Kernel PGD: kernel+user (user NX)
       - User PGD: user-only + trampoline
🔹 Important caveats
Kernel threads (kthreads):

Have task->mm = NULL.

Borrow active_mm from last scheduled user task (lazy TLB trick).

Still see kernel mappings via init_mm.

Lazy TLB:

Kernel threads don’t flush TLB on every schedule.

Saves overhead by holding on to last process’s user mappings.

Memory accounting:

Fork increases mm_users (user refcount).

Exec resets user mappings but keeps mm_count alive until teardown.

Security (PTI):

On meltdown-vulnerable x86, kernel mappings hidden in user PGD.

On ARM, safe by design thanks to TTBR separation.

🔹 Textual Flow Diagram
Boot:
    swapper_pg_dir (init_mm->pgd) setup with:
        - Direct map
        - Kernel text/data
        - vmalloc/fixmap
        - Kernel stacks
    → Shared by all processes

fork():
    copy_process()
      → copy_mm()
         → dup_mm()
            → dup_mmap()
               → copy_page_range()
    Result:
       - New mm_struct
       - Kernel mappings reused
       - User mappings copied as CoW

execve():
    do_execveat_common()
      → mm_alloc()
         → mm_init()
            → pgd_alloc()
    Result:
       - New mm_struct
       - Kernel mappings copied from init_mm
       - User mappings destroyed/rebuilt for new program
✅ Summary one-liner:
Every process inherits kernel mappings (direct map, vmalloc, fixmaps) from init_mm, either via copy_page_range() in fork or mm_init() in execve. User mappings differ: fork → CoW copy, execve → wiped and rebuilt. On ARM this separation is natural with TTBR0/TTBR1, while on x86 PTI complicates the model by splitting PGDs.

ChatGPT said:
Great — now you’re right at the core of how kernel mappings propagate via PGD setup and why PTI adds an extra wrinkle. Let’s unpack this step by step and tie it with everything we’ve discussed (mm_struct, init_mm, swapper_pg_dir, fork/exec, etc.), with all caveats.

🔹 The simple goal
When creating a new process, we need:

User portion: fresh, per-process mappings (mm_struct->pgd).

Kernel portion: shared, copied from swapper_pg_dir (root kernel PGD in init_mm).

👉 Fundamentally, this is:

new_pgd[x] = swapper_pg_dir[x];
for kernel slots of the PGD.

🔹 Added complexity: PTI
Without PTI (Page Table Isolation):
The PGD has both user and kernel entries. Kernel mappings are copied wholesale → done.

With PTI (mitigation for Meltdown on x86):

Each PGD is order-1 (8 KB), i.e. has two halves:

Lower 4 KB → kernel-mode PGD (all kernel + user mappings, user NX).

Upper 4 KB → user-mode PGD (only user + trampoline minimal kernel mappings).

When building a new PGD:

Copy from kernel half of swapper_pg_dir to new PGD.

Also copy the minimal trampoline kernel entries into the user half (so system calls can safely enter kernel).

Switching between the halves is done by macros (SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3(), etc.), effectively flipping a pointer in CR3.

🔹 Synchronizing PGDs across processes
All PGDs in the system are tracked in pgd_list.

New PGD → added to pgd_list under pgd_lock (protects against races).

During early init, before all global kernel mappings are set, sync_global_pgds() ensures:

Every PGD gets kernel mapping updates.

Example: direct map expansion must be reflected everywhere.

After boot:

No new kernel mappings at PGD level (kernel VA space is mostly fixed).

So only P4D/PMD/PTE levels need updates, which are naturally shared.

👉 Caveat:

On x86: P4Ds for kernel VA are shared between all PGDs.

On ARM (TTBR0/1 model): no need to sync kernel mappings separately → TTBR1 always points to the single kernel PGD.

🔹 Flow at init and PID 1
Kernel boots with init_mm pointing to swapper_pg_dir.

In rest_init() → kernel spawns PID 1 (init process).

Calls user_mode_thread() → sets up execution of kernel_init().

That calls run_init_process() → eventually kernel_execve() to exec /sbin/init.

When execve() is called:

mm_alloc() creates a fresh mm_struct.

mm_init() → pgd_alloc() → new PGD is allocated.

Kernel mappings copied from swapper_pg_dir into new PGD (with PTI adjustments if needed).

User portion cleared and rebuilt for init binary’s VMAs.

👉 From this point: every fork/exec works as we discussed:

fork() → copy_page_range() (CoW user mappings, copy kernel slots).

execve() → mm_alloc()/mm_init() (new PGD, kernel part copied, user wiped and rebuilt).

🔹 Textual Diagram (x86 PTI vs no-PTI vs ARM)
=== Boot ===
swapper_pg_dir (init_mm->pgd) = root kernel PGD
   → contains direct map, vmalloc, fixmap, text, etc.

=== fork ===
dup_mm()
   → pgd_alloc()
       → allocate new PGD
       → copy kernel slots from swapper_pg_dir
       → add to pgd_list
   → copy_page_range()
       → copy user PTEs CoW

=== execve ===
mm_alloc()
   → mm_init()
       → pgd_alloc()
           → copy kernel slots
           → clear user slots
       → load binary VMAs

=== PTI active (x86 only) ===
PGD = 8KB
   - lower 4KB = kernel-mode PGD (full kernel+user, user NX)
   - upper 4KB = user-mode PGD (user only + trampoline)
Switching: SWITCH_TO_KERNEL_CR3 / SWITCH_TO_USER_CR3_STACK
🔹 Caveats & subtleties
ARM vs x86:

ARM (TTBR1 for kernel, TTBR0 for user) → no pgd_list syncing needed.

x86 needs pgd_list syncing because kernel PGD is per-process.

Kernel threads:

Have mm = NULL, active_mm = init_mm.

Reuse last user PGD but rely on shared kernel mappings.

Security:

PTI overhead → extra PGD copies, CR3 flips.

On ARM, isolation is free due to TTBR0/1 split.

Scalability:

After early boot, PGD syncing is unnecessary at kernel level because all mappings below PGD (P4D/PMD/PTE) are already shared.

✅ So the essence is:
Every new PGD is seeded with kernel mappings from swapper_pg_dir. On x86 PTI you need two halves of PGD and syncing logic; on ARM TTBR1 ensures kernel mappings are globally shared, so only user half (TTBR0) varies.

You said:
The two key locks at the process address space level are the spinlock
struct mm_struct->page_table_lock and struct mm_struct->mmap_lock which is a
read/write semaphore.
These locks are absolutely critical as they are very heavily utilised and
thus it is useful to examine their usage in detail:
As described in the virtual memory chapter in section 3.1.4, this lock is used
for page table locking at the less-contended higher page table levels, typi-
cally all levels above PMD. There are some nuances to this – operations on
kernel mappings typically use this lock for PMDs unconditionally, e.g. in
__pte_alloc_kernel() which is invoked by vmalloc via pte_alloc_kernel_track()
and of course, if the architecture doesn’t use split locks for PMD/PTEs at all
then this lock will be used for all page table updates.
However, there are cases where the lock is used for non-page table oper-
ations. This used to be more common in the distant kernel past but has now
been narrowed down to only a few instances:
• Protecting stack expansion – In expand_downwards() (typically used with a
stack) and expand_upwards() VMA expansion takes place which results in
thread unsafe fields being updated, specifically the VMA gap calcula-
tion. Since the mmap_lock semaphore permits simultaneous read access, page_table_lock is used to place the entire update process in a critical sec-
tion. This is simply an overloading of an available lock for an entirely
different use.
• Protecting VMA gap calculation – (only applicable if CONFIG_DEBUG_VM_RB has
been set) – A calculation of the VMA subtree gap (see the next section on
VMAs to see what this means) is performed in vma_compute_subtree_gap()
which is invoked in turn by in browse_rb() (via validate_mm()). This
maintains a page_table_lock over the operation, introduced in com-
mit acf128d048c7: mm: validate_mm browse_rb SMP race condition. This
was added because, it this function were to race with vma_gap_update(),
data corruption could occur. Since this update function is invoked
in expand_downwards() and expand_upwards(), and might also hold a read
semaphore at the time (rendering the semaphore useless), using this
lock resolves the data race.
• Protecting the update of the anon_vma field and chain linkage in
__anon_vma_prepare() – Here there may be multiple threads attempting to
perform the same action rendering the update a critical section. Again,
page_table_lock is a convenient lock to use at this stage. See the section
below on reverse mappings for more details on the use of this opera-
tion. The struct mm_struct->mmap_lock field specifies a read/write semaphore object
that is used to synchronise VMAs and any other mm_struct state within the
address space.
It is a very heavily contended lock and used in an enormous number of
places, being arguably one of the most important locks in the entire kernel.
It is therefore worth exploring in some detail:
The struct rw_semaphore object is a lock type which allows concurrent ac-
cess to critical sections for multiple readers, but importantly only permits
writes when no readers are present. It is designed such that readers cannot
starve writers*, though in theory the reverse could occur (however in prac-
tice this should never happen).
The lock is designed such that, if threads are simply reading fields, they
do not contend one another (the state is in theory immutable and thus there
is no reason that they should, though this isn’t quite the case, see the above
note about the use of page_table_lock on VMA expansion).
There are a number of helper functions which wrap common operations

mm_struct->page_table_lock (a spinlock)

mm_struct->mmap_lock (a read/write semaphore)

Let me break this down exhaustively with all caveats, their relationship to everything we’ve already discussed (mm_struct, VMA, page faults, anon_vma, demand paging, etc.), and give you a textual diagram at the end.

🔹 1. page_table_lock (spinlock)
Location: struct mm_struct->page_table_lock

Type: spinlock_t

Scope: protects page table entry updates and some misc critical fields.

Typical usage
Higher-level page table updates:

At levels above PMD (e.g. PGD, P4D, PUD).

Example: __pte_alloc_kernel() in vmalloc paths acquires this before creating new page table pages.

Architectural caveat:

Some arches (like ARM with split locks per PMD/PTE) don’t always use this; x86 and others do.

Unusual / overloaded usage
Sometimes kernel developers reuse it for non-page-table ops (legacy quirks, now minimized):

Stack expansion

Functions: expand_downwards() and expand_upwards()

Why? Expanding a stack VMA changes internal gap-calculation fields.

Problem: mmap_lock (rwsem) can allow multiple readers, so it’s not enough to avoid corruption.

Solution: use page_table_lock for atomic critical section.

VMA gap calculation (debug mode)

Code: vma_compute_subtree_gap() under CONFIG_DEBUG_VM_RB.

Ensures validate_mm() can’t race with vma_gap_update().

Added via commit acf128d048c7.

anon_vma linkage setup

Function: __anon_vma_prepare().

Multiple threads may try to prepare the same anon_vma.

Protects field updates and list linkage.

👉 Caveat:
It’s sometimes used as a "convenient global lock" when other locks are insufficient. This overloading means spinlock contention is a real performance issue.

🔹 2. mmap_lock (rw_semaphore)
Location: struct mm_struct->mmap_lock

Type: struct rw_semaphore

Scope: protects VMAs and mm_struct-wide state.

Semantics
Readers: many allowed concurrently (down_read()).

Writers: exclusive, no readers allowed (down_write()).

Fairness: writers cannot be starved by readers, but in theory readers may starve if writers keep coming.

Usage
Held in almost every mmap-related syscall:

mmap(), munmap(), mprotect(), brk(), etc.

Ensures consistency of VMA tree (red-black tree in mm_struct->mm_rb).

Protects per-process address space layout (mm_struct + VMA list).

Example:

do_mmap() → mmap_write_lock(mm)

find_vma() → mmap_read_lock(mm)

Caveats
Hot lock: one of the most contended locks in the entire kernel.

Deadlock risks: must always acquire in canonical order (never inside page fault handler after taking spinlocks, etc.).

Scaling issue: on very high core-count systems, contention on mmap_lock is a bottleneck. That’s why there are RCU-based ideas like per-VMA locks being explored.

🔹 Relationship between the two
mmap_lock: "big picture" → protects VMA structures and mm_struct state.

page_table_lock: "low level" → protects actual page table updates and a few delicate fields.

Both are needed because:

VMAs are a higher-level abstraction (ranges, flags, anon/file backing).

Page tables are the low-level hardware mappings for these ranges.

🔹 Connection with our earlier discussions
Demand paging:

Page fault path first grabs mmap_lock (read mode) to check/find the right VMA.

If it needs to allocate/modify page tables → also takes page_table_lock.

Copy-on-Write (COW):

Writes require creating new mappings, page table updates → use page_table_lock.

Still need mmap_lock for VMA integrity.

Fork (dup_mmap / copy_page_range):

Needs mmap_lock to walk the VMA tree safely.

Uses page_table_lock while actually copying page table entries.

VMAs and anon_vma linkage:

__anon_vma_prepare() uses page_table_lock for atomicity.

Kernel mappings (vmalloc, ioremap):

Use __pte_alloc_kernel() → requires page_table_lock.

🔹 Textual diagram
User Process Access → Page Fault Trap
    ↓
Kernel checks mm_struct
    ↓
Acquire mmap_lock (read)      // protects VMA tree
    ↓
Find VMA in mm_struct->mm_rb
    ↓
If page table update needed:
    Acquire page_table_lock    // protects page table hierarchy
    ↓
    Modify PTE/PMD
    Release page_table_lock
    ↓
Release mmap_lock
    ↓
Resume process
🔹 Key caveats
Spinlock vs rwsem

page_table_lock (spinlock) → must be atomic, no sleeping allowed.

mmap_lock (rwsem) → can sleep, since VMA operations may need blocking work (I/O for file-backed pages, etc.).

Kernel threads

Still use init_mm->page_table_lock for kernel mappings (e.g., vmalloc).

No mmap_lock since they don’t own user VMAs.

Performance tradeoff

Overloading page_table_lock for things like anon_vma prep is a pragmatic compromise, but increases contention.

✅ So the core picture:

mmap_lock: guards VMA structures (the "map").

page_table_lock: guards PTE modifications (the "territory").
Both are used heavily, in fork, exec, mmap, page faults, vmalloc, etc., and their interaction is central to Linux memory scalability.

Keep this answer handy — it’s the canonical “what each diagram means” + the practical caveats.

1) Big picture: what mmap_lock does and the two lock flavors
mmap_lock (a struct rw_semaphore) is the global address-space/VMA lock inside struct mm_struct.

Readers (down_read): many concurrent readers allowed — used for operations that only examine VMAs or access page tables but do not change the VMA tree.

Writers (down_write): only one writer — used for operations that change the address space layout (create/destroy/resize VMAs, set protections, pin pages, mlock, etc.).

Why it’s hot: almost every process memory syscall and many kernel operations need to read or modify VMAs → enormous contention.

page_table_lock (spinlock) is separate: used to protect page-table updates (PTE/PMD allocations/updates). Many code paths take both locks (read mmap_lock and then page_table_lock) or use them in a carefully defined ordering.

Rule of thumb:

Read lock for “lookups / pinning / common faults / GUP fast path / procfs read / smaps / pagemap reads”

Write lock for “mmap/munmap/mremap/mprotect/brk/fork-copy-mm/exec/mlock/populate/locking that changes VMA or pins pages long-term”

2) High-level practical caveats (you want these remembered for interviews)
Page-faults usually start with an mmap_lock read to find the VMA, but the handler may release mmap_lock while doing I/O, swap-in, or long operations and then return VM_FAULT_RETRY. The faulting instruction is retried after the lock is reacquired. This is central to correctness & deadlock avoidance.

Fault lock-releasing path allows blocking work (reading from disk, swap, file I/O) without holding mmap_lock. This is why page fault code can return VM_FAULT_RETRY and the top-level handler loops.

Write operations (mmap/munmap/mprotect/mlock/etc.) take down_write — these exclude readers and are heavier. Long writes can starve readers or cause contention.

GUP (get_user_pages) / pin_user_pages: common operation used for pinning user pages for DMA; it uses the mmap_lock read path (fast), but the longterm/pin variants may require more guarantees (and may fall into slower paths that re-acquire or upgrade locks). Pinning long-term or doing mlock needs care.

Do not hold mmap_lock while doing heavy blocking work (drivers must avoid taking it if they will sleep a long time); otherwise you can deadlock user code doing memory ops.

Ordering: there’s a canonical ordering: acquire mmap_lock first (for VMA ops), and then page_table_lock when needed for PTE updates. Reversing can lead to deadlocks.

mmap_lock is not per-thread — it protects the process address space. Kernel threads that reuse other process mm may increment mm_count / active_mm and hold references.

Procfs readers (/proc/$pid/maps, smaps, pagemap) mostly take mmap_lock read — must be consistent and avoid races.

3) Figure-by-figure condensed summaries (what your screenshots show)
I’ll convert the flow diagrams into short textual descriptions. For every box I show whether it acquires mmap_lock and whether it is R (read) or W (write) according to the diagrams.

Figure 4-2: mmap() family (mapping/unmapping/exec)
Operations: mmap, munmap, mremap, do_mmap, do_munmap, vm_mmap, load_elf_binary (exec), begin_new_exec.

Locking:

mmap() and do_mmap() → write (down_write) — they modify VMA tree (create VMA).

munmap() / __vm_munmap() → write — destroy range.

execve()/load_elf_binary → allocate new mm + new PGD (mm_alloc()), write operations to set up new mm.

Caveat: mapping creation holds write lock while updating tree; kernel code must not hold it while doing slow blocking I/O.

Figure 4-3: Fork / clone / dup_mm
Operations: fork(), vfork(), clone(), copy_mm(), dup_mmap(), dup_mm(), dup_mmap() is shown as write.

Locking:

dup_mmap() and dup_mm() do heavy VMA copying; take write locks while duplicating mm state.

copy_mm() (for non-thread clone) likewise uses write mode.

Note: when threads share mm (CLONE_VM) they do not duplicate, so less locking needed.

Figure 4-4: Page fault path
High-level: do_user_addr_fault() → handle_mm_fault() → _handle_mm_fault() → handle_pte_fault() → do_fault() → do_read_fault() / do_cow_fault() / do_shared_fault() / filemap_fault() → folio/page allocation → update PTEs.

Locking specifics:

Page fault enters with mmap_lock read to find VMA.

If page allocation / mapping updates required → will take page_table_lock to update PTEs.

If the fault handler must perform I/O (file read or swap-in), it releases mmap_lock while performing I/O, then returns VM_FAULT_RETRY to the higher-level loop that will retry the fault.

filemap_fault() and folio locking may involve folio locks; the fault path will lock_folio_maybe_drop_mmap() — it tries to avoid deadlocks: it may drop mmap_lock, lock folio, then reacquire.

Important: return codes VM_FAULT_RETRY vs VM_FAULT_COMPLETED indicate whether the lock was released during fault.

Figure 4-5: GUP / get_user_pages / pin_user_pages
Operations: process_vm_readv/writev, process_vm_*, get_user_pages, pin_user_pages, get_user_pages_remote, _get_user_pages_fast, gup_longterm_locked.

Locking:

Read lock for common GUP paths (they only need to pin and check pages).

gup_longterm and pinned long-term allocations can be slower and may need different handling (refcounts, long-term pin). Some longterm pin flows reacquire locks differently (diagram shows reacquire points).

Caveat: GUP must be careful with mmap_lock and page faults (pinning may have to cause a fault to allocate page) — slow paths may drop/reacquire locks.

Figure 4-6: mlock() invocations
Operations: mlock(), mlock2(), munlock(), mlockall(), munlockall(), do_mlock().

Locking:

mlock() and mlockall() take write on mmap_lock. mlock needs to prevent pages from swapping so it can alter page accounting / pte attributes — requires write exclusivity.

After write lock maybe release to perform page population; diagram shows __mm_populate() is called after the write lock is released (populating pages).

Caveat: populating pages may fault pages in (causing I/O) — locking strategy must avoid deadlock.

Figure 4-7: madvise() variants
Operations: madvise(), do_madvise(), madvise_vma_behavior(), madvise_populate(), madvise_willneed(), madvise_remove().

Locking:

do_madvise() takes read or write depending on operation (the figure notes lock type depends on madvise_need_mmap_write()).

madvise_willneed() and madvise_remove() may acquire only read in many cases; madvise_populate() may need to re-acquire a read lock after possibly dropping it for I/O.

Caveat: madvise will request population or decommit; population may trigger page faults which may need lock dancing.

Figure 4-8 & 4-9: Core dump and CPU exceptions (page faults from signals / bad frames)
Operations: exit_to_user_mode_prepare, get_signal, do_coredump(), dump_vma_snapshot(), signal handling paths.

Locking:

Core dump needs to snapshot process VMAs → takes locks (the diagram shows dump_vma_snapshot() writing, i.e. write lock).

CPU exceptions that turn into signals need to read VMA info → usually read mmap_lock to resolve problem and handle faults or send SIGSEGV.

Caveat: core dump must produce consistent snapshot while VMAs may be changing; heavy locking is used.

Figure 4-10: procfs interactions (/proc/$pid/maps, smaps, pagemap, mem)
Operations: proc_* read handlers: proc_map_files_lookup(), proc_map_files_instantiate(), pid_maps_open(), pid_smats_open(), pagmap_read(), mem_read() etc.

Locking:

Most proc readers take read mmap_lock (they must read VMA list or page maps safely).

Some proc operations that mutate internal mapping caches may require write or special operations; but usually proc is read-only and holds read lock.

Caveat: /proc/$pid/mem or process_vm_readv may access remote vm pages and pin them, requiring careful GUP logic and mmap_lock use.

Figure 4-11: OOM killer and mm reaping
Operations: oom_reaper()/oom_reap_task(), process_mrelease().

Locking:

OOM reaper reads mm state; it takes read locks to find what to reap; reaper threads may free pinned pages, etc.

Caveat: the OOM reaper needs to carefully race with other lock-holders and may trigger tear-down of mm.

Figure 4-12: prctl() ops (like setting THP/disable)
Operations: prctl(PR_SET_MM_MAP, PR_SET_VMA_ANON_NAME), prctl_set_mm(), prctl_set_vma() etc.

Locking:

Some prctl variants require write (modifying VMA attributes).

Others are read-only and take read.

Caveat: prctl can be used to change mm behavior; it must take locks when it mutates mm.

Figure 4-13: NUMA / migrate pages
Operations: migrate_pages(), kernel_migrate_pages(), do_pages_stat() and do_pages_move().

Locking:

NUMA operations often take read or write depending if they will move pages; moving pages requires exclusive operations and interactions with folio/fallback locks.

Caveat: pages migration may need page pinning, folio locking and coordination with pagefault and swap.

Figure 4-14: miscellaneous (mincore, swapoff, mprotect, try_to_unuse)
Locking:

mincore() is read (does not change mapping).

swapoff() / swapoff related internals or mprotect() may be write.

Caveat: mprotect modifies PTEs and may need to flush TLBs and update page attributes — may also take page_table_lock.

4) Short mapping table (common syscalls → lock mode)
Practical shortlist you can memorize for interviews.

mmap() → write (create VMA)

munmap() → write (destroy VMA)

mprotect() → write (change protections)

mremap() → write

brk() → write (adjust heap VMA)

fork() / clone() (create mm) → write (dup mm)

execve() → write (replace mm)

madvise() → read or write depending on flag (populate / willneed may cause read or extra ops)

mlock() / mlockall() → write (pin pages)

munlock() → write

mincore() → read

process_vm_readv/writev → read (GUP path and pin)

ptrace may need mm manipulation → varies (often write)

/proc/* reads (maps, smaps, pagemap) → read

Page fault path do_user_addr_fault() → start read, may drop lock and later reacquire (fault may block)

Remember: there are many special cases; this table is the typical case.

5) Page fault lock dance: the canonical flow (important)
CPU traps on invalid mapping → do_user_addr_fault() is entered (interrupt context/exception path).

Kernel acquires mmap_lock read to find VMA and check permissions.

If page must be brought in or allocated: it calls handle_mm_fault() which may:

allocate a new folio/page, or

call filemap_readpage() (which does file I/O) or

call swapin (swap I/O).

If I/O needed, kernels normally release mmap_lock (so other tasks can proceed) and perform I/O (sleep), then return VM_FAULT_RETRY. The faulting thread will retry and reacquire mmap_lock.

Once data present, kernel takes page_table_lock and updates PTE; flushes TLB if needed; resumes user thread.

Key interview point: page fault handlers may drop mmap_lock — you must handle VM_FAULT_RETRY and be careful around races (the VMA may have changed while lock was released).

6) GUP (get_user_pages) subtleties
Common use: drivers pin user pages for DMA. They call get_user_pages() or pin_user_pages().

Fast path: try to pin pages while holding mmap_lock read and without causing major blocking.

Slow path: if page needs allocation or copy-on-write, GUP may need to perform faulting & I/O; it then may drop and reacquire locks or use a longterm pin mechanism (gup_longterm_locked) which changes behavior.

Longterm pins are dangerous because they prevent page migration and swapping; the kernel needs proper accounting.

7) mlock and __mm_populate() detail
mlock() is a write operation. The kernel may mark pages as non-swappable and call page population functions to ensure pages are resident.

__mm_populate() is used to fault-in pages (populate) and may be called after lock is managed to avoid blocking while holding the writer lock.

8) madvise(MADV_WILLNEED) / populate behavior
MADV_WILLNEED is advisory but causes the kernel to try to make pages resident. The kernel’s madvise_populate() will either:

do page faults to bring pages in, or

call file readahead if file-backed.

The diagram shows it often releases and reacquires read lock while doing page population to avoid long blocking.

9) procfs and smaps/pagemap note
Tools like ps, pmap, smem and pagemap rely on /proc/$pid/* interfaces. They mostly take mmap_lock read to make consistent view of VMAs and PTEs.

/proc/$pid/mem is special — it can access process address space and uses GUP/pinning and therefore must follow GUP locking rules.

10) Deadlock, ordering, & concurrency rules interviewers expect you to know
Always prefer mmap_lock before page_table_lock if you need both. Reversals will create deadlocks.

Fault code may drop locks; callers must detect VM_FAULT_RETRY.

Do not hold mmap_lock while performing driver I/O or any long sleeps. If you must do I/O, drop the lock first.

Readers (many) vs Writers (exclusive): avoid long-running writers; prefer slicing work or doing work outside the write-critical section when safe.

11) Quick FAQ style clarifications (common traps)
Q: Does a page fault always hold mmap_lock?
A: It starts with a read hold, but fault handlers can release it for I/O; the code will return VM_FAULT_RETRY and reattempt.

Q: Is mmap_lock per-thread?
A: No — it’s per-mm_struct (per address space). Threads sharing the mm (CLONE_VM) use the same lock.

Q: Can kernel code enter page-fault paths while holding other locks?
A: Be careful — if you hold locks that block page fault handlers from completing, you can deadlock. Kernel code must follow lock ordering rules and avoid taking mmap_lock while holding locks that a fault handler might need.

Q: Who uses mmap_lock outside syscall paths?
A: Many kernel subsystems: GUP/pinning (drivers), procfs readers, OOM reaper, core dump, NUMA/migration code, page reclaim, memory hotplug, etc. That’s why it’s one of the most contended locks.

12) Concrete short checklist to memorize for interviews
mmap_lock read: page faults (typical), mincore, proc reads, process_vm_readv, get_user_pages fast, madvise reads.

mmap_lock write: mmap, munmap, mprotect, mremap, mlock, fork copy mm, execve mm replacement, prctl VMA changes.

Page fault may drop lock: always be ready for VM_FAULT_RETRY and changes in VMA while you dropped the lock.

page_table_lock (spin): used for PTE allocation/update; try to grab it after you already hold the appropriate mmap_lock (or as required by architecture rules).

GUP (get_user_pages) rules: fast path holds read; longterm path has special semantics and may change locking.

13) Example interview answer (short script you can recite)
“mmap_lock is mm_struct’s rw-semaphore that protects the VMA tree and mm state. Most read-only operations (page faults, proc reads, GUP) take the read lock; operations that mutate the address space (mmap/munmap/mprotect/fork/exec/mlock) take the write lock. Page faults start with a read lock and may release it while doing I/O or swap-in and return VM_FAULT_RETRY so the fault can be retried — that’s the canonical lock-dance you must describe. Page-table changes happen under page_table_lock (spinlock). Always acquire mmap_lock before page_table_lock and never block the lock for long (I/O) — drop it and retry. mmap_lock is extremely contended; most of the diagrams in Stoakes’ book show where read vs write locks are taken and the special cases (core dump, OOM reaper, prctl, madvise, GUP).”

Link these lock behaviors back to vmalloc/VM creation, VFIO/GUP use-cases, DMA pinning, etc. (so you can explain how driver DMA interacts safely with mmap_lock).

4.3.5.2 Core dump filter flags
Which classes of memory that get core dumped are also stored in the
struct mm_struct->flags fields and specified in /proc/$pid/coredump_filter (or
via the coredump_filter kernel parameter), see the proc documentation for more
details on how to read and set these.
Note that each VMA can override the dumping process altogether by
specifying the VM_DONTDUMP flag. And on the other hand, certain kinds of
VMAs always get dumped, as determined via always_dump_vma() – any VMA
that has a name assigned to it is assumed to always be important, as well as
the vsyscall mapping.
Examining each of these flags, which are processed by vma_dump_size():
• MMF_DUMP_ANON_PRIVATE – Dump anonymous, non-huge private VMAs.
• MMF_DUMP_ANON_SHARED – Dump anonymous, non-huge shared VMAs.
• MMF_DUMP_MAPPED_PRIVATE – Dump file-mapped, private VMAs.
• MMF_DUMP_MAPPED_SHARED – Dump file-mapped, shared VMAs (if the
file is anonymous, e.g. created by memfd(), then this will degrade to
MMF_DUMP_ANON_SHARED).
• MMF_DUMP_ELF_HEADERS – Dump ELF headers. Requires the VM_READ flag to
be set and the VMA to not be offset.
• MMF_DUMP_HUGETLB_PRIVATE – Dump hugetlb private mapping, as deter-
mined via is_vm_hugetlb_page(), i.e. requiring the VM_HUGETLB VMA flag
to be set. Requires VMA_SHARED to not be set. MMF_DUMP_HUGETLB_SHARED – Dump hugetlb shared mapping, determined as
above, only with VMA_SHARED set.
• MMF_DUMP_DAX_PRIVATE – Dumps a DAX (Direct Access for files system, dis-
cussed in DAX documentation) private VMA block. Out of scope for the
book.
• MMF_DUMP_DAX_SHARED – Dumps a DAX shared VMA block. Out of scope for
the book.
The default flags are determined by MMF_DUMP_FILTER_DEFAULT, set-
ting MMF_DUMP_ANON_PRIVATE, MMF_DUMP_ANON_SHARED, MMF_DUMP_HUGETLB_PRIVATE
and MMF_DUMP_MASK_DEFAULT_ELF which enables MMF_DUMP_ELF_HEADERS if
CONFIG_CORE_DUMP_DEFAULT_ELF_HEADERS is configured.
4.3.5.3 Other flags
There are a number of other non-coredump flags which mm_struct objects
can possess. Examining them:
• MMF_VM_MERGEABLE – Used by Kernel Samepage Merging (KSM) logic to mark
a VMA as mergeable. Out of scope for the book.
• MMF_VM_HUGEPAGE – Used by Transparent Huge Pages (THP) (more on this
in the huge pages chapter) to indicate that folios in this process can be
converted into huge pages. Checked by the khugepaged kernel thread on
khugepaged_fork() (called on fork from dup_mmap(). If this flag is set then
__khugepaged_enter() is invoked which marks the mm_struct as available for
use. Checked again on exit in khugepaged_exit() which is called when an
mm_struct is torn down in __mmput().
• MMF_HAS_UPROBES – Used to indicate that the mm_struct has uprobes present
in its address space. Out of scope for the book.
• MMF_RECALC_UPROBES – Indicates that uprobes need to be recalculated for
this mm_struct. Out of scope for the book.
• MMF_OOM_SKIP – Indicates that memory of the process belonging to the
mm_struct should be ignored by the Out Of Memory (OOM) killer. Set
in exit_mmap() when a process is identified to already be an OOM vic-

oom_reap_task() after reaping is complete to achieve the same ends and
in __oom_kill_process() if the process is the global init process (checked
by is_global_init()).
• MMF_UNSTABLE – Set by the OOM killer in __oom_reap_task_mm() to indi-
cate that the address space being reaped is no longer stable, as indi-
cated by check_stable_address_space() and checked by do_anonymous_page(),
finish_fault(), huge page equivalents and memory migration code.
• MMF_HUGE_ZERO_PAGE – Indicates that a huge zero page has been obtained
for the address space via mm_get_huge_zero_page().
• MMF_DISABLE_THP – Disables Transparent Huge Pages (THP) altogether. Set
by prctl() (specifying the PR_SET_THP_DISABLE mode), and can be queriedeither via prctl() using PR_GET_THP_DISABLE or from observing the status in
proc/$pid/status. Checked in hugepage_vma_check() (alongside checking the
VMA flag VM_NOHUGEPAGE).
• MMF_OOM_VICTIM – Set to indicate that a process is a victim of the OOM
killer in mark_oom_victim() and checked via mm_is_oom_victim() which de-
termines whether to set MMF_OOM_SKIP in exit_mmap() as described above.
• MMF_OOM_REAP_QUEUED – Both tested and set in queue_oom_reaper() to mark
that the process will be the subject of OOM repeating and to set up the
timer to do just that.
• MMF_MULTIPROCESS – Indicates that the mm_struct is referenced by mul-
tiple processes. Set when a process is copied via copy_process() in
copy_oom_score_adj() and used in __set_oom_adj() to ensure that the
mm_struct gets pinned (i.e. mmgrab() applied to it to increment its mm_count
reference count.
• MMF_HAS_PINNED – Set by the Get User Pages (GUP) logic in
mm_set_has_pinned_flag() to indicate that FOLL_PIN has been set and
thus the invocation of GUP is intended to pin folios in the process.
Once set, this is maintained for the process lifetime. Checked in
page_needs_cow_for_dma() to determine if folios might be pinned for DMA
(which would have set this pinned flag) and in pte_is_pinned() which is
used by clear_soft_dirty() to clear the soft dirty flag, but explicitly not
when pinned folios could be present. Each contiguous range of virtual memory with similar characteristics (more
specifically ranges which handle page faults* in the same fashion) are repre-
sented by Virtual Memory Areas (VMAs).
These are ultimately the fundamental building block upon which user-
land memory allocations are built – a process has memory mapped at an
address if it has a VMA spanning the base page containing it.
Since we can ‘fault in’ memory on demand, we don’t actually need to
have physical memory allocated or even page table mappings established
for a memory range to be valid, rather we simply mark that it is valid in its
containing VMA.
